The material is up-to-date. In most of the geographies in use today, the treatment of Ethiopia, Manchukuo, and the Philippines, as well as other subjects, is behind the times. This book presents the countries of the world in line with the recent important developments which have taken place. 

A Most Readable Text 

THE OLD WORLD CONTINENTS tells a connected story in a simple, natural, interesting way. 

The thread of the story is not broken by material that destroys reading interest. There are no reading difficulties. The type was especially selected for readability; it conforms to standard requirements for the grade. The paper is durable, unglazed, and of pleasing texture. 

All Material Important to the Subject 

This text is richer in content than other texts, but without padding. The material is confined to usable facts. Continued emphasis on similarities and contrasts stimulates active thinking, clinches the subject, clarifies important principles, and unifies the text. 

Improved Maps Built to Key With Text 

The maps represent a distinct advance in usability. There are maps of many kinds-political, physical, regional, product, etc.—each telling its story clearly. Water areas and boundaries are shown in blue; land areas, in white. Differences in elevation are shown by the simple, natural hachure method. Each important place and each geographic feature mentioned in the text is shown on one or more of the maps. Map exercises bring out the important points of each map and develop skill in map reading. 

Wise Use of Graphs 

Various types of statistical information are shown by means of graphs. With each graph is a legend which helps the pupil to interpret the graph correctly and leads him to make intelligent comparisons and deductions. 

An Unusual and Valuable Plan of Illustration 

The illustration plan adds a unique teaching feature. The pictures have been selected to cover the high points of the units. They are grouped at the beginnings of the chapters and at strategic points within the text. This grouping provides a stimulating preliminary view of each unit and brings out valuable contrasts. The illustrations were chosen after an exhaustive survey. Informative legends call attention to significant details. 

Valuable Teaching Aids 

Material is given at the end of each chapter to fix the important facts. This eliminates much drudgery and planning on the part of the teacher. Under the title I Should Remember, essentials are summarized for study, reference, and review. Under the title Some Things to Talk 

About are stimulating topics for class discussion. Under the title Exercise are carefully framed questions relating to the text. Class Projects develop pupil initiative and provide for group work. 

Statistical tables at the end of the book summarize for reference use important fact material.

PREFACE THE OLD WORLD CONTINENTS is a com plete basal text covering the continents of Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australia.

Like the other books of this series, this text is built in accord with the modern conception of geography as a study of the relations between man and his surroundings. Geography, today, deals with the earth, but with the earth as a stage setting for life, particularly human life. It places emphasis on the great natural regions and shows. how these regions influence the lives and activities of the people who dwell in them. 

The use of the regional method does not mean the ignoring of political boundaries and political units. There can be no question of the value of an understanding of natural boundaries, but the merest glance at recent world history demonstrates that lines established by men have a powerful and far-reaching influence. To be sound, a regional study of geography must frequently consider these important man-made boundaries. Nations constantly extend into and overlap natural regions in odd and significant ways. This overlapping raises striking and suggestive problems for the pupil to think out. The text is distinctive in developing with its regional treatment a judicious recognition of political units. 

Geography, in its new setting, is a vital subject to all of us. It deserves a place as one of the most important subjects in the school curriculum. 

It ought to make a strong appeal to pupils. When properly presented by the regional method it does make that appeal. The pupil has a new and illuminating vision of the world about him, and of the earth as a whole.

In the preceding book of this series, NORTH 

AMERICA AND SOUTH AMERICA, the pupil has been made familiar with the continents of the Western hemisphere. He has learned to interpret the lives and activities of their people in terms of their surroundings. He has become familiar with the regional plan of study.

In studying geography under the regional plan, the pupil has been gaining steadily a breadth of vision. As his power of interpretation has grown, he has begun to feel the magic of geography. 

Cities and countries have become more than mere locations; they have become vitalized as the reasons for their existence, location, and growth have been made clear. But there are other lands to explore and geography continues to be a fascinating subject. So the pupil takes up the study of geography in THE OLD WORLD CONTI- 

NENTS with ever fresh interest and enthusiasm.

In studying each continent the pupil finds new and striking combinations of natural regions. He discovers new and interesting illustrations of the effects of mountain ranges and prevailing winds. 

He learns of old nations and new, of large nations and small, and why the real strength and prosperity of a nation are not always measured by size.

The story of each continent is introduced with a broad view of its great natural regions. Then the countries of the continent are treated, grouped in relation to their general regional location. 

The story of Europe is presented first. There is the customary introductory view of the great regions of Europe. Then comes the detailed story of the continent. Three times, however, this story takes the pupil beyond the bounds of Europe first, in considering the Mediterranean region, where the natural features and climatic conditions are such that the story of the lands bordering the Mediterranean sea is best presented as a whole. This carries the pupil into northern Africa. Again, in the study of Russia, the pupil travels beyond the borders of Europe into the great Russian lands of Asia. Finally, in the study of Turkey, the pupil is taken into Asia Minor.

The story of Africa follows that of Europe, as the Dark Continent is so closely linked with European countries through colonization. It is a distinct and vivid picture that is presented of Africa. Full advantage is taken of the many opportunities for vivid and effective contrasts in this mysterious land.

The story continues with Asia, a country of ancient nations and strange and picturesque civilizations. Again, in Asia, the interest of the pupil is caught and held by exceptional new illustrations of the effects of regional and climatic environment.

The picture of the Old World continents is completed with the story of Australia, retold in somewhat fuller detail than in the earlier text of the series, PEOPLES OF OTHER LANDS. 

The text throughout is thoroughly readable. It creates interest, then holds it. In style it is simple, direct, and unencumbered with technical terms. It paints clear and vivid pictures and so leaves distinct, clear-cut impressions. Full advantage is taken of the many opportunities for striking comparisons and contrasts between regions and between countries. The effects of natural differences in environment are clearly shown.

There is no dry mechanical formula by which all chapters are shaped. The approach to the several units of study is not always the same. 

Often some special distinguishing feature of a section or region is first emphasized, so that the pupil's attention is caught and he finds himself eager to go on. This variety of approach gives a refreshing quality to the story as a whole. iii

iv 

PREFACE 

Supplementing the text are many reference maps and graphs, specially drawn for this book. 

They are built to key with the text. There are general relief maps, maps showing regional boundaries overlaid on political boundaries, straight political maps, and special informational maps. 

Each has been built to tell its own story in the most understandable way.

These maps set a high standard of simplicity and usability. Mountains and valleys, plateaus and plains are shown on special relief maps by the hachure method, which gives the pupil a real visual impression of topography. Each surface looks much as it would actually look if one could view it from far above. Such maps are far clearer to the pupil than color maps, which present no real picture and which require for their interpretation constant reference to a color key. Hachures are, moreover, by far the easiest symbols of surface contour for the child to reproduce. Other types of maps included in THE OLD WORLD CONTI- 

NENTS show countries, states, cities, regions, and other areas clearly, unconfused by overlying physical symbols.

The clearness of the maps in this book is enhanced by the use of blue to show water areas and to emphasize significant boundaries. Shore lines stand out sharply where white land areas meet blue water areas.

The boundaries of countries, states, and regions are clear-cut-blue lines against a white background. Each area stands out as a sharply-defined unit. Maps of this type have marked advantages in readability over maps of many colors, as the most casual comparison will show. Strong testimony to the effectiveness of this type of map is its increasing use by leading map makers.

The photographic illustrations of THE OLD WORLD CONTINENTS also supplement the text and add to its vividness. The pictures are examples of what can be accomplished by a wise selection based on importance of subject, teaching value, and artistic quality. They are grouped to tell their story most effectively and to make the most of opportunities for striking comparison and contrast.

The placing of the illustrations in groups, so far as possible at the beginnings of the chapters, gives the pupil a stimulating preliminary survey of each unit. These photographs, which cover the high points, create a desire on the part of the pupil to read the text. Live and effective legends strengthen this desire, and guide the pupil in the intelligent interpretation of the pictures. 

Following the text on each unit area, under the heading I Should Remember, is a summary of important points. This is helpful for quick reference and for review. Under the title Some 

Things to Talk About are listed general topics for discussion. There are Exercises, consisting of groups of questions which emphasize main points and guide the teacher in her further questioning. 

There are also Map Reading Exercises, based upon the story units. At frequent intervals, Class 

Projects are outlined. Thus abundant provision is made for well-balanced emphasis on the salient points of each study unit.

The 

As a further aid to the proper study of geography, and to provide in full for all pupil activities in the subject, there is published sep arately the IROQUOIS GEOGRAPHY WORK BOOK ON THE OLD WORLD CONTINENTS. 

This is a very complete book, covering in exercise form all the regions included in the basal text, and closely keyed with the text. material is comprehensive and is exceptional in its variety. It keeps the pupil wholly alert, and eager for each new page. There are effective outline maps, map exercises in varied forms, exercises on map sketching, provision for picture study, and an exceptional series of drill exercises built in the best modern forms-completion, matching, selective, true-false, naming, etc. There is adequate provision for periodic reviews. All necessary directions are clearly and definitely stated.

This basal text, THE OLD WORLD CON- 

TINENTS, provides an unusually worth while treatment of all the continents other than North America and South America and of their natural regions and main political units, presented in so vivid a way that the real picture of these lands is lastingly painted on the pupil's mind. 

The separate WORK BOOK provides all drill material for pupil activities. Taken together, the two books make complete text and drill provision for the geographical study of the continents of the Eastern hemisphere. Not only do they make geography fascinating to study; they make it refreshing to teach.

MOUNTAINS AND LOWLANDS IN EUROPE 

1. A group of mountains in the Swiss Alps, a part of 

Europe's high mountain region. The high mountain region extends east and west across southern Europe, and juts down into the southern peninsulas. It contains a number of ranges of mountains, the most famous of which is the Alps. Many of the Alps mountains are very high and are continually snow-capped. Great glaciers move slowly down their sides. This view shows one of the high protected valleys in Switzerland. Here is good pasture land for dairy cattle. Some of this pasture land is level, and some is on the steep slopes of the mountains. There are many valleys like this in the high mountain region, 2. A scene in southern England, in the lowland region of Europe. This view shows a rich farming area around an old British town. The ancient castle tells us that people have lived in this fertile district for many centuries. Trees line the roads and grow in the fields and pastures. England is a tree-loving country. In the background is the Bristol channel, an inlet of the Atlantic ocean. Winds blowing from the ocean bring the rain which keeps the land productive. This village is as far north as the bleak northern tip of Newfoundland, but

England's climate is kept mild by the warm waters of the 

Gulf stream,

1. A mountain of the Northwest highlands, in Norway.

These highlands are old and worn down, so that their peaks are not sharp and rugged like those of the Alps. 

Most of the mountains of Norway's coast rise from the very edge of the water, and the ocean extends into their valleys making safe, deep anchorage for ships. Busy little towns have grown up on these natural harbors. 

The mountains of the British Isles are also part of the 

Northwest highlands. 

2. On the plains of Germany. The lowlands of Europe extend through many countries, and the western winds from the Atlantic provide them with moisture which makes dense woods and heavy crops. The German lowlands have many productive farms. 

3. In the lowland country of the Netherlands. At the right is the sea. The wide bank is a dike built to hold the sea back. The houses beyond the dike are built on land below sea level, and the dike is needed to protect them from the ocean. The Netherlands has many square miles of land below sea level, protected from the ocean by dikes like this one. 

4. A lowland scene in the Rhine basin. This is the waterfront of the city of Cologne, Germany, on the

Rhine river. Notice the river boats. The Rhine has several important tributaries and is connected by canals with other rivers of central Europe. Its many navigable rivers and canals help make the lowlands the most important region of Europe.

THE CONTINENT OF EUROPE 

On the other side of the world from North and South America, with the Atlantic and

Pacific oceans rolling between, are the continents of the Eastern hemisphere-Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australia.

Back in the days when only the Indians lived in North and South America, many of the peoples of Europe had developed advanced civilizations. They had many cities, with beautiful cathedrals and other great buildings. They had universities where men learned to become writers, artists, and scientists. They had stately ships, with which they carried on trade throughout the known world. It was in an effort to find a new trade route between 

Europe and Asia that Christopher Columbus discovered new lands in the Western hemisphere.

When other explorers followed Columbus and the continents of the Western hemisphere became known, they were given the name of the New World. The continents of the East ern hemisphere then became known as the Old World. Although discovered later than the Americas, Australia is considered an Old World continent because it is in the Eastern hemisphere.

Two of the Old World continents are joined together in one large body of land. The western part of this land is the continent of Europe. The eastern part is the continent of 

Asia. Because no ocean separates Europe from Asia the vast expanse of the two continents is sometimes called Eurasia. 

Although Europe and Asia form one body of land, Europe is far ahead of Asia in civilization and progress. It is peopled almost entirely by members of the white race, divided into many different nations. These nations and the 

United States have brought about most of the progress of the modern world. 

The European nations have been greatly influenced by the continent in which they live. 

The relief map of Europe and the regional OF map on page 2 show us a very different sort of continent than North REGIONS or South America. There are old, EUROPE worn-down mountains; great, low, inland plains; and high, rugged mountains.

But the mountains and the plains extend in a generally east and west direction instead of the north and south direction of the mountain ranges and plains of North America. 

Northwest Highlands. The old, worn-down mountains of Europe are in the northwestern part of the continent. They are parts of a range which once extended from the Arctic ocean to the Bay of Biscay. They now include the Scandinavian mountains, the highlands of the British Isles, and one small highland area on the Atlantic coast of the mainland, south of the British Isles. They reach their greatest altitude on the Scandinavian peninsula, which is the only place where they have any very great effect on climate or on the occupations of a whole nation. 

Lowlands. The lowlands of Europe extend across the British Isles, take in much of the western mainland of Europe and part of the 

Scandinavian peninsula, and widen out to include most of eastern Europe from the Arctic ocean to the Black and Caspian seas. As they extend east from the coast, these lowlands open a path for the western winds across practically the entire continent. 

Central Uplands. Find on your map the 

Central uplands of Europe. Here are some of the most carefully tended forests in the world, and great mineral deposits that have helped in the industrial growth of the countries of this region. 

High Mountain Region. The high mountain region lies in a belt across the southern part of the mainland. It includes the Pyrenees, the 

Alps, and the Carpathian and Caucasus mountains. Running down into the two great peninsulas which jut out into the Mediterranean sea are other mountains. 1

THE CONTINENT OF EUROPE 

3 If the high mountains of Europe ran north and south along the entire western coast like the ranges of North and South America, much of Europe would be a desert waste. As it is, the lowlands are open to the sea, and the prevailing westerly winds carry their moisture far inland. These winds blow across the warm 

Gulf stream, which flows northeastward along the shores of the British Isles and the Scandinavian peninsula. They pick up warmth and moisture from the water, and thus keep the temperature of the northwestern part of the continent mild and bring abundant rainfall. 

As a result, northwestern Europe has a much more moderate climate and can support a far greater population than cold and sparsely settled Labrador, which lies in North America in about the same latitude.

The eastern section of the lowlands of Europe is too far from the ocean to get the benefit of the Gulf stream, and has a continental climate with great differences in temperature in its various parts. 

Mediterranean Region. What is known as the Mediterranean region follows the Mediter ranean coast line of Europe, extends to the northern border of the Black sea, and includes the western part of Africa's northern coast.

Here the summers are dry and warm, and the winters are mild with moderate rainfall. The soil is rich enough for varied crops. 

Productive Areas. The unproductive areas of Europe are not great. Because of extreme cold, the northeastern part of the continent, which is shut off from the warm westerly winds by the mountains of the Scandinavian peninsula, consists largely of tundras and forests; but even the tundras can be used for herding reindeer. Many of the mountains of the Scandinavian peninsula are so rugged that they are of little value except for timber and mineral deposits. Practically all the rest of

Europe is intensively farmed. Even in the high mountains, where you might expect to find little farming, the lower slopes are terraced for fields and the higher slopes are used for pastures. The needs of Europe's great population demand that all possible land shall be used.

Effect of Coast Line and Navigable Rivers. 

Since very early times, Europe's long, irregular coast line has been of great value. It has made a great deal of land accessible to the sea, and the warm ocean waters moderate the climate. 

Irregularities of the shore make excellent natural harbors. On many of these, cities have grown up as commercial ports for the various European countries. Many of the natural harbors are estuaries of long, navigable rivers. 

These rivers make a path for commerce to countries and cities far inland. The Rhine, the 

Danube, and the Rhone are three such rivers. 

Since the Rhine and the Danube both flow through several countries, and are so important commercially, they have been "internationalized." That is, they have been opened to the commerce of all nations. Besides these three rivers, there are many other rivers that are navigable for miles. For long distances east and west of the Rhine, a great system of canals joins one river to another, so that inland cities can ship goods to the sea by more than one water route. Rivers have done much to build up commerce.

In population, Europe stands second only to huge Asia, although in area she is only fifth. The densest population is in manufacturing districts, where POPULATION 

the people live very close together. The areas of medium population are the sections where the people cultivate small farms intensively. 

The sections of least population lie near the Arctic ocean and along the crest of the 

Northwest highlands in the Scandinavian peninsula.

Parts of the European continent have been inhabited for many thousands of years. 

Europe had many great and powerful CITIES cities at the time of the discovery of America. Some of them were very old at that time. Many of the early European cities were entirely independent of any power outside their walls. Now there is only one "free city" which belongs to no country. Most of Europe's ancient cities still remain, governed by the countries in which they are located and filled with the art and beauty of the past. A few have fallen into unimportance. With so early

EUROPE 

a start, Europe today has numerous cities highly developed in art, literature, and culture, and to a large extent skilled in manufacture. 

From earliest times, great trade routes have led to Asia across the lowlands of Europe, and rivers have served as car- 

TRANSPORTATION riers for commerce. As the continent developed, canals were dug and railroads built. When railroads were built through the Alps, some of the finest roadbeds of the world were laid, and the longest tunnels in the world were blasted and dug through solid mountains. Europe is also ahead of other continents in the development of aviation. Luxurious cabin planes run on regular schedules in all directions from the great centers of population.

A study of the countries of Europe should be of the greatest interest to every American. 

From these far-away lands have come many of our people. If we know about their home countries we can better appreciate what they have brought to America and why they came to our United States.

1. North America and South America, in the Western hemisphere, are known as the New World continents. Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australia, in the 

Eastern hemisphere, are the Old World continents. 

2. Europe is the western part of a great body of land known as Eurasia, made up of the continents of Europe and Asia. Europe is largely peopled by members of the white race and is far ahead of Asia in civilization and progress. 

3. The surface of Europe is very different from that of North or South America. The high mountain ranges and the central plains extend mainly in an east and west direction. 

4. The Northwest highlands are made up of old worndown mountains. They extend through the Scandinavian peninsula and the British Isles to the European mainland. 

5. The lowlands of Europe extend across the British 

Isles, include much of the western mainland of 

Europe and a part of the Scandinavian peninsula and widen out to include most of eastern Europe from the Arctic ocean to the Black and Caspian seas. 

They are swept by the prevailing westerly winds. 

6. The Central uplands of Europe contain rich mineral deposits and valuable forests. 

7. The high mountain region lies in a belt across the southern part of the mainland of Europe. It includes the Pyrenees, the Alps, and the Carpathian and Caucasus mountains. Other mountains extend into the Mediterranean peninsulas of Europe. 

8. The Mediterranean region follows the Mediterra nean coast of Europe to the northern border of the 

Black sea.

It also includes the western part of Africa's northern coast. This region has warm, dry summers and mild winters with moderate rainfall. 

9. The greater part of Europe is productive and is intensively farmed. 

10. Europe's long and irregular coast line and her many navigable rivers encourage commerce. Some of the rivers have been internationalized. 

11. Europe is second in population among the continents. 

12. Europe has many large and very old cities which are important commercially and are interesting because of their many relics of the past. 

13. A network of canals, railroads, and airlines provides Europe with good transportation.

In this quaint but typical English cottage lived the girl whom William Shakespeare married in 1582. The rooms of the cottage are just as they were when Shakespeare sat with Anne on the high-backed seats which still stand on each side of the fireplace.

Just off the mainland of Europe is a group of islands clustered together between the 

North sea and the Atlantic ocean. 

They are the British Isles.

LOCATION 

AND 

SHAPE 

From the shores of Europe, as from the shores of other continents, flat plateaus extend out under the sea for considerable distances before the real depths of the ocean are reached. These underwater plateaus are called continental shelves. 

At one time the shelf which now surrounds the British Isles was above water and the present islands were part of the mainland. When the land sank the lower lands disappeared below the surface of the water, and the higher lands were cut off by the ocean and became islands. 

The shelf which surrounds the British Isles is about six hundred feet under water. Its shallow parts are excellent fishing grounds. 

The largest of the British Isles, Great Britain, is separated from the mainland by only a narrow strip of water called the English channel. This island is broad at the south and narrower towards the north. The southern part includes England, with the little country of 

Wales to the west. The northern part is Scotland. To the west of this island, across the 

Irish sea, lies Ireland. Around these two main islands are possibly 5000 smaller islands, all included in the British Isles.

OF THE ENGLISH PEOPLE 

Hundreds of years ago the land that is now England was called Britain and was inhabited by a people known as the Britons. 

THE STORY From Scotland and Ireland came fierce warriors, the Picts and the 

Scots, to raid, rob and murder. 

The Britons appealed to two peoples from the mainland of Europe-the Angles and the Saxons-to help them. The Angles and Saxons sent warriors across the sea and drove the Picts and Scots back into their own lands. Then, instead of going home, the Angles and Saxons conquered Britain, renamed it Angleland, or England, and drove the unfor- tunate Britons into the mountainous western part of the island, a region now called Wales. 

Later still came the Normans from northern

France, who conquered the Angles and Saxons and blended Norman civilization with the earlier ones.

These events of long ago gave us our present distribution of peoples in England and the other countries of the British Isles. In Scotland lives a thrifty, serious people, the descendants of the early Picts and of a tribe of Scots who moved over from Ireland. The people of Ireland are emotional and poetic. 

They are descended from the early Scots and other tribes who have always lived on the island of Ireland. The English show the characteristics of Angles, Saxons, and Normans; they are a steady, methodical people, a nation of conquerors and empire-builders. The people of Wales, like their Briton ancestors, are quiet and retiring. They take great pride in the oldfashioned customs and costumes that survive in many parts of their land.

THE BRITISH 

The large island made up of England, Scotland, and Wales is called Great Britain. Until recent years Great Britain governed Ireland, but a few years ago EMPIRE Ireland was divided into the Irish Free State, with its own government, and 

Northern Ireland. The Irish Free State in cludes the greater part of the island. Northern

Ireland is included with Great Britain and the surrounding islands in one government called the United Kingdom, with the king of England at its head.

Since the early days of exploration the men of Great Britain have been famous sailors, explorers, traders, and colonizers. As Great 

Britain became crowded her people settled in large numbers in Canada, Australia, and New Zealand. Gradually they gained control of many different parts of the world and founded colony after colony. Today Great Britain controls more land than any other nation. Great OWC-2

East

Britain and her dependencies make up the 

British empire.

There are British lands in every continent. 

Canada, in our own continent, is a member of the empire. A little corner of South America is known as British Guiana. Australia and a great part of Africa belong to the British empire. India and Burma in Asia add many millions of dark-skinned people to the subjects of the British crown. It is said that the British empire includes almost one-fourth of all the land on the globe, and nearly one-fourth of all the people. One cannot help feeling amazed that the little country of England, not quite so large as our single state of Alabama, should be the heart of the world's largest empire. 

How does Great Britain feed all its people? 

What do they do for a living? How has Great 

Britain grown to be so important? Why has it such a large navy and merchant fleet? The answers to these and many other such questions are found by studying the position, surface, climate, and industries of the British Isles and the character and needs of the British people. 

POSITION OF BRITISH ISLES 

If a man who is hardworking and intelligent opens a store on a corner where trade flows all about him, his chances for success are good. If you will look at the map on page 66, showing world trade routes, you will see that the Atlantic ocean is crisscrossed with lines between the ports of eastern North America and western Europe. These are the busiest ports of the world and the Atlantic is the busiest ocean. 

Now that South America is waking up, her steamships swell the traffic of this ocean thoroughfare. The British Isles, lying on these trade routes, are like the man on the busy corner. Their position is very favorable. They are centrally located for trade with the important land areas of the world. 

The fact that the British Isles are cut off from the mainland of Europe made their people independent. Although they exchanged goods easily by sea with European countries, the same sea has for centuries protected them from invasion, and they have been able to explore and settle distant lands. The sea encouraged shipbuilding, until the British merchant marine-the total number of freight and passenger ships-became the largest on earth. 

SURFACE 

The Northwest highlands cover parts of Great Britain, but they have no such great skyscraping peaks as are found in our western states. Scotland has highlands in the north and in the south, with a stretch of lowlands between the two. These lowlands have an outlet on the east coast in the Firth of Forth, and on the west coast in the 

Firth of Clyde. Firth is the Scottish name for a drowned valley, like that of the Hudson river, into which the sea entered between high hills when the land sank in olden times. 

The highlands extend from southern Scotland into northern England, forming the Pennine range, which runs north and south almost to the center of England. Central and southeastern England are largely flat but have some hills. Wales is a mountainous country. 

Ireland has a central plain with highlands north, south, and west. Here and there are great stretches of marshy land, called bogs. 

These are generally overgrown with heather and low bushes. In the bogs are found beds of peat, or partially decayed vegetable matter, which is used as a fuel.

An ice sheet once covered all the British Isles, and is responsible for their many beautiful lakes. The lakes of England, Ireland, and 

Scotland have long been celebrated in song and story. These lovely lakes attract many visitors each year.

CLIMATE 

We have seen that the Gulf stream and the westerlies bring warmth and moisture to much of Europe. No part of 

Europe is more helped by them than the British Isles. The Isles are in the same latitude as the cold and sparsely settled coast of Labrador in North America, but their climate is more like that of British Columbia, which gets warmth and moisture from the Japan current. The winters are temperate and the summers are mild, and there is ample rainfall. The islands have one of the best possible oceanic climates, which helps make Great Britain one of the most densely settled and one of the busiest industrial regions of the earth.

EUROPE 

The climate of the British Isles does not vary so greatly from summer to winter as does that of our New England. The highlands, of course, are colder than the lowlands, and the north has more cold weather than the south. 

There is often snow during the winter months, but as a rule it does not heap itself up in banks and drifts that last for days. The rivers of the British Isles seldom freeze, and the surrounding waters are never ice covered. The country is open, therefore, to commerce and fishing all year round. In summer, there is a freshness and greenness about the whole British Isles, because there is no excessive heat to dry up the growing things. The grass is so green in Ireland that it is called the Emerald Isle. The eastern part of Great Britain is somewhat drier because it receives less moisture than the western section.

In such an even, temperate climate as that of the British Isles people thrive. They feel vigorous and ambitious. This climate of the

British Isles has helped to decide their industries. It has encouraged agriculture, helped cattle raising, and favored the growth of manufacturing. 

Mists and fogs are very common in the British Isles. The city of London is especially known for heavy fogs which sweep in from the sea very suddenly and settle down over the city. They are often so thick that they shut out everything but blurs of light from the street lights. It is rather exciting to be on the streets of London when one of these fogs descends. BRITISH

INDUSTRIES 

Great Britain's power in the world is largely due to her manufacturing industries. Even if a man has a fine business location, the commercial world will pass him by if he has nothing attractive to sell. In addition to being on the "busy corner," this island nation has very fine goods to sell. 

Growth of Manufacturing. There are several reasons for the growth of manufacturing in

Great Britain. The industries and the commerce started in a small way and grew up gradually. We know how this took place in our New England section. We remember the fishermen and traders who sailed up and down the Atlantic coast. We know that factories centered around the waterfalls. We know how the factories attracted many workers, until there were more people than the land could feed.

A development much like this took place earlier in Great Britain. Nearness to the sea made the men fishermen, explorers, and traders. They visited new lands and founded colonies. To these colonies Great Britain could sell goods, and from them she could get raw materials. This naturally encouraged manufacturing. The presence of iron, coal, and other raw materials on the islands themselves also helped. Great Britain's population increased, until her farm lands could no longer feed all the people.

With the coming of machinery, the factories increased in number and size. The English are an inventive race. The steam engine, the locomotive, and spinning and weaving machinery were all invented by Englishmen. 

Growth of Commerce. With these inventions the factories produced more goods. Commerce grew. Little towns became cities. Great ships began to carry British goods to all parts of the world. They brought back to the mother country the wheat, the meat, the sugar, and the coffee that her people needed. They brought, too, raw materials to be used in the growing factories.

Today only the United States can equal 

Great Britain in commerce. The big seaports of the British Isles are visited by ships from many countries, and British merchant ships are a familiar sight in every port of the world as they go about the business of the mother country. Besides her great merchant marine 

Great Britain has a powerful navy to protect her merchant ships and to guard the shores of the British Isles and British rights all over the world. 

Mining and Use of Coal, Iron, and Other Minerals. But Britain's big seaports, fast ships, large cities, and mammoth trade would probably never have been were it not for two gifts which nature has hidden in the ground. They are coal and iron. These two minerals make it

possible to run factories, to build ships and make them move, and to build and run the great locomotives which connect factory and seaport. The iron and coal deposits are near each other and extend from central and northern England into southern Scotland. Limestone is used in smelting pure iron from iron

Though Great Britain imports some iron ore from Sweden, Spain, northern Africa, and other countries, she has plenty of coal and to spare. In southern Wales there are large deposits of coal, and Cardiff has become the greatest coal-exporting city of the world. 

Ships from British ports carry coal to 

France, Italy, and South America. They take it to Ireland and others of the British Isles that have little or no coal of their own. They also supply many coaling stations where British ships may call in their travels for a fresh supply of fuel. 

The United States leads the world in coal production, but Great Britain exports more than we do. Our country is so large, our railroads cover so many thousands of miles, our industries are so varied and great that we use most of the coal that we produce. Except for the United States and Great Britain, there are few countries that have coal to spare. 

Where coal and iron are found close together, great steel and iron industries have grown. We saw such a situation in Birmingham, Alabama. This city was named for the older steel center of Birmingham, England, which earlier became famous through having the same advantages. At Pittsburgh, too, we saw that iron ore could be brought great distances to be smelted at the coal mines. In the same way the British import iron ore from foreign lands to be smelted at Cardiff and other seacoast coal fields. Both Great Britain and the United States are fortunate in these resources. The lack of them is one of the great obstacles which prevent the progressive countries of South America from becoming important in world industry. 

Birmingham, the great British steel center, is centrally located and is connected by rail with industrial cities to the east, west, south, and north. So this city supplies iron and steel and manufactures machinery needed in her neighbors' many industrial plants, shipbuilding yards, and locomotive factories. Besides machinery, Birmingham makes a large number of small iron and steel articles.

There are other centers of the iron and steel industry in England and in southern Scotland. 

In northeastern England, around Newcastle on the Tyne, there are large deposits of coal. 

Newcastle exports coal, is an iron and steel center, and builds steel ships. Sheffield has long been famous for its pocket knives, shears, and cutlery. These small steel articles are profitable products for an interior city, because they are valuable and may be cheaply transported on account of their small size.

A great industry which has grown up in Great Britain because of her deposits of coal and iron is the building of ships. Glasgow in 

Scotland leads the world in this industry. 

Though Glasgow is not on the coast, her people have deepened the river Clyde so that large steamers can come right up to the city docks.

Many great ships are built in Glasgow and are launched on the Clyde.

Hull in England and Belfast in Ireland are also ship-building cities. Belfast has no coal, but it is near English ports which ship out thousands of tons every year. Both Hull and 

Belfast have good harbors. When ships are

EUROPE 

launched and leave these harbors they often take their first cargo right with them. Belfast exports linen goods and other products of northern Ireland. Hull ships out iron and woolen manufactures.

Besides iron and coal the British Isles have deposits of lead, tin, and copper, which are used in varied industries. Some of these industries are branches of the iron and steel industry, and all of them are largely dependent on the supply of coal. A number of English cities have large watch factories. Glassworks are pretty well scattered throughout industrial Great Britain. There are factories where needles, pens, and pins are turned out by the millions. Small brass wares are a valuable source of income to many cities. Firearms, hardware, steel wire, and countless other metal articles are shipped to South America, Australia, and Africa. 

Woolen Industry. Great Britain produces woolen, cotton, and linen goods as well as her many metal manufactures. As you study the textile industry of Great Britain keep in mind our textile section of New England, and you will notice that the growth of the industry followed along the same lines in both places. 

Woolen cloth was woven in England before cotton, and the woolen mills of Great Britain still turn out fine tweeds, rich carpets, and the softest of yarns. Nobody can be sure when the industry began. Some historians say that the 

Romans brought it to the British Isles nearly 2000 years ago. At any rate, wool was woven into cloth on hand looms in the early homes of the English. Great Britain was later the place of refuge for skilled weavers from other European countries, who were driven from home by religious persecution. They taught the British their skill, and presently British woolens became famous and found a ready market throughout Europe.

When machinery replaced hand weaving, the first factories were built on the border of the Pennine range, where water power was to be had. The shire, or county, of England called York, east of the range, became the natural center of the wool industry because the sheep which furnished the raw material were pastured on the nearby hills. The eastern slopes of the Pennines are drier than the western. They are not so good for agriculture, but are excellent for sheep raising. 

When coal came into use in making steam to run heavy machinery, Yorkshire obtained coal from nearby mines and remained the woolen center. Leeds, in Yorkshire, is the leading city of the woolen district. The neighboring city of Bradford makes very fine broadcloth, a soft, smooth fabric of heavy wool. 

Factories have been established farther north and south. Scottish tweeds have a large sale in all cool countries of Europe and America. 

Throughout industrial Great Britain are other towns engaged in making clothing, blankets, hosiery, sweaters, carpets, and the many other woolen products of our markets. 

Sheep are still raised in England and Scotland, but all the sheep raised in the British Isles do not begin to supply the woolen factories with all the material they need. Some wool is imported from Argentina and Uruguay, but New Zealand, South Africa, and especially

Australia supply the bulk of the wool which the factories need. 

Cotton Industry. Cotton is now the leading manufacture of Great Britain. Woolen cloth was made before cotton, but the British gradually added the cotton industry to the woolen. 

Cotton was first woven by hand on small looms in the homes of the weavers. When the steam engine was invented machinery was devised to spin and weave the fiber many times faster than by hand. The weavers were angry when they first saw the machines being installed in factories, and made a great deal of trouble. They feared the machines would drive them out of work and they would starve. But that did not happen. As the factories grew larger more workmen were needed, and more cotton was manufactured and sold.

The cotton industry is centered in Lancashire, a district west of the Pennines. Here the westerly winds keep the air constantly moist. 

While cotton fibers are being spun they must be moist or they will break, and the natural dampness of this region attracted the early factories. Plentiful coal helped greatly. Mod-

1. A Scotch weaver making woolen cloth on a hand loom. Before the invention of weaving machinery, all cloth was made on hand machines. Nowadays there are very few of these old-fashioned looms in use. Cloth is made in Great Britain by machinery of the same kind as is used in the mills of New England and other parts of our country. 

2. A pit pony hauling coal in a mine in Wales. Mines are commonly called pits in Great Britain. British mines do not have so much machinery as American mines. In some of our mines we use electric trains to haul the coal to the shaft but in Wales they use horses. Most of the horses remain all their lives in the depths of the mines, and never see daylight. 

3. A scene in an English steel works. In the center of the picture we see the mouth of a Bessemer converter, which is a machine for making steel. This converter is full of very hot liquid iron. A blast of air blowing through this iron is burning out the impurities and helping to change the iron into steel. Great Britain is one of the leading countries in the manufacture of iron and steel and of goods made from these metals. 

4. Gathering peat from a bog in Ireland. The blocks of peat which are piled up to dry were cut from the pit. 

Peat is plant material in the first stages of its change to coal. When dry it burns readily. Peat is used for fuel in 

Ireland and in many parts of Europe where coal and wood are scarce.

1. A farm in Ireland. The chief industry of Ireland is raising livestock. Most of the farms of the country are small, but cattle, horses, sheep, and hogs are raised on them. Butter and cheese are among the leading exports of Ireland. These farm products are shipped largely from 

Dublin for the use of people in England. 

2. These little pigs went to market. They are waiting for buyers in the market place of an Irish town. The buyer of these little pigs will take them to his farm, where they will grow large. Pigs are among the most important farm animals of Ireland. The people of the many large cities in England eat a great deal of bacon, and much of this bacon is supplied by Ireland. 

3. Dipping sheep, in the mountains of Wales. Sheep are raised in many parts of the British Isles which are too mountainous for agriculture or cattle raising. The men in this picture are washing a large herd of sheep in a liquid that will keep insects from their skins. The sheep in the background are awaiting their turn to enter the tank. 

4. An English fishing village on the shore of the English channel, with fishing boats tied alongside the dock. Nets in which the fish are caught are piled on the deck of the largest boat which we see in the picture. Fishing is an important occupation of the English, and provides much of their food.

No cotton can be grown in Great Britain, for the summers are too cool. Much is imported from India and Egypt, and even more from the United States. The cost of sea shipment is not great, the country has coal to run the factories, her workers are skilled, and her foreign market is established. Therefore Great Britain has become the leader in this profitable trade. 

More cotton than woolen cloth is sold. It is cheaper and lighter, and is much more comfortable to wear in warm countries. A list of cotton articles might begin with dresses, sheets, pillowcases, and curtains, and would reach a hundred articles in no time at all. Cotton is used by itself, or mixed with wool, linen, or silk. Cotton cloth is made in fine grades and coarse grades. Almost everyone everywhere makes use of it in some way. It is worn by laborers in the fields of China, by miners in the coal mines of the United States, and by workers in the jungles of the Amazon. No wonder the making of cotton is a great industry. The cotton products of Great Britain are an important reason for her greatness.

Manchester is the chief city of the cotton industry. Years ago all Manchester's shipping was done through the port of Liverpool. But as her exports and imports increased, the city dug a thirty-five mile canal which gave it a direct outlet to the sea. Ships now come up to the city's docks.

As in the woolen industry, there are numbers of towns and cities where many thousands of people spin cotton and weave and dye cotton cloth, or make it into finished articles. Like the woolen industry, the cotton industry has spread north into Scotland, where the city of 

Glasgow is the center. 

Linen Industry. Another textile which is widely used is linen. Linen is made from a plant called flax. As flax grows very well in the damp climate of Ireland, that country is a center for linen manufacturing. Very fine linen is made in the city of Belfast on the east coast of northern Ireland. Manufacturing in

Ireland is done largely on the east coast where coal can easily be brought from England and Scotland.

Besides using the flax grown in Ireland, Belfast imports flax from Poland, in central Europe. The Irish have become very skilful in making linen, and the cloth they weave is of fine quality and brings a good price.

Other Textile Industries. The making of silk is included in the textile industries of the British Isles. The Scottish city of Dundee imports jute, from which it manufactures rough cloths called burlap and gunny cloth. These are made into sacks and bags for use in shipping goods. It would not be possible to tell in detail about all the textile industries of the islands, as each has its own special history. 

But you have read enough to know that their textile products are very important to the British Isles and form a large part of their exports. 

Fishing. Almost every one of the ports of the British Isles is a fishing center, just as are almost all the ports of New England. The shallow waters of the continental shelf are excellent feeding grounds for cod, haddock, and herring. The fishing industry employs more than 70,000 men and provides the country with an important source of food. The life of a fisherman requires bravery and endurance and teaches great skill in seamanship. The fishing fleet is a fine school for seamen for the merchant marine and naval service of their country.

The principal fishing centers are London, Hull, and Grimsby in England, and Aberdeen in Scotland. But there are scores of small villages all along the coasts of the British Isles whose men earn their living on the sea. 

Farming. All these varied industries keep thousands of people running machines in factories, burrowing in long tunnels underground for coal and iron, working huge cranes in the shipbuilding yards, and sailing fishing boats.

These people must eat. The farming sections of Great Britain can do only a little towards supplying this army of workers with food. The rocky upland regions cannot be cultivated. 

And often where the surface is suitable, the rainfall is much too abundant. As a result only

EUROPE 

a relatively small part of the land is under cultivation, though the land that is farmed is worked carefully and well. 

The farming sections of the British Isles are largely meadows and pastures, with winding country roads and quiet rivers. Cattle graze upon the hillsides and country people sit peacefully in the evening outside pretty cottages whose roofs are thatched with straw. Some of the homes are several hundred years old, and have housed many generations of a single family.

The best farming lands are in southeastern England, where the rainfall is less abundant. 

Much wheat is grown here, although not nearly enough to supply the needs of the people. The United States, Canada, and Argentina send quantities of wheat to the British

Isles. The summers are not hot enough for corn, but barley, oats, and potatoes grow very well in the cool, moist climate. Besides potatoes, other vegetables and fruits are grown. 

Potatoes form the chief crop of Ireland.

Most of them are used in that country. Some of the people practically live on this crop. 

The agricultural products of Scotland are potatoes, barley, and oats, with vegetables and some fruits, but agriculture is not very extensive.

Much of England is divided into vast estates, which are subdivided into farms. The owner of an estate rents out the farms, and his tenants are called tenant-farmers. If the owner understands farming and helps his tenants, this system of tenant-farming works out very well. 

But if he is interested only in collecting his rents, the result is dissatisfaction and often poverty for the tenants. In the Irish Free 

State, an agricultural country, the government helps the tenants to buy the lands they farm. 

As a rule an estate is not so intensively cultivated as are small privately owned farms. 

The estate owner does not want all his lands plowed up into fields. He wishes to keep his parks and preserve his hunting fields. Often he is interested in cattle raising, and this requires pasture land and hay fields.

Stock Raising. Many fine breeds of cattle are raised in the British Isles. The farmers have made a study of stock raising and go about this industry in a scientific way. As a result the 

Isles export more animals for breeding purposes than any other European country. Even the tiny Channel islands of Alderney, Jersey, and Guernsey produce world-famous dairy cattle. 

Stock raising is really more important than the raising of cereals. The climate of Ireland and of western Great Britain is very favorable for hay raising and for good grassy pastures. 

Because of the abundant moisture the grass is always fresh, and the animals can graze out of doors all the year round.

On the rocky hills and in the drier regions of the British Isles there are large flocks of sheep. Perhaps you remember that sheep raising also flourishes in the drier regions of our own country, because sheep do not need as good pasture as cattle. The mutton from 

British sheep is famous for its quality. 

The barren and unproductive highlands of Scotland have long been used for sheep raising, and Scottish shepherds and their flocks have roamed these hills for many centuries. 

Ireland's chief industry is stock raising, and she has many cattle, sheep, horses, and hogs.

Ireland produces a fine grade of bacon, which has a good market in Great Britain. 

Dairying. Dairying is extremely important in all the farming sections of the British Isles. 

The many large cities demand great quantities of milk, cheese, butter, and eggs. Here again, the abundant rainfall, which keeps the grass fresh and green, benefits an industry. Dairy products are among Ireland's chief exports. 

They go for the most part to England. England buys dairy products from Denmark, the 

Netherlands, and several other countries.

SEAPORTS 

Trade with foreign lands requires harbors, and nature has given them generously to the British Isles. Their coast lines are very irregular. When the continental shelf sank, the sea flowed into many river mouths and formed estuaries. As the tides rise and fall their rushing waters keep these estuaries from being blocked with silt, and at high tide ships can pass far up the streams. 

Many of these estuaries have famous ports.

The Thames has London. The Bristol channel has Bristol and Cardiff. Liverpool on the

Mersey, Hull on the Humber, Glasgow on the 

Firth of Clyde, and Edinburgh on the Firth of 

Forth are other examples.

Great Britain's second city in size is the shipbuilding port of Glasgow, which is the outlet for many products of industrial Scotland. 

Edinburgh is an old Scottish city which has long been famous as a center of culture and learning. It is rich in history and here many great men have lived and died. Edinburgh's university is known throughout Europe. 

Liverpool is perhaps more familiar to Americans than other British ports, as trade with the United States centers here. Grain, meat, and raw cotton enter the country through 

Liverpool. Outgoing ships carry away the many products of industrial England. 

On the English channel are the ports of 

Plymouth, Portsmouth, and Southampton. 

Liners enter Southampton's deep harbor to land passengers, who there take train for London. Plymouth is a naval station. This is the port from which in 1620 the little band of Pilgrims set sail in the Mayflower. Dover, on the Strait of Dover, is a port for travel between 

France and England.

On the east coast of northern England is Hull, on the Humber river. Hull exports the manufactures of Sheffield, Leeds, and nearby cities. Newcastle, on the Tyne, is also an important port. These east coast ports trade with many places on the North sea and the Baltic.

Before the American continents became important in world trade, the eastern ports of Great Britain were nearest to the markets of that day. Now the western ports are facing the greatest markets and are the most important seaports, with the exception of London. 

In Ireland, Dublin and Belfast are the chief ports. Dublin, an old town with an interesting history and an ancient university, is the cultural center of Ireland. It is the capital of the 

Irish Free State and the largest city of the island. Dublin has seen much bloodshed and bitter fighting in years gone by. Belfast is the capital of Northern Ireland. Cobh, or Queenstown, in the Irish Free State, is a port of call for liners and a naval base for Great Britain. 

The wealth of Ireland is centered mostly in these cities.

The trade of Ireland and Scotland is largely with England, and the ports that are nearest England are the important ones. The ports of western Ireland and northwestern Scotland have not grown in importance, because they face away from nearby markets and because they have fewer products to ship. 

It is not surprising that in Great Britain, with so much seacoast and such a small amount of land area, no one lives more than seventy miles from the sea. This seems very odd to us, because in our own country millions of people live more than a thousand miles from any coast, and many live and die without ever seeing the ocean. The wheat from our western wheat fields, the cattle from our Great plains, the flour from the mills of Minneapolis must all be transported many long miles before they reach a seaport and are ready to start on their ocean journeys to other lands. In Great Britain, especially in industrial England, transportation is quite simple. Seaports are within an easy journey. Rivers, canals, and railroads form a honeycomb of lines in the small interior, and link up the factories with the great ships that ride at anchor in the harbors, ready to be off with their cargoes.

The most famous port of the British Isles, and the oldest English city, is London, the capital of the British empire. Centuries ago, when the British Isles LONDON were just barbarous islands, a rude fort stood on the high ground at the head of the estuary of the Thames. This high land seemed a good place from which to build a bridge across the Thames, and a little village grew up around the bridge. The village became the town of 

London, then a city, and, later, the largest city of the world. It is fifty miles from the sea, but big ocean steamers make their way upstream and unload their cargoes in the very heart of the city. London is a great fishing port and a railroad, shipbuilding, and manufacturing center. It handles enormous quantities of goods in transit, collecting and shipping the manufac-

EUROPE 

tures of British cities and sending them foods and raw materials from far lands. 

Ships bring to London valuable cargoes of meat, wheat, and butter from Canada and Australia. Africa sends gold, diamonds, hides, and tropical products. London is a great market for tea imported from Asia. That continent also sends to London tin and jute. The exports of London include iron and steel goods, machinery, clothing, and almost every other article that men make for sale.

London, with its museums and universities, is the cultural center of England. It has scores of historic landmarks, and is the home of England's king. The great houses of Parliament extend along the Thames. Here are made the laws of the United Kingdom and of many dependencies of the British empire.

Westminster Abbey is a large and stately church that has shared the country's history. 

In it are monuments and memorials to the famous dead of the British Isles-memorials to explorers, orators, writers, warriors, and many other types of men. James Watt, who did so much for industrial England by inventing the steam engine, has a tablet here. In the Poet's 

Corner is a memorial to Longfellow, one of our American poets. Many a famous king and queen has been crowned in Westminster

Abbey, and many of them are buried here. 

In another part of London is a place far different from the Abbey. This is the Tower of 

London, a prison among whose prisoners have been many famous people. Even some of the kings who received their crowns so proudly in the Abbey were later brought to the Tower as prisoners to await their fate. This Tower of London has a sad but fascinating history. 

In a part of London called Greenwich is a famous observatory, on the meridian from which longitude is measured. Greenwich has been given the meridian o°, and all other places in the world are spoken of as being so many degrees east or west of Greenwich. 

Not only London but all of the British Isles have a great appeal to travelers. All want to see the Irish countryside, the his APPEAL TO toric castles and cathedrals, the little fishing villages, the universi- 

TRAVELERS 

ties at Oxford and Cambridge, the Shakespeare country centering around picturesque Stratford on Avon, and the lovely lake sections of England, Ireland, and Scotland. The lakes of Ireland are especially beautiful in their settings of rich green. The lakes of Scotland are famous as well, and so are the Scottish highlands. There are many ruins of old castles in 

Scotland. The Scottish highlanders, in their plaid kilts, marching to the skirling of the bagpipes, are not soon forgotten.

THE PEOPLE OF  

As you would expect, the city of London is the most densely populated place in the British 

Isles. Of the 48,000,000 people who live in the Isles, about onesixth live in London. Next come the manufacturing and shipping centers-Glasgow, Birmingham, Liverpool, Manchester, Sheffield, Leeds, Dublin, Belfast, Edinburgh. Throughout the farming sections the population is less dense, and in the rugged highlands there are very few people.

Because of the crowded conditions in industrial Great Britain, many of its people leave home to start life over again in some other land. Great numbers have moved to the 

United States, Canada, and Australia, where they now form a large part of the white population. We know that in our own country they generally take an intelligent interest in public affairs, work hard, and educate their children well.

The English, the Scotch, the Irish, and the Welsh-all descended from northern European races-share certain qualities. They love adventure. They are energetic, independent, and resourceful.

In every field of life, people from Great Britain have left a fine record. We have learned some of their gifts to modern machinery. They have made many scientific discoveries. Their writers have given the world prose and poetry that will live forever. They have sent out great explorers who have carried the British flag to the ends of the earth. And they have gone into parts of all the continents and have established 

British rule in many lands.

1. The British Isles are just off the mainland of 

Europe, between the North sea and the Atlantic ocean. They are on the great trade routes between the progressive continents of Europe and North America. 

2. Being cut off by themselves, the people of these islands have become resourceful and independent. 

But they are near enough to the mainland of the continent to carry on trade. Great Britain is industrial rather than agricultural, and depends upon its commerce and its manufacturing for its existence. It must import many of its raw materials, and food for its people. It must keep a large merchant marine and a large navy. 

3. Scotland has highlands in the north and south, with lowlands in the center. The Pennine range of mountains runs south from Scotland through northern England almost to the center of England. 

Central and southeastern England are largely flat. 

Wales is mountainous. Ireland has a central plain with highlands north, south, and west. There are famous lake regions in Ireland, Scotland, and England, left by the ice sheet. 

4. The latitude of the British Isles is the same as that of Labrador, but the Gulf stream warms the British 

Isles and gives them an oceanic climate. The westerly winds leave much moisture on the western coast and slopes, and a lesser amount on the eastern. 

5. The population of the British Isles is so great that there is not enough land to raise the needed food. 

Wheat, meat, sugar, coffee, butter and other food products are imported. 

6. The iron and coal beds in the British Isles extend from central and northern England into southern Scotland. There is a rich supply of coal in southern Wales. Cardiff has become the greatest coalexporting city of the world. Great Britain exports coal to her colonies, to France, Italy, and South

America, and to her coaling stations. She imports some iron from Sweden, Spain, and northern Africa. 

7. Birmingham, England, is an iron and steel center. 

Sheffield manufactures steel cutlery. Glasgow, Hull, and Belfast are shipbuilding centers. 

8. The making of woolens was first carried on in the homes. Now it is a great manufacturing industry. 

Yorkshire is the center of the industry. This is on the drier side of the mountains, and sheep raised here furnish raw material for the factories. Much wool is also imported, especially from Australia. 

9. Cotton manufacturing is the most important British industry. It centers on the west side of the Pennines, where the atmosphere is moist and the cotton fiber may be easily handled. Manchester is the leading cotton city. Raw cotton is imported from the United States, Egypt, and India. 

10. The chief manufacture of Ireland is linen. The flax is grown in northern Ireland and is imported from Poland. Belfast is the center of the industry. 

11. Southeastern England is largely agricultural. Wheat, vegetables, and fruits are raised, and sold to the cities. Potatoes, barley, and oats are grown in the 

British Isles. Potatoes are the chief crop of Ireland. 

12. Raising farm animals is an important occupation. 

The drier regions support large numbers of sheep. 

Dairying is a prominent industry, and much milk, butter, and cheese are shipped to the cities. Ireland supplies England with dairy products. The animals of the British Isles are of excellent stock and many are exported for breeding purposes. 

13. Fishing is an important industry of the British 

Isles and provides a valuable source of food. 

14. Uneven coast lines give the British Isles many fine harbors. Glasgow is on the Firth of Clyde, and is the second city in size. Liverpool, on the

Mersey river, imports the raw materials and exports the products of industrial England. Cardiff and Bristol are on the Bristol channel. Plymouth, Portsmouth, and Southampton are on the English channel. Hull on the Humber river and Newcastle on the Tyne are both important seaports. Cobh, Dublin, and Belfast are Irish ports. 

15. London is the oldest city in England. It is located fifty miles inland on the estuary of the Thames. 

It is a center of culture, and the seat of the British government. Edinburgh is the cultural center of 

Scotland, and Dublin of Ireland. 

16. The people of the British Isles are descended from various races of northern Europe. They are intelligent, vigorous, and resourceful. They have emigrated in large numbers and settled in many different parts of the world. The British are well known in science, art, invention, and many other fields of life.

The fish are drying on racks on the shore. They will be exported to countries which use more fish than their own fishermen can supply. Norwegian fish are shipped to many countries, and in return, products of those countries are brought to Norway. 

3. A Norwegian whaler. The crew of this small but powerful steamer has been killing whales in the icy waters of the Antarctic. The whales are securely fastened to the boat and are being towed to a shore station. 

There they will be cut up, and the valuable whale oil will be boiled from their fat. Norway is now the leading nation in the whaling industry.

1. Harvest time in southern Sweden. Hardy grains grow well in the Baltic lowlands of the country. Hay is needed to feed the farm animals through the cold winters, and is an important crop. The land is not sufficiently flat and the fields are not large enough to make practical the use of great harvesting machines. Horse-drawn machines are widely used. 

2. Logs at a Swedish lumber mill. These logs were cut in distant forests and were floated downstream to the mill. They are now waiting to be sawed. They are held in one place by booms, which are floating fences made of logs chained together. Find them in the picture. The piles of sawed lumber beyond the mill look like small houses. 

3. A Swedish paper mill. The single machine in the picture makes 30,000 tons of paper a year. Sweden has extensive evergreen forests and many streams which furnish plenty of clear water and power. These advantages make wood pulp and paper important among her manufactures. Swedish pulp is exported even to the United States. 

4. A view in Stockholm, the capital and principal seaport of Sweden. Stockholm is a large and very beautiful city. This view shows its opera house on the right, the tower of its city hall, and bridges which lead to the royal palace. The river boats are important means of transportation in Stockholm, as part of the city is built on islands.

THE SCANDINAVIAN PENINSULA 

Far in the northwestern part of Europe lies the Scandinavian peninsula, the largest peninsula of the whole continent. From north of the 70° parallel, beyond the Arctic Circle, it stretches southwest for 1,200 miles almost to the 55° parallel. The two countries which lie in the Scandinavian peninsula are the kingdom of Norway, to the west, and the kingdom of Sweden, to the east. North Cape, in Norway, is the most northerly point of the continent of Europe.

SURFACE 

Europe's Northwest highlands run northeast and southwest through the peninsula.

Their main ridge, called the Kiolen mountains, forms a part of the boundary between Norway and Sweden. This ridge is the watershed between the two countries. To the west of the Kiolen mountains is a high plateau, formed of very old, hard rock, well weathered. The plateau rises sharply from the sea, leaving no coastal plain. To the east the mountain slope is much longer and more gentle. Much of Sweden is rolling lowland with many small hills. There are tundras in the northern parts of both countries. 

Long ago northern Europe, like northern

North America, was covered by a great glacier. 

This glacier scooped out valleys, cut deep gorges in the mountains of the Scandinavian peninsula, and formed many glacial lakes and waterfalls like those in New York state. Except in the Alps and the Pyrenees, southern Europe had no ice sheet and so has few lakes. 

The coast of Norway is fringed with islands which were formed by the sinking of the land. 

The islands are tops of mountains which have sunk beneath the sea. The largest island group is called the Lofoten islands.

The sea, flowing between the islands and the Norwegian coast, has made in many places deep, protected channels like those of the Inside passage off the coast of British Columbia and southern Alaska. The sea has also entered the sunken river valleys, forming long, 17 deep bays or fiords. Through these fiords, as through the fiords of Alaska and British Columbia, boats may sail for many miles through quiet waters past some of the loveliest scenery in the world.

If we were to judge the climate of the Scandinavian peninsula solely by latitude, we should expect to find a very cold, bleak CLIMATE land. But we should be wrong, for the warm Gulf stream and the prevailing westerlies do much to offset the peninsula's far north latitude. The Gulf stream flows along

Norway's coast, as it does along the coasts of the British Isles. The westerly winds carry the Gulf stream's warmth over the western part of the peninsula. Here the winters are much milder than farther east in Europe, and the ports are open the year round. 

Even as far north as Hammerfest on the 

Arctic ocean the country is habitable. And 

Tromso, though it lies in the North Frigid zone almost as far north as the 70° parallel, is a city of over 10,000 people. In the Western hemisphere, this same 70° parallel crosses Baffin island, a large island which lies near the mouth of Hudson bay. Baffin island, however, is far away from the warm Gulf stream. It has no cities, and practically no inhabitants. 

The nearby waters are jammed for many months with ice, through which passage is very difficult. Were it not for the Gulf stream, the climate of the Scandinavian peninsula would be as cold as that of Baffin island.

The westerly winds cool as they rise to cross the mountains between Norway and Sweden, so the eastern coast of the peninsula is much colder. Even as far south as Stockholm the harbors are closed for months each year by ice.

But the climate is not so severe as that of the same latitude in northeastern North America, where the cold Labrador current sweeps along the coast. Many people live along the Gulf of
