LAND OF THE MIDNIGHT SUN 

Because Norway stretches so far north into the Frigid zone there are nearly three months each winter when the sun does not shine at all in the northern part of the country. Then for nearly three months in the summer it shines both night and day. These summer nights are like long twilights followed, not by darkness, but by dawn. Though all places in the same latitude as northern Norway have the same long periods of light and darkness, Hammerfest and North Cape are the only places easily reached where one may see the sun shining at twelve o'clock at night. So northern Norway is called the "Land of the Midnight Sun," and tourists from many lands visit it. 

AGRICULTURE 

Even as far south as Stockholm daylight lasts in midsummer until ten o'clock at night. 

This helps to make up for the shortness of the growing season in this land where there are few agricultural advantages.

The soil of Norway is thin and stony, and less than one-fortieth of it is cultivated. The best farming lands are in the south of the country where the land is low, though there are farms along some of the west coast fiords. As you would expect, the people of Norway raise what they most need-potatoes, grains, and forage crops for their cattle. The uplands are grazing lands for sheep, cattle, and the small, sturdy horses which are used to carry goods between the farms and the little villages. In the summer the girls and young boys of the highland farms lead the animals to pasture on the hillsides, far above their homes. When the long winter settles down the animals are brought back home to be fed in the barns. 

The men and the older boys care for the soil and raise and gather the crops. As the climate of Norway is very moist, hay grows abundantly. But before it can be used it must be piled on racks, away from the ground, to dry. 

It is a long, painstaking task to dry out enough hay for even a few cattle. 

Farming in Norway is done largely with hand tools, because the ground is unsuited to the use of large agricultural machinery. 

Sweden's lowlands along the Baltic sea are the best farm lands of the peninsula. Here hay, oats, rye, barley, sugar beets, potatoes, and wheat are all grown. There is less moisture in the lowlands of Sweden than in Norway, because of the protecting mountains to the west, so the hay is more easily dried. Dairying is extensive, and butter and cheese are shipped away. Oxen are used for plowing, and some farm machinery, manufactured in 

Sweden, is in use.

FORESTS AND THEIR USES 

Much of the Scandinavian peninsula is forest land. Great tree-covered slopes extend from the Kiolen mountains to the farmlands in Sweden. The country has hundreds of lumber, pulp, and paper mills. The timber is cut into boards and used for building purposes. It is also made into firewood and small articles, such as toys and matches. Matches from the 

Scandinavian peninsula are sold in many different lands. The wood pulp is shipped to many countries to be made into paper. Much of it goes to the United States, so perhaps the paper in one of your books was made of pulp from a Swedish forest. Norway, too, has many paper mills, and she has long used much of her timber for building. Most of the buildings in both countries are built of wood. AND

WHALING 

One of the first purposes for which Norway's trees were cut was the building of fishing boats. The men of Norway have been fishermen from early times, FISHING and fishing remains one of the most important industries. Along the coast of Norway the waters are shallow and provide excellent feeding and spawning grounds for cod, mackerel, herring, and salmon. Near the shores of the Lofoten islands great numbers of cod are caught and codfishing is the real business of the islanders. All along the shore may be seen the little wooden shacks of the fishermen built close to the water. The Norwegian fishermen can work the year round because the waters of their fishing grounds do not freeze in winter. 

Vessels from Norway sail to the Arctic ocean and to the Antarctic to hunt seal, walrus, and

EUROPE 

whale. The seal and walrus are valuable for their skins, and the whale for oils. Fish provide the Norwegians with food, and fish and fish products are among their most important exports. Most of the exported fish are canned. 

We receive many Norwegian sardines. There are important exports of dried fish also, particularly to southern Europe. The city of 

Bergen is the largest center for the products of the fisheries. Bergen is on a fiord which provides an excellent harbor.

Scandinavian countries have other industries which are gradually increasing in value. Norway has

WATER POWER valuable silver deposits. Cop per, zinc, and lead are found in both countries. Both countries, too, have iron, though Sweden's iron industry is the more important. Iron is found in the far north of

Sweden and also in the southern part. As the country has no coal, most of the ore from her mines is exported to Great Britain, Germany, and other countries. Swedish iron is of such excellent quality that it is used largely in steel industries where a particularly fine grade is needed, as in the making of cutlery. The people of Sweden use it in making delicate parts for watches and clocks.

A number of smelting plants and steel mills have been built in southern Sweden. Their fires are fed by coal imported from other lands or by charcoal made by the partial burning of wood. 

Another substitute for coal used in both

Norway and Sweden is water power. The glacial lakes are fine reservoirs, from which the water runs off in swift streams and waterfalls. Long used for running mills, the water power is now being turned into electric power in many hydroelectric plants. The electric power is used not only to supply lights and to run trolleys and railroad trains but also to run manufacturing plants. The water and power are both very valuable to the pulp and paper mills.

Though the use of water power is constantly growing in both Norway and Sweden, only a small part of the vast supply has as yet been developed. As more and more of it is harnessed to factory wheels the industrial importance of the Scandinavian countries should become greater. 

Not quite 3,000,000 people live in Norway, and a little more than 6,000,000 live in Sweden. 

Most of the people of Norway live in the cities and villages AND CITIES POPULATION 

along the fiords and on the islands. Very few live in the uplands. In

Sweden most of the people live in the southern section and along the lowland plain. 

The three largest cities of the Scandinavian peninsula are Stockholm, Oslo, and Goteborg.

Stockholm is the capital of Sweden, and the home of its king. Since the city is on the Baltic, it is well situated for trade. Though the 

Baltic freezes over in winter, ice-breaking ships keep Stockholm's port open. Traffic also goes out of Stockholm by way of rivers and canals to Goteborg, a port of western Sweden near the North sea. Stockholm has so many canals that it resembles Venice in Italy, a city built on many islands. You may sometimes hear it called the "Venice of the North." 

Oslo, or Christiania, the capital of Norway, is in the best farming section of the country and is the country's leading seaport. Norway's longest railroad runs north from Oslo to

Trondhjem on the west coast. Trondhjem was once the capital of the country and has an ancient church where many of the old-time

On the whole, the Scandinavian people are well educated. Their far northland has taught 

PEOPLE 

them to be hardworking and thrifty. 

As the rugged highlands offered few means of making a living, the men of Norway early turned to the sea and became hardy fishermen or brave and adventurous sailors. 

Centuries ago men from Scandinavia plowed the seas in ships and explored unknown lands. 

In very early times these Norsemen, as they were called, settled on the shores of Iceland and Greenland and, long before the coming of Columbus, even touched the coast of North America.

From those long-ago times Norway has had many ships and many sailors. Today her merchant vessels carry products for other lands besides their own, and this business of transportation is one of Norway's greatest occupations.

The men of the lowlands have struggled to make their rocky soil productive, and as a result have become an intelligent, painstaking people.

Because of the hardships of life at home many thousands have come to the United States from Norway and Sweden. They have settled in the central farming districts, or in the lumbering and mining sections. Healthy, determined, thrifty, and painstaking, they make good citizens.

The literature of Norway and Sweden shows us that their people are patriotic and are lovers of beauty. These countries boast many writers, artists, musicians, and inventors. 

The same fearless love of adventure and accomplishment which took the early Norsemen to unexplored parts of the world is still a trait of these people. Early in the nineteenth century, Keilhau, a Norwegian, made the first scientific trip to the region of Svalbard, or 

Spitzbergen, far north in the Arctic ocean.

Nansen, another Norwegian, was one of the greatest Arctic explorers. The Norwegian 

Roald Amundsen discovered the South Pole in 1911, and, in 1926, flew from the islands of Svalbard in a dirigible balloon across the north polar regions to Alaska. Sven Hedin, the great 

Swedish explorer, has reached parts of central 

Asia which no other white man has seen. 

If you read the adventures of these men you will feel like saying, as did the ancient Norsemen-"Skoal! to to the Northland," which means, Hail! to the Northland-the beautiful, rugged country from which such heroes come!

The peninsula extends from north of the 70° parallel almost to the 55° parallel. The Northwest highlands run through the peninsula. The Kiolen mountains lie between the high plateau of Norway and the lowlands of Sweden. The coast line of Norway is fringed with islands and fiords. 

2. The climate of the western part of the Scandinavian peninsula is mild because westerly winds bring warmth from the Gulf stream. Norway's ports are open the year round, while some of Sweden's, on the Baltic, are closed a part of each winter by ice. 

Sweden has less moisture than Norway because of the protecting mountains in the western part of the country. 

3. The soil of Norway is thin and stony and agriculture is limited. Cattle, sheep, and small, sturdy horses are raised in Norway. The Baltic lowlands of Sweden are the best farm lands in the peninsula. 

Oats, barley, rye, sugar beets, potatoes, and a little wheat are grown. Dairying is extensive and butter and cheese are exported.

Norwegian ships now transport goods for many other countries besides their own.

1. A Danish dairy farm. Denmark is a low, level country with large areas of good pasture land, well suited to dairying. More than a third of the entire country is devoted to grazing lands for dairy herds. So well does the dairy industry flourish that Denmark exports more butter than any other country in the world. Notice the large windmill. Windmills are used in Denmark to pump water and, sometimes, to grind grain.

Much of the work in the small fields is done by hand. 

The people of Denmark are skilful farmers.

Copenhagen is an important seaport. It lies on a strait connecting the North and Baltic seas and so is right on a main route of sea traffic. Products of the interior of the country are brought to Copenhagen for shipment.

DENMARK, THE NETHERLANDS, AND BELGIUM 

The lowland plains of the mainland of Europe extend from the western coast of 

France and the shores of the North sea, to

Europe's eastern boundary. In the western part of these plains, bordering the North sea, there are three lowland kingdoms, Denmark, the Netherlands, and Belgium. All three are small countries lacking many of Nature's most valued gifts, but each has prospered by making use of what it has at hand.

DENMARK AND HER POSSESSIONS 

In studying about the countries of the world, you have seen that different ones have different industries and that each trades the things it makes for what it needs. It is this trade between countries that helps to furnish the people of the world with the food they eat, the clothes they wear, the tools with which they work, and the other necessities of life. 

In looking back over what you have studied, you might call Chile the world's nitrate field, England one of the earth's great factory districts, and Mexico one of the chief mineral lands. As for Denmark, we may describe that little country as one of the famous dairies of the world, for its dairy products are known far and wide.

POSITION, CLIMATE, AND PEOPLE 

Denmark forms part of the lowlands of 

Europe. It includes the peninsula of Jutland and a group of islands lying at the entrance to the Baltic sea, very close to southern Sweden.

The people of Norway, Sweden, and Denmark have many of the same characteristics, but each country has its own language and its own government. Their natural boundaries of mountains and water have kept the three lands separated into different nations.

There are about 3,500,000 people in the kingdom of Denmark.

Denmark is a low, level little country with many fresh, green meadows. The climate is cool and the country has many mists and fogs. 

It is only twice as large as our one state of 

Massachusetts. There is no coal, there is no iron, and there is no water power. There are few forests and no mountains, and the sandy soil is poor. But there is abundant rainfall, so this cool, damp country has fine grasslands. 

DAIRYING AND OTHER 

About three-fourths of the country is in farm lands, and about half of this is pasture. 

Grains, vegetables, and fodder crops are grown for home use. 

These are valuable crops, but FARMING the pasture lands are even more important. Lacking forests and minerals, Denmark has turned to dairying and to the raising of swine and poultry. By hard work and good business methods these industries have been made successful.

In developing their dairy industry the Danish people went to work intelligently. Their dairy machines are the best. They have studied and experimented until dairying in Denmark is carried on in the best way known to modern times. People from other countries often go to 

Denmark to study the Danish methods of dairying.

The Danish people are said to make the best butter in the world, and they export more of it than any other country. Much goes to England and much is packed in cans and is shipped to far distant lands. Many of the farmers sell all the butter they make, and they themselves eat margarine or some other butter substitute.

The skimmed milk left from butter making is used to fatten hogs. Danish bacon has fully as good a reputation as Danish butter.

There are large poultry farms in the country, 25

EUROPE 

and the eggs and meat are important Danish exports.

With the smallness of its area, its position so far north, and its lack of forests, minerals, and water power, Denmark might easily be one of the least progressive countries of the world.

But instead of that, this little country has developed the industry best suited to its conditions and now has a world-wide reputation for its products.

COOPERATIVE 

MARKETING 

Do you remember how the fruit-growers of

California work together, or coöperate, in marketing their goods? The farmers of Denmark have adopted the same coöperative system in marketing their farm products. The butter, eggs, cream, cheese, and meats are sent to factories where they are prepared for shipping, sold, and shipped. If men work together in this way instead of each man for himself they save money in transportation, in packing, in advertising, and in selling their goods. 

Buyers as well as sellers benefit by coöperative associations. Each association makes very strict rules, and its members must observe them. If a member is found to be sending out a second-grade product as first-grade, he is fined or dropped from the association and his goods are no longer accepted. In this way the associations earn a good reputation, people learn to depend on them, and their members find a ready market for their products.

OTHER 

INDUSTRIES 

There are a few other industries in Denmark besides dairying. The shallow waters along the coast are good fishing grounds. The country has a merchant fleet of good size, and many 

Danes are engaged in trading. A fine clay found in Denmark is used in making pottery and porcelain.

FUEL As there is no coal in Denmark, peat is used for fuel. Peat is a form of decayed vegetation found in marshes or bogs. It is common in countries having a moist atmosphere and low temperature. People go to the bogs to get their fuel, and cut the peat out in chunks, just as we sometimes see sod cut in our own country. Peat has to be dried before it can be used. What coal Denmark uses comes from neighboring countries.

COPENHAGEN The one important seaport of Denmark is the city of Copenhagen. Built on a strait between the Baltic and the North seas, Copenhagen is right in the line of trade. Ships traveling from the west can sail to the city around the tip of Jutland or through the Kiel canal which cuts through the southern end of the peninsula. The city has always been a port of refuge in storms, and in this way earned its name, which means "Merchant's Haven." 

Copenhagen is the manufacturing center, the commercial center, the shipping port, the cultural center, and the capital of Denmark. 

The king lives here and here the lawmaking bodies assemble. The city has a fine university and a museum.

There is a monument in Copenhagen interesting to both children and grown-ups. It is erected to Hans Christian Andersen, the famous Danish author who wrote The Ugly 

Duckling and other favorite fairy stories.

ISLAND POSSESSIONS

Some of her early possessions Denmark has now given up. She once owned the island of 

Iceland, but a few years ago she gave the Icelanders their independence and made Iceland a separate country. About the same time she sold the Danish West Indies, now called the 

Virgin islands, to the United States.

One of the possessions that Denmark has retained is the Faroe islands, which lie out in the Atlantic north of Great Britain. Sheep are raised there and cod are caught in the nearby waters. The islands supply Denmark with fish and mutton for food, and with wool and codliver oil for export. 

Greenland, another Danish possession, lies northeast of North America. The interior is a vast ice-capped plateau. This ice moves slowly towards the shore, where it breaks off in great icebergs. Down the east coast of Greenland flows an ice-cold current from the frozen north. The climate of this coast is so bitterly cold that nobody lives there and the country is dreary and desolate. Greenland's few inhabitants are Eskimo fishermen and fur-hunters who live on the narrow belt of tundras along the southwest coast. Danish traders deal with the Eskimos in a few trading settlements from which they ship furs and seal-oil to the busy little homeland.

THE NETHERLANDS AND HER POSSESSIONS 

Southwest of Denmark is the little kingdom of the Netherlands, often called Holland, the home of the Dutch people. The name means lowlands, and the kingdom is rightly named. 

One-fourth of its surface is actually below sea level. Most of the land of this country was formed by soil brought down from the mountains by the Rhine river. The wide delta which the river has built up forms a great part of the country. The Netherlands is flat, with no water power, no forests, no mineral resources. Its greatest natural advantage is its position at the Rhine's mouth.

This position makes the Netherlands an open front door for the trade of Germany and

COMMERCE 

central Europe. Great Britain, France, and Belgium are near neighbors and are connected with the Netherlands by canals, railroads, and sea routes. 

Goods brought to Dutch ports by ocean steamers are reloaded onto river boats and canal barges and distributed to inland countries. 

Goods from the interior of Europe come down the Rhine to the Netherlands and are reloaded onto ocean steamers for foreign ports. Germany, especially, uses this great river waterway, for it is her nearest route to the west. 

The Netherlands lies right in the path of the greatest European trade, and this fact has made it a very important commercial nation. 

In addition to the commerce which the 

Netherlands handles for other nations, she has imports and exports of her own. Chief among the imports are coal, iron, steel, cotton, and foodstuffs.

CITIES 

The chief cities of the Netherlands are Rotterdam and Amsterdam. Each has a fine harbor and is an important trading center. Rotterdam is on one of the Rhine mouths. Amsterdam is on the Zuider Zee, an inland bay, connected with the North sea by a ship canal. All Dutch cities are clean and well laid out, and both these ports have fine buildings, streets, and highways. Canals run through the cities and cut the land into islands, connected by bridges. The canals are used as we use streets, and people go along them in boats as we go along our streets in automobiles.

On a branch of the main canal connecting 

Amsterdam and Rotterdam stands The Hague, the capital of the Netherlands. In this quaint old city have been held many international conferences to promote world peace.

The Rhine delta, like the deltas of the Nile and Mississippi, has deep, rich soil. Formerly much of it was covered by shallow waters of the sea. The 

Dutch hit upon a plan for turning this section into farm lands. They built 

PUSHING BACK THE SEA

EUROPE 

walls, or dikes, around the shallow waters and then pumped the water into the walled-out sea.

They also built high banks along the Rhine and other streams to keep them from overflowing the lowlands, and dug a network of canals and ditches to carry off the water brought by heavy rains.

TEXEL I. 

We can hardly think of Holland without thinking of its longarmed windmills.

These are a sort of trade-mark of the country. They were erected to pump the water into the sea. 

Holland lies in the path of the prevailing westerlies, and has local winds that blow across its flat surface in many directions. The windmills can be kept turning most of the time. Gasoline pumps are now replacing many of the picturesque wind- mills. 

The lands drained by the canals and pumps are called polders. The chief reason for draining the polders was to make room for a growing popula- tion. The population is still growing, The Hague Scheldt

Rive Haarlem used. The crops are largely vegetables, grains, sugar beets, flax, and flower bulbs. The farmers raise poultry and export great numbers of eggs.

The Netherlands is truly a lowland country. By shutting out the sea with dikes, much land called polders has been added which is actually below sea level. In time, a large section of what is now the Zuider Zee will become Dutch land. and the Dutch are still extending their land. 

They are now draining parts of the Zuider Zee, and expect to add many square miles in this way.

The polders have fine farm land and excellent pasture. The farms are small, and the farmers 

AGRICULTURE AND DAIRYING 

usually live in little villages or in nearby towns and cities. 

Every possible foot of land is made into butter, cheese, condensed milk, and milk chocolate, all of which are important exports. 

People who enjoy the fragrance of hyacinths and the bright beauty of tulips find the Netherlands attractive for its great fields of these blossoms. The plants are grown for their bulbs, the export of which is a source of much wealth. The bulb industry centers around the city of 

Haarlem. Long experience has made the Dutch expert in this industry. The bulb farmers hold frequent contests, and prizes are given for the finest products. This encourages the production of new and beautiful varieties.

The Netherlands will never be a leading manufacturing country, for it has no coal and iron. Peat bogs supply fuel, but coal must be imported.

MANUFACTURES 

There are, however, plentiful deposits of fine clay. From the clay are made the famous Delft china and the bricks and tile which are the chief building materials of the country. In the

larger cities machinery and cotton textiles are manufactured from imported materials. Cotton cloth is the most important export of the country. One of the chief industries of the 

Dutch is the cutting and polishing of diamonds. Amsterdam is one of the great centers of this trade.

FISHING 

The North sea fisheries are important in feeding the country, and herring figure largely in the foreign trade. Fishing gives an occupation to many Dutchmen, and the fishing fleet of the seacoast villages numbers several thousand vessels. Since the country has many small streams and canals with houses built along their banks, fishing for family needs may be done almost from the doorsteps.

COLONIES 

The Dutch have long been sailors and traders, and their colonies are found in many parts of the world. The Netherlands and the colonies together are known as the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

On the piers at Rotterdam and Amsterdam the visitor sees goods from the far-away Indies and South America alongside the German and

Dutch goods awaiting shipment to foreign lands.

Dutch Guiana. The Netherlands holds one of the three parts of the country of Guiana in 

South America. Dutch Guiana is a hot land with few white people. A large part of the population lives in the capital, Paramaribo. 

Some sugar, molasses, cacao, coffee, and bananas are exported to the mother country. 

Dutch West Indies. Two little groups containing six islands in the Caribbean sea consti tute the Dutch West Indies. Of these the principal island is Curacao. The products are not very important. They consist principally of cattle, salt, and phosphates. Curacao has refineries for oil from the South American mainland. 

Dutch East Indies. Most important of the 

Netherlands' possessions are the Dutch East

Indies, which lie southeast of Asia, as the map on page 174 shows us. They are nearly sixty times the area of the mother country and nearly one-fourth as large as the United States. 

To a commercial country like the Netherlands these islands are very important, for they give her tropical products to trade with Germany and other countries, and they also buy great amounts of her exports. 

The Dutch East Indies are crossed by the Equator and lie in the equatorial rain belt. 

In past ages their many volcanoes covered large parts of the islands with lava. The lava soil is rich and deep. Some of the volcanoes are still active, and earthquakes occur from time to time.

The Dutch gained possession of these islands almost as soon as the sea route around the Cape of Good Hope was found. In those times the spices of the islands were the important product, for spices were demanded in Europe to preserve food. This fact led to naming the Moluccas, one of the groups of islands, the 

Spice islands. The most important of the islands now is Java, which is very fully developed. Sumatra is also well advanced. Parts of Borneo and New Guinea belong to the

Netherlands, but they are little developed and are inhabited largely by savage tribes unfriendly to white men.

The Dutch have developed the East Indies by forming large plantations, on which the native East Indians and immigrants from Asia supply cheap labor under the direction of white men. These plantations raise rice to feed the islanders, and important export crops of sugar, rubber, tea, tobacco, and coffee. The islands are part of the greatest rubber-producing area of the world. The rubber is mostly sold direct to the United States, but the other crops are marketed through Rotterdam and Amsterdam. 

Copra, the dried meat of coconuts, is prepared for shipping to the home country, where the valuable oil is pressed from it. Other products are tin and petroleum, tropical fruits, spices, and cinchona bark, from which quinine is made. All these products are valuable in themselves and their transportation gives employment to many Dutch ships and people. 

The population of the Dutch East Indies is nearly 50,000,000, over six times that of the mother country. The island of Java is most densely populated. Batavia, Java, is the capital of the colonies and the chief seaport and city.

OWC-4

EUROPE 

The Dutch East Indies were long the only source of tropical products for Europe and 

North America, and have brought great wealth to the mother country. Parts of South 

America and other continents have now begun large production of these materials, but the demand of temperate lands is so great that a market is assured for any amount likely to be produced. From what we know of the thrifty, industrious, and determined Dutch, we may expect that they will hold and increase their business in tropical products.

BELGIUM AND HER POSSESSIONS 

The second most densely populated country of Europe is Belgium, the smallest of the lowland countries. It is smaller even than the 

Netherlands, but has about 300,000 more people. 

To the northwest, Belgium has a short coast line along the North sea. To the north is the Netherlands. 

To the south is the great country of 

France. To the east is Germany. At 

Belgium's extreme southeast corner lies the tiny independent state of Luxembourg.

Not all of Belgium is lowland. 

The southeastern part lies in the Central uplands of Europe where there are timber forests 

SURFACE and fine grazing lands. But if AND CLIMATE 

you should travel south from the Netherlands into northern Belgium you would find the two countries very much alike.

On every side you would see dikes, polders drained by ditches, flat farm lands, and dairy cattle contentedly grazing. The climate in general is cool and moist. 

The picturesque Belgian countryside is divided into the tiniest of farms, so small that you would be inclined to call them gardens. As in the Netherlands, the land is well suited for farming. 

AGRICULTURE 

Since there are a great many people in Belgium, and very little farm land, the earth is intensively cultivated so that it yields fine large crops. Farms in Belgium produce twice as much wheat and over three times as many potatoes to the acre as do those of the 

United States. Potatoes are the leading food crop. 

Hardy grains and sugar beets are also grown. The largest crop of the country is mangels, which are large beets grown to feed the hogs and cattle. Flax and tobacco are other valuable crops, and bulbs and flowers are raised. 

Farming is so important that even those who work in the factories, the mines, or at the docks are encouraged to plant small gardens about their village homes. These may be tended by the women and children, or by the workmen themselves in the evening, and they produce food for many families. 

Dairying is a leading industry of the farms. 

On many of the small farms in Belgium, dogs, instead of horses, are used to draw the products to market. It is a familiar sight in a Belgian village to see a dog harnessed to a little

wagon full of shiny milk cans, patiently waiting while his mistress sells the milk. 

The Belgians raise rabbits for food. These animals are fed partly on the weeds from the gardens. When they are fine and fat the rabbits are killed. Their meat is eaten and their pelts are sold for making felt, or for other purposes. 

COMMERCE 

Belgium is not so well situated for commerce as the Netherlands. It has no good seacoast harbors, and most of the streams which flow across the country have their outlets to the sea in the Netherlands, rather than in Belgium. But the Belgian people have offset these disadvantages by a network of railroads and canals. So well have they succeeded that Antwerp, their chief port, is one of the most important in Europe, even though it is not actually on the sea. 

Antwerp is near the mouth of the Scheldt river. The city is connected by ship canal and railroad with Brussels, the capital city of Belgium, lying almost in the center of the country. Railroads and canals also connect Antwerp with all other parts of Belgium. Like 

Rotterdam, Antwerp handles a large trade between the colonies of its own country and the industrial countries of central Europe. The city is a shipbuilding center and is among the chief diamond markets of the world. Ostend, on the North sea, is the port next in importance to Antwerp. Boats ply between Ostend and the English port of Dover, and Ostend is connected by ship canal with the French port of Calais.

In the valley of the Sambre and Meuse rivers, west of the Central uplands region, there are rich deposits of coal, iron,

RESOURCES, and limestone.

As these min- 

MANUFACTURES, AND INDUSTRIES erals are most important for every kind of manufacturing, they have added much to the wealth of Belgium. They are the basis for industries which support more people than trade or agriculture could support, and it is for this reason that Belgium has a larger population than the 

Netherlands. Here, as in England, the limestone found near the coal and iron deposits is an aid to the production of iron and steel, and these products are Belgium's principal exports. 

Throughout Belgium there are many smelters.

In the city of Liege there are factories for the manufacture of iron and steel products, including firearms of many types. The coal and iron fields of Belgium touch those of France to the south. Besides these minerals the country has deposits of zinc, and its clay and sand are used in the making of pottery, glass, and cement which Belgium sells all over the world. 

The northern part of Belgium was once known as Flanders. Long years ago the Flemish people, as the inhabitants of Flanders were called, started the textile industry which is still flourishing there. The cool, moist climate is especially suited to the manufacture of cotton. 

Except for flax, which grows in Belgium, little raw material for textiles is produced in the country, and quantities of wool, cotton, and even flax are imported for the making of cloth and thread. Ghent and Bruges are centers of textile manufacturing. They have been connected by deep canals with the sea, and can place their wares directly aboard ship. 

Belgium is still famous for one of its oldest industries—the making of lace. Even in this day of factories, this work is done extensively by hand in the homes. Exquisite pieces of lace are skilfully made of finest thread. Some of these pieces are so delicate that they are used only as altar cloths, to trim wedding dresses, or on garments for royalty. They are considered great treasures and bring enormous prices. Much of this handmade lace is sold for export. 

The quaint old city of Brussels, famous the world over for the manufacture of rugs and carpets, is a commercial center for the lace industry. One of its noted buildings, the Hotel de Ville, or City Hall, has a stone tower carved in an elaborate pattern. One writer describes this tower by saying that it reminds him of the Belgian lace which merchants and tourists from many countries come to see and buy in the city. Brussels also makes fine gloves.

You would find it interesting to listen to the conversations of different groups of people in Belgium, though probably you

A LAND OF TWO LANGUAGES

EUROPE 

would not be able to understand all they were saying. Belgium has two official languages—

Flemish, spoken largely by people from the northern part of the country, and French, spoken mainly by those from the southern part. In addition, German and English are freely spoken in the markets and shops and along the docks.

RELIGION AND 

EDUCATION 

Busy as they are with their farms, their mines, their commerce, and their industries, the Belgians have not allowed the religious and educational sides of their lives to go undeveloped. Nearly every Belgian village, however humble, has an exceptionally beautiful little church, and there are numerous wayside shrines. Belgium has four universities, of which the largest is that of the city of Louvain. 

Leopold II was king of the Belgians from 

1865 to 1909. He was an alert, businesslike sovereign, much interested in the welfare of his country. Seeing how the Netherlands was profiting by having colonies in the Dutch East

THE BELGIAN CONGO 

Indies, he became interested in newly explored lands in the rich Congo basin of Africa.

Largely through his efforts, Belgium acquired a good part of this region in west central 

Africa. It is now known as the Belgian Congo. 

Find it on the map on page 132. 

The Belgian Congo is about seventy-seven times the size of little Belgium. It is larger even than the Dutch East Indies. It has an outlet to the sea through the Congo river. At present it is inhabited by native tribes, with a very few Belgians to govern them and trade in their products. But the tropical jungles have rich products. Palm oil and some wild rubber are produced to be refined in Antwerp.

Rubber plantations have been started, and coffee and sugar are successfully cultivated. Rice is grown for local food, and cotton cultivation is promising. Belgium receives great quantities of copper from the Congo, and gold, silver, diamonds, and ivory are all valuable additions to its trade. A good deal of the commerce is with Great Britain. The United States receives copper and palm oil in return for automobiles and petroleum.

1. Denmark is part of the lowlands of Europe. It includes the peninsula of Jutland and islands at the entrance to the Baltic sea. Its people are much like the people of Norway and Sweden. 

2.

Denmark is a low, level country, with a cool, moist climate. Its principal industry is dairying. By the use of the best modern methods, the Danes have made their dairy and meat products known all over the world. 

3. Fishing is an industry of Denmark. Many people are engaged in trading. The chief mineral is a clay which is used in making pottery. There is no coal, and peat is used for fuel. Some coal is imported. 

4. Copenhagen is Denmark's seaport, its capital, and its manufacturing, business, and cultural center. 

5. Denmark owns Greenland and the Faroe Islands.

These possessions furnish Denmark with fish and mutton for food, and with furs, seal-oil and codliver oil for export. Greenland is a cold country, with very few inhabitants. Iceland was formerly a Danish possession, but is now independent. The 

Danish West Indies, now the Virgin islands, were purchased by the United States. 

6. In the Netherlands lies the rich Rhine delta. Much of the Netherlands is below sea level, having been reclaimed from the sea by the building of dikes and the draining of the land. 

7. To make room for their growing population, the 

Dutch are draining parts of the Zuider Zee. 

8. The Netherlands has excellent pasture lands and well kept farms. Dairying is extensive. Butter, cheese, and milk chocolate are manufactured and exported. The raising and selling of flower bulbs is a great industry. 

9. The Netherlands is not a great manufacturing country because she lacks coal and iron. Clay is plentiful. From it are made bricks, tile, and a fine grade of china, called Delft. Textiles and machinery are manufactured from raw materials which are imported. The cutting and polishing of diamonds is one of the country's chief industries. 

10. Many Dutch people engage in fishing. The Netherlands' fishing fleet comprises several thousand vessels. 

11. The Netherlands is the open doorway for the traffic of the Rhine river, the path of trade between interior Europe and the west. It is an important commercial country. At its great ports, Rotterdam and Amsterdam, products from all over the world are exchanged. The Hague is the capital of the country.

12. The Dutch have long been sailors and traders. 

Among their colonies are Dutch Guiana, the Dutch 

West Indies, and the Dutch East Indies. Of these, the most valuable are the Dutch East Indies. These tropical islands export rubber, tea, coffee, sugar, spices, cinchona, tropical fruits, tobacco, tin, and petroleum. 

13. Belgium, the smallest of the lowland countries of 

Europe, ranks second in density of population. 

France, Germany, Luxembourg, and the Netherlands are bordering countries. Northern Belgium resembles agricultural Holland in appearance. The southeast corner of the country lies in the Central uplands, where there are forests and good grazing lands. 

14. The people of Belgium grow wheat and hardy grains, potatoes, flax, sugar beets, tobacco, mangels, flower bulbs, and flowers. Dairy cattle are also raised. 

15. Belgium has no good seacoast harbors. Most of the streams flowing through the country have their outlets to the sea in the Netherlands. Railroads and canals have helped to offset this disadvantage. 

Antwerp is one of the largest ports of Europe. 

16. Belgium has deposits of iron, coal, and limestone, zinc, clay, and sand. Her manufactures include iron and steel products, glassware, pottery, and cement. 

Raw materials for textile manufacturing are imported. They include wool and cotton. 

17. Belgium has a vast colony in Africa known as the 

Belgian Congo. The colony supplies gold, silver, ivory, diamonds, rubber, and palm oil. These resources increase the commerce and wealth of the mother country.

1. Stacking wheat in northern France. Notice the pointed tops of the finished stacks. In northern France it often rains during the harvest season, and the farmers in this picture have stacked their grain so that water will run off. If rain soaked the wheat, the crop would spoil. 

In our drier spring wheat belt the farmers do not need to pile their crop so carefully.

LOWLAND AND PLATEAU COUNTRIES OF WESTERN EUROPE FRANCE AND HER DEPENDENCIES 

Great Britain, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, the Netherlands, and Belgium are all kingdoms. The country of France is a republic, with a government somewhat like our own. 

France may be said to have three coast lines, one to the north, one to the west, and a third to the southeast. Along the

COAST LINES 

north, its shores are lapped by the waters of the North sea, the Strait of Dover, and the English channel. The Strait of Dover lies between France and England.

Though this strip of water that separates their lands is only twenty-one miles wide, the people of France and England are very unlike. They speak different languages and have different habits and customs. This is also true of 

France and her other near neighbors.

On the French side of the Strait of Dover is the port of Calais. Opposite it on the English side is Dover. Between the two ports ships pass continually, laden with passengers, mail, and goods of many kinds. 

The western shore of France is part of 

Europe's Atlantic coast. On the Bay of Biscay is Biarritz, one of the famous beach resorts of the country. France has a number of such playgrounds that are international rather than French, for their visitors come from all over the world.

The blue waters of the Mediterranean sea wash the southeast coast of France. This is a lovely stretch of land, the eastern part of which is known as the Riviera. Because of its mild climate the Riviera is a famous winter resort where the wit, beauty, and wealth of the world gather each year.

On the Riviera, near the Italian border, is one of the world's midget countries, the principality of Monaco, under French 

MONACO 

protection, but with a government independent of France. Though the country has an area of only eight square miles and has less than 25,000 inhabitants, each year hundreds of thousands of pleasure seekers visit its chief town, Monte Carlo. The profits of the great Monte Carlo gambling establishment, the Casino, pay all the expenses of the government and a large income to the Prince of Monaco.

Andorra is another tiny European country, perched high up in the Pyrenees mountains between France and Spain, and ANDORRA protected by the two countries.

Andorra is the smallest republic in the world. 

About 5000 people live in its six small villages and make their living by tending flocks and herds. The only way to reach this shut-away land is through steep mountain passes during the summer months, when they are not blocked by snow.

There are a few French villages, as well, in the Pyrenees. They nestle in the sheltered valleys between the mountains, where the people do a little farming besides caring for their sheep and cattle.

Just as the Pyrenees form a high wall between France and Spain, the snow-capped 

Alps rise between France and

Italy. Mont Blanc, the highest BOUNDARIES peak in western Europe, lies

LAND 

on this border with its summit in France. The lower Jura mountains divide France from 

Switzerland, and the Vosges mountains lie just west of the Rhine where that river separates 

France and Germany. The forested Ardennes highlands are along part of the Belgian border, but along only part. The rest of this boundary line is low. Because the Vosges mountains and the Ardennes forest gave strong natural protection, the Germans chose the low Belgian border by which to enter France at the opening of the World War.

Besides its various highland sections, France has a great stretch of lowland, as much of the western part of the country lies in the Atlantic lowland plain.

SURFACE 

35

EUROPE 

The south central part is a high plateau. 

The province of Brittany, which is the peninsula between the Bay of Biscay and the English channel, is lower upland country. 

The prevailing winds of France are westerly, warm and moisture laden, and with no mountains to block their way they sweep 

CLIMATE 

in from the ocean across the country. 

Just as in the case of the British Isles, these westerly winds give France a milder temperature than other countries in the same latitude. 

As France is farther south than the British Isles, its climate is somewhat warmer. When the winds strike the highlands to the east they lose much of their moisture, so eastern France has even more rainfall than the western lowlands. All the country has enough for agriculture.

The sheltering highlands in the southeastern part of France help to give the southeast coast a truly Mediterranean climate. The winters are mild with moderate rain and the summers are hot with very little rain. The coast is swept by the warm winds from the Mediterranean sea and the vegetation is varied and rich.

Much of France has a longer growing season than the British Isles. Also, France is nearly twice as large as the 

AGRICULTURE 

British Isles, and has much more farm land. Then, too, it has nearly 7,000,000 fewer people. For these reasons France can raise almost enough food to feed her people, while the British Isles have to import a great many food supplies. Of the nearly 50,000,000 inhabitants of the British Isles, about fourfifths are city-dwellers. Of the more than 

40,000,000 people in France, over half live in villages or in the country and work the land. 

From that fact alone, you can draw a comparison between industrial France and industrial British Isles, and agricultural France and agricultural British Isles. 

You would be surprised at the care with which French farmers farm their lands. No plot of ground is too small to be cultivated. In the most unlikely places—even high up on the mountain slopes where there happen to be fertile, protected areas-you will see little patches of wheat, barley, rye, or potatoes. 

In the British Isles, you will remember, much land is owned by a rather small number of wealthy men, who rent it out to tenantfarmers. In France the farmers usually own the land themselves and so they take more pride in it. Therefore it is more carefully farmed and better fertilized, and raises larger crops. 

The farm products of France vary with the climate, as they do in every country. Northern 

France grows the more hardy products. Potatoes

FARM PRODUCTS 

and oats, wheat, and other hardy grains are grown, and fields of sugar beets furnish the raw material for the sugar refineries scattered about France. France does not grow quite enough wheat for her people, and must import some from Australia and Argentina. Apples are the chief fruit of this region. 

The people of Brittany engage in dairy farming and market gardening. The products are shipped across to busy England. Sheep raising is very important in Brittany, and an especially fine type of strong, active draft horses, called Percherons, are bred nearby. 

Corn, tobacco, and wheat are grown in the southern part of the country. Upon reaching the Mediterranean region you still see wheat and barley, which grow well in this section of winter rains and dry summers. 

VILLAGE LIFE 

In France, as in a number of European countries, most of the farmers live in villages near their farms. All over France there are these little villages, each no more than a cluster of houses around a church, a store, and possibly a garage, with the beautifully tended fields lying all about.

It may be that one reason the French have held to this arrangement is that they are a very sociable people. They enjoy company, and their greatest daily pleasure is to get together in the evening and talk over the events of the day. They are not idle while they talk. The women are often making bits of lacework, and you would be amazed at the prices that will later be paid for these bits of lacework in a city shop.

These little farming communities have a

FRANCE AND HER DEPENDENCIES 

37 pleasant, restful air. Sometimes a village will be guarded by frowning mountains or by an old stone castle. Sometimes one seems to have just sprung up beside a quiet river.

But perhaps the greatest source of wealth is the vineyards. From as far north as Paris 

VINEYARDS 

these vineyards stretch south throughout the country. They extend up the valleys of the Rhone, the Seine, and the Garonne rivers and along many of their branches. Every village has its vineyards and produces its share of wine and raisins made from the grapes. The drinking water in France is poor and much of it unhealthful. Light wines are used by all the people. France also ships to many other countries famous brands of wine which bring large prices, and wine is one of her chief exports. 

Bordeaux is the chief wine seaport.

FISHING 

Another French export is fish caught by the fishermen of Brittany. These fishermen journey as far as Newfoundland for cod and haddock. The coasts of Brittany are well known for sardines and tuna-fish which are canned for export. The fish-packing industry gives work to many people, both men and women.

One of the chief industries of France is the silk industry. Silk is a thread obtained from the silkworm, which is raised in

SILK INDUSTRY 

great numbers in France. For the first part of its life, the silkworm feeds greedily on the leaves of the mulberry tree, which is grown especially to supply this food. 

On reaching full growth, the worm spins about its body a cocoon made of a long, very fine fiber. When the cocoon is completed, it is heated to kill the silkworm. The fibers of several cocoons are then unwound together to form a single strand. They are delicate, and this operation needs much skill. The strands formed in this unwinding are called raw silk. 

Several strands must be spun together to make one thread firm enough for weaving into cloth. 

Because of the time and the care that it takes to unreel the silken fibers from the cocoons, this industry can flourish only in a country where labor is cheap and the people very skilful and careful. 

The weaving of silk is a very ancient industry that started in China. The person who first had the idea of unreeling the fiber of a little silken cocoon and spinning that fiber into thread must have had a great deal of imagination and patience. The story goes that a 

Chinese empress developed this industry and invented the loom for the weaving of the cloth. 

For years the Chinese kept secret the source of this silk thread but finally some of the silkworms were smuggled out of the country, and the industry was started in other lands. 

In France the mulberry trees grow along the Rhone valley, and it is here that the silk industry of the country centers. Lyon is the chief city for the making of silk, but St. 

Etienne and Paris are also silk centers. The silk-manufacturing industry of France is so great that the country must import additional raw silk from the Far East.

OTHER France has other textile industries, which center about the city of Lille in industrial northern France. Here labor is plentiful and transportation good. TEXTILES 

The province of Lorraine is the center for the cotton industry. All the raw material for this industry must be imported, and France buys a great deal of cotton from the United States. The sheep raised here and there about France supply some of the raw material for woolen factories, although wool must be imported from Argentina and Aus tralia. The flax from agricultural France goes

EUROPE 

to the linen factories, but European Russia is called upon to furnish still more. The imported cotton, wool, and flax enter the country at Cherbourg or Havre, and are sent by river and canal to the factory towns. 

France does not supply the world with so large a quantity of textiles as Great Britain does, but she is very famous indeed for the quality of those that she does supply. Her fine cotton and silk fabrics share the lead among her exports. Some French towns specialize solely in ribbons, others in velvets, and still others in shawls and tapestries. We have already mentioned the beautiful and fine lace made by the women of the little country villages. It is beautiful and fine simply because they take so much pride and pains in their work. This is a characteristic of the French. 

What they make they wish to make perfectly, and they will toil over a piece of work until it is beautiful, sparing neither their eyes, nor their hands, nor their patience.

Because of the artistic sense of the French people, Paris has become the fashion center of the world. The dresses made by the French are sold to the United States and other countries, and copied for sale in these foreign lands. 

Southeast of Lyon is Grenoble, as famous for its dainty gloves as is Paris for its gowns. 

ARTISTIC PRODUCTS 

Near the Riviera the city of Grasse distills expensive perfumes from the fields of flowers which surround it. Paris and many other cities make jewelry of unique designs from the silver and gold of the colonies and gems from Antwerp and Amsterdam. One especially famous art ware is French pottery, which has special qualities of delicacy and beauty. The lovely 

Haviland china is made in the city of Limoges. 

Sevres produces fine shell-like porcelain.

COAL AND IRON 

The real backbone of French industry, however, is the supply of iron and coal. Near 

Lyon, between the Saone and the Loire rivers, is a fine coal and iron district whose chief cities are St. 

Etienne and Le Creusot. St. Etienne uses part of its coal in the manufacture of silks, and both towns have tremendous iron works which produce locomotives, firearms, structural steel for making buildings, and every sort of iron ware. This district was rushed with work during the World War, when the northern coal and iron mines were held by the Germans. 

These northern mines, near the Belgian border, were returned after the war, at the same time as the provinces of Alsace and Lorraine, which had been taken from France by Germany in 1870. Both have coal and iron deposits, and Alsace also produces potash, salt, and petroleum. To make up for the damage done to her coal mines during the war, France was also given temporary control of the coal mines in the Saar basin of Germany, just north of Lorraine. The coal and iron supply makes northern France the most important industrial district and the most densely populated region of the country.

METAL PRODUCTS 

France puts her artistic sense and her pride in turning out something fine and beautiful into her metal industries as well as into her textile industries.

Among her iron and steel products are delicate steel tools, clocks, watches, firearms, locks, and any number of other things that require patience and skill to make. There are also factories which make large machinery, locomotives, and automobiles, but France also imports many of these from the United States and Great Britain.

COMMERCE, SEAPORTS AND TRANSPORTATION 

These varied products bring France a large foreign trade. It is not so large as the foreign trade of the United Kingdom, for the French have less need than the British for food from other countries. French trade also needs fewer ships in proportion to its value, because the products which France exports are not so bulky as those shipped from most of the British ports. 

Transportation between the different sections of France is especially good. Most of the important cities are located on the four large rivers which flow through the country. On the Rhone river is Lyon. On the Seine is 

Paris, with Havre, the port of Paris, at the river's mouth. On the Loire are Orleans and 

Tours. On the Garonne are Toulouse and Bordeaux.

SEAPORTS OF FRANCE 

​(1) French Line. (2) (3) French Government Tourist Information Bureau. 

1. The port of Havre. This harbor has fourteen ship basins, or enclosed docking spaces like those in the picture. Its eight miles of docks are never idle. The city lies near the mouth of the Seine, and river boats from Paris meet liners from England and America at its docks. 

Its harbor is the busiest on the Atlantic coast of France. 

Because many Paris-made goods are shipped from Havre, the city is often called "The port of Paris." 

2. Bordeaux, on the Garonne river. Bordeaux is sixty miles from the river's mouth, but in spite of its distance from the ocean it is one of the chief seaports of France. 

Although Bordeaux is a shipbuilding and manufacturing city, it is chiefly known as a great wine market. More wine has been exported through Bordeaux than has been shipped through any other seaport in the world. 

3. A French fishing port. The boats anchored in the bay are part of a fleet of 800 that sail from this port to fish off the coast. From June to December, between three and four thousand people are kept busy catching or preserving sardines. During the winter months, old fishing boats are repaired and new ones built. Notice how small the boats are. They would not do for deep-sea fishing on the broad Atlantic.

FRENCH CITIES AND INDUSTRIES

1. Paris seen from an airplane. This view shows the 

Isle of the City, one of the oldest parts of Paris. Notice how the Seine river cuts the city into sections. On the island, the church facing the open square is the famous Notre Dame cathedral. Paris is one of the world's most beautiful cities. Thousands of Americans visit its museums, public buildings, and shops every year. 

2. Weaving silk at Lyon. The machines in this factory make cloth from silk thread. Lyon, on the Rhone, is the chief center of the French silk industry. Silkworms are raised in the Rhone valley. Some of the raw silk used in the factories at Lyon is produced near the city, and the rest is imported.

Marseille is the busiest port in France.

Europe, and many of its products are sold in American stores.

FRANCE AND HER DEPENDENCIES 

39 With these rivers connected by a fine system of canals and with many railroads and highways, all parts of the country are in touch with one another. France is also closely joined with her neighboring countries. By means of the Rhone-Rhine canal, Marseille, the important Mediterranean port of France, is connected by water with Germany, Holland, and Belgium. Across the south a canal joins the 

Mediterranean with the Atlantic ports. Many goods going from one country to another cross France by water. Products sent from Italy to England often go across France instead of through the Strait of Gibraltar. France, therefore, has a fine position in the path of business and trade. Besides her railroad, river, canal, and highway system, France has developed a fine airplane service between Paris and other important cities of Europe.

The harbors of France are not so deep nor so large as those of the British Isles. But as 

France does not have the large merchant marine and navy that Great Britain has, her harbors are quite sufficient for her needs. 

The chief seaport of France is Marseille, on the Mediterranean. Marseille owes its importance to France's trade with her great colonies in north and east Africa, and to her trade with the Far East and Australia. All this trade centers in Marseille. The city is located near the mouth of the Rhone river and is connected with the river by a barge canal. The Rhone valley is the direct route to northern France and Germany. From Marseille go a variety of manufactured goods to Asia and Africa.

Among its imports are raw silk, tea, wool, and wheat. Copra, palm nuts, peanuts, flax seed and other oily seeds are received in huge quantities. Marseille presses out their oil to make soaps and cooking fats. 

From the port of Bordeaux, wines, silks, cottons, machinery, and toys go to South America and Mexico, and coal to Africa. Bordeaux is the chief port for exporting wines. Through this port wool, hides, sugar, coffee, copper, and nitrate enter from South America and Mexico. 

From West Africa come gums, ivory, and rubber.

Havre, connected with Paris by the Seine river, is the chief port for products from the United States. Here we send our cotton, petroleum, copper, and machinery, and from Havre we receive clothing and lingerie, silks, furs, leather goods, and fine cotton fabrics. This same port sends silks, butter, eggs, and cattle to England, and imports from that country textiles, machinery, coal, and tin. Cherbourg is an American passenger port.

PARIS 

Paris, the beautiful capital of France, is one of the world's largest cities, with a population of more than 2,800,000. Paris started more than 1400 years ago as a little settlement on an island in the Seine. As years passed it spread to both banks of the river and reached out for miles on all sides. Today it is a city of old, narrow, winding streets, of broad boulevards, of lovely parks, of great churches and cathedrals, of little outdoor restaurants, of marvelous shops and hotels, of old palaces, and of great museums. The Louvre, once a palace, is now one of the world's most famous art museums. In the halls and galleries of this beautiful palace are examples of the finest painting and sculpture of the world, as well as marvelous tapestries, fine porcelains, and rare jewels. On the south side of the Seine is an interesting part of Paris called the Latin Quarter. Here are many of the city's fine colleges and universities. And here live the thousands of students from different countries who have come to Paris to study.

Lying in the lowland plains of France and on the river Seine, Paris is easily reached and has become the natural center for roads, railroads, and river traffic. Here many railroads meet, bringing travelers and trade from every land. Paris is also a center of airplane travel.

Much of the raw material brought to Paris is used in the city's manufacturing, for Paris is the greatest manufacturing center of the country. The varied list of her products includes automobiles, machinery, tools, cutlery, glass, rubber goods, furniture, leather goods, and jewelry. As Paris sets the styles for women's clothes, gowns, coats, and hats are made here in enormous quantities.

EUROPE FOREIGN POSSESSIONS 

extent and value of her colonies. These colonies serve a double purpose; they are sources of valuable raw material and also markets for the products of the mother country. Then, too, when the mother country becomes overcrowded, her people can settle in the colonies. 

France owns French Guiana in South America, which she uses as a prison colony. In 

North America she owns the two small islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon, off the southern coast of Newfoundland. These serve as bases for French fishing fleets. A number of small islands of the West Indies belong to France and raise some sugar and cacao.

In Asia, France owns the southeastern country of French Indo-China, where rice, cotton, sugar, coffee, tea, coconuts and some rubber are raised. Other Asiatic possessions are five towns in India which serve as trading centers. 

The large island of Madagascar, off the east coast of Africa, is French property. Here darkskinned natives raise rice and cattle. And here colonists from Europe are developing plantations of cacao, coffee, and sugar cane. Vanilla beans, which yield the much used vanilla flavoring, come from Madagascar. 

The mountainous Mediterranean island of

Corsica and many small islands in the south 

Pacific belong to France. The Pacific islands serve as coaling and repair stations. Along the coasts of Corsica olives and other fruits are grown.

Besides all these widespread possessions, France owns the countries of Algeria, Tunisia, and most of Morocco in northern Africa, as well as French Equatorial Africa and other countries of west and east Africa. Find these

French possessions on the map on page 132. 

The northern countries of Africa, through which stretch the Atlas mountains, have a 

Mediterranean climate with winter rains and hot, dry summers. The native people are mostly Arabs and Berbers and are white. They are very skilful in making leather articles by hand and in weaving rugs. The climate is attractive to the French, and many people from the mother country have found pleasant homes in these countries. France has spent vast sums here to establish schools, irrigate dry lands, and teach the natives better farming methods. She has built telegraph and telephone lines, and has connected all parts of the 

Mediterranean region with the seaports, by means of roads and railroads.

Both the natives and the European colonists farm the fertile lowlands along the coast and in the valleys of the Atlas mountains. They raise much wheat and barley, and grapes, olives, and other fruits. The cork oak, from whose bark cork is made, grows in this region. Besides the weaving of rugs, the making of wine and corks are growing industries of the north African colonies.

Being rich in iron ore, zinc, and lead, Algeria and Tunisia export all three. As France has iron of her own and to spare, the African ore is sent to Great Britain. The other metals go to France.

The fact that trade can so quickly and easily be carried on between the mother country and her north African colonies makes these colonies of great value to France. They provide a market for her own goods and supply her with foodstuffs, olive oil, phosphate, and cork. 

The chief cities of the north African colonies are Algiers, the capital of Algeria, and Tunis, the capital of Tunisia. Both are on the coast and are important seaports. Fez is the capital of French Morocco.

Parts of French West Africa and French 

Equatorial Africa lie in the sandy wastes of the great Sahara desert where desert conditions and the immense cost of development have hindered progress. But parts also lie in the grasslands of the Sudan, that region of 

Africa to the south of the desert. Here the natives are negroes. Those in the northern part of the Sudan raise flocks of goats, sheep, and cattle. Farther south the natives live in little villages of mud huts and do some simple farming. A leading crop is peanuts, from which the oil is extracted at Marseille. Still farther south are rain-forest lands which export palm oil and palm nuts, cacao, and ivory. 

Except for the Mediterranean countries of

Africa, the large French colonies are hot countries, not suited for settlement by white men.

FRANCE AND HER DEPENDENCIES 

43 The French are developing them to supply raw materials and foods for the home country. 

They are educating the natives so that they may produce more materials for the French to buy and so may earn more wealth with which to buy manufactured goods from France. 

1. France lies between the Atlantic ocean and the 

Mediterranean sea, with Spain to the southwest and 

Belgium, Germany, Switzerland, and Italy to the north and east. 

2. The surface of France is divided into lowland plain in the west, plateau in the south central part, and highlands in the south and east. 

3. The Mediterranean region of France has mild, moderately rainy winters and hot summers with little rain. The rest of France has a moderate climate. 

The prevailing westerly winds bring warmth and moisture to the country. 

4. France is more an agricultural country than the 

British Isles. It has more farm lands, and a warmer climate than the Isles. There are about 

40,000,000 people in France, over half of whom live in small farming communities. In the north of 

France grow the hardy vegetables and grains. 

Brittany engages in dairying, market gardening, and sheep raising. The French vineyards extend along most of the river valleys, and wine is an export. Along the Mediterranean grow tropical fruits and nuts. Mulberry trees flourish along the 

Rhone valley and furnish food for silkworms. 

5. Among the industries of France, the weaving of silk is very important. Lyon is the silk center. 

Linen, cotton, and woolen factories are located in northern France. Much of the raw material must be imported. Fine workmanship is a characteristic of French products. 

6. Coal and iron are found in northern, northeastern, and east central France. Northern France is the chief industrial section. After the World War, Alsace and Lorraine, which have coal and iron deposits, were returned to France. France was also given temporary use of the coal mines in the Saar basin. France has another industrial section around 

St. Etienne where there are coal and iron deposits. 

7. Besides iron and steel machinery, the French make smaller metal products which require much skill. 

8. There are many railroads in France, and four large river systems well connected by canals. Marseille is the chief seaport of France. Other important ports are Bordeaux, Havre, and Cherbourg. 

9. Paris is one of the world's largest cities. It is the capital and chief trade center of France. 

10. France owns much land in Africa, the island of 

Madagascar, and a number of other possessions. 

The African possessions are important because they supply France with the raw materials which she needs, and provide a market for her manufactured goods.

1. The river Elbe at Hamburg. These are the wharves of a famous steamship company that carries freight and passengers between Germany and the United States. Very likely some of these vessels are loading with steel wares and potash for New York, and others are unloading 

American copper and meats for German use. Compare the Hamburg water front with that of Rotterdam, shown opposite page 26. Both cities are river ports. 

2. The Tempelhof airport at Berlin. This airport is a center of airplane transportation lines. From here passenger planes fly in every direction. Europeans travel in airplanes more than Americans do. 

3. A railroad bridge in the Black Forest, in southern 

Germany. Germany is a "through passage land" for railway travel. Fast express trains run from her principal cities to almost every country of Europe. Notice the thick growth of the forest beyond the railroad. The Germans have not allowed their forests to be cut down without replacing the cut timber with new trees. 

4. A canal in Hamburg. In all the northern lowlands of

Europe, canals are an important means of carrying goods. 

This narrow canal brings goods from the Elbe wharves to the back doors of the houses. Larger canals connect 

Hamburg with many other cities of the northern lowlands.

GERMANY'S MOST FAMOUS RIVER 

(1) (2) German Tourist Information Office. 

1. The Rhine from one of its high banks. 

The great rock is the Rock of the Lorelei. There, according to legend, lived a beautiful maiden whose singing lured fishermen to their deaths. In the stream we can see a passenger steamer and two freight barges. The freighters are long and wide. They remind us of the freighters on our Great lakes. There is also a tug boat pulling some small barges. The Rhine is connected by canals and other rivers with most of northern and central Europe, and with a great river of southern Europe, the Danube. 

Freight may be carried by boat from the Rhine river ports to almost any part of the continent. Notice the automobile road which follows the river bank. 

2. Castles on the Rhine. The castle on the right was built in olden times. Its owner was a robber baron, a nobleman who forced travelers on the river to pay him for the privilege of passing. Another such castle is across the river, and there are many others along the steep river banks between Bingen and Bonn. They add much to the beauty of this most beautiful part of the river. On the hillside we see terraced vineyards. Here grow grapes for which the Rhine valley is famous. On the river and along its banks we see indications that the valley is an important route of travel. There are river boats steaming busily along, a railroad on the nearer bank, and a broad highway on each side of the river.

LOWLAND AND PLATEAU COUNTRIES OF WESTERN EUROPE GERMANY 

The country of Germany has many near neighbors. There is Denmark on the north; the Netherlands, Belgium, and France on the west; Switzerland and Austria on the south; and Czechoslovakia and Poland on the east.

As East Prussia is part of Germany, its eastern neighbor, Lithuania, must be added to the list.

Germany is also bordered by the North and 

Baltic seas.

SIZE, GOVERNMENT, AND POPULATION 

Before the World War Germany was a powerful nation with foreign possessions, mostly in Africa, and with much more land in Europe than she has today. By the treaty which closed the war, she lost her foreign possessions and gave up parts of her home land to each of several neighbors. To France she gave the provinces of Alsace and Lorraine, and to Poland valuable lands in the eastern part of the country. And since the war Germany has become a republic.

The Germany of today is not much larger than our one state of California, yet its population is more than half that of the whole United States.

There are three natural regions in Germany.

The northern part of the country is a lowland plain. The southern part

AND CLIMATE is an upland plateau. The NATURAL REGIONS 

third region is the valley of the Rhine.

The westerly winds sweep across the northern plain, making the temperature mild. All of Germany has plenty of rain because there are no north-south mountain ranges to shut out the moisture-bearing winds. 

The northwestern part of Germany near the

North sea coast has much fog during the winter months, just as England has. As the ocean winds lose their moisture passing from the west to the east, so they lose some of their warmth, and eastern Germany is colder than western Germany. 

Usually, difference of latitude makes a difference of warmth, and you would expect to find the southern part of 

Germany warmer than the northern part. This is not the case. The climates of northern and southern Germany are about alike because the altitude of the plateau in the south offsets the difference in degrees of latitude between the two regions. In Mexico, you remember, the southern part of the plateau was cooler than the northern part because it was much higher. 

There are warmer spots in southern Germany, but they are in the valleys of the rivers which This map shows the distribution of annual rainfall in Europe.

Because it lies in the path of European travel from east to west and from north to south, Germany has been called the "through passage land" of Europe. Over its railroads and rivers go endless streams of people and goods from every land.

THE PLAIN IN THE NORTH 

The plain in the north of Germany is part of Europe's great lowland region which starts in the British Isles and broadens as it goes east, reaching its greatest width in Russia. 

The plain is not quite so flat in Germany as it is in the Netherlands. Some of it is beautiful rolling country. Here the surface and the soil are the result of a glacier which in past ages came down from the north and covered the region. When at last the ice melted away, it left uneven places in the surface of the land, dammed up streams, and formed lakes and swamps. The soil left by the glacier is sandy. 

Agriculture. This sandy glacial soil is rather poor, but with the use of potash and other fertilizers and the right methods of farming it is made to produce good crops. You remember that this is true of the soil of the 

Atlantic Coastal plain in our own country. To feed their people the Germans have to produce as much food as they possibly can on their limited amount of land. For this reason they have carefully studied methods of farming and have established experiment stations all through the farming region. Their study and hard work have resulted in large crops from what seemed unpromising soil. 

Agriculture is the chief occupation of the lowland plain of Germany. Farms are small and well kept and all the land is used. Women and men work together in the fields. Even the dogs help pull plows and draw small carts filled with farm produce. As in France, the farmers live in villages and go back and forth to their work each day. 

Potatoes are the principal crop. Germany raises about fifteen times as many bushels of potatoes as the Irish Free State and over three times as many as the United States. Although potatoes are skilfully and scientifically grown in our country, Germany gets about 20 per cent more potatoes from an acre than we do.

The potatoes are used for food and for making starch and alcohol.

Oats, rye, and other hardy grains are extensively grown. Rye bread is a favorite food of the Germans. Corn is not grown to any great extent because it needs a hotter climate than 

Germany can provide. 

Hay and mangels, or fodder beets, are grown for feeding animals. The dry hay and the juicy mangels combine to make a very good diet for cattle and horses.

Sugar beets are a very valuable crop. It was a German scientist who discovered that sugar can be made from the sugar beet. Before that time, sugar came wholly from sugar cane.

Careful selection and breeding have produced beets that give surprising amounts of sugar, and more beet sugar is made in Germany than in any other country. After the extraction of the juice, in which the sugar is found, the pulp that is left is used to feed hogs and cattle. 

Stock Raising. Cattle, hogs, and horses are raised in the pastures of the lowland plain. 

Some sheep are also raised. The cattle are of both the beef and the dairy varieties. Hogs are fattened on corn in our country, but in Germany they are fattened on the waste of

47 the sugar beet and on acorns and other forest nuts. The wool from the sheep is manufactured into woolen cloth. The horses are of high grade and are in demand in the markets of Europe.
