Cities. There are not many cities in the lowland region of Germany, but those which do exist are very important. The most important are Berlin, Hamburg, Bremen, and Stettin.

Berlin, the capital of the German republic, is the third largest city in the world. It is not only the center of government but of commerce and manufacturing as well. Located in the center of the lowland region, Berlin has a fortunate position for trade. The Spree river, which flows through the city, is connected by canals with both the upper Elbe and the Oder. 

Over these rivers vessels reach Berlin, filled with goods to be distributed in the region round about or to be shipped to other countries. Both the Elbe and the Oder, as well as other important navigable rivers of Europe have been internationalized, or opened to the trade of all nations. 

Navigable waterways, railroads, and highways lead from Berlin in every direction, and the city is a center for many of the airplane lines which regularly carry passengers and mail from one European country to another. 

Part of Berlin is very old, but much of it has been built since it became the capital of the German empire in 1871. The newer part has grown very rapidly and has none of the interesting atmosphere of the older, quainter cities of Germany. It is more like a modern, progressive city of the New World. Its wide boulevards and stately public buildings are much like those of Washington. One of the famous streets of Berlin is Unter den Linden (Under the Linden Trees), a mile long and very wide, with stately rows of trees on each side. It stretches from the imposing Brandenburg Gate to the former imperial palace and other fine public buildings. In the heart of the busy city is a great wooded park, called the 

Thiergarten (Zoo). A remarkable collection of animals is in this park. Berlin is a center of culture, with its National Art Gallery, its famous Royal Opera House, its theatres, its Academy of Science, and its noted universities. 

Berlin is important as a manufacturing city because it is in easy reach of raw materials and coal for its factories. It manufactures jewelry and watches; silk, cotton, and wool goods; machinery; chemicals; glassware; paper; shoes and clothing.

Hamburg, Bremen, and Stettin are all important river ports, railroad centers, and manufacturing towns. Each has a harbor suitable for large steamers but so far inland as to be safe from ocean storms. Each is a shipbuilding center and manufactures machinery and textiles. 

Hamburg is the chief of Germany's commercial ports, and only New York and London

EUROPE 

have more trade. It is on the wide and navigable Elbe river, and its miles of riverfront harbor are filled with ships from many parts of the world and river boats from the interior of the country. Through busy Hamburg goes much of the produce of the interior, as the city is connected with the industrial towns of 

Germany not only by water but also by rail. 

Bremen is on the Weser river. Both the 

Elbe and the Weser flow into the North sea, which is never frozen over. Hamburg and 

Bremen have an advantage over Stettin, on the Oder. The Oder flows into the Baltic sea, and so Stettin is not in as close touch with the outside markets of the world. This fact alone accounts for Stettin being a smaller and somewhat less important port. On the other hand,

Stettin lies nearer Berlin and the great industrial district of eastern Germany and western Poland.

The Kiel Canal. Years ago ships from the 

Baltic seaports had to sail the length of Denmark's eastern coast to reach the North sea.

But now the Kiel canal cuts through German land to the south of Denmark and joins these two seas, shortening the journey by many miles. The canal is internationalized and is wide and deep enough for ocean steamers. 

East Prussia. The part of Germany known as 

East Prussia lies in the lowland plain. East

Prussia is cut off from the rest of Germany by a part of Poland and the Free City of Danzig, which Germany lost in the World War. Agriculture and the raising of sheep and cattle are the principal occupations. The chief city is Königsberg.

The plateau in the south of Germany is part of Europe's Central uplands region. The surface of the plateau is varied, THE PLATEAU having some old, worn-down mountains and some broad val- 

IN THE SOUTH 

leys cut by rivers. 

Forests. The German names for many of their mountains include the word wald which means forest. This is because the mountains are covered with trees-evergreens, pines, oaks, and beeches. Forests cover one-quarter of the surface of Germany. Among the best known is the Black Forest in the southwestern part of the country.

The Germans give their forests as intelligent care as they do their fields. Foresters appointed by the government see that the forests are protected from harm. A certain amount of lumber is cut from the forests each year, and enough young trees are planted so that the new growth always equals the amount cut. The trees that are cut are used for lumber and the making of paper. Paper and wood pulp are important exports. The forest underbrush is cleared out from under the trees to lessen the danger from fires. This underbrush the thrifty 

Germans use for fuel. They use small trees, cut to thin the forests, and limbs trimmed from larger trees as poles on which to raise beans and hops. The hops are used in making beer, the popular drink of Germany.

Wood Carving. The Germans carve many beautiful things out of wood. In the winter months, when there is no work in the fields, whole families spend their time indoors carving furniture and making toys out of wood. The quaint old city of Nuremberg is a center for the toy industry. Here, too, are made watches and jewelry and gold and silver ornaments. 

Valleys. Where the rivers have cut their way through the plateau, there are fertile valleys filled with small, well-kept farms, which are worked with every care. Wheat, barley, rye, hops, tobacco, and grapes are grown. The valley of the upper part of the Elbe is a rich growing section. So is the valley of the 

Danube river. This river rises in the Alps mountains and flows through the southern part of Germany on its way east to the Black sea.

In its fertile valley, cattle raising is an important industry. The Rhine river and its tributaries run through valleys famous for their vineyards and wines.

The Rhine river is perhaps the most important river in Europe. It is known to the traveler for the beauty of its 

AND VALLEY 

scenery and for the fasci- THE RHINE RIVER 

nating stories that have grown up about the castles along its shores. 

To the commercial world of Europe, the Rhine has been known from early times as one of the chief waterways for commerce and trade.

EUROPE 

The river rises in the glaciers of the Alps mountains in Switzerland, flows into the Lake of Constance, then west along the border between Switzerland and Germany to the city of Basel. Here it turns north between Germany and France. At Karlsruhe it becomes wholly German. From Basel to Mainz, the river's valley is twenty miles wide, with the steep, forested slopes of the Black Forest on the east and those of the Vosges mountains on the west. A valley of this kind, lying between steep walls some distance apart, is called a rift valley. This rift valley of the Rhine is known as "The Garden of the Rhine" because it has such fertile land, and because nearly every crop of a temperate climate will grow in it. Here are fields of cereals, hops, tobacco, and fruits. On the sunny, terraced slopes of the hills are rows and rows of vineyards. The towns are not built close along the river but are a few miles back.

At Mainz, the river broadens as it winds westward around the Taunus mountains. At 

Bingen, it turns north and follows a narrow valley through the lower Rhine highlands to Bonn. In this narrow valley the hills rise close on either side and there is hardly room for the railroads and highways that follow along the river banks. This is the most beautiful and picturesque part of the river. In its narrow course it winds in and out through the gorge. Steep hillsides covered with terraced vineyards rise on either side. There are old castles perched high up on the hilltops, some still lived in, some in ruins. These were built as strongholds by the barons of the Middle Ages. Each has romantic tales woven about it. Here, one may see a little town spread lengthwise in the narrow valley between the river and the hills. There, one may see jagged rocks of curious shapes that add to the picturesqueness of the scenery. 

Quite in contrast to this beautiful part of the river is its course from Bonn to the North sea, which it reaches through the Netherlands. 

After leaving Bonn, the river grows broader, the banks are flat, and the steep hillsides are replaced by the lowland plains. Along the banks are many cities and towns busy with factories.

The Rhine river is navigable from its mouth to Basel, in Switzerland, and is open to the trade of all nations in times of peace. The river's whole length is 700 miles, and, though neither its source nor its mouth is in Germany, 450 of its 550 navigable miles are in or beside 

German land.

The most important tributaries of the Rhine are the Moselle, the Main, and the Neckar. 

The Moselle, on the west, flows from France, and the Main and the Neckar, on the east, flow from southern Germany.

Along the valley of the Rhine are railroads and highways, and many bridges connect the banks. All this makes the Rhine and its valley a very important trade route. But what makes the route even more important is the fact that it is connected with other trade routes, reaching far and wide.

Between the Vosges mountains, which border the Rhine on the west, and the Jura mountains, which lie south of the Vosges, there is an opening called the Burgundy Gate. Here the Rhine-Rhone canal connects the Rhine valley with the valley of the Rhone and opens a way to the Mediterranean port of Marseille. 

North of the Burgundy Gate there is no break in the mountains until near the French city of Strassburg, on the Rhine. From Strassburg a railroad passes through a gap in the mountains and leads to Paris by way of the cities of Nancy and Metz. Through this same gap a canal has been cut which connects the Rhine with the Marne river, a tributary of the Seine, thus giving a water route to Paris. 

On the east the Main river is connected by canal with the Danube, which flows into the 

Black sea. This makes a pathway between the

Rhine valley and the Turkish city of Istanbul and the countries of southwestern Asia.

Because of all these connections the products not only of Germany but of countries farther inland may be shipped through the valley of the Rhine. The commerce which passes over the Rhine is now somewhat greater than that which passes over our greatest river, the Mississippi.

1. Cologne's cathedral. Cologne is an ancient city on the Rhine river. Its beautiful cathedral is very old. It was not completed until six hundred years after it was begun. Europe has many other celebrated cathedrals. 

2. Berlin's Unter den Linden. Many Americans are well acquainted with this wide boulevard. The name means "Under the Lindens," and was given the street because of the rows of linden trees which shade its roadways and its central walk. Berlin is the capital of Germany and the third largest city in the world. 

3. A scene in the steel mills of Essen. Essen is in the 

Ruhr basin, the center of the steel and iron industry of Germany. Like the Pittsburgh district in our country, the 

Ruhr has rich coal mines and can get plenty of iron ore for its blast furnaces from nearby. In this picture we see a machine called a steam hammer forging a shaft, or beating it into shape. The huge shaft is very hot. It is hung from chains which turn it slowly over and over. 

As it turns, the steam hammer strikes terrific blows which pound the hot metal into the desired form.

1. Heidelberg, on the Neckar river. The buildings on the hillside are part of Heidelberg University, one of the oldest and most famous of the many universities of Germany. Some of its buildings were erected more than five centuries ago, before America was discovered. 

Neckar river is a tributary of the Rhine, and river steamers carry many tourists to this old German town. The 2. Old buildings in a German town. The houses and the tower are just as they were built hundreds of years ago. 

The tower bridges the street. In olden times, when governments were not strong and there was more disorder than at present, the tower contained a gate which could be shut to keep robber bands out of the city. We see another tower at the foot of the hill. The house facing us is made with walls of timber and plaster in a style that is common in German buildings of past times.

The people of the city come to the market to buy their supplies. Markets like this are found in most of the cities of Europe. Market day is an important day in Germany.

TRADE ROUTES OF GERMANY 

many, you remember, has the Elbe and Weser rivers which carry goods to the North sea through the ports of Hamburg and Bremen, and the Oder which leads to the Baltic through the port of Stettin. The Danube is connected by canal with the Elbe as well as with the Main.

In addition, fast express trains from Paris cross Germany to Berlin and rush on to Leningrad and other cities in Russia, or pass through Germany on their way to Istanbul and other cities of southern Europe. Germany's lowland plain makes an easy route for railroads. 

Its central position, its waterways, its railroads, its airways, and its ocean ports, explain why Germany has become so important a country in trade and commerce. Her most important imports are raw materials for her factories and foodstuffs for her people. 

SOME CITIES ON ROUTES OF TRADE 

Many cities have grown up where the routes of trade cross each other. Berlin has grown rapidly because of trade routes which pass through it north, east, south, and west. Coblenz is located where the Moselle river joins the Rhine, and Mainz where the Main flows into the Rhine. Mannheim is at the meeting place of the Rhine and the Neckar. 

Just as many important cities have grown up along the Mississippi and its tributaries, so have many developed along the tributaries and the main stream of the Rhine.

MINERALS 

With her natural resources and the ease with which she can get raw materials and ship away her products, it is not surprising that Germany should be one of the world's greatest manufacturing countries. Among the richest of Germany's resources are her mineral deposits-coal, iron, copper, potash, zinc, and lead. These are found in many parts of the country, especially along the lower Rhine, in the Harz and Thuringerwald mountains of central Germany, and in the district of Silesia to the east. 

Before the World War Germany's mineral deposits were much greater than they are today, and the country held the lead among European countries in the manufacture of iron and steel products. At the close of the war most of the rich Silesian coal fields went to 

Poland. Alsace and Lorraine, rich in iron, went to France. The coal mines of the Saar basin were given to France for fifteen years, but were returned to Germany in 1935. Today, the most important German coal fields are the very rich mines in the basin of the Ruhr river, a tributary of the Rhine. Some iron is mined in the Ruhr region and in eastern and central Germany, but not nearly enough to supply the country's many factories. The loss of the Lorraine iron mines was a great blow to Germany. 

France needs the coal from the Ruhr basin for smelting her iron and Germany needs the iron of Lorraine for her manufactures. An arrangement for interchange has been made, to the benefit of both countries.

The largest supply of copper found in Europe is in the region of the Harz mountains of Germany. Potash is found here, too, and there are large quantities of it all through the plateau country, east of the Rhine. Even with the loss of the large fields of potash, salt, and petroleum in Alsace, Germany still has immense resources of potash. Potash is used in the making of fertilizers, glass, soap, pottery, gunpowder, and in dyeing and bleaching.

Germany owes much of her high position in the industrial world to her resources and trade routes, but

MANUFACTURES 

she owes no less to the industry and skill of her people. The Germans are intelligent, hardworking, and determined, and are celebrated the world over for doing very thoroughly whatever they do at all. Their scientists are continually experimenting to develop new products and better ways of making old, and have given Germany a great deal of special knowledge that has helped make her a great nation. The Ruhr basin and Silesia not only have extensive iron and steel manufactures, but they also make special kinds of steel that are used for special purposes. The hardware and machinery from these districts are in demand in other countries. The textiles of the 

Rhine valley, central Germany, and Silesia are not so artistic as those of the French but are of great durability and are very well made.

EUROPE 

Fine pottery and china are made from clay found in the uplands section. 

Perhaps the greatest triumphs of German skill are found in her chemical industry. We have seen that German chemists taught the country to obtain sugar from beets. They have gone still farther, and have enabled the country to produce beautiful dyes and valuable medicines from coal wastes. The great potash deposits gave Germany a start in the chemical industry, but its growth in the dye industry came from the discovery, in 1868, that the coal tar left over from purifying coal gas could be made into coloring substances not only as good but actually better than the vegetable dyes then used for cloth. British chemists made the same discovery at about the same time, but the Germans developed it so much faster that in ten years Germany had almost full command of the dye industry of the world. 

She lost it only at the time of the World War, when the United States and other countries were forced to make their own dyes because they could import none from Germany.

MANUFACTURING CITIES 

Manufacturing cities have grown up in many parts of Germany. The busiest manufacturing section is in the Rhine valley north of Cologne, where the Ruhr basin supplies iron and coal. Essen, the manufacturing center of the Ruhr basin, makes locomotives and machinery. Cologne is the chief commercial city on the Rhine. It manufactures perfumes and refines sugar. It is noted, too, for its wonderful cathedral. China is manufactured near the city of Dresden. Leipzig and Munich are centers of the book trade of Germany. Their great publishing houses have made a fine art of printing and binding books. Munich makes beer, scientific instruments, watches, and jewelry. Breslau turns out cotton, woolen, and linen goods. Chemnitz makes iron, steel, and textiles. Jena manufactures field glasses, opera glasses, and miscroscopes. Frankfort, Mannheim, Elberfeld, and Barmen are centers of the chemical industry. 

Most German cities have stately, handsome public buildings. Some of the cities are very old and quaint, with narrow, winding streets and many things of historic interest. The Germans are fond of statuary, especially of wartime subjects, and there are many beautiful works by noted sculptors in the city squares. 

The Germans are a well-educated people. 

They have twenty-one universities, the best known being at Berlin, GERMAN EDUCATION Heidelberg, Leipzig, AND CULTURE 

Bonn, and Munich. They have many trade schools where their people are trained to do well the work of the farms and factories. The German child is taught from his earliest days to appreciate art. In the fine art galleries of Berlin and Dresden and Munich you will see the rich and the poor, the young and the old, all enjoying the great pictures and paintings. The Germans are also taught to love and appreciate good music. No occasion is complete to the German without good music.

One especially well known school of music is the Conservatory at Leipzig.

The problem of the German people is to regain the position they lost by the World War. They are a thrifty, hardworking, industrious people and by making every effort they are again building up a nation that commands the world's respect.

1. Germany is a republic. It has a large population in proportion to its size. 

2. Germany has as near neighbors all three of the lowland countries as well as France, Switzerland, Austria, Poland, Lithuania, and Czechoslovakia. It has coast lines on the North and Baltic seas. 

3. The natural regions of Germany are a lowland plain in the north, an upland plateau in the south, and the Rhine valley. 

4. The climate of Germany is temperate. The prevailing westerly winds from the Atlantic ocean make the climate milder in the western than in the eastern part. There is plentiful rainfall. The climates of the north and the south are equalized because the lower latitude of the south is offset by its higher altitude. 

5. Agriculture is the chief industry of the lowland plain. The Germans farm scientifically. The chief

GERMANY 

53 crops are potatoes, hardy grains, and sugar beets. 

Cattle, horses, hogs, and some sheep are raised. 

6. There are some large cities on the plain in the north. The chief cities are Berlin, the capital, and the ports of Hamburg, Bremen, and Stettin. Berlin is the third largest city in the world. It is centrally located with many railroads and waterways radiating from it. It is important in commerce and manufacturing, and as a cultural center. Hamburg on the Elbe and Bremen on the Weser are important ports on navigable rivers flowing to the 

North sea. They are shipbuilding centers. Stettin on the Oder is a busy port connected with the Baltic sea.

The North and Baltic seas are connected by the Kiel canal. 

7. East Prussia is separated from the rest of Germany by the Free City of Danzig and part of Poland. 

The chief city is Königsberg. 

8. The plateau in the south is part of Europe's Central uplands region. It has a varied surface. Old worn-down mountains and broad valleys are scattered through it. Most of the mountains are covered with forests. The Germans give their forests the same scientific care they give their farms. The wood is used for lumber, paper, fuel, and the making of furniture and toys. Nuremberg is a center for toy making and manufacturing. 

9. Where the rivers have cut through the plateau, there are intensively cultivated valleys, in which grains, hops, tobacco, and grapes are grown. The valleys of the Rhine, Elbe, and Danube rivers are fertile farming sections. 

10. The Rhine river is the outstanding river of Europe because of its scenery, its history, and its industrial and commercial importance. It has three sections: (1) the fertile valley from Basel to Mainz, with steep, forested sides, called "The Garden of the Rhine" and used for the cultivation of fruits and grains; (2) a picturesque narrow valley through the lower Rhine highlands; (3) the lower part flowing through the lowlands of Germany and the Netherlands to the North sea. The river is navigable to 

Basel, and railways and highways parallel its banks. 

11. The Rhine river with its branches is very important as a trade route. With it are connected trade routes to the Rhone valley and to Paris. The valleys of the Main and Neckar are trade routes to southern Germany. 

12. Other trade routes of Germany are: (1) by way of the Danube to the Black sea and Istanbul; (2) by way of the Elbe and Weser to the North sea; (3) by way of the Oder to the Baltic sea; (4) across the plains by railroads connecting Berlin with Paris and Leningrad. 

13. Germany has a fine system of waterways, railroads, and airways which with its central position make it very important in trade and commerce. Many important cities have developed where routes of trade cross each other. 

14. Germany is rich in minerals, especially coal, iron, copper, and potash. The most important coal fields are in the Ruhr basin. Iron is now mined in the

Ruhr valley and in eastern and central Germany. 

Germany has the largest supply of copper in 

Europe, and immense resources of potash. Potash helped to found the German chemical industry. 

15. Germany manufactures iron and steel products, chemicals, dyes, textiles, china, and beet sugar. The busiest manufacturing center is in and near the

EVERYDAY LIFE IN SWITZERLAND 

1 4 

1. Swiss farmers hauling bundles of hay. Alpine slopes are so steep that in many places wagons and carts cannot be used. American farmers would not need to work so hard for such a small amount of hay. But the men of 

Switzerland are glad to do so, for in their country hay is scarce, and they need all they can get to feed their dairy animals. 

2. A mountain girl with her pet goats. Many goats are raised in Switzerland because they can find food on high mountain sides where dairy cattle might starve. They give rich milk and need less care than cattle. But where there is good pasture, dairy cows are raised. 

3. An electric train leaving the St. Gotthard tunnel. 

Railroads are very costly to build and operate in Switzerland. They must cross deep ravines, wind and twist through narrow gorges, and pass through long tunnels under mountains. The famous tunnel in the picture enters the rock at this point and comes out on the other side of the mountain, nine miles away. 

4. The workshop of a Swiss watch factory. No people in the world are more skilful than the Swiss at manufacturing fine watches, and watches are important among

Switzerland's exports. Notice that each worker uses an electric motor. The electricity comes from water power, as there is no coal in this mountain country to furnish power. 

5. Making Swiss cheese in a mountain dairy. People all over the world like Swiss cheese and cheese-making is an important Swiss industry.

SIGHTS IN THE SWISS ALPS 

1. The Matterhorn. This beautiful peak lies on the frontier between Switzerland and Italy. Its summit is nearly 

15,000 feet above the sea. For many years no man could climb its steep, slippery sides. Now, however, men often reach its top. During the summer the village at the foot of the mountain serves as headquarters for many mountain climbers. 

2. This mountain climber has reached a high crag in the 

Alps. He is looking down upon a Swiss village thousands of feet below. Every summer people come from distant parts of the world to spend their vacations climbing in the pure mountain air. These people have money to spend, and their trade is very profitable to the Swiss. 

Swiss innkeepers and shopkeepers are kept busy entertaining the visitors and furnishing them with things they need. 

3. Swiss children bringing home a supply of wood. The 

Swiss gather every twig and dead branch from their forests, for they have no coal. These children are pushing a sled over the bare ground. It takes the place of a cart, which would be used in a more level country. 

4. The Castle of Chillon on Lake Geneva. This old stronghold is one of the most famous sights of Switzerland. It was old when the Pilgrims came to America. 

Its damp dungeons below the level of the lake have held many prisoners in years gone by.

HIGH MOUNTAIN COUNTRIES 

SWITZERLAND, AUSTRIA, AND CZECHOSLOVAKIA 

The chief mountain systems of North America extend north and south on either side of the continent, and breaks in the ranges are few and far between. The lowlands lie through the center of the continent, shut in by the mountains, and, like the highlands, extend north and south. 

How different is Europe! Europe's chief mountain wall and lowland plain run east and 

EUROPE'S MOUNTAIN WALL 

west. Being open to the sea, the western lowlands are warmed by the moisture-laden westerlies, and even the eastern lowlands have rain enough for crops. Though the mountain wall extends across the continent, wide openings break it into separate parts and make possible passes for transportation routes.

The Cantabrian, the Pyrenees, the Alps, the 

Carpathian, and the Caucasus mountains form the main divisions of Europe's mountain wall. 

Find them on the map of Europe, page viii. 

The Cantabrians and Pyrenees follow the northern border of Spain. The Caucasus lie north of the boundary where southeastern Europe meets the continent of Asia. These mountains have always served as barriers to trade and invasion.

MOUNTAIN COUNTRIES 

The ranges of the Alps and the Carpathians stretch through the high mountain countries- 

Switzerland, Austria, and Czechoslovakia. In these countries the HIGH mountains are high, young, and rugged. There are many passes through the Alps, but most of them are so high and so snow-blocked in winter that they are not practical routes for trade.

The climates of Switzerland and Austria are influenced by altitude and by the warm winds from the west and south. The sheltered valleys are warm; the lower slopes of the mountains are cool and the heights are cold, barren, and snow-covered. Czechoslovakia has a more continental climate. All three countries have plenty of rain for crops, brought by the warm winds which blow from over the Atlantic. 

SWITZERLAND 

One trait of most mountain people is a strong love of liberty, and the Swiss are no exception. Many, many years ago the people living in one mountain valley were quite independent of those living in other mountain valleys round about. Each group managed its own affairs. But as time went on these intelligent people noted that they were surrounded by strong nations who were always anxious to gain more land. To protect themselves from their grasping neighbors the people of the mountain valleys decided to unite. This happened before the discovery of America. The people of the different valleys were separated by natural barriers. They spoke different languages and had different religions. But they united against their common foes and formed themselves into a nation with a republican form of government. 

As the years went by people of many countries, oppressed by their rulers, came to live in 

Switzerland. Frenchmen, Germans, and Italians came, and although they kept their own languages they became citizens of Switzerland. 

Even now there is no one national language in the country. French, German, and Italian are spoken in various parts of the land and all three languages are recognized as official.

SWITZERLAND 

KS Switzerland is a beautiful country of picturesque mountains, lovely lakes, and swift, tumbling streams. Mountains cover a large part of its surface. Many of the highest peaks are capped with snow the year round. The melting snow feeds many streams which help to form the Rhone, the Rhine, and other great rivers. There are a number of passes through the high mountains. Find Simplon Pass and St. Gotthard Pass. boulders, trees, houses and everything in its path are swept along. Sometimes a whole village is buried beneath an avalanche with its snow, ice, earth, and rock.

The snow fields and glaciers on the mountain tops feed many small streams and lakes. 

DRAINAGE 

As in the Adirondack mountains of our own country, the streams flow in every direction. This is called radial drainage. We see on the map on page viii four stance, and Lucerne are famous for their beauty. One of the thriving industries of the 

Swiss people is caring for the tourists that come in summer to climb the mountains and enjoy the cool climate and lovely scenery, or in winter to take part in winter sports for which the country is famous the world over. To provide for these guests, Switzerland has many inns and hotels.

The whole country of Switzerland is not

SWITZERLAND 

57 

USES OF THE LAND 

quite half the size of our one state of Maine, and yet it has over five times the number of people. With all their visitors as well as their own people to care for, the Swiss are forced to make the best possible use of all their land. The valleys and lower mountain slopes are used for intensive farming. Vineyards surround many of the 

Swiss lakes. Higher on the mountain slopes, where crops cannot well be raised, cattle and goats are pastured. Still higher are the forests; first hardwood trees, then evergreens. These forests are as carefully tended and cut as the German forests. They must supply both fuel and the lumber for the building of houses. 

Above the tree line are the jagged, bare rocks, and higher still the snow fields. These snow fields furnish one great resource of which the Swiss are making more and more usemountain streams whose power can be harnessed to furnish electricity. 

INDUSTRIES 

But even with such careful use of their lands, these thrifty people are unable to raise all the food needed to support a large population. Like the New 

Englanders, they have been forced to turn to manufacturing and commerce, so as to have products to exchange for the goods they need. 

A larger part of the people in Switzerland are engaged in manufacturing than in any other country in the world.

From the milk of their dairy cattle they make condensed milk and cheese. With milk they use cacao from tropical lands to make delicious chocolate. Many of the Swiss men are expert in making beautiful wood carvings, and all over the country, often in their own homes, the Swiss women are making by hand the soft laces and beautiful embroideries for which the country is well known. 

The Swiss, like the people of Denmark, are without iron and coal. They are also without seaports, and can reach the sea only through other countries. So the manufacture of heavy machinery or other bulky products for export is out of the question. These people have to content themselves with the manufacture of small, fine things whose value lies in the beauty of workmanship. They make fine watches and clocks, and laces and ribbons.

The country's most important exports are these watches and clocks, light machinery, artistic embroideries and textiles, and cheese. 

We buy Swiss watches and Swiss cheese, and sell automobiles in return. Raw cotton and silk are imported to supply the Swiss textile industry. With the increasing use of water power, manufacturing will continue to grow in importance. 

Switzerland has fine highways especially on the plateau, and miracles have been performed in the building of her railroads. Routes to the north 

TRANSPORTATION 

are not difficult, but in olden times southern Europe could be reached only through a few passes across the Alps. In spite of the difficulties of building railroads through a mountainous region, Switzerland has built fine ones and in several places tunnels have been cut through mountains, or under high passes. 

Two of these tunnels are very famous-the St. Gotthard, nine miles long, and the Simplon, twelve miles long, the longest in the world. 

Since Switzerland is without seaports, her roads and railroads and the Rhine river are the chief means of export and import. When the project of widening and deepening the Rhone river through France to the Swiss border has been completed, water transportation to the Mediterranean will be opened to this little republic.

Switzerland has a population of more than 4,000,000 people. The distribution is uneven, being densest in the manufacturing districts of the plateau.

Here raw materials can be transported with greater ease and here, too, the climate is warmer.

POPULATION 

Most of the important cities of Switzerland lie on the plateau. Zurich is the largest city. 

It is a railroad and manufacturing cen- CITIES 

ter, especially noted for the manufacture of silk textiles. Bern, the capital of the country, is noted more for the beauty of its surroundings than for any industry. It is one of the great centers for the visitors who flock to this mountain country. Basel is noted for its ribbon manufactures. Geneva, a quiet,

EUROPE 

beautiful city on Lake Geneva, is a manufacturing and educational center. Here are made most of the famous Swiss watches and many very delicate and accurate scientific instruments.

THE LEAGUE 

In the past, Switzerland has been able to avoid taking sides in the many wars that have again and again changed the

OF NATIONS boundaries of the countries of 

Europe. It has been possible to do this because the land is easy to defend. Moving armies into Switzerland has always been too difficult a task to tempt the military leaders of a stronger nation. At length, Switzerland came to be considered the best place for the representatives of warring nations to meet and settle their disagreements. It was at Geneva that representatives from the United States, Great Britain, Switzerland, Italy, and Brazil met in 1872 to settle the questions raised by the activities of English-built Confederate commerce raiders during the Civil War. It was also at Geneva that representatives of many of the great countries of the world met in 1927 to consider the reduction of their armies and navies. Now many of the leading nations of the world have formed the League of Nations, with its headquarters at Geneva.

The purpose of the league is to have the representatives of the various nations settle peacefully the differences between one country and another, thus doing away with such destructive wars as have been waged in the past. 

AUSTRIA 

Before the World War Germany had a great and powerful neighbor to the south and

BEFORE east of her. This was the empire 

THE WAR of Austria-Hungary, a rich land stretching through the center of

Europe, with its southern border on the Adriatic. The empire of Austria-Hungary was made up of a number of small nations, each speaking a different language and having its own interests to a great extent. Some of them were conquered countries whose people longed for independence.

When the war came to an end there came an end to Austria-Hungary as well. By the terms of the treaty of Versailles Hungary was separated from Austria. In losing Hungary, Austria lost much fertile farming land along the Danube river. Czechoslovakia became an independent country and with Czechoslovakia went the empire's richest coal and iron mines. 

Poland took part of the plain lands to the north. To Italy, Austria lost the important ports of Trieste and Fiume on the Adriatic, together with some surrounding lands. When 

Jugoslavia took the remainder of the old empire's Adriatic coast, Austria became an inland country with access to the sea only through other countries.

Austria, now a republic, is no longer a world power. The land left to her after the World 

War is an area about the size of the AFTER state of Maine. This land is mostly THE WAR mountainous, although in the north there is some fertile lowland along the Danube river. The Alps in Austria are lower than the 

Alps in Switzerland and therefore can be more generally used for forests, pasture, and farming. Still, the possibilities for agriculture are so limited that Austria must depend mainly on manufacturing to pay for the food imported for her more than 6,500,000 people.

In manufacturing, the country still has the foundations of her former industrial greatness-the skilled workmen, the established reputation, electricity, some coal and iron, and much water power from mountain streams and rivers. She imports necessary raw materials. 

She has one great advantage over the empireher people are mostly of one race and speak one language-German.

PRODUCTS 

Today Austria is struggling to make the most of both her agricultural and manufacturing possibilities. The hardy grains and vegetables are being grown.

Dairying is increasing in importance, and sheep, hogs, and horses are being raised. Textiles, fine leathers and shoes, paper and wood pulp, machinery, automobiles, and many other

VIENNA 

Vienna, the capital of the republic of Austria, is at one of the main crossroads of Europe, and owes much of its greatness to this central position on the continent. In the old days Vienna was the center of the wealth and industry of the empire and of the politics of all Europe. With the 

Imperial palaces, the many beautiful and stately homes, the famous churches and museums, and the great university, the city was one of the gayest, wealthiest, and busiest capitals of the continent. It was also a cultural center, one of the greatest musical centers of the world, and an important manufacturing center. Now, with many of the rich sections of the empire gone, the city no longer has the sources of raw material and the markets that it once had. Vienna, as the capital of a small republic, is very different from the glittering capital city of the empire. But even with far less wealth and a much smaller population, it is still a large and important city. 

The continuing importance of Vienna is in a large measure due to excellent transportation lines that meet in the city. 

CROSSROADS OF Find Vienna on the map on page 40. It lies in a break

TRANSPORTATION 

in the high mountain region, between the Alps and the Carpathians, in one of the valleys that connect the great lowland area of Europe with the plains of the Danube river. 

Paris is reached from Vienna by railroads which follow the Danube river west into Germany and take the Strassburg route to the French capital. Berlin may be reached by following the same route through the mountains, turning north not far from the western boundary of Czechoslovakia, through Leipzig to 

Berlin. Another route leads north through 

Prague to Berlin. Still another leads through the central pass of Czechoslovakia, known as the Moravian Gate, or Corridor, to Berlin and the ports along the Baltic and to Warsaw and cities of Russia. Vienna also has airplane connections with many important cities of Europe. 

To the southeast, the Danube river leads to the Black sea, cutting through the Transylvanian Alps in a narrow passage called the 

Iron Gate. From Vienna, railroads follow one river valley after another southeast through Bulgaria to Istanbul on the Strait of Bosporus. 

Another road follows the rather low land south along the Morava and Vardar river valleys to 

Saloniki on the Aegean sea. Still another southern route skirts the eastern slopes of the 

Alps to the two seaports, Trieste and Fiume.

So, north, south, east, and west the great railroads of Europe seem to center in the valley where lies the city of Vienna. It will be interesting for us to watch for ourselves, from year to year, to see if Austria will be able to rebuild her old time greatness around her one industrial and commercial center, Vienna. 

CZECHOSLOVAKIA 

Czechoslovakia has been a separate nation only since the World War. Before the war its lands were part of the empire of Austria- Hungary. At the close of the war, the three districts, Bohemia, Moravia, and Slovakia, joined together and formed the republic of Czechoslovakia with Prague as the capital. 

The district of Bohemia is a plateau with fertile soil for agriculture, rich coal and iron fields, and many well developed manufacturing cities. Moravia has more lowland than Bohemia, but it too has iron and coal mines as well as some industrial cities, and broad valleys of rich farm land. The Moravian Gate, or Corri dor, is in Moravia. Slovakia is mountainous. 

Though it has some gold and silver and some fine forests, its farm lands are poor, and it is the most thinly populated district. 

POPULATION 

The long, narrow country of Czechoslovakia is little larger than our state of Arkansas. The population of about 14,500,000 is made up of different races. In the western part of the country, in Bohemia and Moravia, are the Czechs, an educated, capable, patriotic people. In the eastern part are the Slovaks. The Slovaks have less educa-

EUROPE 

tion than the Czechs and are far less progressive. Their chief industries are farming and forestry. Many Germans also live in Czechoslovakia, mostly in the western section. 

CLIMATE AND AGRICULTURE 

Because of its inland position, Czechoslovakia has a continental climate, and its differences in altitude increase the variations in temperature. Sugar beets and potatoes are raised in great quantities, and wheat, rye, oats, and barley are important crops. Much livestock is raised. There are large vineyards, and in the fertile, protected valleys many fruits are grown. 

In her natural resources Czechoslovakia is indeed fortunate. Forests supply more wood 

NATURAL RESOURCES 

than is used in the country, and they are being replanted yearly.

It is said there is hardly a mineral that is not found in her mountains. Clays and sands of unusual quality form the basis of two important industries-glass and porcelain manufacturing. We know that there are iron and coal. Other minerals are manganese, used in making steel, and the precious metal radium. With all this mineral wealth, and with the modern manufacturing plants built in the days of Austria-Hungary, this small republic has a wonderful start.

TRANSPORTATION AND TRADE 

Except for its lack of seacoast, Czechoslovakia is well located for commerce. The natural routes of Bohemia lead north, while those of 

Moravia open to the south. 

The railroad between Berlin and Vienna crosses the country, as do both the road from 

Warsaw in Poland to Trieste on the Adriatic and the line which connects Switzerland with 

Poland. The Elbe river, rising in Czechoslovakia, offers fine water transportation to the 

North sea or to the Baltic through the Kiel canal. The Danube connects Moravia with the south. All these routes open up good markets for the commerce of the country. Her chief imports are cotton and wool for her textile factories, raw materials for her other industries, and food stuffs. She exports textiles, sugar, iron and steel goods, glassware, and shoes.

The fine cotton goods and glassware are familiar to American shoppers.

PRAGUE 

Prague, the capital of the republic, is one of the very old cities of Europe. The older parts of the city lie along the banks of the 

Moldau river, a branch of the Elbe. 

Their narrow, crooked, cobblestone streets and quaint old stone houses, churches, and bridges carry us back hundreds of years in the history of the world. The city of Prague has long been a cultural center and has a fine university. 

Prague stands on a plateau, rimmed round with mountains. Because of these mountains, the city is not easily reached from all parts of the country, though its transportation lines do connect it with many important cities of other countries. Not only is Prague a commercial and manufacturing center, but it is rapidly becoming one of the large and important cities of central Europe. The rich resources of the surrounding plateau add greatly to its importance. 

Here are manufactured industrial machinery, railroad cars, cotton goods, and chemicals. 

OTHER CITIES 

AND 

INDUSTRIES 

The city of Pilsen is noted for the making of beautiful Bohemian glass and machinery.

Karlsbad is noted for two very different industries. It is a famous health resort, with inns and hotels which care for people from all over the world who come to drink the mineral waters. Deposits of kaolin, a very fine quality of clay, near Karlsbad, have led to the manufacture of beautiful porcelains in that city. Brunn, like Pilsen and Prague, is noted for making machinery. 

A number of great iron and steel foundries are scattered throughout the country, chiefly where there are iron and coal mines close together. The extensive forests supply raw material for many paper factories. Many of the natives of Bohemia are skilled in the making of jewelry by hand and this product, made in the homes, is an important export of the country. Textiles and laces are widely manufactured, especially in the Elbe valley.

Czechoslovakia is also noted for the colorful embroideries done by its women. 

With improved transportation, a strong and wise government, and the use of one national language, we may hope to see this small republic become a real commercial power.

SIGHTS ON A TRIP THROUGH THE MEDITERRANEAN 

3 2 (1) (3) (4) Publishers' Photo Service, N. Y. (2) Copyright E. M. Newman, from Publishers' Photo Service, N. Y. 

1. The Rock of Gibraltar, at the western entrance of the

Mediterranean sea. Our steamer passes close to this towering rock. Gibraltar is owned by the British, who have made it one of the strongest fortresses in the world. Guns are placed high up in the rock to protect the entrance to the Mediterranean, and from a signal station on top guards examine all approaching ships. 

2. A Roman aqueduct in Spain. We leave our steamer and take a trip to see this bridge, with its many arches. 

It was built by the ancient Romans to carry water across a valley to an ancient city. The water flowed through a covered trough on the top of the aqueduct. Notice its height, over a hundred feet. So skilful were the Roman builders that the great structure, built without cement, is still in good condition after 1800 years. 

3. The Riviera, in southern France. Our steamer anchors in the harbor of Monte Carlo, which lies along the shore with mountains in the background. The fine climate, the beautiful scenery, and the gay times to be had at Monte Carlo attract many people of all nations to the Riviera. 

4. Vineyards on the island of Capri. In the Bay of

Naples, Italy, we find this small island rising steeply out of the sea. Besides the vineyards and gardens planted on the terraced hillsides, we must surely visit the Blue Grotto, the most beautiful of the island's many sea caves.

SIGHTS ON A TRIP THROUGH THE MEDITERRANEAN 

SAVOY HOTEL 

1 3 

1. Ruined temples in ancient Athens, Greece. The high hill is the fortified part of the old-time city, the Acropolis. 

On it stands what remains of the magnificent temple called the Parthenon. It was built about 2300 years ago and was one of the most perfect examples of old Greek buildings. 

2. Port Said, Egypt, near the eastern end of the Mediterranean. This is a seaport at the entrance to the Suez canal, which is controlled by the British. The lighthouse guides ships to the harbor, where many take on coal before continuing on their way. 

3. The Suez canal, between the Mediterranean sea and the Red sea. This narrow waterway saves ships sailing between Europe and the Far East from making the long voyage around the south of Africa. We see the sands of the desert stretching into the distance on both sides. The canal was dug through desert sands. The British bought the canal from the ruler of Egypt to connect eastern British possessions with their home country. It is now open to ships of all countries. 

4. An Algerian shepherd and his flock. We cruise back along the southern coast of the Mediterranean to Algeria, and get a glimpse of this French land in Africa. The lonely shepherd has raised his sheep on the thin, rocky pastureland and is now leading them to market. This dry land is better suited to sheep than to cattle and horses.

THE MEDITERRANEAN SEA AND SURROUNDING LANDS GENERAL CHARACTERISTICS 

Between Europe and Africa lies the greatest inland sea in the world, the Mediterranean.

Its warm blue waters extend more than 2200 miles in an east-and-west direction. From

Marseille, in France, to the northern coast of Africa the width of the Mediterranean is about 450 miles. Farther to the east the Italian peninsula stands out between the Mediterranean and the Adriatic, for about 600 miles. If the 

Mediterranean sea lay within the borders of the United States it would reach from New York bay across our country nearly to California. Naturally this immense inland sea has a great effect upon the lands which border it. 

The Mediterranean region extends through about fifteen degrees of latitude, or from 

CLIMATE 

about 46° north latitude to about 

31° north latitude. Nearness to the great landlocked sea makes the climate of all the surrounding lands mild the year round, while the cold winds from the north are shut off by Europe's east-west mountain ranges which shelter the seacoast.

Most of the lands bordering the Mediterranean have what is known as a Mediterranean climate, with moderate rainfall in winter and hot dry weather in summer. The winter rains are brought by the prevailing westerlies which blow over this region in wintertime. The dry weather is caused by the belt of horse-latitude calms which extends over this region in summer. The true Mediterranean climate has only two seasons, one wet and one dry.

The Pacific coast of California and the Atlantic coast of the United States from New York to Savannah lie in about the same degrees of latitude as the Mediterranean region. 

Southern California is much like the Mediterranean lands in climate, but the Atlantic coast has a more oceanic climate, with four seasons and abundant rain the year round. 

The greater part of the crops of the Mediterranean region get their needed moisture from 63 the winter rains. During the long, hot, dry summer months crops require irrigation. As water for irrigation is scarce, only those countries which can afford to build large dams irrigate to any extent. These are Spain, Italy, and 

France. The dams hold back water from the rainy winters for use in the dry growing season. 

The mild climate of the Mediterranean lands tends to make the people easy-going and satisfied with farming and tending flocks instead of earning a living by manufacturing. There are few industrial centers on the shores of this sea. 

Many centuries ago the lands bordering the Mediterranean were all that was known of the world. Men who write of ancient lands believe that the Mediterranean carried the first tiny ships of man.

EARLY HISTORY 

The Phoenicians. Among the earliest sailors and traders known to history were the Phoenicians. They lived in what is today the country of Syria at the eastern end of the Mediterranean. Forests of wonderful trees, called the cedars of Lebanon, furnished tall, straight masts and fine lumber for their tiny ships. The first ships did not sail out of sight of land but kept near to the shores. Then, as the many islands of the sea offered frequent stopping places and made stepping-stones for the early traders, they began to venture farther and farther out on the Mediterranean until gradually this whole sea became known to them and they had visited every land in the thenknown world. Along the northern coast of

Africa, settlements were founded as tradingposts by the daring Phoenicians. One of the most important of these African settlements was Carthage, near the present city of Tunis.

Carthage was destined to grow into an important city and a great trading center. 

As time went on, the Phoenicians in their small ships ventured through the Strait of Gibraltar and out onto the broad Atlantic. OWC-7

EUROPE 

They sailed as far north as the British Isles. 

Here was found a metal called tin. For this they traded African ivory and eastern spices, gold, and sandalwood. The Phoenicians used the tin with copper to make bronze, a metal which they are believed to have been the first to make. From the region of the Baltic, the traders got amber to use in making jewelry. 

As the Phoenicians needed a simpler form of keeping records than the picture writing which had come into use in Egypt, they invented the first alphabet of twenty-two letters. 

The Phoenicians' alphabet, their knowledge of sea craft, and their seacoast colonies were their most important contributions to civilization. 

Greeks and Romans. Phoenicia declined and other Mediterranean nations became important. The people of Greece lived in small city states, each of which had its own government. As the city states were near the sea, the Greeks became a seafaring nation. They were also great colonizers and planted many colonies on the shores of neighboring lands and nearby islands. But above all they were real students of government and lovers of freedom and beauty. The ancient Greek sculpture and Greek writing, both prose and poetry, are as fine as any the world has yet produced. 

Greece gradually fell under the power of the Romans, a nation of warriors living in Italy. 

The Romans were not content with conquering Greece and the Greek colonies of the Mediterranean. They became trade rivals of rich and powerful Carthage across the Mediterranean, and waged a series of wars with the Carthaginians. At last they captured and destroyed Carthage. In the years which followed, the Romans conquered most of the known world of their day.

Many of the works of the Romans remain today in the form of Roman roads, bridges, aqueducts, temples, and theatres which are found in practically every land bordering the Mediterranean.

Even the mighty power of Rome was not lasting. Far to the north of Rome, in forestcovered central Europe, there were wild tribes of barbarians. For hundreds of years the 

Romans held these tribes at bay, and even conquered some of them, but in time great barbarian armies crossed the mountain passes of northern Italy and overcame the Roman empire. 

Changes in Trade and Commerce. But with the passing of one powerful nation after another, the Mediterranean still remained the heart of the trade and commerce of the known world. In the Middle Ages two Italian cities, Venice and Genoa, grew enormously wealthy by handling the trade between the Far East and the lands of central and western Europe. 

Spices, tea, jewels, silks, gold, and ivory passed through these ports.

Still later the countries of western Europe sought direct ocean routes to the rich Orient. 

Slowly new ideas of the size and shape of the earth grew up, and new sea routes to the East were sought. Finally a brave explorer succeeded in sailing to India around the south of 

Africa. Others started boldly across the Atlantic ocean, discovering the vast new lands of 

North and South America, and the world became known, not as a comparatively small sea surrounded by land, but as great land masses, called continents, surrounded by even greater oceans. 

In the years following the discovery of

America the Mediterranean became steadily less important as a trade route. But in the late years of the nineteenth century it again became important when a canal was cut across the Isthmus of Suez, that narrow, sandy strip of land between the Mediterranean and the Red sea. From very early times goods had been sent by caravan across this isthmus from the Mediterranean shore to the shore of the Red sea, there to be reshipped. When the Suez canal, about 100 miles long, was finished, trade passing through the Mediterranean found an eastern outlet by water through the sea-level canal into the Red sea and thence to southern and eastern Asia and Australia. People came to realize that the Mediterranean was now the most direct water route between Europe and the great trade centers of Africa, Asia, and Australia. Rivers, canals, and railroads began pouring goods into Mediterranean ports to be reshipped to far-away lands. Great Britain,

GENERAL CHARACTERISTICS OF THE MEDITERRANEAN LANDS 65 

who owned and had fortified the Rock of Gibraltar guarding the western entrance to the Mediterranean, also acquired and fortified the canal, and so gained control of both entrances to the Mediterranean. The many interior railroad, river, and canal routes which now connect with the Mediterranean make this control less important today than it once was. 

MODERN TRADE 

Today in the chief Mediterranean ports of Europe cargoes of tea, oil seeds, cotton, wool, hides, and raw silk from Africa, Asia, and Australia are exchanged for the textiles, iron and steel machinery, grain, and flour of European countries. Although far from being the center of the world trade, as it once was, the Mediterranean is of great commercial importance, and the Suez canal handles more commerce than the Panama canal. 

Much of the Mediterranean trade of today is "through" trade. Local commerce, that is, trade between the Mediterranean ports, is of much less importance than foreign commerce, except the trade between north Africa and 

Marseille. That is true because all parts of the Mediterranean region produce similar crops. Surrounded by rugged mountains which provide little good land for commercial crops, many of the ancient ports have lost their importance. Their population is sparse, they buy little from other lands and the warm climate discourages the manufacture of goods for export. So the Mediterranean ports themselves do little to stimulate trade on the sea. However, tunnels, railroads, and canals are being built in increasing numbers to connect the north of Europe with the south, and to form transportation lines for commerce to the Mediterranean.

Certain of the Mediterranean countries- 

Spain, Italy, Greece, Morocco, Algeria, Tu 

MEDITERRANEAN COUNTRIES 

nisia, Libia, and Egyptdepend on the Mediterranean sea routes. They are the true Mediterranean countries. The other countries which border on this great sea depend upon it much less, and some of them make little use of it. Using the map on page 

62, find their names.

The high mountain ranges which border most of the Mediterranean region have had a great influence on the peoples of the region. In early times they protected the coast countries from attacks by barbarian tribes from the interior. Because the 

MOUNTAINS 

ranges also formed a barrier against inland travel or expansion, the early Mediterranean peoples turned their backs on the land and faced the sea. Still there are some comparatively low places in these mountain ranges and with the development of the nations of Europe these passes came to serve as connecting links between the center of Europe and the Mediterranean lands.

COAST LINE 

AND

ISLANDS 

Another natural feature which had a great influence on the early Mediterranean nations was the irregular coast line. 

Study your map, page 62, and notice the many peninsulas and islands and the indentations of the Mediterranean coasts of the various countries. The mountain background made the people seafarers, and the many islands dotting the sea encouraged short, comparatively safe trips from island to island in the little ships of the day with their sails and oars. See how naturally Sicily, frequently a battleground in the past, seems to lead from southern Italy to northern Africa. Notice how ships from

Genoa, in Italy, could avoid much of the open sea by sailing along the coasts of Corsica and 

Sardinia on their way to Africa. And see, too, how the islands of Crete and Cyprus must have tempted Grecian ships toward Syria and the eastern end of the Mediterranean!

RIVERS 

Because of the mountains, the rivers of the Mediterranean lands are mostly short and are navigable for only short distances inland. The two great exceptions to this are the Rhone, in France, and the Nile, in 

Egypt. Though these rivers are highways of commerce, they are handicapped by deltas. 

These deltas form partly because of the sediment brought down by the streams and partly because of the fact that the Mediterranean has no strong tides, such as we find at work about the British Isles, to wash silt from the river mouths. The Po, in Italy, has the same dis-

advantage as a trade route.

Very little is left of the stately forests that once lined the Mediterranean shores. In early times the forests were wastefully cut 

FORESTS 

to furnish lumber for shipbuilding or wood for fuel. There is not enough rainfall to produce rapid forest growth, so the forests have not grown up again. Now fuel is very scarce, and most of the houses are built of stone in the absence of suitable lumber. 

PRODUCTS 

In certain parts of the Mediterranean region, the population is dense. As farming land is scarce, every bit of it must be used FARMS AND and so the hillsides are terraced. 

Often these terraces are so small that the fields must be spaded up because there is not room to plow them. Even where a field is large enough to be plowed, the crops usually bring in so little beyond the need of the family that there is no money to invest in modern machinery. Furthermore, lack of education prevents the people from using new methods. 

The most important grain crops of the Mediterranean region are wheat and barley. Subtropical crops-olives, dates, oranges, lemons, and figs are grown throughout the region. 

Chestnut and almond trees flourish, and on sunny, terraced hillsides there are vineyards.

As not enough food can be raised to feed the people of the region, much food must be imported.

Fish, especially sardines and tuna-fish, are taken in quantities along the shores. Since meat is scarce, fish and olive oil serve as important food products of this region as well as important exports.

DOMESTIC ANIMALS 

Few cattle and horses are raised, for the scanty rain does not give rich enough pastures. 

The animals of the region must be able to find their food in rough, rocky pastures too poor for crops. 

Sheep are raised for their wool, and goats are the common dairy animals. There are a few oxen and many tiny, sure-footed donkeys, which can forage on the steepest hillsides. 

Camels from the desert regions are common carriers of loads in northern Africa. 

Except for Spain, the Mediterranean countries are poor in coal. There is a little lignite, which is a soft coal of poor quality. Spain, Algeria, and 

Tunisia have good deposits

MINERALS AND MANUFACTURING 

of iron, but little of the metal is used in manufacturing, most of the ore being exported. Industry is generally limited to the products which can be made by hand-fine fabrics and rich tapestries, leather goods, and jewelry.

There are important deposits of stone and other minerals which are exported in considerable quantities. Sulphur, phosphate rock, marble, and zinc are among these resources. 

The Mediterranean is no longer the center of the known world, but it is still a great avenue of commerce. It is the main road from 

Europe to north Africa, Australia, and the Far East, and great liners and freight boats now plow through the blue waters which carried the first tiny ships of the adventurous Phoenicians.

1. The Mediterranean is the greatest inland sea. 

2. The Mediterranean gives the bordering lands a mild climate the year round. The Mediterranean region has two seasons, a dry season in summer and a wet season in winter. The mild climate tends to make the people easy-going and satisfied to live by agriculture and tending flocks. 

3. In ancient times the Mediterranean was the center of the known world, and around it grew up the civilization of Europe. The Phoenicians began sea commerce on its waters, and were succeeded by the Greeks, who in turn gave place to the Romans. 

Rome was overthrown by barbarians. In the Mid dle Ages the cities of Genoa and Venice controlled most of the trade. With the discovery of other routes to the Far East, the Mediterranean became less important but recovered much of its importance with the opening of the Suez canal. 

4. Much of the Mediterranean trade is what is called "through" trade. There is comparatively little trade between the different ports of the Mediterranean region, except between North Africa and Marseille. 

5. The rivers of the Mediterranean lands are short. 

Only two, the Rhone and the Nile, are navigable for any great distance. Because they carry much sediment and because the tides of the Mediterranean are not strong enough to wash away silt from their mouths, the Rhone, the Nile, and the Po all have deltas which handicap their usefulness for trade.

SCENES IN SPAIN AND PORTUGAL 

3 2 4 

(1) (2) (4) Spanish Tourist Information Office, N. Y. (3) Consulate General of Portugal, N. Y. 

1. A valley in the Pyrenees, north of Barcelona, Spain. 

Until recent times, the Pyrenees have shut Spain and Portugal away from the rest of Europe. Even now, only three railroads have been built across or through the mountains. In these days of airplanes, however, the mountains are ceasing to be a barrier. 

2. The Court of Myrtles in the Alhambra, an ancient castle near Granada, Spain. The court is named from the myrtle bushes that surround the pool. The Moors who built this castle have been dead hundreds of years, but their skill is still one of the wonders of the world. 

Notice the delicate lacy carving in the court and the strong tower which was built for defense. 

3. Portuguese sardine fishermen with their boat. All along the coast of Portugal, natives put out in their clumsy boats, searching for schools of sardines. The sardines caught in these waters are small, and excellent for canning purposes. They are important in Portugal's trade. 

4. The Guadalquivir river and the docks at Seville, Spain. The Guadalquivir is the only navigable river in 

Spain. Ocean steamers use it safely as far inland as 

Seville, and the city is a shipping center. 

We notice, however, that the Guadalquivir is not so busy with shipping as the Elbe at Hamburg or the waters of New York harbor. This is because Spain is not an active industrial and commercial nation.

HERE AND THERE IN SPAIN

(1) Copyright E. M. Newman, from Publishers' Photo Service, N. Y. (2) (3) (4) Publishers' Photo Service, N. Y. 

1. Sheep grazing on the Spanish plateau. The dry central region of the Iberian peninsula is of little use for most agriculture. Sheep, however, thrive on the sparse vegetation, and their fine wool is an important product. 

The Merino breed of sheep, noted for its fine wool, is famous the world over. 

2. A carnival time in Spain. Carnival days bring gay crowds of people into the city streets. Farmers and shepherds come from the country to see the sights, and tourists from the United States and other countries mingle with the merrymakers. Balconies with iron railings are common on houses in all Spanish countries. People can sit on them and enjoy the sights in the streets below. 

3. A grove of cork oaks in Spain. A large part of the world's cork comes from the Iberian peninsula, and it is a very profitable product to both Spain and Portugal. 

The rough, light-colored outer bark on these trees is cork. Where the trees look dark, the cork has been removed. If all the cork were taken from a tree at one time the tree would die. Where the cork is carefully cut away a new bark forms in a few years. 

4. The business section of Madrid. Spain is not all carnivals and narrow, picturesque streets. Here, in the very center of old Spain, are modern office buildings, very beautiful in design,

THE MEDITERRANEAN SEA AND SURROUNDING LANDS THE IBERIAN PENINSULA 

Southern Europe has three great peninsulas. The one to the west includes the countries of Spain and Portugal and is called the Iberian peninsula.

HISTORY OF SPAIN AND PORTUGAL 

The story of Spain goes far back in the history of the world. Its coast was visited by the early Phoenician sailors as they skirted the shores of the Mediterranean. Then Spain was owned by powerful Carthage. Next it was conquered by the mighty Romans, who held it for some hundreds of years and looked upon it as a grain field and a treasury of minerals. After Rome fell, the barbarian tribes from the north seized Spain, and, at length, in the eighth century, it came into the hands of the dark-skinned Moors from northern Africa.

The Moors established a capital city at Granada. Nearby they built the Alhambra, the ancient castle of the Moorish kings, which still exists. The outside of the Alhambra is severely plain. Within, it is filled with beautiful tiles and marbles and with delicate wood carvings and skilfully inlaid ceilings. The 

Alhambra was only one of many marvelous buildings erected by the Moors. The city of 

Cordoba was noted for its beautiful buildings. 

The Moors also built roads in Spain, and dug irrigation canals, some of which are still in use. 

The history of Spain is practically the history of Portugal up to the twelfth century. 

Then Portugal broke away from Spain and became a separate kingdom. Today both are republics.

The Moors were driven from Spain near the close of the fifteenth century, and not long afterwards the Spaniards began the great exploring and colonizing ventures which gained them lands in the New World. It was the 

Spaniards who conquered Mexico and Peru and who claimed the southern and western parts of what is now the United States. They also claimed most of the West Indies and the Philippine islands. And they built up a rich trade between the countries of the Western hemisphere and their homeland of Spain. 

In the meantime, and even previously, the Portuguese sent exploring expeditions down the west coast of Africa. This resulted in the discovery of an all-water route around the Cape of Good Hope to India. There are still 

Portuguese possessions along Africa's coast. 

Other brave men from Portugal explored parts of South America and claimed the lands now known as Brazil. Here the Portuguese language is still spoken, though the country is now independent. Both of the Iberian countries have now lost all of their New World possessions. As the mother countries little by little became less powerful the distant colonies became more independent. Some were lost as a result of European wars, and others revolted and established governments of their own. 

With such a background, let us turn our attention to the Spain and Portugal of today and see what effects the natural conditions of the peninsula and the character of the people themselves have had on the development of the countries.

The Iberian peninsula is a little larger than France. The latitude of Madrid, the capital of Spain, is about that of New York 

City. Lisbon, the capital of Portugal, is only about a degree and a half farther north than San Francisco on our western coast. 

SIZE AND POSITION 

Both Spain and Portugal extend farther west than any other of the mainland countries of Europe, and they are closer to the coast of Africa than any other European country. 

SURFACE 

Let us travel quickly around the Iberian peninsula, noticing the natural features. 

Across the northeast border of Spain tower the Pyrenees. Being almost without passes, these mountains have been a nearly complete barrier between Spain 69
