EUROPE 

and France, and have served in a great measure to cut Spain and Portugal off from the life and industries of the rest of Europe. To the northwest the Cantabrian range, an extension of the Pyrenees, forms a rugged coast line along the Bay of Biscay. On the west, and south to the Strait of Gilbraltar stretches the Atlantic coast line, broken here and there by fine harbors. On the southeast and east, from Gibraltar to Cape de Creus, the shores are washed by the Mediterranean.

The interior of the Iberian peninsula is a broad plateau stretching from the Pyrenees south to the Sierra Nevadas, another high and snow-capped range. The plateau is streaked with smaller ranges and is fringed about with narrow bits of coastal plain. Here and there fertile river valleys slope from the interior towards the sea. The two largest valleys are drained by the Ebro and Guadalquivir rivers, the Ebro flowing southeast, the Guadalquivir flowing southwest.

A spur of the high Cantabrian mountains forms a part of the east-west boundary between Portugal and Spain. For a part of its length the north-south boundary follows the courses of three rivers. 

None of the rivers of the Iberian peninsula is very large. All flow rapidly through deep gorges, and are therefore of little aid 

RIVERS 

to commerce. Tortosa at the mouth of the Ebro receives ocean steamers, but the river itself is suited to boats of only small draft. 

The Guadalquivir is navigable to Seville and is the only navigable river of the peninsula. 

Because of its exposed position in the path of westerly winds, the northwestern Atlantic coast of Spain and Portugal 

CLIMATE 

receives heavy rainfall. Here the summers are mild and the winters are cool. 

The winds lose most of their moisture rising to the plateau, so the plateau itself and the Mediterranean coast of Spain are much drier than the northwestern coast. The Mediterranean coast of the peninsula is also much warmer than the northwestern coast because of the protecting mountains to the north, and the hot, dry winds from Africa. Nearness to the Mediterranean keeps the temperature of the eastern coast of Spain fairly even the year round.

Because of lack of rainfall, the interior of the plateau is a semi-arid region. Varying altitudes cause a variety of temperatures, but as a whole the plateau has a continental climate. 

Small sections of the plateau are watered by narrow streams, or are irrigated by snow waters from the mountains. 

AGRICULTURE 

Farmers on the plateau raise chiefly wheat, oats, barley, and rye. Potatoes are an important food. Vineyards flourish along the lower slopes of the gorgeous Sierras as they do in the valleys of California. They line the valleys of the 

Ebro and the Guadalquivir rivers and grow at the foot of the Pyrenees near Barcelona. 

Some of the grapes are made into wine; others are dried and sold as raisins. Both wine and raisins are important exports. About the Gulf of Valencia there are rows and rows of orange trees. Because parts of the Mediterranean coast are so very warm, such sub-tropical products as oranges, lemons, dates, figs, and almonds are plentiful. More and more of the land here is being made useful through irrigation. Yet everywhere we find agriculture carried on by the most old-fashioned methods. 

On the slopes above the vineyards olive trees are grown. Olives are another of the peninsula's most important products. Quantities of unripe olives are pickled and sold for export. The ripe olives are picked and crushed to make olive oil, which we use in salad dressings, and which the Spaniards use on bread and in cooking in place of butter. When the oil is removed from the ripe olives, the pulp is fed to cattle and hogs. 

Parts of the Iberian peninsula, especially along the coast of Portugal, are heavily forested with cork oak trees. The corks which we use are a product of their bark. Once the trees grew wild but they are now cultivated in groves. They are a valuable source of income to the people of the country. Stoppers for bottles, soles for shoes, parts of life preservers and life boats, and varieties of floor coverings are made from cork. Cork is our most valuable import from Spain and Portugal,

SPAIN AND PORTUGAL 

73 

DOMESTIC ANIMALS 

You have probably noticed that where we have found plateaus we have nearly always found sheep. The Iberian peninsula is no exception. Sheep raising is one of the great occupations of Spain, and wool is one of the country's exports. Spain is the native land of merino sheep, whose wool is softer and finer than any other. Many merinos have been taken to Australia and to other sheep-raising countries. Some cattle are raised along the rainy western coast, but for the production of milk the Spaniards raise goats more extensively than dairy cattle. Goats, you will remember, thrive on rough, stony pasture, such as is found on the plateau. Oxen are used for plowing. Sure-footed little donkeys, much like the burros of Mexico, take the place of horses.

MINERALS 

Spain and Portugal have good mineral resources. These include deposits of coal, zinc, lead, quicksilver, copper, iron, and sulphur. The lead, zinc, copper, and quicksilver are found mainly in the Pyrenees and along the eastern and southern coasts of the peninsula. The quicksilver, or mercury, is exported to other countries where it is used in the tubes of thermometers and on the backs of mirrors. The iron and the coal are found most extensively in the Cantabrian mountains, in the region about Bilbao. This port, on the 

Bay of Biscay, ships iron ore to the smelters of the Cardiff coal fields in England. Manufacturing is increasing in Bilbao as the Spaniards are now gradually waking up to the fact that there is more money to be made in exporting finished products than raw materials. Because the wealthy people of Spain were so long uninterested in her industries, the Spanish mines are mostly worked with foreign capital.

On the whole the products of Spain and Portugal are so similar as to discourage trade between the two countries. 

You will remember how difficult it was to build railroads in the high mountain countries of South America. The Ibe- TRANSPORTATION 

rian peninsula, though lower in altitude, has so uneven a surface that it presents similar difficulties to the builder of railroads. Until recently there were very few railroads in the peninsula. Even today only three cross the Pyrenees, and two of these have been built through the low passes near the ends of the mountain range. These railroads connect Spain with the other European countries. Shorter railroads connect with these and with each other in a loose network, of which Madrid is the center. 

In general, the highways of the Iberian countries are poor, but there have been recent government appropriations for the building and repairing of roads in Spain. This is an indication of progress. The country also has several air lines. Although transportation is still poor and inadequate, it is improving. 

Most of the people of Spain and Portugal live along the western coast and along the 

Mediterranean. The central section is thinly settled. Much of the population is concentrated in the cities, so in general distribution is very uneven. 

POPULATION 

The people of these countries are divided into two distinct groups-the upper, or socalled "gentleman" class, and the working class.

The upper class, the highest born and best educated men and women of Spain and Portugal, do not always use their talents to help make their countries richer or more powerful. 

They have fine homes, lovely gardens, and plenty of servants. With these luxuries they are content. Their families have been raised for generations with the idea that a gentleman must not work or interest himself in industry. 

So, until very recently, most of the upper class people have thought themselves too good for work, and many still think so. 

Because of this belief of the wealthier class, agriculture, other industries, and the development of natural resources have been left to the less educated people. Their work has been inefficient because they have no way of learning the best methods of working or farming. 

So they are not prosperous, and many of them are too poor to send their children to school at all. Because of the general lack of education the natural resources of the countries are still largely undeveloped. A compulsory edu-

EUROPE 

cation law, however, is beginning to be enforced, and we may expect better education to lead to improvements.

The habits and customs of the Iberian countries are similar. The people are so fond of pleasure that nearly every great saint's day or political holiday is made the occasion for closing the shops and planning special amusements. Bullfighting, for centuries a popular amusement, may be seen in Lisbon, Madrid, and many other cities and towns. Dancing and singing are popular pastimes. The Spanish and Portuguese are light-hearted peoples and know well how to enjoy themselves. 

The towns and cities of the peninsula are quaint and colorful. The houses are built of stone or stucco, and are colored pink, yellow, blue, green, or lavender. In the cities there are modern business sections and broad highways and boulevards.

CITIES 

Madrid, the capital, is the loveliest of Spanish cities. Should you visit it on a holiday you would find it filled with lights and music and gaily dressed men and women. It truly pictures the character of the light-hearted and laughter-loving people of Spain who let work take care of itself. 

Madrid entertains not only her own people, but thousands of visitors every year. 

Lisbon, in Portugal, is somewhat like

Madrid. It also has its carnivals, and there are many fine buildings. But its location on the finest harbor of the peninsula makes Lisbon a busy commercial center. Here ships are built, sardines are packed, and many products are imported and exported. Cork products, paper, pottery, chemicals, and woolen goods are manufactured. 

Oporto, north of Lisbon, has a smaller harbor but greater commerce, since it is backed by a rich farming region. Grapes raised nearby are made into the famous port wine, which is Portugal's chief export.

Cadiz is the most southerly port in Spain. 

Like Bilbao, it exports minerals-largely lead, copper, and iron. The Mediterranean cities of

Barcelona, Malaga, and Valencia, in a region of rare natural beauty, export wines, fruits, olive oil, raisins, and almonds. Barcelona is the chief manufacturing city of the peninsula.

Silk, cotton, and woolen goods are made there; also drugs, furniture, leather goods, and machinery. Except in Barcelona, manufacturing is not yet far advanced, and Spain must import so many manufactured goods that their value exceeds that of her own exports. The effect is to reduce the wealth of the country. 

Among the inland cities of interest are Cordoba, Seville, and Toledo. Cordoba is famous for its leather goods. Seville is the center of the porcelain industry. This city has a beautiful cathedral, the tower of which was built by the Moors. It is said to be the burial place of Christopher Columbus and his two sons. 

Toledo, on the Tagus river, was once the capital of Spain. 

Have you noticed how many of the cities mentioned are seaports? These are sure to become much more important if Spain continues to work her mines and increase the number and variety of her manufactures.

COLONIES 

Spain now has few colonies to claim her attention. These include Spanish Morocco, in northern Africa, famous for grapes, leather goods, tiles, and cork; Rio de Oro on Africa's west coast, a fishing center; and Spanish Guinea, on the Gulf of Guinea, which produces cacao, coffee, sugar, palm nuts, and rubber. Spain also owns the Balearic islands east of her mainland in the Mediterranean, and gets from them almonds and olives. 

The Canary islands off the northwest coast of Africa are perhaps the most important colony, for they are a coaling station and also produce important crops of bananas. Find all these

Spanish possessions on the map, page 132. 

Portugal has more colonies than her larger neighbor. Her explorers were the first to visit the Cape Verde islands off Africa's west coast. These islands, the Azores, and the 

Madeiras southwest of Portugal, now belong to Portugal. The Azores and Madeiras produce early vegetables and fruits for European markets. All three island groups serve as coaling stations. Locate these on the map, page 66. 

In Africa, Portugal owns Angola, Mozambique, and Portuguese Guinea. Angola, or

SPAIN AND PORTUGAL 

75 Portuguese West Africa, lies between the Equator and the Tropic of Capricorn on the west coast. Mozambique, or Portuguese East

Africa, is a little farther south than Angola and on the east coast of the continent. Portuguese Guinea is on the western coast. Angola produces cotton, sugar cane, coffee, and cattle. 

Mozambique exports coconuts, sugar, and cotton. Portuguese Guinea exports some hides, and palm oil made from palm kernels.

Portugal has also lands in Asia. On the west coast of India are the ports of Goa and Daman and the settlement of Diu, which is on a little island near the mainland. The three send 

Portugal salt and the useful steel-making metal manganese. Besides these Indian dependencies, Portugal owns the island of Macao off the coast of China, and half of the East Indian island of Timor. Find all these on the map on page 174.

All of Portugal's foreign possessions together, like those of the Netherlands and Belgium, are many times larger than the mother country. Since the homeland is small, many citizens have gone to the colonies to make homes and to take care of the commercial and industrial interests there. None of the colonies has a very great white population compared with the number of natives living there, but the Portuguese language is widely used in all of them. There are more people speaking 

Portuguese in countries outside of Portugal than there are in the mother country herself. 

The colonial possessions of Spain and Portugal, however, are less valuable than other countries' colonies in the same regions. The 

Iberian nations have not had the money to develop them and their full value must wait for the growth of railroads and other means of trade and communication. 

1. Spain and Portugal lie in the Iberian peninsula.

The Moors took possession of Spain in the eighth century. They built many fine buildings, roads, and irrigation canals. Soon after regaining the country from the Moors, the Spaniards carried on foreign exploration and conquest which gained them much land in the New World. Portugal, too, gained New World colonies. But both countries later lost these lands. 

2. The Iberian peninsula is a little larger than France.

It is the most westerly part of the European mainland and the nearest to Africa. Its coast line is largely regular, but has some fine harbors. 

3. The surface of the peninsula is largely plateau, broken by several mountain ranges and a few valleys. It is fringed by bits of coastal plain. 

4. The northwestern coast of the Iberian peninsula is very rainy and has mild summers and cool winters. The Mediterranean coast is drier and warmer in winter and summer. The interior is a semi-arid region with a continental climate. The Mediterranean coast is irrigated in a few places. Parts of the plateau are made productive by snow waters from the mountains. 

5. The rivers of Spain and Portugal are not large. 

They flow rapidly through deep gorges. The one navigable river is the Guadalquivir. 

6. Hardy grains are grown on the plateau. Grapes are raised on the lower mountain slopes and along the river valleys. Valencia produces oranges. Other products of Spain's Mediterranean coast are olives, oranges, lemons, figs, dates, and almonds. 

7. Oxen, goats, and donkeys are raised. Donkeys are used everywhere as beasts of burden. Sheep raising is an important occupation and wool is one of the exports. 

8. The Iberian peninsula has large mineral deposits. 

They include lead, zinc, quicksilver, copper, iron, and coal. 

9. Most of the people of the peninsula live along the coastal plains. The central section is thinly settled. 

There are two distinct groups of people—the highborn "gentleman" class and the working class. As many of the people are poor and uneducated the resources of the countries are undeveloped. Transportation is poor. 

10. Madrid is a beautiful city, typical of Spain. Lisbon, in Portugal, is like Madrid in many ways, but is more of a commercial city, with varied industries. 

Oporto, also a seaport, exports wine. Cadiz exports lead, copper, and iron. Barcelona is the largest manufacturing city of the peninsula. 

11. Spain has possessions in Africa and owns the 

Canary and Balearic islands. Portugal owns the 

Cape Verde islands and the Azores and Madeiras. 

She owns, too, Angola, Mozambique, and Portuguese Guinea in Africa, some ports in India, and some islands off the coast of Asia. These colonies are undeveloped because of the poverty of the 

Iberian nations.

1. Rome and the Tiber river. Rome is the capital of 

Italy, and was the center of the Roman empire. It is called the Eternal City because it is already more than 2500 years old and many believe that it will exist forever. This picture was taken from the roof of St. Peter's church in Vatican City, the headquarters of the Roman Catholic Church. Vatican City does not belong to Italy. 

It is the smallest independent state in the world.

It is one of many relics of ancient days to be seen in Rome. The bridge in the foreground is known as the Angel bridge, because of the many statues of angels with which it is decorated.

ITALY'S SUNNY SOUTH AND SICILY 

PL 

1. An Italian fish dealer. The people of southern Italy are noted for their happy ways and cheerful dispositions. 

This fish dealer seems to enjoy his work. Probably business is good, as the people of this section eat a great deal of fish. 

2. Macaroni drying in front of a macaroni factory in 

Naples. Macaroni is made from a wheat flour paste. 

A machine forms the paste into tubes. After the tubes are made they are hung on racks to dry in the sun, like tobacco in our country and hay in Norway. Nobody seems to worry for fear that dirt from the street will settle on the macaroni. 

3. The Bay of Naples, with Mount Vesuvius beyond.

Notice the long piers which protect ships from heavy waves. Naples is a picturesque city, with many queer and interesting sights, and most tourists to Italy visit it. 

The bay is noted for its beauty. Many immigrants have come to America from Naples. 

4. The crater of Mount Vesuvius, one of the most active volcanoes in the world. Its eruptions have done much damage. The city of Pompeii, buried by Vesuvius many centuries ago and recently excavated, is one of the attractions of the vicinity of Naples. 

5. A hillside in Sicily. With its hot, rainless summers, Sicily does not have rich fields of grass for dairy cattle. 

To supply their milk, the Sicilians raise goats because goats live well on such scanty pasturage as we see here. 

The little building at the end of the road is a wayside shrine.

THE MEDITERRANEAN SEA AND SURROUNDING LANDS ITALY 

Lying on the second of southern Europe's great peninsulas, and extending north of it into the Alps, is the country of Italy. The Italian peninsula has often been called a great boot, stretching southeastward into the Mediterranean sea toward Egypt. This boot is about 600 miles long, and the whole of Italy is only about 760 miles. So you can see that most of Italy's land is on the peninsula. The southern tip of 

Italy is near the 38° parallel. Rome, near the center of the boot, has a latitude of 42°, about the same as New York City's. And northern

Italy reaches almost to the 47° parallel. But in spite of its length, Italy's area is less than two and a half times that of New York State. 

Unlike Spain, Italy has no plateau bordered with narrow coastal plains. The Apennine mountains extend through the length of the peninsula. Along all the eastern coast and part of the western coast there are lowlands between the mountains and the sea. The lofty Alps form a crescent about northern Italy and extend into Italy itself. 

Between the Alps and the Apennines lies the valley of the Po river, running east and west. 

Naturally the crescent of the Alps forms a partial barrier between Italy and the rest of 

SURFACE PASSES 

Europe. But the Alps, unlike the 

Pyrenees, have several passes, through some of which railroads have been built.

The first pass to be used for travel was the lowest-the Mt. Cenis pass. It is about 3800 feet above sea level and leads from Italy to 

France. The Brenner pass leads to Austria, and since the World War has been completely controlled by Italy. The St. Gotthard, famous for its beauty, lies between Italy and the lake region of Switzerland. A railroad tunnel beneath this pass is one of the main travel routes between northern and southern Europe. Another tunnel connecting Italy and Switzerland is the Simplon tunnel built under the Simplon pass. This tunnel is over twelve miles long, the longest of its kind in the world. 

Work on it was begun at both ends, and so exact was the engineering skill with which it was planned that the two shafts under construction met perfectly.

The mountains of Italy, both the Alps and Apennines, are young and rugged. There are evidences of old volcanoes throughout the peninsula. 

The great quantities of lava which these old volcanoes once poured forth have made the soil about them rich. 

VOLCANOES AND EARTHQUAKES 

In the south of the peninsula there are still active volcanoes. Vesuvius, near the Bay of 

Naples, is about 4,000 feet in height. It is one of the most active volcanoes in the world, and is eternally smoking. Etna, about two miles high, is on the island of Sicily just off the southwest end of Italy. These volcanoes have erupted from time to time, often destroying much property and killing many people. Earthquakes are common in parts of Italy, and the surface in places is cracked and broken by them. ert.

CLIMATE 

Italy, in the Mediterranean region, has two seasons, a wet one in winter and a dry one in summer. In the summer hot winds known as Siroccos blow over the peninsula from Africa's burning des- Because of this, southern Italy is very warm and dry. Here farming without irrigation is almost impossible, and artificial means of watering have been used for many years. 

Because of its high altitude, northern Italy is much cooler than southern Italy. The valley of the Po has warm summers and mild winters because the mountains shut out the cold winds from the north.

Because their country has a large number of people who must be fed, the Italians carry on much agriculture. Their richest farm lands are in the Po basin. The 

PO BASIN 

77

EUROPE 

Po river rises in the Alps, flows east across much of northern Italy, and empties into the 

Adriatic sea. Hundreds of years ago the Po basin was an arm of the sea, but silt brought down from the mountains by the Po and its tributaries has built up an alluvial plain and a rich delta at the river's mouth. The land along the lower part of the river is so low that embankments have been built along the river to protect the nearby farms from flood. 

The warm valley of the Po has a long growing season. Its soil is deep and rich and fertile. The Po and its tributaries supply water for irrigation. All these facts combine to make the basin a wonderful agricultural section. One of the chief crops of the valley is rice. In fact, the valley of the Po with its rich

Italy cannot raise enough wheat in her limited area to feed all her people, but she does raise quantities of it in the Po valley. Corn, too, is grown and Italian boys and girls eat plenty of corn-meal mush, a cheap and nourishing food. Flax and hemp furnish fibers for textile manufactures, and mulberry trees are raised to feed the country's many silkworms. Italy produces more raw silk than any other European country. Most of the Italian farmers use modern farm machinery and modern methods of farming. 

It is no wonder, with these advantages for agriculture, that the Po valley has a greater population than any other section of Italy, and that several large and progressive cities are located there. Most of these cities are built where small valleys open into the Po valley. 

Milan, in the heart of the valley, is the second largest city of Italy. Nearly a million people live there, and it is a great center for textile manufacturing and trade. 

THE TIBER PLAINS 

Other parts of Italy are less suited for farming, but everywhere the occupation is carried on as extensively as possible. The 

Tiber river rises in the Apennines and flows south to the Mediterranean. Along its course, as along the

Po, there are rich plains, and good farm lands extend southward from the mouth of the Tiber along the coast. The country about 

Naples is especially productive. are 

Throughout this section vegetables grown in quantities. They are a food well suited to the warm climate, and extensive irrigation allows the production of two or more crops of one kind on the same soil in the same year. In some places the land is terraced to make room for more crops. By terracing and irrigation, the Italians have made much of their land productive.

Very often in Italy one sees two kinds of crops growing on the same land. Products which grow on the ground, such as peas and market-garden crops, are planted between the rows of grape vines or fruit trees. This process is called intercultivation. 

TREE PRODUCTS 

Lemons, oranges, olives, and varieties of nuts are grown extensively in southern Italy, for they require warmth and can thrive in the dry climate.

Two of Italy's most important trees are the olive and the chestnut. Olives furnish both oil and food. The oil is used in the preparation of many foods, and in the making of ointments. The Italian chestnuts are very large and are eaten boiled or roasted. They often take the place of potatoes in the daily fare. 

These nuts are also ground into a sort of meal which is mixed with flour and used for the making of bread.

USEFUL 

In the crowded market sections of Italy one sees many small wagons loaded with farm products. These wagons are drawn by small, shaggy horses or more ANIMALS often by donkeys. Larger loads are hauled by oxen, the chief draft animals of the country. There are ample grazing lands for all these animals, for they do not require rich

ITALY 

79 pasture. Sheep and goats graze by the hundreds under the olive trees and on the mountain slopes in southern Italy.

In addition to these animals, many of which are raised throughout all the Mediterranean countries, Italy raises a great many 

DAIRYING cattle, largely for dairy purposes. 

Dairying is carried on in the northern part of the country where there is sufficient rainfall for rich grazing lands for the herds. Cheese is exported, about half of it to our country. 

Goat's milk, too, is used for cheese making.

Little meat is used by the Italians in comparison with the amount used by the people of cooler countries. As a 'substi- 

SUBSTITUTES tute for meat these people use 

FOR MEAT olive oil and fish. Sardines are taken in quantities from the Adriatic, and tuna-fish are caught in the Mediterranean north and south of the mouth of the Tiber. 

Although Italy has good fisheries, they are not sufficient to supply the amount of fish needed, and thousands of tons of fish are imported each year.

MINERAL RESOURCES AND WATER POWER 

Italy suffers from a lack of coal, and although she has some iron, her mines do not produce nearly all she needs. But north of 

Trieste, in a piece of land gained at the close of the World War, there are mines of mercury, or quicksilver. These deposits make Italy a rival of Spain in the production of mercury.

At Carrara, which is in the mountains southeast of Genoa, white stainless marble and alabaster are quarried. The marble is used in buildings and statuary, the alabaster in vases.

These materials have long been used by Italy's famous artists. Sulphur is mined in Sicily, and zinc in Sardinia.

Italy's water power makes up for the lack of coal. The Italians have built generating plants which supply electricity to the cities, the mills, and the factories. Iron and coal are imported in large quantities and used in making steel and machinery. This industry centers in the Po valley, where Turin makes automobiles and railway cars, and Milan makes locomotives and many other kinds of machinery. 

Except for these iron goods, other manufactures of Italy are an outgrowth of her own raw materials. Several cities engage in making textiles- 

MANUFACTURES 

linen, woolen, and silk. The finer kinds of cloth require artistic skill in which the Italians are well gifted. Silks and tapestries, beautifully designed and woven, are exported. 

Genoa makes hats, one of the important exports to the United States. Rayon, or artificial silk, is another valuable export. Exquisite laces, straw plaiting, and jewelry are also made, largely by hand. Some of the jewelry is made of coral taken from the Mediterranean. 

At first the coral looks like weathered branches of sea growth, but rubbing and polishing bring out its lovely colors, which vary from rosy pink to fainter tints. Tiny bits of colored glass and stone are put together in what is known as mosaic ware. 

And we must not forget in our list of Italy's manufactures one of the commonest of all, carried on alike at home and in the factoriesthe making of macaroni. Macaroni is a coarse wheat flour moistened to form a paste. When the paste is made it is run through machines from which it comes out in long strings or tubes. These are hung on bars to dry. When they harden they will keep indefinitely without losing their food value or spoiling. Macaroni has become so popular in many countries that the Italians export quantities of it.

Grape wine is popular in Italy and, like macaroni, much of it is made at home. The wine made for export is drawn off in great casks for shipment, and the making of these casks furnishes another occupation for many people. 

Olive oil, here as in Spain, is prepared to be used in salad dressings or in cooking.

COMMERCE PORTS 

Textiles make up a large part of Italy's exports. Others are fruits and nuts, chemicals, olive oil, cheese, and such foodstuffs as macaroni. Italy's exports AND are worth more than those of any other Mediterranean country except France.

Italy, too, buys more goods than she sells. 

The wheat which she imports to feed her people and the raw cotton, coal, iron, and machinery to supply her factories are nearly half

EUROPE 

again as valuable as her exports. But Italy is working hard to develop her resources, and expects that in time she will export enough to pay for what she buys.

Much of Italy's commercial importance depends on her central location and on the trade which passes through her ports between the Mediterranean and the interior countries of 

Europe. Genoa, famous as a trade center before the days of Columbus, is the chief port for the Po basin and is connected with Germany by a fine direct railroad line. Trieste controls the trade of Austria through the Brenner pass. 

The possession of Trieste, Fiume, and the surrounding land gives Italy nearly full control of the commerce of the Adriatic. 

Beautiful and historic Venice, southwest of Trieste, is a city built on islands connected by countless bridges. Between the islands are waterways or canals which serve as streets, and the Venetians use long graceful Italian boats called gondolas as we use automobiles. 

Venice was once a foremost port of the Mediterranean world. The finding of new routes to the East and the growth of trade on the Atlantic diminished its commercial importance. 

Although the opening of the Suez canal partially revived the trade of Venice, the city today is more famous for its history and its beauty than for its commerce.

Brindisi is the only other port of any size on the west coast of the Adriatic. Naples, on the Mediterranean coast, is one of the most interesting cities in the world. It is literally packed with people and is Italy's largest city. 

The city lies in the center of an agricultural district and handles a large part of southern 

Italy's foreign trade. Naples has hydroelectric power, and manufactures sugar, textiles, and many other products. The Bay of Naples, on which the city is located, is the most beautiful bay in Europe.

A TOURIST LAND 

All Italy, with its warm, sunny climate, its mountains, and its excellent resorts, is a delight to tourists. Nestled in the 

Italian Alps are Lake Como and 

Lake Maggiore, rivals in beauty of the lakes of Switzerland. The Italian

Riviera is as lovely as that of France, and the Lido is a famous resort near Venice. Many places are hallowed by the memories of statesmen, poets, and teachers. And there is the great city of Rome from which the ancient Romans spread their power over the whole of Italy and most of the known world of their day. 

One might live for years in Italy's capital city of Rome and not see all of it. But this is not surprising when you consider ROME that it has taken over 2,000 years for the city to become what it is today. It had its beginning hundreds of years before Christ was born, and was originally built on two hills near the banks of the Tiber river. Now it occupies seven hills and its territory extends on both sides of the Tiber. 

Let us take a bird's-eye view of some of 

Rome's many points of interest. See the Appian way, the road of the Caesars, leading from the temple of Mars to the gates of the city and beyond the gates toward Brundisium, as Brindisi was once called. This road is so old and worn and yet so solid that it seems to have been formed by nature itself. Once it rang with the tread of Roman soldiers returning from their wars. Yonder is the Roman Forum, an ancient square surrounded by the city's principal buildings. Once it echoed with the voices of Pompey, Cicero, Caesar, and the other great Roman statesmen of ancient times. 

Over there are the ruins of the Coliseum, an enormous amphitheater, or stadium, where the Romans watched the gladiators, strong and able-bodied men, fight to the death for the amusement of the public. In the Coliseum, too, many early Christians were thrown to lions because of their faith. 

Note the entrances to the gloomy catacombs, underground burial places where the early Christians fled to worship. And see those stately columned buildings, temples to the Roman gods. The Romans used rounded arches extensively in their buildings, bridges, and temples. This form of arch is found today in modern structures all over the world. 

Northwest of the Tiber, but within the limits of Rome, is Vatican city, the center of the Roman Catholic Church and the smallest in-

ITALY 

81 dependent state in the civilized world. In it are the world's largest church, St. Peter's, and the buildings in which lives the Pope, the head of the Church. The city is under the control of the Catholic Church and is independent of the Italian government. Its buildings are renowned for their magnificence and contain priceless works of art. The Vatican library holds some of the most famous collections of books and records. 

These are only a few of the things that make 

Rome famous. Italians everywhere, whether natives of Rome or not, are proud of their capital city.

CAPRI 

Italy has many interesting sights besides. 

Rome. There is the blue expanse of the Bay of Naples broken by a few islands. One of these is Capri, famous for its scenery and for the ruins of numerous villas of ancient times. Capri is near the city of Naples and commands a fine view of the bay. The shores of the island have many sea-caves. The most beautiful is the Blue Grotto. The cave is so named because the daylight enters it through only a small opening, and the water in the cave gives the grotto a rich blue shade.

ANCIENT CITY OF POMPEII 

"And don't forget to see Pompeii!" the traveler from Italy tells us. Pompeii was completely buried in 79 A.D. by the lava and ashes of Vesuvius, but it has been excavated. So well were the buildings of Pompeii

Pompeii con- structed that parts of them are still standing and even pictures painted on the walls can still be seen.

The city of Florence is famous for its art galleries. It also has many fascinating shops where one may find attractive jewelry and lovely mosaics. The city is also a center for making straw hats, mats, and baskets.

FLORENCE SAN MARINO 

Another place of historic interest is the tiny independent republic of San Marino, whose thirty-two square miles are picturesquely situated in the Apennines, south of the Po valley. San Marino claims to be the oldest state in all Europe. 

The islands of Sicily and Sardinia are parts of the kingdom of Italy. In the long-ago days when Rome and Carthage were powerful, Sicily lay between them SICILY

AND in the middle of the Mediterranean SARDINIA sea, a veritable stepping stone from

Italy to Africa. Naturally the island became a famous battleground. Its central position in the Mediterranean region also made it a great trade center. Like other islands, Sicily was a haven for the small primitive ships of those days. As passing centuries have brought new and swifter means of transportation, trade and travel have passed Sicily by and today the island is poor. 

Sicily has a typical Mediterranean climate.

Palermo is its chief city. It exports sulphur, chestnuts, and fruits, especially lemons. The sulphur is found in very large quantities near 

Mount Etna. Recently Louisiana and Texas have far outstripped Sicily in the production of sulphur.

Sardinia, the large island northwest of Sicily, is mountainous and has a Mediterranean climate. Copper, iron, lead, zinc, and other minerals are found on the island, but the mines are little developed. Granite, marble, and clay are quarried to some extent, but the people are mostly farmers.

With her more than 40,000,000 people, Italy is far more densely populated than Spain. 

This is especially true of the Po valley and the lowland coastal regions. The only places in Italy which are not crowded are the mountain tops. 

POPULATION 

Because Italy is so crowded and because the ways of making a living there are so few, thousands of Italians have moved to other lands. Many have come to the United States, Brazil, and Argentina. These younger countries offer them work and opportunity. 

COLONIES 

Italy's largest colonies are Libia and Ethiopia, in Africa. Libia is mostly undeveloped desert. Numbers of Italians have settled here and are endeavoring to raise dates and other tropical fruits. Sponge fishing is an important coast occupation. Tripoli is the chief port.

Ethiopia, conquered by Italy in May, 1936, may in time supply homes for Italian settlers. 

The high central plateau has a favorable cli-

mate, although the lowlands are too hot and unhealthy for white people. Ethiopia has good agricultural and pasture lands and undeveloped mineral resources. A railroad connects the interior with the French port of Jibuti, on the Red Sea. 

Eritrea and Italian Somaliland are smaller and less important possessions of Italy in Africa. Both are dry and unproductive. Find all these possessions on the map, page 132. 

Besides her African possessions, Italy owns the Dodecanese islands in the Aegean sea. The people of these islands are Greeks. They raise grapes and vegetables for export.

1. Italy lies in the central part of the Mediterranean region. Its surface is largely mountainous. The 

Alps are in the north. A central range, the Apennines, extends the length of the peninsula. This range slopes east and west to coastal plains along the Adriatic and part of the Mediterranean coasts. 

2. The crescent of the Alps forms a partial barrier between Italy and the rest of Europe, but passes allow trade and travel. 

3. There are evidences of volcanoes in all parts of 

Italy, and in the south there are active ones. Of these the most famous are Vesuvius, near Naples, and Etna, in Sicily. 

4. Italy has a wet season in winter and a dry season in summer. Irrigation is necessary, especially in the southern part which is very warm and dry. 

The northern part is cooler than the southern part. 

5. The Po delta and plain have the finest agricultural land in Italy. Wheat, corn, rice, flax, and hemp are grown there. More people live in this valley than in any other part of Italy, and here are several large and progressive cities. Milan, in the heart of the valley, is a trade and manufacturing center. 

6. Another good agricultural section stretches along the Tiber plains and southward along the Mediterranean coast, especially about Naples. Here vegetables, grapes, olives, and citrus fruits are grown. 

Intercultivation is practiced. Chestnuts form a popular food of the Italian people. 

7. Oxen are the chief beasts of burden in Italy.

Horses and donkeys are also used. Goats are raised for their milk, and sheep are extensively raised in the southern part of the peninsula. In the northern part dairying is carried on. Cheese is exported. Fish and olive oil are used in place of meat. 

8. Italy has deposits of quicksilver, or mercury, and some zinc is mined, but the country is lacking in coal. Water power in part makes up for this lack. 

Coal and iron are imported. Turin makes automobiles and railway cars. Milan and Turin are centers of steel industries. Most of Italy's other manufactures are an outgrowth of her own raw materials. These manufactures include textiles, jewelry, straw goods, olive oil, wine, and macaroni. 

Carrara has stainless white marble. 

9. Italy's commerce depends largely upon her central position among the countries of the Mediterranean and the location of two of her ports, Genoa and 

Trieste. Genoa is the chief port for the Po basin and has a direct rail line to Germany. Trieste, on a line with the Brenner pass, is a port for Austria. 

Two other ports on the eastern coast are Venice and Brindisi. Italy has nearly full control of the commerce of the Adriatic sea. Naples, on the western coast, is the largest city in Italy and handles a large part of southern Italy's foreign trade. 

10. Italy offers many attractions to the tourist. These include pleasant climate, delightful scenery, and fine resorts. The whole country is rich in historic scenes and places. A few of the places to visit in 

Rome are the Appian way, the Forum, the Vatican, temples of Roman gods, and the Coliseum. Other points of interest in Italy are the Bay of Naples, Pompeii, and Florence. 

11. Italy's island of Sicily, because of its central position in the Mediterranean region, was once important, but newer and swifter means of travel have taken its trade away. Today the country is poor. Its chief city, Palermo, exports fruits and sulphur. Sardinia belongs to Italy. 

12. Italy has a dense population. Because of crowded conditions in the homeland thousands of Italians have migrated to the United States, Brazil, and Argentina. 

13. Italy has a few colonial possessions of which the largest are Libia and Ethiopia, in Africa. Others are 

Eritrea and Italian Somaliland, in Africa, and the

THE MEDITERRANEAN SEA AND SURROUNDING LANDS FORMER GLORY GREECE 

Greece lies on the third or easternmost peninsula of southern Europe-the Balkan. Greece is about the size of the state of New York, and has a population of somewhat over 6,000,000 people. We hear very little of its present activities but some 2,500 years ago the Greeks were the greatest nation in the world. Greece had famous orators, writers, statesmen, athletes, and sculptors. Its buildings were of great size and beauty. The marble statues by its sculptors were so lovely that they have been reproduced time and again. And we still read the writings of its famous men. The Greek merchant fleet was large and commanded great respect, for Greece was a commercial nation whose sailors were fearless and adventurous.

But Greece had one great handicap. The country is very mountainous and the different ranges divide the land into separate sections. 

Because of this the Greeks were not a united nation. Each section was free and independent, ran its own affairs, and was known as a city-state. These city-states were jealous of one another and there was much warfare between them. Then, other countries came to be envious of the glory and culture of Greece and made war on the Greeks. And so, weakened within by lack of unity, and attacked by enemies from without, Greece at last lost its power. For a time it was governed by the country of Macedonia which lay to the north and is now a part of Greece. Then it was conquered by the mighty Romans. Other nations followed the Romans but at last Greece became an independent kingdom and, a few years ago, a republic.

Every year many visitors from all parts of the world go to the ancient Greek city of 

ATHENS 

Athens to see the beautiful buildings and the works of art that have existed since the days when Athens was at the height of her glory. Perhaps the best-known building is the Parthenon, one of the splendid temples built on a great hill overlooking the city. The Parthenon was almost destroyed in a war, but is now being rebuilt. 

Today, Athens is the capital of the republic of Greece and is still a center for Greek education and culture. But, beautiful and interesting as is the modern city, it is the ruins of ancient works of former days that fascinate visitors.

BOUNDARIES 

We do not wonder that the Greeks early became and still are a nation of traders and sailors when we look at the location, the surface, and the surroundings of their country. Lying in the southern part of the Balkan peninsula, Greece looks out to sea on the east, the south and the west. It is bounded by the Aegean, the 

Mediterranean, and the Ionian seas. Its coast line is a maze of gulfs, inlets, peninsulas, and harbors. As in England, no part of the country is very far from the sea. 

SURFACE 

About four-fifths of Greece is mountainous, and only about one-fifth of the country is suitable for cultivation. Its surface is as varied as its coast line. The rugged mountain chains lie everywhere. The most important chain is the Pindus, which is an extension of the Dinaric Alps. In places the mountains come straight down to the coast and disappear under the sea, to appear again farther out in the form of islands. There is a limited coastal plain, most of which is pro ductive. The districts of Thessaly and Mace donia have fertile lowlands, but much of the soil in the rest of Greece is rather barren. The rivers are short and rapid, and there are many lakes. The country is a mixture of mountains, lowlands, plateaus, and river basins. 

In general, the climate of Greece is Mediterranean, with the usual mild winters and the hot, dry summers. But, of course, CLIMATE different altitudes of the country 84

1. Modern Athens from the Olympic stadium. The build ings of the ancient Greeks were once the most beautiful in the world. Tourists still come to Athens to see their ruins. But the newer part of Athens is worth seeing, too. 

Its broad streets, handsome homes, and fine public buildings make it one of the world's most beautiful cities. 

2. A steamship passing through the Corinth canal. The narrow neck of land which is cut by this canal once separated the Gulf of Corinth from the Aegean sea. In former days vessels traveling from one to the other had to make a much longer journey because there was no passageway connecting them. This four-mile short cut was planned centuries ago by the Romans, was begun by the French, and was completed in 1893 by the Greeks. 

3. Harvesting rye in Greece. Modern machinery is rare in this country, and old farming methods are still widely used. In our country a machine would cut and thresh this grain in one operation. But Greek farmers cut it with sickles, tie it up in bundles, and carry the bundles to the barn, where they thresh the rye by hand.

Here goods come for export from those of the Balkan states which have arranged with Greece to make use of her northern seaport. Saloniki was once a Turkish town and the slender towers are the minarets of Mohammedan churches, or mosques.

SCENES IN NORTH AFRICA 

3 22 

1. Primitive farming in North Africa. These Arabs have never seen a steel plow. They live in one of the backward parts of North Africa where modern machinery has not yet been introduced. Notice the homemade, wooden spades. Farming with such tools is a slow, hard task, and the amount of ground one man can till is small. 

2. Plowing with a tractor in Egypt. Farm machinery is still new to most of North Africa. Ox-drawn plows are more familiar sights than tractors. But the use of machinery is rapidly increasing there, which gives American and European manufacturers new markets. 

3. A French-built road in the Atlas mountains. Until the coming of the French the Atlas district had poor transportation. Roads were rough trails over rocks and sand, and travel was slow and dangerous. Notice the way in which this fine road has been cut through solid rock. The building of good roads is only one of the many benefits which French rule has brought to North Africa. 

4. The harbor of Algiers, the capital of Algeria. About a hundred years ago a French army besieged Algiers and defeated the pirates who held the town. Since that time the old pirate stronghold has become one of the busiest and most important of French ports. Notice the merchant ship loading at the dock. The ship in the foreground is a French battleship.

GREECE 

85 affect the climate greatly. In the uplands and in the north the winters are often severe, with snow and raw, cold winds. Rainfall throughout the country is light even in winter, and the land needs to be irrigated. 

PRODUCTS 

Along the western coast grow the products of a Mediterranean climate. Olives, raisins, oranges, lemons, figs, and wines are among the chief products. Grains are also grown to a great extent, though wheat and flour are the leading imports. Some mulberry trees are raised. The region along the southern border of the Gulf of Corinth is used for growing small, seedless grapes which are dried to make small raisins, called currants.

These currants are one of the chief exports of Greece, and many thousands of people depend upon the currant industry for their living. 

The lowlands of Macedonia make good tobacco lands, and tobacco is the chief export crop of Greece. Grazing is carried on in all the upland areas. The country also has mineral wealth. The mines produce lignite, iron, and chromite, which is used in making steel. Lead and magnesia are also exported. The forests of Greece have been terribly wasted, but the land is being reforested.

TRANSPORTATION 

The mountainous character of the country has good effects as well as bad. The mountains furnish minerals and grazing lands, and help to make the people independent and freedomloving by separating them from others. But, as in ancient times, the mountains make it very difficult to unite the country. Many sections are entirely cut off from their neighbors, and the building of roads and railroads is slow and expensive. Interior communication is still poor, though it is being gradually improved. After many years of work, the Corinth canal has been cut across the Isthmus of Corinth, connecting the Gulf of Corinth with the Aegean sea.

Greece has good harbors, but they were of more importance to her in the days of her glory than they are today. Piraeus is the harbor of Athens. Saloniki, at the mouth of the Vardar valley, has a beautiful harbor, and is one of the chief cities of Greece. Some of the Balkan states, through treaties with Greece, have arranged to use this seaport as an outlet for their products. Patras is the port that exports the huge shipments of currants that leave Greece every year. Greece owns the island of Crete and many small islands in the Aegean sea, as well as the many islands near the country's western coast. 

The people of Greece struggled through long years of cruelty, misery, and poverty under their different captors. This has put them sadly behind in the progress of the world. 

Much of their work is done in a very simple and primitive manner, and they have few industries. But we must never forget the world's debt to Greece. A great deal of all that is fine and good in our times may be traced directly back to that country whose statesmen and whose scholars were wise, and whose ideals were beauty and truth. 

1. Greece was once a great nation, but through wars of ancient days and lack of unity it has lost its power. Athens still has many ruins and these attract visitors each year. Every country owes much to the early Greek writers, orators, statesmen, and sculptors. 

2. Greece is the southern part of the Balkan peninsula.

Its coast line is extremely irregular, with many harbors, gulfs, and peninsulas. About four-fifths of the country is mountainous, and about one-fifth is suited to cultivation. The Pindus mountains are an extension of the Dinaric Alps. This country has many plateaus, and here and there a limited coastal plain. Much of the soil is poor, but the lowlands of Thessaly and Macedonia are fertile. 

3. Greece has a Mediterranean climate. But in the uplands and to the north the winters are often severe, and the winds are cold. Rainfall is light. 

4. On the western coast grow the fruits and grains of a Mediterranean climate. Along the southern border of the Gulf of Corinth small seedless grapes are dried into currants, which form a chief export of Greece. The tobacco of Macedonia is the most important export crop of Greece. 

5. Inland communication is poor, because of the mountainous character of the country. The Corinth canal connects the Gulf of Corinth with the Aegean sea. Piraeus is the harbor of Athens, which is the capital of the republic. Patras exports currants. 

Saloniki has a beautiful harbor and is one of the chief cities of Greece.

THE MEDITERRANEAN SEA AND SURROUNDING LANDS NORTH AFRICA 

The countries of northern Africa are not young, vigorous countries, such as we consider our own to be. They are old

AN ANCIENT lands, whose people are de- 

LAND 

scended from ancient races that have lived under Africa's hot sun for many centuries.

In the course of history the Phoenicians visited northern Africa and established colonies there. Then came the Romans. The north 

African region was once one of the great granaries of ancient Rome. That empire needed many such granaries to supply her cities and her great armies. There are still many remains of the Roman occupation-such as walls, parts of buildings, tombs and aqueducts, built so well that they have lasted all these centuries. 

Other conquerors followed the Romans, and then for many years pirates swarmed along the coast.

These attacked many vessels, seizing their cargoes and either killing their passengers and crews or carrying them off to be sold as slaves or held for ransom. More than a hundred years ago the power of the pirates was broken by our own United States navy. 

Today, the countries of northern Africa are moving gradually towards order and progress. 

They are being caught up in that great bond of trade which is tying the whole world together. You will notice on the map on page 

62 that Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libia, and 

Egypt are the northernmost countries of 

Africa. But only the French lands of Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia are really Mediterranean in climate and in products. 

Across Morocco, northern Algeria, and northern Tunisia extend the young, rugged

THE 

ATLAS 

DISTRICT 

Atlas mountains, lifting in places to heights of 14,000 feet. Like all mountains the Atlas affect the countries through which they extend. They cause the winds to lose their moisture in rain, they provide grazing lands for cattle, and they hide rich stores of minerals. 

Between the inner and outer ranges of the Atlas mountains lie plateaus which are used for raising grain and for cattle grazing. Between the Atlas mountains and the sea is a coastal lowland known to the natives as the Tell. This lowland is from fifty to one hundred miles wide and supplies fruits and vegetables for European markets.

Products. As the Atlas district has a Mediterranean climate, the usual crops of a Mediterranean climate are raised. Wheat and barley are among the cereal crops. The subtropical fruits-oranges, figs, olives, and grapesgrow in abundance. From the olives, olive oil is made for export. The grapes are made into wine or are dried to make raisins. Wine is exported. Mulberry trees grow well, and silkworms are raised. The cork oak which grows on the mountain slopes furnishes cork for export. Morocco sends poultry and eggs to England. Tobacco crops swell the exports of 

Algeria. Dates grow in the desert oases.

There are many grazing lands on the great tablelands and in the elevated valleys of this region, and large herds of cattle roam the broad pastures. Sheep have been raised here for many centuries and numbers of them are shipped to France. The horses and mules and native cattle are of excellent types, and hides and leathers form a large part of the exports of this region. 

From the mountains are taken iron ore, zinc, phosphate rock, copper, lead, and other minerals.

Trade and Seaports. The greatest trade is with France, who controls all of this territory but a part of Morocco. And, of course, where there is commerce there must be seaports.

The most important are Algiers, the capital of 

Algeria, and Tunis, the capital of Tunisia. The imports that come into these cities from 87

THE MEDITERRANEAN LANDS 

France and other countries include cotton cloth, tea, sugar, machinery, automobiles, hardware, and other manufactured products.

Progress. After the Roman rule, the growing of grain was neglected for many years, and it has taken hard work for France to build this industry up once more. The French have sunk artesian wells, taught the natives scientific agriculture and the use of fertilizers, and introduced modern machinery. They are building good roads and railroads, and they have established some telephone and telegraph lines.

Population. The natives of the Atlas countries are mostly Arabs and Berbers. Besides the natives there are many colonists from France, Spain, Italy, and other lands. The colonists cultivate the fertile northern coast.

The Arabs live on the plains. The Berbers live in the mountains, and, as a protection against wandering bands of robbers, they still live in walled villages. Many of the natives are nomads, or wanderers, who drive their flocks from one pasture land to another.

The dress of the natives is suited to the climate. Some dress in long, white flowing garments, as white reflects the sun's heat away from the body. Many wear white turbans, and others wear fezzes, red caps with tassels. Men often wear bright baggy trousers. One sees women whose faces are covered so that only their eyes show.

Mohammedanism is the chief religion of the natives. The Mohammedans cling stubbornly to old ways, saying that what was good enough for their fathers is good enough for them. They have opposed the improvements of the French and hindered the progress of the country.

LIBIA 

To the east of the Atlas countries is the Italian colony of Libia. Libia is mostly desert land with here and there a rich oasis which produces fine dates. Along the coast there is more rainfall and some farming is done. The main crop is esparto grass, used in making paper and rope. Sponges are gathered near the shores and many are exported. 

Tripoli is the chief city. It is both a seaport and the starting place for caravan routes across the desert.

East of Libia is the country of Egypt. Here as in the Atlas countries we find a curious mixture of races, customs, and beliefs. 

Egypt's climate and products, however, are different from those of the other Mediterranean lands.

EGYPT 

The history of Egypt goes back much further than that of any of the countries you have studied. The early Egyptians were slim brown people. They were very remarkable builders. Out of huge heavy blocks of stone they built the mighty pyramids, which still stand today. They built the Sphinx-an enormous stone figure, having the body of a lion and the head of a man. On the walls of their temples they carved pictures which give a history of their life and their country. 

Climate. Because it is in the belt of the drying northeast trade winds, much of Egypt is desert with mile upon mile of nothing but sand. 

Along the Mediterranean coast a small strip of land receives a fair amount of rain. But the rest is for the most part dry, except for an occasional storm. The temperature is high during the day, but the land cools off rapidly at night.

The Nile. The Nile river rises in the belt of heavy rains near the Equator, and flows north through the eastern part of Egypt. Each year the river overflows its banks and spreads a layer of fine fertile silt over many miles of its valley. Some of the silt which the Nile brings down from the mountains is carried along and added to the river's delta. The delta of the 

Nile is one of the most fertile regions in all the world. The British have built a great irrigation dam across the Nile at Assuan, which holds back flood water until it is needed. Then it is let into irrigation ditches. Through the overflow of the Nile and through artificial irrigation, great areas of desert land are made to produce two or three crops a year. 

Products. Cotton is the chief crop of Egypt.

Egyptian cotton is considered especially good as it has a long fiber. Most of this cotton goes to the British Isles. Other crops include dates, oranges, lemons, pomegranates, vegetables, sugar, and grains. One also sees a wide variety of flowers.

NORTH AFRICA 

89 

British Influence. 

For many years Egypt was a part of the British Empire, and the bulk of its trade was with Great Britain. Today 

Egypt is an independent country, but Great Britain is still favored in commerce, and has certain rights which protect her investments in irrigation projects, in railroads, and in the Suez canal. All of these have helped to develop 

Egypt. 

Great Britain controls the Suez canal, connecting the Mediterranean and the Red sea, and therefore the shortest water route from 

Europe to the Far East. Ships, at one time, had to go all the way around Africa to reach these eastern markets, but the Suez canal has done away with that long, tedious journey.

This canal reaches from Port Said on the 

Mediterranean to Suez on the Red sea.

The Cape-to-Cairo railroad will be another great link in transportation controlled by England. This road will run from Cape Town at the southern tip of Africa to Cairo, on the delta of the Nile, a distance of 7,000 miles. It will be one of the world's longest railroads.

SIZE RUSSIA THE UNION OF SOVIET SOCIALIST REPUBLICS 

In point of size Russia is the giant country of the world. North and south it stretches from the Arctic ocean to the Black sea, and east and west it spreads from the Pacific almost to the Baltic sea. This immense country lies in two continents. The western part is in Europe and the eastern part in Asia. 

When Europe and Asia are spoken of as a connected whole they are called Eurasia, and 

Russia is an Eurasian country.

GOVERNMENT 

Before the World War this vast land was known as the Russian empire. It was ruled by an emperor, the Czar, who had absolute power. The common people were allowed almost no voice in the government. The Russian empire was even larger than the Russia of today.

The World War years worked many changes in Russia. In 1917 a revolution within the country overthrew the Czarist government and weakened Russia's hold over many parts of its empire. Finland and the three Baltic countries of Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia seized the opportunity offered by these internal troubles to establish their independence. Bessarabia declared itself independent and later joined 

Rumania. Following the World War, most of the Russian territory within the ancient borders of Poland was included in that reunited country. Find these countries on the map, pages 18-19.

From the rest of Russia's territory a number of republics were formed which united under the name of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, abbreviated U. S. S. R. A soviet socialist republic is a republic governed by a council or committee of its workers, the government having the control of the railroads, factories, lands, and other means of producing wealth. Moscow is the center of all government. 

The great majority of Russia's millions of people are poor and unschooled. For cen 

POPULATION 

turies they have had few rights.

Only since the forming of the Soviet Union have they had a voice in the affairs of their country. They are trying very hard to form a government which will work for the good of all, and the eyes of all the world are watching their efforts. They have not yet been educated up to their new responsibilities, and progress has been very slow. The new government has lacked funds to establish schools and develop the resources of the country. 

The very size of Russia makes problems of transportation, government, and industry very hard to solve. Then, too, Russia is made up of a number of different peoples. Most of them are Asiatic, but they belong to various races of Asiatics and speak different languages. 

Because Russia extends from about 77° to about 37° north latitude we know that it must have a variety of climates in spite of the fact that its surface is generally low and level.

CLIMATE 

A small strip of country along the Black sea has a Mediterranean climate, but the great central part of the Soviet Union has a continental climate. The summers are hot but the winters are long and extremely cold. One of the coldest regions in the world is in the northern part of Asiatic Russia. Throughout most of

Russia the frosts set in early. From October to 

March there are apt to be bad storms. Across the open spaces wild hurricanes sweep, bringing biting blizzards. Even on the arid plains east of the Caspian sea it becomes bitterly cold in winter, although there is seldom snow.

The winds that sweep so freely across Russia bring only a little rain. They have left so much on the countries of western Europe that little remains for this great country so hemmed in by land. Throughout the central parts of both European and Asiatic Russia the rainfall is fair, and is usually sufficient for agriculture. North and east of the Caspian sea the rainfall is slight and the land is so dry that irrigation is necessary for the raising of crops. In the far north also there is little rainfall. 91

RUSSIA 

93 In the west-central part of European Russia is a low plateau. Rivers have cut through the plateau dividing it into rounded hills 

SURFACE 

called the Valdai hills. From this plateau the land sweeps out in all directions in vast, low, slightly swelling plains, broken by many rivers, canals, and lakes. Beyond the 

Ural mountains the plains extend through most of Asiatic Russia and are bordered on the east by wide stretches of uplands and mountains.

The mountains of the Soviet Union are of different types. There are the old, worn Ural mountains which form part of the boundary between Europe and Asia and are too low to be a serious barrier to transportation. There are the young, high, rugged Caucasus mountains which also divide Europe and Asia.

These mountains are even higher than the Alps and naturally they are very hard to cross. 

In the extreme eastern part of the country, in Asia, are the low Stanovoi mountains, and in the southern part are young rugged mountains which are part of the Altai range. Find these mountain ranges on the map, page 92.

One part of Russia is even below sea level. 

This region borders the Caspian sea. The Caspian sea has no outlet, but the water evaporates as fast as the rivers supply it. Because there is no way for the dissolved salts brought in by the inlets to escape, the Caspian is steadily growing saltier. The water there is much more salty than that of the ocean.

TUNDRAS In the Arctic region of Russia, as in Alaska and Canada, there are tundras, with growths of mosses, lichens, shrubs, and quick-flowering plants which spring up and blossom during the short summer. The tundras are peopled by nomads or wandering folk who drive their herds of reindeer from place to place seeking pasture. The reindeer meat provides the people with food and the reindeer hides are made into clothing. 

South of the tundras stretches the forest belt, which extends clear across the Soviet 

Union to the Pacific. So great is the

FORESTS 

extent of the forest belt that it should supply abundant lumber for many years to come. The northern forests contain evergreens, whose timber is exported. This belt has dense softwood forests broken by many marshes and thickets, and numerous lakes and swampy meadows. During the long, cold winter deep snow covers the ground for many months. 

Here and there in the forests are villages built in cleared spaces. The people that live in this region raise oats and potatoes and other hardy crops during their short summers. In the winter they hunt and fish, trap fur-bearing animals, and cut down timber for shipment in the spring. The wild animals which roam the 

Russian forests furnish some of the loveliest and most valuable furs that can be bought. 

The southern part of the forest belt contains both hard and soft woods, and lumber and wood pulp are valuable exports. In this forest belt the soil is more dry and marshes are less numerous than in the evergreen belt. The surface is more rolling, and much more of it is cleared and farmed than in the forest belt to the north. There are more little villages, set closer together, and the crops are somewhat more varied and abundant. Wheat, rye, and barley are seen in the fields about the little settlements.

South from the forests of European Russia and western Asiatic Russia there is the famous

EUROPE BLACK EARTH 

Russian black earth belt, the

OR WHEAT BELT soil of which is probably as fertile as any soil in the world. 

It is black from the vegetable mold which has been accumulating in it for many centuries, and is extremely rich-the best possible soil for the raising of wheat.

The villages are numerous in this region, and the peasants are somewhat better off than those farther north, for this is the great wheat region of Russia, one of the most extensive grain belts of all the world. Many nations turn to Russia for the grains that their own limited fields or poor soils cannot supply. This black earth region resembles our prairies, but is even more fertile, and Russia is a close rival of the 

United States in the production of grain.

Besides the ever-present wheat, there are acres upon acres of oats, rye, barley, and hemp. 

Potatoes are the largest, although not the most valuable, food crop. Flax, too, is raised in enormous quantities and is exported to the linen factories of France and Ireland. Sugar beets are one of the chief crops, and sugar refineries are increasing in Russia. The tobacco crop is also important. Corn is raised in the southwest part of the region. Sunflowers are grown for a valuable table oil which is pressed from their seeds. The western part of this agricultural section is the richer, as towards the east the rainfall is less and the winters are longer and colder.

Besides growing crops, the farmers of this district raise cattle and carry on a large dairy industry.

Agriculture is the chief industry of the Russian peasant. But even this chief industry has been carried on in a very crude and slow manner with the poorest of tools, many of which were homemade. In the past, the land was owned, not by the peasants themselves, but by the villages, and was redistributed among the peasants each year. One year a farmer would have a certain plot of land outside the village, and the next year his neighbor might have that land and he would be given another plot. Or sometimes tenant-farming was practised, the land being owned by rich men and rented out to the farmers.

Neither of these systems has worked for the good of the country or for the happiness of the people. A farmer easily loses his ambition if he knows that the land he works this year may be taken away from him next year, or that a
