The present Russian government is trying to work out a system of distributing the land in a fairer manner. 

The Russians are great admirers of American farm machinery, and are buying much of it from us. Because the individual peasants are too poor to buy machines, a village often buys them and the farmers rent them. 

The grain fields and the black earth region give way on the south to what is called the steppe, a grassy plain which covers thousands of square miles 

THE STEPPE 

east, north, and west of the Caspian sea. As

RUSSIA 

95 there is not enough rainfall on the steppe for farming, it is used as grazing land. The people of the steppe are nomads who wander over the plain with their large herds of cattle, sheep, goats, and horses. The steppe, in addition to being grazing land, also has large deposits of coal and iron. It is, too, the home of the Russian Cossacks, or cavalrymen, who are counted among the most daring horseback riders in the world.

The part of the steppe which is in Asia is called the Kirghiz steppe and the nomads who live there belong to the Kirghiz tribes. 

South of the Kirghiz steppe is a stretch of desert land, the lowland of Turan. Here little

DESERT 

grows except in the southeast part, where irrigation is carried on. The people of this section raise fruit, vegetables, grain, and mulberry trees, upon whose leaves silkworms are fed. The people are very skilful in the making of silk rugs and shawls. The irrigated land produces nearly as much cotton as the whole of Egypt. This cotton is used in 

Russian mills. 

Along the Black sea, where there is a mild climate, grapes, olives, and figs are grown. 

Wheat, barley, sugar beets, tobacco, flax, and hemp are also grown in this region. 

BLACK AND CASPIAN SEA REGION 

Russia is a near-rival of the United States not only in the production of grains, but in the production of petroleum as well. There are rich oil wells around the city of Baku, on the Caspian sea. Many of the Russian railroads are run by oil. It is unfortunate that these oil wells are on the inland Caspian sea, as the oil must be piped to Batum on the Black sea and exported from there. It is also sent up the Volga, which is connected by canal with the White sea and the Baltic sea. 

The Caspian sea and a number of smaller bodies of salt water in this region supply another natural resource of this section of Russia-salt. The sea water is heated and evaporated, leaving the salt behind. 

The entire northern part of Asiatic Russia is known as Siberia. Siberia contributes a great deal to the fur and mineral output of Russia. Furs are our most im 

SIBERIA 

portant import from Russia. The animals that live in the intense cold of Siberia grow very thick furs, which bring a high price. They include sable, ermine, fox, bear, and beaver. 

Platinum, which is even more valuable than gold, is found in Siberia, and varieties of precious stones also come from there. Along the route of the Trans-Siberian railroad, which crosses both European and Asiatic Russia, little towns have sprung up which do some manufacturing and are trading centers for furs and minerals. Dairying is an important industry along this route.

WATER ROUTES AND SEAPORTS 

Notice on the map on page 92 the rivers of this country. Since ancient times, Russia, especially European Russia, has had a means of local transportation in its rivers.

These rivers are as a rule broad, placid streams, making their way in enormous curves across the vast plains. In Asiatic Russia, the largest rivers flow north into the Arctic ocean. This shows that that part of Russia slopes decidedly to the north. In European Russia rivers flow in all directions. This means that European 

Russia has radial drainage. The Volga, Dnieper, Don, and Dvina in Europe and the Ob, Yenisei, and Lena in Asia are all navigable for much of their lengths, for the levelness of the country prevents the waterfalls and rapids so frequently found in the rivers of North and 

South America. 

Unfortunately, however, the climate unfits the rivers for large boats. In summer, because of light rainfall, many of the rivers become low. Even the Volga gets so shallow at certain times that only vessels of light draft can navigate it. In the winter the streams freeze. 

Many of them are frozen by the middle of October and by the middle of December nearly all of them are ice-covered. The Siberian rivers flow north into an ocean that is almost continually ice-bound.

The Dvina river flows north into the White sea and has Archangel as its port, although for many months of the year it is a frozen port. 

The Pechora flows into the Arctic ocean. The 

Neva flows into the Gulf of Finland at the point where Leningrad is located. To the

EUROPE 

south, the Dnieper, the Don, and the Dniester flow into the Black sea. These southern rivers are all navigable and are of great value because the Black sea is open the year round while the White and Baltic seas are frozen over for so much of the time.

European Russia's longest river, the Volga, flows into the Caspian sea, which is unfortunate, as the Caspian sea has no outlet. A canal is planned between the Volga and the Don rivers to carry shipments to the Black sea and so to the Mediterranean. To the north, you remember, the Volga is connected with the 

White and Baltic seas.

In order to travel from the Black sea to the Mediterranean, ships must pass through the Strait of Bosporus, past the city of Istanbul (Constantinople), which belongs to the country of Turkey. It has happened in the past that in time of war Turkey and Russia have been on opposite sides, and Russian shipping could not go through this strait. In time of peace, however, the Bosporus is very useful. 

Great grain shipments leave Russia's Black sea port of Odessa by this route for European ports. Much grain is also sent north through

Leningrad, and oil is shipped from Batum. 

Though railroads connect the main cities of European Russia, the Soviet Union has few 

RAILROADS 

miles of rail for the size of the country. However, the building of the Trans-Siberian railroad was a long step forward. The Trans-Siberian railroad is about 

6000 miles long and links the eastern and western parts of this far-flung country. It runs from western Russia to the port of Vladivostok on the Pacific coast, and also connects with Port Arthur, a city in Manchukuo held by the Japanese. The Trans-Siberian railroad puts 

Siberia in touch with the outside world and offers an outlet for its minerals and furs. It also gathers up the agricultural, mineral, and forest products of European Russia and carries them to ports in the east and west. 

It is partly due to lack of proper transportation that the natural resources of Russia, in- 

MINERALS 

cluding the soil, the vast forests, the pasture lands, and the mineral deposits have been little developed. Coal, iron, gold, copper, and platinum are found in the Ural mountains and in many places throughout the Soviet Union. Manganese comes from the Caucasus mountains. Silver and zinc also form part of Russia's undeveloped wealth. 

FISHING 

One Russian industry of some importance is fishing. Men living near the White sea earn their living by fishing and by catching seals. Those along the Caspian also catch seals, and fish for sturgeon. The eggs of the sturgeon are considered a great delicacy. They are salted and sold under the name of caviar.

Manufacturing on a large scale is still undeveloped in the Soviet Union. This is true partly because the people are untrained in factory work. In 

MANUFACTURING 

the larger cities, however, factories have been slowly increasing in number since the World War. Most of the industry of the country is directed by the government, which is working hard to increase manufacturing. The making of cotton goods is one of the leading manufactures, and in addition to the large Russian crop much cotton is imported from the United States. The making of sugar from sugar beets is another industry.

CITIES 

Moscow. Moscow, the capital and largest city of the Soviet Union, is also its chief manufacturing city. It specializes in cotton, wool, and linen textiles, in leather goods, and in machinery. This city is about the size of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and is located in the central part of European Russia. 

For years its famous churches, monasteries, and palaces have been an attraction to visitors. 

Moscow is a commercial city with many interesting markets and bazaars. Through it go the country's grain, oil, furs, and other products on their way to the seaports. This famous inland city is within reach of rivers which lead in every direction and is the railroad center of the Soviet Union.

Stalingrad. Russia's Soviet government, in its effort to increase manufacturing, has developed on the Volga river a new industrial city, Stalingrad. With modern methods and modern machinery, it hopes to build here a great center of industry for southern Russia.

RUSSIA 

97 

Leningrad. Leningrad, on the Gulf of Finland, has an unusual history. In the early days it seemed unlikely that there would ever be a city where Leningrad stands, as the land was damp and marshy and the climate unhealthful. 

But Russia had a powerful ruler, named Peter the Great, who wanted, he said, a window through which he could keep his eye on the other nations of Europe, all of whom he distrusted. He decided to have a city on the Gulf of Finland, dampness or no dampness, and a city he eventually had. Workmen died by the hundreds, and whole villages of people were obliged to break up their homes and move to the new city to provide inhabitants for it. The city was first known as St. Petersburg, later as Petrograd, and now as Leningrad. It is 

Russia's second largest city and exports grains, furs, minerals, and other Russian products. 

Kiev and Odessa. Kiev is a very old city which lies near the black earth region and is a market center for its products. The city has textile plants, iron and steel works, sugar refineries, flour mills, and tobacco factories. 

Odessa, on the Black sea, is a milling center and a grain-exporting seaport. It has long been an important trading city.

1. Russia, or the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, stretches from the Arctic ocean to the Black sea, and from the Baltic to the Pacific ocean. The western part is in Europe and the eastern part in Asia. West-central European Russia has a low plateau, from which the land sweeps in broad, slightly swelling plains. Its surface is cut by rivers into rounded hills. Around the Caspian sea the land is below sea level. Between Europe and Asia tries the population is scattered. There are few large cities, many farming communities, and great areas where no one lives at all. Both countries are more agricultural than industrial. 

The latitudes of the two countries are about the same, and the vegetation and natural resources are very much alike. In the severely cold regions of the north are the tundras.

South of them stretch the forests with their timber and fur-bearing animals. Then come the wheat fields and grazing lands. There are dairy farming and fruit growing in each country, and in each there are large deposits of coal and other minerals. 

But Canada has a most excellent natural waterway to the Atlantic ocean in the Great 

Lakes and the St. Lawrence. Her railroad system, although not much greater in miles than that of Russia, includes three transcontinental lines and many other lines in the more important districts. So, while the two countries have much the same resources, Canada's better transportation gives her an advantage in marketing her products.

Then, too, our own industrial country to the south takes about one-fourth of Canada's exports. Russia's markets are farther away and harder to reach. Canada has had a more generous government and better schools, and her people have enjoyed many more rights than have the Russian peasants. The Canadians are better educated, more skilled at their work, and more accustomed to the use of machinery than the Russians. Canada's exports are two-and-one-half times those of Russia. 

The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics must go through a long period of development before it will reach an importance in the world corresponding to its size.

2. Along the Black sea Russia has a Mediterranean climate. The climate of central Russia is continental, with very cold winters and hot summers. In the north the winters are very cold. The winds do not bring much moisture. In the arid Caspian sea region irrigation must be practiced in order to grow crops.

3. Russia has a number of different regions. In the north are the tundras with their growths of mosses, lichens, and quick-flowering plants. Here nomads live with their herds of reindeer. South of the tundras is the immense forest belt. The northern part is an evergreen or softwood forest. The southern part has both soft and hard wood. The timber is a valuable export, and forest animals are trapped for their fur. There is a little farming done in the northern part, and much more in the southern part of the forest belt. 

4. South of the forest belt is the black earth or wheat belt. Here are the famous grain lands. Among the important crops are wheat, oats, rye, barley, flax, sugar beets, potatoes, and tobacco. Dairying is carried on. 

5. South of the black earth belt is the steppe, a grassy plain which is used as grazing land. This grassy plain supports large herds of cattle, sheep, goats, and horses. 

6. In the region around the Black sea the fruits of a 

Mediterranean climate are grown. There are great oil wells near Baku on the Caspian sea. In the arid Turan lowland, south of the Kirghiz steppe, the people weave rich rugs and shawls of silk, and cotton is raised by irrigation. Along the Trans- 

Siberian railroad the dairying industry has developed. 

7. The drainage of European Russia is radial. In 

Asiatic Russia the more important rivers run north, as the land slopes in that direction. Many of Russia's rivers are navigable. 

8. The seaports and sea routes of northern Russia are closed for many months of the year. The river Volga is European Russia's longest river. 

The most important railroad in all Russia is the Trans-Siberian line, which connects western Russia with Pacific ports and opens up an outlet for the products of Siberia. Russia's railroads are not sufficient for the country's needs. 

9. Russia is rich in minerals, but the deposits have been little developed. There are coal and iron deposits in many sections. 

10. Little progress has been made in manufacturing, though factories are increasing in the larger cities. 

The more important cities of Russia are Moscow, Leningrad, Stalingrad, Kiev, Odessa, and Vladivostok. 

11. Russia is like Canada, in that it covers a large area, has a population mostly rural, and is rich in mineral resources. The range of latitude of these two countries is about the same and their products are very similar. Canada's government is better developed than Russia's and her people are better educated and are more skilful workmen. The smaller country has developed the greater international trade.

BORDER COUNTRIES BETWEEN RUSSIA AND WESTERN EUROPE FINLAND AND THE BALTIC STATES 

At the close of the World War four parts of western Russia became four independent republics. These are the republics of Finland, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. Find them on the map on page 19. 

FINLAND 

The long rugged country of Finland lies in the north of Europe, between Russia and the 

Scandinavian peninsula. It is over twice the size of our state of Missouri but has only about the same number of people. For centuries 

Sweden controlled the land of Finland, and the Swedes established fine schools there and trained the people in many ways. Later Finland became a badly ruled possession of Russia, with whom she had constant struggles to preserve her rights. But finally, at the close of the World War, Finland became independent. 

SURFACE 

AND SOIL Like so much of Europe, the land that is now Finland once lay in the path of an ice sheet. As a result, a good part of the area of the country is made up of lakes, marshes, and streams.

The higher lands have thin soil. The soil of the lowlands is coarse. Many of the lakes are connected by canals, and in places they form the only means of inland transportation. 

Fine forests of both soft and hardwood trees cover over half of Finland's surface and belong to the forest belt which extends far to the east across Russia. The coastal plains are the farming lands. In fact, her latitude, her forestcovered sections, and her coastal farming regions make Finland very much like her neighbor, Sweden, across the Gulf of Bothnia to the west.

INDUSTRIES 

Finland is an agricultural land in spite of the country's far northern latitude and its short growing season. This is possible because during part of the summer the sun hardly disappears at all, and the long hours of sunlight make crops grow and ripen rapidly. Rye, oats, barley, flax, and potatoes are raised in large quantities. On the rougher parts of the lowlands, especially in the south of Finland, cattle, sheep, pigs, and horses are raised. Dairying is one of the main industries. The fine forests are carefully tended. 

Because of the long seacoast and sheltered harbors, many of the people have turned to the sea for a living, and fishing is an important industry. Both copper and gold are mined near the Russian border. Streams dropping from the highlands to the coastal plains furnish water power, which is used in running factories in place of coal. Some manufacturing is done but is limited largely to the pulp and paper industry and to the making of textiles. 

Finland's main imports are machinery and food stuffs which her own factories and farms do not supply. She exports pulp, paper, lumber, and other forest products, and the butter and cheese of her dairy industry. Most of this trade is with the United Kingdom, Germany, and the United States.

The population is sparse and not at all evenly distributed. The most dense population is along the southern shore, cen- POPULATION tering in the capital and seaport, Helsingfors, or Helsinki. This is an interesting city with wide streets and fine public buildings. 

The people living along the Gulf of Bothnia are mostly of Swedish descent. 

Those who live in the northern tundra part of Finland, Norway, and Sweden are called Lapps and the land they live on is known as Lapland. Like other dwellers in the frozen north, the Lapps could hardly live without their herds of reindeer. They eat reindeer meat, drink reindeer milk, and wear clothes 100

The people of Finland are unusually well educated. This small country has a fine school system and three universities. With their advantages in education, their commerce, and their natural resources, the people of Finland are prosperous and progressive.

THE BALTIC STATES-ESTONIA, LATVIA, AND LITHUANIA 

South of the Gulf of Finland and bordering the Baltic sea are the three small republics of 

Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. These three are often called the Baltic states. In size all three together are a little larger than Missouri. 

Their total population is half again as large as that of Missouri. In surface, climate, occupations, and history they are so much alike that we can study them together. 

HISTORY 

Long ago, a league of German crusaders, called the Knights of the Sword, took possession of a large part of these small countries. Under the protection of the Knights other Germans came to the region, where they became lords, or nobles. The earlier inhabitants were forced to work as serfs without pay on the estates of the nobles. 

They had no education and their lot was a very hard one. With the passing of time, this region came under the Russian rule. The serfs were freed by law, but really their condition was not much better. It was almost impossible for a common man to obtain land of his own.

Naturally the people wished for better education, better living conditions, and a chance to develop their natural resources. With the World War their opportunity came and they declared their independence and set up governments of their own. The large estates were now broken up and no one man was allowed to hold more than a fixed number of acres. Much of the land was divided into plots of a few acres each and was given to the poor people for the growing of crops. Now the people of these countries are doing their utmost to improve education, agriculture, and manufacturing. 

The surface of the Baltic states is low, slightly rolling, and covered to a large extent with lakes and marshes. Though the soil is not very good, farming is the most important

Riga, the capital of Latvia, Memel, the principal seaport of Lithuania, and Reval, the capital of Estonia.

Reval and Riga are transit ports-ports through which goods pass on their way to other countries. Ocean vessels are loaded with the products brought in over the Trans-Siberian and other railroads, and the railroad cars are reloaded with goods brought from all over the world in ships. Riga is also a transit port for the commerce of the Duna river. Both the 

Duna and the Niemen rivers are connected by canals with Russian river systems and form outlets for many products of inland Russia. 

Kovno, the capital of Lithuania, also has considerable transit trade as a railroad center and a river port. Reval, Riga, and Kovno are very old cities, and the old and new sections of each make strange contrasts.

BUFFER STATES 

Such small states between strong surrounding nations are often called "buffer states.”

They help to keep the larger countries from disputes over boundaries, and their rights are usually guarded by the stronger nations. On the other hand, they are so small and weak that often in times of war they serve as highways of invasion between one country and another. Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania are buffer states between 

Russia and Germany.

BORDER COUNTRIES BETWEEN RUSSIA AND WESTERN EUROPE SURFACE POLAND 

In times past the country of Poland might well have been called the battle-field of Europe. 

Lying in the very heart of the continent, Poland is entirely without natural boundaries except on the south, where the Polish lowland rises to the crest of the Carpathian mountains. The rest of the country is just great, level plains with no barriers to shut out enemies.

HISTORY 

Two centuries ago Poland had for neighbors Russia on the east and Austria and the German state of Prussia on the west. All three nations were strong and powerful. They were envious of each other and again and again met in Poland to fight out their differences. Even Sweden, from the north, and Turkey, from the south, invaded parts of this unfortunate country. 

At that time Poland had much more land than at present, but its government was not strong enough to hold the country together or to make the people realize that they must unite for protection. Greedy nobles were interested only in enriching themselves. Under these nobles, with their large estates, was a class of peasants very like the unfortunate serfs of the Baltic states. 

Because there was no real unity in the country, even among the nobles, Poland grew weaker and weaker. Seeing this state of affairs, the powerful neighbors agreed among themselves to divide, or partition, Poland, each taking the parts nearest to its own boundaries. 

Three times they helped themselves, until there was no Polish land left. The city of 

Krakow for a short time remained a free city, but finally went to Austria. 

During the World War, the lands which had once been Poland were again the battleground between Russia, Austria, and Germany. Towns, cities, and factories were almost wiped out, and forests and fields suffered from the inroads of warring armies. But although they had no country which they could call their own, the Poles still felt that they should be a separate nation, and at the close of the World War they regained part of their ancient lands from the three countries that held them. Since the war we once more find a country called Poland on our maps. This country is now a republic. 

Today, Poland is a little less than threefourths the size of France, and about three times the size of New York state. In Poland, as in the Baltic states, the new government is breaking up the great estates, making it possible for the Polish peasants to own the land they work. This means prosperity for the people. And prosperity for the people means prosperity for the nation. Education is also being advanced. The part of the country regained from Germany and Austria is well supplied with schools, and the people living there are trained in the latest farming and manufacturing methods. The people in the section regained from Russia, however, are about on Russia's low educational level. What is true of the people in the regained lands is equally true of the lands. The farms in the west have been well cared for, while those in the east are in poorer condition.

AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS 

On the low plains in northern Poland and on the rolling land at the foot of the Carpathians where there are rich farming lands, we find the usual crops of central Europe-potatoes; rye, oats, barley, and wheat; sugar beets; and flax. Part of the potato crop is used for making alcohol. The flax is exported to Ireland and Belgium. Hogs and poultry are raised.

Poland has considerable mineral wealth in addition to her rich soils. Around Krakow in the Silesian district there are mines of coal, iron, zinc, and salt. 

Poland mines more coal than either Belgium or Russia. In Silesia are many 

MINERAL RESOURCES 

104

POLAND 

105 smelters and factories for the making of iron and zinc goods. Petroleum is found in southern and eastern Poland.

The forests of Poland, which lie in both the northeastern part of the country and in the southern highlands, provide much lumber and wood pulp.

FORESTS COMMERCE 

In times of peace, Poland's central position in Europe, with almost no natural boundaries, is an enormous advantage. Most of the great east-west and northsouth trade routes cross Poland's level plains.

It is easy for the country to import and export goods. She has the use of the Free City of 

Danzig as a seaport. She is also rapidly developing her own Baltic port, Gdynia, at the end of that narrow strip of land called the Polish Corridor which leads to the sea between 

Germany and East Prussia. The Vistula river and its tributaries open up the interior of Poland to water transportation. A canal connects the Vistula river with the Dnieper river system in Russia, making another transcontinental waterway.

Poland's exports include lumber, coal, woodpulp, zinc and other metals, and hogs and eggs from her farms. The chief imports are fertilizers and chemicals, machinery, metals, raw cotton from the United States, and wool. 

THE FREE CITY OF DANZIG 

Poland has a number of well developed cities, many of them dating from very early days. 

But let us first visit Danzig, the city at the mouth of the

Vistula river. The history of this city is very closely bound up with that of Poland, and although Danzig is now a free city and an international port, her importance to Poland is still great. No one knows just when Danzig was founded. Very early in

European history the strong fortifications of this city did much to protect its independence. 

But its early existence was a stormy one, and time and again it lost its freedom and fell under the control of some neighboring country. Before the World War it was a German port, but since the war it has governed itself under the protection of the League of Nations. Many old fortifications have been torn down to make room for the newer city, but there still remain quaint houses and beautiful old buildings dating back to the Middle Ages.

Commercially, Danzig is one of the important transit ports of Europe, because of its location as a Baltic port, a river port, and a railroad center. It is trying to increase its commercial importance by manufacturing into finished products many of the raw materials that pour into the city. The city has huge steel foundries, sugar refineries, and flour mills. 

Shipbuilding is one important industry that dates back many years. Danzig is noted as a market for amber. Amber is a clear yellow substance as hard as stone. It was originally the sap of trees. The best amber is cut and polished to make jewelry; cheaper qualities are used in making varnish.

POLISH 

Warsaw. Warsaw, located on the Vistula river, is the present capital of Poland. It is at the crossing of natural north-south and east-west travel routes. These CITIES 

routes have served, in times past, as paths for invading armies. Today they are valuable trade routes. Warsaw is a very beautiful and interesting city, with many palaces, wonderful old churches, and fine public buildings. Situated in the midst of a fertile plain, Warsaw was an early distributing center for the products of the region, and the Vistula river made export of these products easy. 

Later, Warsaw became a railroad center with lines to Vienna, Kiev, Moscow, Leningrad, Danzig, and Berlin. Because of its fine transportation, nearby iron and coal fields, and central position in Europe, Warsaw rapidly developed as a manufacturing center, with great iron foundries and textile mills. 

Krakow. Krakow, the old capital, is a storehouse of historical treasures. It has many old and famous churches. Among these, Stanislaus cathedral is probably the most interesting. 

Here, in olden times, the kings of Poland were crowned. It is also the burial place of some of 

Poland's most famous men. The university in 

Krakow was opened long before Columbus started on his westward cruise. But Krakow does not live entirely in the past. It has modern industries and is a trading center. The upper Silesian coal fields, just northwest of

EUROPE 

this famous old city, are a great aid to manufacturing. Salt mines that have been worked for hundreds of years lie within a few miles of Krakow. Machinery and chemicals are important manufactures.

Other Cities. 

Posen is located in a rich farming district, is on a navigable tributary of the 

Oder river, and is also a railroad center. Lodz, located near iron and coal fields, has textile mills, and great plants where machinery and chemicals are manufactured.

The Polish people are naturally lovers of freedom. In the past, they have objected to being ruled by anyone.

FUTURE 

This prevented the formation of a strong central government, and made the land a prey to other countries.

Now the Polish people are working to restore their trampled land. They are building for the future-beginning great industries, educating their citizens, learning to govern.

They are overcoming their handicaps caused by the long invasion, and the name of Poland is becoming more and more important in international affairs. But for years to come the future of this country without natural boundaries will depend upon continued peace in Europe. 

1. Poland, in the center of Europe, is without natural boundaries except on the south. The country had been partitioned among Austria, Russia, and the 

German state of Prussia but after the World War parts of Poland were reunited as an independent republic. 

2. The estates of the nobles are being broken up to provide farm land for the poor people. Education, already good in sections of Poland formerly held by Germany and Austria, is being improved throughout the country. 

3. Poland raises the central European crops of cereals, potatoes, flax, and sugar beets. The mineral resources are coal, iron, zinc, salt, and petroleum. Wood products, coal, zinc, and other metals, hogs, and eggs are exported. 

4. Poland is crossed by north-south and east-west trade routes. On the Baltic shore of the Polish 

Corridor is the port of Gdynia. The Vistula river has long been important commercially. 

5. Danzig is an independent city which Poland uses as a seaport. The city governs itself under the protection of the League of Nations. It is important as a transit port and manufacturing center.

Warsaw, the capital of Poland, is a distributing and manufacturing center. Krakow, the old capital, is important historically as well as industrially. 

Posen is a railroad and distributing center. Lodz is a manufacturing city.

THE PLAINS COUNTRIES OF THE DANUBIAN PLAINS : 

HUNGARY AND RUMANIA 

We have studied the Danube river as an important route of trade extending from Germany to the Black sea. Now we are to follow its course across the plains through Hungary and 

Rumania. Flowing between the

Alps and the Carpathian mountains through an opening called the Carpathian Gate, the Danube continues through Austria, forms part of the northern boundary of Hungary, and then winds south across the country into Jugoslavia. Farther on, the river forms part of the southern boundary of Rumania as it flows generally eastward between the Transylvanian Alps and the Balkan mountains. This mighty river has cut its way through these mountains in a narrow passage, the western end of which is called the Iron Gate. From bordering

Rumania on the south, the Danube turns north and then east and flows into the Black sea.

Near its mouth it has formed a large delta, with many lakes and channels.

The countries of the Danubian plains, Hungary and Rumania, were quite different in size 

HUNGARY AND RUMANIA BEFORE THE WAR AND 

AFTER and in natural regions be fore the World War. Hun gary was a part of the Austro-Hungarian empire and had an area of about 125,000 square miles, which is a little larger than New Mexico. After the war, when the country became an independent republic, its territory was reduced to less than one-third its former size. 

Rumania, on the other hand, had an area before the war of about 53,000 square miles. But after the war it gained lands which gave it more than twice its former area.

In their regions of plain and mountain, there were changes too. Hungary lost all of her mountains and some of her plains. 

SURFACE 

The present Hungary is practically all plain, watered by the Danube and its tributaries. Only in west-central Hungary is the plain broken by low hills. All about Hungary are the Carpathians and ranges of the Alps, but her borders do not touch them.

Rumania, which used to be all plain with only bordering mountains, is now part plain and part highland. The Carpathian mountains curve to the south and in Rumania form the Transylvanian Alps. These mountains divide the plains of Hungary and western Rumania from Rumania's eastern plains. In the middle of Rumania the mountains surround a central plateau.

Danube. We know that where the soil is fertile, agriculture is usually the chief occupation of the people, and it is so on the Danubian plains. So much grain is raised on the plains that they have been called the bread-lands of Europe.

The plains of Hungary have the longest growing season in all central Europe. Over half the land is cultivated, and 

AGRICULTURE 

the rest is in forest and pasture. The summer rain and the hot weather are good for the growing of corn, and corn is one of the chief crops. Wheat and the other hardy grains are also important. One large crop is potatoes; and sugar beets, grapes, and tobacco are grown. Cattle, sheep, and hogs are raised on the grasslands in the eastern and southern plains of Hungary. Hungary is one

European country which produces more grain and meat than its people need. Its western neighbor is Austria, which needs food badly, and wheat and flour, cattle, and hogs pour out of Hungary to Vienna. Timber, coal, and manufactures are received in return. 

Rumania, too, has agriculture and stock raising as its chief industries, and it also exports food supplies. Its soil is rich and black. 

Corn is the chief crop and the chief export. 

The hardy grains, potatoes, and tobacco are other important crops. There is less rain in the eastern part of the plains, and grasses take the place of cereal crops near the Black sea.

Here cattle and horses are pastured. There is stock raising, too, on the highlands. In summer the cattle and sheep graze on the Transylvanian highlands, and in winter are brought down to the lowlands for shelter. Hogs are exported. There are vast forests in the mountains-oak, beech, and ash. Building lumber is an important item in export trade. 

Rumania has minerals in her mountains, including lignite-which is a poor kind of coaland rock salt and petroleum. 

Petroleum is also found near the

MINERALS 

shores of the Black sea. Rumania refines her petroleum with American machinery and exports the products. Hungary has no important mineral deposits.

BESSARABIA 

Much of the land that Rumania received after the war came from Hungary, but she also got back from Russia some territory which had once been hers.

Between the Pruth river and the Dniester lies Bessarabia, which became part of Rumania after the World War. In the north, Bessarabia is hilly. The farmers who live there cultivate crops of corn and hay and wheat, and pasture livestock. Along the shores of the

Pruth and at the mouths of the Danube Bessarabia is marshy and treeless.

CITIES 

Budapest is the capital and chief trading center of Hungary. It is really two cities, Buda and Pest, separated by the

Danube river. The two cities are connected by a number of beautiful bridges and are considered as one city. Budapest is one of the most delightful cities in Europe. Situated in the midst of a great grain-growing region on an internationalized river, it has naturally become a shipping center. 

Railroads pass through it in every direction. Like Minneapolis, it has become a flour-milling center. It also manufactures beet sugar and farming tools. Cotton is imported, and the textile industry is growing in importance. 

Bucharest is the capital of Rumania and its largest trading center. Many of the wealthy landowners make their homes in this city. 

Galatz, on the Danube, is the chief wheat-exporting town. Constantsa, on the Black sea coast, is the great petroleum port.

The natives of Hungary, the Magyars, came originally from Asia. They form a good part of Hungary's evenly distributed population. They are consid-

109 brave, proud, and well-mannered. The upper classes are well educated. Much of our most beautiful music has been composed by the Hungarians. The peasants are ignorant and backward but there is an effort being made to improve their education.

The Rumanians take pride in claiming their descent from the ancient Romans. Their language is based on the Latin tongue. As a nation, they are thrifty and intelligent and fine looking. The Rumanian women are noted for their beauty. Most of the poorer classes can neither read nor write. Some of the peasants and herdsmen live in the narrow valleys cut by the rivers through the Transylvanian highlands. But most of the people live on the plains. 

Hungary has good railroads leading to the countries on every side of her, and to the port of Trieste. Those of Rumania are less extensive. Both countries, however, depend largely on 

TRANSPORTATION 

the Danube to carry their bulky freights of foodstuffs and animals. The Danube is over twice as long as the Rhine and has nearly as much importance as a commercial waterway. 

Like the Rhine, it has been made an international river, which means that all nations may use it. It flows through rich countries and has many cities and towns along its banks. 

Food products, manufactured articles, and lumber travel up and down it on steamers and barges. The commerce may go up the Danube into southern Germany, or it may cross through Czechoslovakia by the canal which connects the Danube with the Elbe, and so reach central Germany. Or it may travel down the Danube into the Black sea and through the 

Strait of Bosporus to the Mediterranean sea, and so reach distant parts of the world.

VIEWS IN A LAND OF MOUNTAINS 

1. A scene in the mountains of the Balkan peninsula. "Balkan" is a Turkish word that means "mountain," and this peninsula is one of the most mountainous lands in the world. But although there are many ranges and peaks, the mountains of the Balkan peninsula are only about half as high as the Alps. They form difficult trade barriers because they are rugged and numerous and run in every direction. 

2. Waterfalls in the Balkan peninsula. There are natural sources of water power everywhere in the Balkans. 

Mountain streams could easily be made to furnish electricity for manufacturing. But the people of the Balkans are farmers and shepherds who know little of modern industry. They let most of this power go to waste. 

3. Sheep grazing in the Balkan peninsula. This sloping mountain pasture has very thin soil. Notice the rocks that show above the surface. Farming would not be profitable here. There are many places in the Balkans like this one, where stock raising is the only industry. 

4. On the Adriatic coast of the Balkan peninsula. The steep range of mountains that rises from the shore shuts off the coast from the interior. As no east-west valleys and no navigable rivers cut through the mountains, there are no great seaports on this coast. The fine Adriatic harbors are little used. The people of the small seacoast villages, like the one in this picture, live by fishing and entertaining tourists.

THE BALKAN REGION 

East of the Adriatic sea is the mountaincovered Balkan peninsula. It contains four countries known as the Balkan states-Greece, Jugoslavia, Bulgaria, and Albania. Part of the country of Turkey also lies on the peninsula. 

Greece, because of her Mediterranean climate, was considered with the Mediterranean countries. Turkey, because most of it lies in Asia, is not strictly a Balkan state. The other three are alike in many ways, and may be considered together.

SURFACE 

The surface of the Balkan peninsula is a tangle of mountains and valleys. As you will see by the map on page 62, the mountains in the Balkan peninsula are the Dinaric Alps and the Balkan and Pindus mountains. The Dinaric range extends southeast from the Alps along the Adriatic sea. The Balkans extend east through Bulgaria to the Black sea. The Pindus mountains extend south through Greece. Except in Albania there is almost no coastal plain. 

There are stretches of lowland along the Danube river, which flows through the northern part of Jugoslavia and forms most of the northern boundary of Bulgaria. There are also bits of lowland along the Maritza river in southern Bulgaria. Besides these valleys there is the Morava-Vardar valley in Jugoslavia.

This valley is the one great natural trade route of the peninsula and one of the oldest in the world. Through it the Morava river flows north and the Vardar flows south, their sources nearly meeting. The two together have cut a valley which connects the interior of Europe with the Aegean sea. Today railroads follow the valley and there is talk of connecting the two rivers by a canal.

The coasts of the Balkan states, of course, have a moderate climate because of the influence of the nearby waters. The westerly winds crossing the mountains leave much of their moisture on the western coast. The eastern coast has less rainfall. 

CLIMATE STATE OF DEVELOPMENT 

The mountains of the Balkan states are well forested, but are not well suited for agriculture, so farming is of little importance. Cattle raising and sheep raising are the principal industries. In the more primitive parts of the countries the people spend nearly all their time on the hillsides with their flocks and herds. 

There are some mineral deposits in the Balkan states, including coal, iron, copper, aluminum, silver, lead, and platinum. Mountain streams supply water power, but until recently the people have scarcely worked the mines at all, and the water power has long been going to waste. There is very little manufacturing. 

POLITICAL DIFFICULTIES 

Long ago the Turks gained control of most of the Balkan region, and they held that control for many years. Their rule was harsh and oppressive, and little or no progress was made under their government. But as time went on small groups of people gained their independence and formed separate states. All of these little states are now included in Jugoslavia, Bulgaria, Albania, and Greece. Jugoslavia gained much territory from Austria-Hungary after the World War. The Turks now hold only a small part of the peninsula.

The population of the Balkans is sparse compared with that of other countries of southern Europe. The people are a mixture of races and creeds and speak different languages. 

Then, too, natural boundaries separate one small group from another. There is no one important center for trade or transportation. 

These things have made the Balkan groups distrustful of one another. Each has been afraid of coming under the control of some other group. There have been constant friction and petty quarrels among them which have prevented them from uniting into a single strong nation. While they have been busy settling wars and disputes, their valuable resources have remained undeveloped. Education has 111

EUROPE 

been neglected. Living conditions and farm methods have not been improved. Exports, which might be of value to many countries and which would help the Balkan states to build up wealth and prosperity, have not increased. 

All these characteristics of the Balkan states have been advantages to those European countries with interests in the East. You will see from your map on page 62 that their position makes the Balkans the gateway between 

Europe and the southwestern countries of 

Asia. Knowing this, you can easily understand why these other European countries did not care to see one single strong nation controlling this important gateway.

JUGOSLAVIA 

Jugoslavia, the largest of the Balkan states, is about the size of Oregon. The Adriatic sea and Italy form the western boundary. Mountains rise abruptly from the sea, and form a natural barrier between the interior of the country and the west coast. From the mountains the land slopes generally east to the Morava-Vardar valley.

As the mountains are unbroken by east-west valleys or by navigable rivers, and as few railroads reach the Adriatic coast, there are no large seaports. The shore is broken by islands and fiords. This mountainous coastal section is the province of Dalmatia, and fewer people live here than in any other section of the country. The people of Dalmatia are mostly fishermen and seamen. Do you remember another rugged country of Europe whose fiord coast is the site of many fishing villages? 

The western part of Jugoslavia has the most rainfall, but the interior has enough rain for the raising of corn and wheat. The interior has hot summers and cold winters. Plums grow in the northern part of the country, and, in the valleys between the mountains, pigs, cattle, sheep, and goats are raised. Grapes and tobacco, hemp and flax are valuable crops.

The only industries carried on to any extent in factories are the milling of flour and the weaving of carpets. In their homes the women make cloth, brightly colored and some of it striped. These gay cloths they make into aprons and scarfs. They do a great deal of knitting with yarn spun from wool which comes from the many sheep. Such manufactured articles as iron and steel goods and machinery are imported. The leading exports of the country are lumber, wheat, livestock, and copper. Though Jugoslavia has no important port on the Adriatic, she can carry on foreign trade through the Italian port of Fiume. 

Belgrade, the capital of Jugoslavia, is also its chief city. It is located on the Danube and so is on the river trade route between the 

Black sea and Germany. Through it pass railroads which lead to Berlin and Vienna, to 

Istanbul in Turkey and to Saloniki, the chief port of Greece.

Belgrade is so far north that it is not a natural political center for Jugoslavia, and the more remote mountain districts know little about what goes on in their capital city. 

Most of the wealthy people of Jugoslavia live in Belgrade. They are owners of large farms and vineyards which are usually run by up-to-date methods and yield abundant crops. 

With the exception of these wealthier people, the Jugoslavs are uneducated and do not know how to make the best use of their land or resources.

The name Jugoslavia means the country of the southern Slavs. To the north lies Czechoslovakia, another country whose people are largely Slavs. 

BULGARIA 

Bulgaria, the next state in size, is a little smaller than Kentucky. It has three natural regions, very distinct from each other. They are the plains about the Danube river, the plains about the Maritza river, and the mountainous district which lies between these two lowlands. This country has in general a continental climate with cold winters and hot summers and a moderate amount of rainfall. The mountains protect the lowlands south of them. The eastern section gets the sweep of the winds from the central plains of Russia, and this adds to the coldness of the winters there. 

The mountains are rich in coal. Vineyards line their slopes, and sheep graze there in large numbers. In the Danube valley wheat and corn are raised. Wheat is the most important grain

JUGOSLAVIA, BULGARIA, AND ALBANIA 

113 crop. Silkworms, tobacco, and roses are raised in the valley to the south. 

Bulgaria is very famous for its roses. Many, many acres of land are devoted to them. It seems strange that a country which is poor and undeveloped should spend much time and labor on flowers which our country raises largely for their beauty. The roses in Bulgaria, however, are put to a very practical use. They are made into attar of roses, an exquisite perfume which brings a high price and is a chief export of the country. The Bulgarians also export tobacco, cattle, eggs, and grains, though their farming methods are largely of the simplest. They import machinery, metals, and textiles. 

Bulgaria carries on trade down the Maritza valley to the Aegean and also by ship across the Black sea. Varna on the Black sea is the chief port. Sofia is the capital of the country and has rail connections with northern countries. The railroad from Belgrade to Istanbul passes through Sofia. Philippopolis, on the

Maritza, is Bulgaria's busiest industrial city. 

The smallest of the Balkan states is Albania, whose capital is Tirana. Albania has a low- 

ALBANIA 

land coast with mountains behind it, and the country's climate is mild. 

There is only one railroad, no important manufacturing, and few schools. Farming and cattle raising are the principal occupations. On the lowlands the people raise the usual Mediterranean products-olives, lemons, and grapes.

The Albanians are a restless, excitable people. They are largely Mohammedans, but do not hate Christians as do many other races of their religion. During their spare hours the villagers amuse themselves with native games and folk dances. Like the Italian and Spanish people they celebrate many holidays and festivals. 

The Albanians are believed to be the original inhabitants of the Balkan section. They owe their present backward condition largely to the fact that they are separated by mountain walls from even their nearest neighbors; that, unlike the Jugoslavians and the Bulgarians, they are not on trade routes; and that they have naturally fierce dispositions and do not seek contact with other peoples.

OF THE 

The Balkan states can be improved in several ways by the establishment of sound progressive governments, the exten sion of education, the improvement FUTURE of agriculture by modern farming BALKANS 

methods, and the development of forests, mines, and water power. All these things will mean an industrial growth and will lead to increased trade and the building up of each country's treasury. Years of peace, rather than war and oppression, should give the Balkan countries a future very different from their past. 

 1. The Balkan states of Jugoslavia, Bulgaria, and 

Albania lie east of the Adriatic sea in the Balkan peninsula. They are a tangle of mountains and valleys, the ranges being the Dinaric Alps and the Balkan mountains. The countries have little coastal plain and only a few lowlands. The lowlands are along the Danube and Maritza rivers. Besides the valleys of these rivers there is the great trade route between interior Europe and the Aegean sea-the 

Morava-Vardar valley. 

2. The climate of the Balkans is, in general, continental. The western coast of the peninsula receives the most rainfall. 

3. The chief industries are the raising of cattle and sheep. The land is not well suited for agriculture. 

The chief crops are grains and fruits. There are deposits of coal and metals in the mountains but the mines are little worked. There is little manufacturing. Carpet weaving and flour milling are carried on in Jugoslavia. Bulgaria manufactures attar of roses for export. Albania has no important manufacturing industries. 

4. Jugoslavia carries on trade and transportation by way of the Danube river and the Morava-Vardar valley. Jugoslavia has railroad connections with 

Berlin, Vienna, Saloniki, Istanbul, and the Italian port of Fiume. Bulgaria ships over the Black sea and down the Maritza valley to the Aegean sea. 

5. The people of these countries are a mixture of races, creeds, and tongues. Education in general is lacking. Their backward condition is due to their early conquest by the Turks, whose rule was oppressive, to their natural surroundings which prevent much communication or unity among them, and to the many wars which have long occupied their time and interest.

THE TURKEY 

When the ancient Roman empire was at the height of its power, it included most of the known world-from the British Isles

TURKS on the north and west to Egypt and Palestine on the south and east. As the empire's strength failed, it became too difficult to rule so vast a region from Rome. So the eastern city of Byzantium, located at the outlet of the Black sea, was made a second capital. There were now two emperors, one in 

Rome to rule the western part of the empire and one in Byzantium to rule the eastern part. 

After a time, the name of Byzantium was changed to Constantinople in honor of the 

Emperor Constantine.

Long after the city of Rome was captured by barbarous tribes from northern and central Europe, Constantinople remained a capital of the Roman empire. It was not until 1453, about a thousand years after the fall of Rome, that the eastern capital was finally captured and the empire came to an end. 

The conquerors of the eastern empire were the Ottoman Turks, a warlike race from central Asia. Not content with seizing Constantinople, they swept west and north, overrunning most of the Balkan peninsula and even gaining a foothold in southern Italy. As they already held much of southwestern Asia, their empire was now very great. The Turks ruled their possessions badly, and one can trace the extent of their conquests as well by the backward condition of the lands as by the mosques, or churches, and other Turkish buildings which they erected. Their government was so bad and incompetent that it called forth the protests of people in every Christian nation. Turkey became known as "the sick man of Europe." Turkey's location, however, was so favorable that none of the great powers was willing to allow any of the others to occupy it, and Turkey long held her empire on that account.

Nevertheless, little by little, the Turks have lost most of their lands. They were driven from their Italian foothold soon after gaining it. As war followed war, they lost many of their possessions in the Balkan peninsula, and from the lands they lost the independent Balkan states were formed. During the World 

War, they lost the greater part of their broad 

Asiatic possessions.

MODERN 

It does not seem likely, however, that the Turks will lose the rest of their possessions. 

They are now becoming a progressive nation. They have given up TURKEY their old form of government, a monarchy ruled by an emperor known as the Sultan, and now have a republic with its capital at Angora (Ankara), in Asia. Constantinople, now everywhere known as Istanbul, is no longer the capital.

Today, the Turks are abandoning ancient oriental styles of clothing in favor of modern fashions. They have established schools for the education of their people. They have abandoned their old oriental alphabet and adopted the alphabet which is used in most of the leading countries of the world. 

The Turks still occupy the important little stretch of land between Europe and Asia cut by the Bosporus. They also occupy an area in 

Europe about the size of Massachusetts, between the Bosporus and the city of Adrianople. 

This small territory is important principally as a trading center. In Istanbul railroad traffic from Europe to Asia crosses sea trade from the Mediterranean to the Black sea. The Bosporus is narrow and deep, and the city's fine crescent-shaped harbor called the Golden 

Horn gives safe anchorage and docking space to ships from every corner of the world. ISTANBUL These facts give Istanbul wonderful advantages as a trading city, both for buying and selling and for transit trade. At one time or another almost every great power has wanted to own this crossroad. Russia long hoped to seize it as a means of com- 115

EUROPE 

manding the routes to the Black sea and her southern ports. Germany had in mind a Berlinto-Bagdad railroad system which would lead from Berlin through Constantinople to southwestern Asia and the Arabian sea, bringing the products of the East Indies to the Prussian plains. Because of her interests in Egypt and

India, Great Britain violently objected to both these plans, and Turkey continued to hold the Bosporus. Today, however, the Bosporus has been internationalized under the protection of the League of Nations and is open to the trade of all nations.

Istanbul is a city of contrasts. On its many hills are the marble palaces of the former sultans and the old walls and fortifications that defended the city in days gone by. We can see the most modern liners and wharf machinery, and, in the same view, the shining domes of the old Mohammedan mosques, whose delicately pointed minarets, or prayer-towers, are the skyscrapers of the city. Around each minaret, high above the ground, is a little gallery from which at certain hours of the day men called muezzins summon the faithful 

Mohammedans to pray. When their voices are heard, the work of the city stops while its inhabitants spread tiny prayer rugs, turn their faces toward their holy city, Mecca, and kneel in prayer. Mecca is a city of Arabia in Asia. 

On the Asiatic side of the Bosporus you will notice a little village of odd-shaped houses. 

This is Scutari, where many of the Turkish business men live. Pera, a part of Istanbul, is on the European side of the Bosporus. This is the section where most of the Europeans live, and here are the foreign embassies, modern hotels, and public buildings of the city. 

Most visitors are chiefly interested in Stambul, the native section. Here are the great bazaars and workshops of the natives. In these bazaars, or open-air stores, the merchants sit cross-legged in their funny wide trousers, with turbans wound about their heads. The bazaars are hung with those rich rugs for which Turkey is so famous. Here you may buy artistic little articles which the Turks make so well from cotton, wool, leather, and metal.

In the narrow, dirty streets of Stambul people of many different races pass and repass all day long. Jews and Persians and Arabs and Greeks walk the streets of this Turkish city in their native costumes, talking their native languages. In the more modern parts of Istanbul the streets are wider, and one sees electric lights, street cars and automobiles. 

Here the men and women dress much as we do. 

Although many ships enter the Golden 

Horn, Turkey contributes really very little to the trade that is forever on its way through her chief city. European Turkey is now too small to have large exports, and Asiatic Turkey ships through its seaport of Smyrna (Izmir) on the Aegean sea.

TURKEY 

Asiatic Turkey includes the peninsula of

Asia Minor, and extends east beyond the eastern end of the Black sea. The pen insula of Asia Minor lies between the IN ASIA 

Black and the Mediterranean seas. 

Except for the Mediterranean shore it is for the most part an arid plateau, bordered on the south by the Taurus mountains, which shut out the rain.

Along the west coast the mountains have sunk below the sea, making an irregular coast line with good harbors. The shores are bordered by narrow lowland belts, which have a Mediterranean climate. Here are small farms where fruits, barley, and wheat are raised. The soils of the interior are good when they are watered. Irrigation is practised, but the methods are primitive and the farming tools are crude. Tobacco and cotton are raised, and cereals, figs, almonds, grapes, and olives. Mulberry trees grow here and many people raise silkworms.

The drier lands are used for grazing and large numbers of people depend for a living upon their herds of sheep and cattle. Angora goats supply the hair for mohair cloth. Smyrna has some textile manufacturing, and oriental rugs are woven in the homes or in little workshops. Turkey's mineral wealth of coal and iron has scarcely been touched. Petroleum is now exported.

Tobacco is the only export of great importance, but there is a good trade in raw cotton, wool and mohair, and raisins, figs, and

TURKEY 

117 nuts. The native rugs, among the finest in the world, find a ready market in Europe and the

United States. 

Turkey in late years has begun to encourage new farming methods, and to enter the ranks of progressive nations.

EARLY AFRICA PHYSICAL FEATURES OF AFRICA 

Of the six continents Africa is the least developed. History tells us that in ancient times the lands in the Nile delta and along the Mediterranean coast reached a high state of civilization. In fact, in the very early days northern Africa was more advanced than was the European side of the 

Mediterranean. Egyptian civilization dates back into the dim haze of early history, and the Moors of North Africa were interested in education while Europe was still peopled only by barbarians. But to the south of the Mediterranean lands lay a great desert which shut off the central and southern parts of the continent from exploration and colonization. For long years most of Africa-a land of dark people, dark forests, and dark deeds-lay unknown, avoided, and even feared. It was called the Dark Continent. And even the great civilizations of the northern coast fell long ago into decay.

POSITION 

Africa is the second continent in size. It stretches for some five thousand miles from north to south. In the northeast it 

AND SIZE joins Asia. At the Strait of Gi braltar it is only nine miles from 

Europe, but a journey by fast steamer from 

England to Africa's southern tip takes seventeen days.

The map shows us that Africa is broad at the north, with a huge shoulder jutting into the Atlantic ocean. The Equator crosses it just below this shoulder. The southern part of the continent is narrower.

RELIEF 

Africa is different from other continents in that it has little very high or very low ground. 

Plateaus are the most common feature of the surface. Only Australia has fewer mountains. The coastal plains are narrow and the mountains are comparatively few and scattered. 

Plateaus. The plateau regions of Africa are of two types. The northern and western parts of the continent consist mainly of low tablelands. The southern and eastern parts are largely made up of high plateaus. A diagonal line extending from the middle of the African coast of the Red sea southwest to a point just south of the mouth of the Congo river will very nearly divide the low from the high plateaus.

The greater part of the plateau region in the north of Africa is occupied by the desert table-land of the Sahara. This vast plateau stretches across the northern part of the continent for hundreds and hundreds of miles. 

The high table-lands of Africa, lying in the south and east, rise to three or four thousand feet and in some places more. In southern 

Africa is a vast interior plateau. In the east central part is a plateau on which lie all the great lakes of the continent. To the north this upland becomes the forest-covered Abyssinian plateau, rising as high as 8000 feet above sea level. 

Mountains. The high mountains of Africa are arranged in small, scattered groups, instead of in long chains like those of North and South 

America. The highest African mountains are about the same height as the Rocky mountains but there are no peaks which equal the towering Andes.

In the northwest, bordering the Sahara table-land, are the parallel ranges of the young, high, rugged Atlas mountains. Find them on the map, page 124.

The eastern part of Africa is its most mountainous section. Crossing the high Abyssinian plateau are ranges whose peaks reach heights of 15,000 or 16,000 feet.

In east-central Africa, astride the Equator, are the Ruwenzori mountains, which are not extensive but are high. Near Lake Victoria is a group of high volcanic peaks which have given a rich black lava soil to the region. The best-known of these volcanoes is Mt. Kilimanjaro, the highest peak in Africa, with an elevation of 19,445 feet. Just north of it Mt. Kenya 119

AFRICA 

reaches 17,000 feet.

The Drakensberg mountains, which are in southeastern Africa, are the highest part of the southern highlands. These mountains parallel the coast.

There are low ridges in western Africa near the coast. In all parts of the continent the detached groups of mountains slope to the plateaus.

Coastal Plains. In most parts of the continent to reach the interior one must first cross the narrow coastal lowlands from which rise sharply the plateaus and mountains. Few of 

Africa's coastal plains are more than three hundred miles wide, and in some places there is almost no plain at all.

AFRICAN LAKES AND RIVERS 

are East-central Africa, a district of high tablelands and heavy rainfall, is the lake region of the African continent. The lakes feed many rivers and useful for navigation.

Lake Victoria is one of the most important. 

Although Lake Superior in our country is the largest body of fresh water on earth, Lake Victoria in Africa is a close second. It is almost as large as the country of Scotland. 

East of the Congo basin is a chain of long, narrow lakes. These lakes lie in what is known as a rift valley caused ages ago by the breaking of the earth's rock formation. Lake Tanganyika and Lake Nyasa, the most important of the rift valley group, are among the largest lakes in the world.

The usefulness of the rivers for transportation is limited by waterfalls and rapids. Those that flow east from the east-central highlands have short, rapid courses. Those that flow in other directions are longer, for they cross the broad table-lands. These table-lands drop abruptly to the narrow coastal plains, and the rivers flow over the ledges in rapids and waterfalls. As the coastal plains do not extend far inland, the rivers usually have falls or rapids near their mouths.

The Nile. The best-known African waterway is the Nile, the upper stream of which, the White Nile, rises in Lake Victoria. From the lake the Nile wends its way north for half the length of the continent before it enters the 

Mediterranean sea. Its four thousand miles drain an area of more than 1,100,000 square miles.

Find the Nile on the map on page 132. A study of its course tells us a great deal about the unequal rainfall of Africa. We see that the southern half of the river is fed by many tributaries, and that the northern half is one single stream. The reason is that the upper half lies in or near regions of heavy equatorial rains which pour a great volume of water into the main stream through a number of important branch streams. The most important branch of the Nile is the Blue Nile. In the northern half of its course the Nile river flows through the flat, sandy desert land, where no rains add to its flow or give it tributaries. It finally empties into the sea less water than it had when it left the tropics.

Although considered a navigable river, the Nile is obstructed by many sand bars and a series of cataracts along the section from Assuan to Khartum. During the seasons when the water is low, river traffic is hindered and steamers must stop their trips until the water rises again. Because of these hindrances the 

Nile above Khartum is not so important a means of transportation as the railroads. 

The Congo. The map on page 124 shows us that the Congo has many branches and that some of its tributaries are very long. This tells us at once what kind of rainfall the Congo basin has. The Congo is shorter than the 

Nile, being less than three thousand miles long, but it carries more water. Rising in Lake 

Tanganyika, the river turns and twists and finally makes its way to the Atlantic ocean. 

It drains more than 1,400,000 square miles, most of the area being in the belt of equatorial calms.

In spite of the fact that its course is blocked in places by rapids, the Congo river is a great highway of travel, because it flows largely through a jungle area where it is difficult to build long stretches of railroad. Below Stanley pool is a series of cataracts, around which a short railroad has been built. Above Stanley pool the Congo is navigable to Stanley falls, around which it has been necessary to build

PHYSICAL FEATURES OF AFRICA 

121 another railroad. The Congo makes its way through grasslands, rain forests, and fields of rice and cotton. Down it are sent cargoes of rubber, ivory, gold, palm oil, and a gum called copal. 

The Niger. The Niger river rises 150 miles from the Gulf of Guinea, into which it flows after describing a great semicircle. The area which the Niger drains is a little less than 

600,000 square miles, a territory one-fifth the size of the United States. Navigation on this river also is interrupted by rapids, but it is open to steamboats for almost five hundred miles from its mouth. Down the Niger come palm nuts and oil, ivory, rubber, and peanuts.

The Zambezi. The Zambezi river, although much smaller than the three mentioned, is about sixteen hundred miles long and drains an area of more than half a million square miles. Its course, before it finally flows into the Indian ocean, is like a letter S. Like most 

African rivers, it is interrupted by falls and rapids. At Victoria falls it takes a dizzy downward plunge of 400 feet, nearly three times the height of Niagara's plunge.

The Zambezi flows through rain forests, through a cattle country, and through a mineral country. It passes orchards and fields of cotton, grains, and rice. It is navigable for four hundred miles from the sea, and many products are brought down it to the ocean ports. 

These four African rivers-the Nile, the

Congo, the Niger, and the Zambezi-are among the greatest in the world. The Congo is second only to the Amazon in the size of its drainage basin, and no other continent except 

South America has four rivers with so great a total drainage area. The Mississippi, greatest in drainage area of our own continent, is well behind the Congo in this respect and only a little ahead of the Nile. 

Waterways as Travel Routes. Without these inland waterways the development of Africa would be even more difficult than it is. The rivers of Africa bore along the rude boats of the black people for many centuries before the white man penetrated into this dark continent. 

But for the rivers, explorers could not have made such extensive travels as they have. 

Today the rivers provide passage for modern steamboats, but now, of course, we have other ways of moving about. With the coming of the white man short railway lines have been built from the coasts into the interior, and also around cataracts and waterfalls. Today even the truck and the airplane are being used to open up the interior of this vast continent. 

1. Africa is only nine miles from Europe at the Strait of Gibraltar and it is joined to Asia. It is the second largest continent in the world and is crossed by the Equator. 

2. Africa is a continent of plateaus. The low Sahara table-land occupies much of the north of the continent. The high table-lands are in the east and south. 

3. Africa is not a mountainous continent. The eastern part is the most mountainous section. The highest mountains of Africa are about the same height as the Rockies but are lower than the peaks of the 

Andes. The important ranges are the Atlas mountains, the Abyssinian highlands, and the Ruwenzori and Drakensberg mountains. Near Lake Victoria is a group of volcanic peaks, the best-known of which is Mt. Kilimanjaro. 

4. Africa has very narrow coastal plains. places there is almost no plain at all.

Africa. This is a region of heavy rainfall. 

6. The African rivers are useful as routes of transportation, despite the falls and rapids along their courses. The four chief rivers of Africa are the 

Nile, the Congo, the Niger, and the Zambezi. 

7. East-central Africa is the lake district of the continent. Lake Victoria is the most important of these lakes. A chain of lakes of this district lies in a long rift valley.

AFRICA'S POSITION  

Tropic of Cancer

The climate and vegetation of the continent of Africa are affected by its shape; by its plateaus, lowlands, and moun EFFECT OF tain ranges; and by the trade winds, just as are the climates of all the continents. But the position of Africa is the chief cause of its climatic belts.

Africa extends about an equal distance north and south of the Equator, and less than a thousand miles beyond either tropic. The continent, therefore, lies almost wholly in the Torrid zone and does not have the great differences in temperature of most other continents. A trip north from the

Equator would be through belts having the same types of natural vegetation as a trip south from the Equator. 

If you went north, you would pass through a belt of rain forest, a grassland area, a desert, and a region with a Mediterranean climate. A trip south would lead through similar belts. Equator
