the west coast to the mouth of the Congo river. Eastward, it extends more than half way across the continent nearly to Africa's lake region and to the headwaters of the river Nile.

On the east coast, extending from the Equator nearly to the Tropic of Capricorn, is another area of rain forests. This coastal lowland, in addition to being near the equatorial belt of heavy rains, lies in the path of the southeast trade winds. Along the coasts, the rain forests contain many great swamps of mangrove trees, whose trunks are connected by roots which rise high out of the water and form a dense tangle which boats can hardly penetrate.

A voyage up the Congo river would show us that this region is much like the great 

Amazon basin in South America. We should find the same dense forests, matted together with vines so as to be almost impassable. Like the Amazon basin, the Congo basin is a network of streams. The streams drain into the 

Congo river, and the water flows to the ocean carrying large quantities of silt which discolors the Atlantic for miles out from shore. Africa is the home of the negro race, just as South America was once largely inhabited by Indians, and in the forests of the Congo will be found tribes of negroes as savage and uncivilized as the jungle Indians of the Amazon basin.

The jungles of the Amazon basin, however, are thicker than those of the Congo basin, for the Amazon is in a region of even heavier rainfall than the Congo. The Congo basin is protected on the east by high African mountains, and a great deal of the moisture from the southeast trade winds falls on their eastern slopes before the winds reach the Congo basin.

In South America no east-coast mountains cause the trade winds which sweep the Amazon basin to lose their moisture. Then, too, the Congo jungle, because it is on a table-land, is somewhat cooler than the low Amazon region. 

The Congo basin, although it includes some twenty-five thousand square miles of matted forests, has many more clearings than the Amazon jungle. It is in these productive clearings that the native negroes make their homes. 

Usually a group of them choose a place close to a stream and clear away the forest to make room for a village. This is a difficult task in the matted growth and doubly difficult when done with crude tools. When the huts have been put up a garden is planted with corn, yams, and manioc. When the people of a village have used the soil for so long that it has lost its fertility, the village is moved. Again the laborious task of making a clearing is begun. 

Of the native African tribes, the Pygmies are the most interesting. They are a small people, some of them only three feet high. 

They are very ignorant and backward and do not clear the land for farms. They depend for food principally on wild animals. They are skilful hunters and, like some tribes of South 

America, use poisoned spears and arrows.

Jungle Products. Few of us would be as skilful as the black people at gathering the natural resources of the jungles. To get the long, white ivory tusks that bring such a huge price, it is necessary to kill elephants. The natives often capture elephants by digging pits which they cover with leaves. Elephants fall into the pits and are then slain by the hunters. 

The ivory tusks are saved to be sold, and the meat is cut up, some being used for a great feast and the rest being smoked for later use.

Both soft and hard woods grow in the rain forests. Mahogany and dye woods are among the most valuable timbers. Because of the difficulty of getting wood out of the forests and down to the seaports, this great source of lumber is little used. 

Oil palms are scattered throughout the

African jungle. The oil of the nuts has come to be of great value in the manufacture of soap, margarine, and lubricating oil. The fruit of the oil palm grows in great bunches at the bases of the leaves. The bunches or cones of fruit are cut by natives who walk up the palms with the aid of strong ropes. A single cone from these trees may contain as many as seven hundred nuts, each of which is as large as a horse chestnut and about the same color. The nuts

AFRICA 

are boiled in water to remove the outside shell. 

This shell is lined with a fiber that is rich in oil. During the boiling some of the oil rises to the surface. The natives skim this off to use in cooking. The fibers are then crushed into a pulp and again boiled. The oil is again skimmed off and placed in casks. The nut kernels are also valuable for oil. They are dried and sent to Europe, where they are ground and the oil is pressed out of them. For long years before the white man discovered the value of palm oil, the natives used it for cooking and to rub on their bodies to protect them from sun, rain, and insects.

Another valuable product of this region is gum copal. This is the sap of certain tropical trees, which hardens when exposed to air. The gum is often found in the beds of streams where it has been washed down by the heavy rains. It is used to make varnishes.

As in the Amazon basin, rubber is gathered in the depths of the African jungles. Cacao has also been introduced into Africa and now forms one of the most valuable products of the Equator region. Vanilla beans grow here and are shipped away to furnish flavoring. 

The Congo basin is rich in copper and gold, and diamonds may be found in the beds of old creeks and rivers. Until the white man came to Africa, however, these diamond fields were undeveloped.

The rain forests of the east coast lowlands produce about the same products as the jungles along the Gulf of Guinea and the Congo river. In the east coast rain forests, the stripping of the bark from the mangrove trees is an important industry. This bark is shipped to Europe where it is used in tanning hides.

The jungle belt stretches for many miles on either side of the Equator. Then to the north and to the south, the matted, GRASSLANDS darkened jungle gives way to more open forests and clear spaces become more and more frequent. Beyond the forests are grasslands or savannas, just as there are beyond the jungles of Brazil. This is the game country of Africa. Here live the lion, king of beasts, the striped zebra, and many graceful varieties of antelope. Leopards, giraffes, and the rhinoceros also roam the open grassland plains. Wild animals are especially abundant here because antelopes and zebras feed on grasses and herbs, and flesh-eating animals, such as the lions and leopards, prey on the grass-eating beasts. 

The northern and the southern regions of the African grasslands stretch in broad belts across the continent. The grasslands north of the Equator extend across the low table-land, over the high Abyssinian plateau, and down to the east coast. The southern grasslands of 

Africa extend east in a broad belt from the Atlantic to the rain forest of the east coast and stretch northward to join the northern belt of grasslands near the east coast. They also reach to the south, into the temperate plateau of the Southeastern highlands.

The Sudan. The part of the northern savannas between the Atlantic and the plateau of Abyssinia is known as the Sudan. 

As you travel north across the Sudan from the jungle you pass through a belt of grass and forests and then grassy plains and come to a region of scanty vegetation and uncertain rainfall. Beyond this is the Sahara desert. 

The African grasslands, like those of South

America, are caused by the shifting of the equatorial rain belt. When the sun is directly overhead near the Tropic of Cancer, the Sudan has a rainy season. Its dry season occurs as the sun moves toward the Tropic of Capricorn and carries a rainy season to the southern grasslands. During the rainy season there is a quick, luxuriant growth of vegetation on the grasslands which is withered during the great heat of the dry season. The west coast of the northern grasslands has a somewhat heavier rainfall than other sections of this region. 

The Sudan is inhabited almost entirely by negroes. Many of the tribes of this region are more advanced than the primitive peoples found in the jungles.

Like nearly all grassland regions of the world, the Sudan affords pasturage for sheep and goats. As the southern part is well watered by streams, the soil is good for farming. In the northern part of the Sudan, where

there is the least amount of rain, the people are nomads, who wander from place to place to find food for their cattle, sheep, camels, and goats. On this northern border where the grass is sparse there have been dreadful famines in years of scanty rainfall. 

In the more rainy southern part of the Sudan, near the jungle, are great numbers of native villages where the negroes do simple farming. The people of the southern Sudan, unlike the less civilized tribes of the jungle, get their food principally from their gardens and flocks. 

There are mineral deposits of tin, lead, iron, silver, and salt in the Sudan. Few African minerals were developed before white men came into the continent, but the natives of the Sudan have worked tin mines for centuries. 

Southern Grasslands. Like the Sudan grasslands, the broad region of grasslands to the south is caused by the shifting of the equatorial rain belt.

The grasslands of the south lie principally on higher table-lands than the grasslands of the Sudan, and are therefore cooler. On the plateau to the east, their elevation is so great that Europeans find the climate temperate and comfortable. The southern part, called the veldt, has a climate much like that of the higher western plains of the United States. 

The Southeastern highlands shut off heavy rains and prevent the growth of forests. 

This veldt region has light rains and not enough water for irrigation, so there is not much agriculture. Like our own western plains, however, it offers good grazing. Sheep are the most important animals, and fine wool is produced in great quantity. In the dry western districts of the grasslands are Angora goats, which can live on the coarsest and most worthless plants and whose long hair makes fine mohair cloth. Farther north are cattle, and corn and wheat are raised. The eastern plateau and the tropic savannas are well suited to corn and cattle raising. 

The southern grasslands are very rich in minerals. One of the greatest copper-producing districts of the world is here. Other minerals of the region are tin, iron, gold, asbestos, and chromite, which is used in making certain hard steels.

Traveling away from the Equator across either the northern or the southern grasslands, one reaches a desert. Nearly half of

Africa is covered by areas of rocky 

DESERTS 

or sandy waste, which produce little and form great barriers to the interior of the continent. 

The northern desert, the Sahara, is the largest desert in the world. In southern Africa is a desert known as the Kalahari. 

Sahara Desert. Something of the great size of the Sahara may be judged from the fact that it covers about one-third of the entire area of Africa. It stretches across the continent from the Atlantic ocean to the Red sea. It extends to the Mediterranean on the northeast but in the northwest it is cut off from the sea by the Atlas mountains. In the south it merges into the grasslands of the Sudan. This vast area is almost as large as the continent of Europe. If it were laid on the United States with its northern edge along the Canadian border, its southern sands would reach the Gulf of Mexico, and its length would cover our country from the Atlantic to the Pacific. 

As you travel over the Sahara you will discover that it is not just a flat, sandy waste. In fact much more of it is bare, rocky plateaus and hills. Your desert journey will also convince you that the daily temperatures of the 

Sahara are extreme. When the burning sun glares down on the sand and rock, the temperature often climbs to 130°. However, the air cools quickly at night and sometimes there are frosts. 

The Sahara is really a part of a desert area that stretches beyond the borders of Africa and on into Asia. The prevailing winds that blow over the low Sahara table-land are the northeast trade winds. These winds blow from the dry interior of Asia toward the Equator and have little chance to pick up moisture. 

Consequently they have little moisture and bring very little rain indeed. The north of 

Africa is so wide that the desert is not affected by winds from the sea.

Occasionally, especially during the rainy seasons along the Mediterranean, short showers

AFRICA 

will occur in the desert. Rain which falls on the slopes of the Atlas mountains forms streams that flow out into the desert. But after flowing a short distance the river waters are lost in this vast sea of sand and rock. The courses of the rivers, being dry most of the time, make good roads. Some of the water, however, collects beneath the rock and soil, or flows along as underground streams. It comes to the surface as springs or may be reached by wells. Around these springs vegetation grows luxuriantly and people establish homes. 

These fertile places in a deşert are called oases. 

Some of the oases are large and have several villages which they supply with food. Some give food to only a few families. 

The oases make it possible to cross the Sahara. For centuries the long, slow caravans have used them as resting places at which they secured fresh supplies of food and water. Experienced Arabian guides are needed to pilot the lumbering camels over the indistinct routes that lead from one oasis to another. The camels, which rock and sway under their loads of valuable merchandise, are the most important of the desert animals, for they can eat and drink enough at one time to last them during a journey of several days.

The oases of the Sahara show that the desert land is really very fertile and lacks only water to transform it into a productive region. 

The people on the oases raise for their own use vegetables, grain, and fruit, but the great 

Sahara desert produces little of commercial importance except dates. 

Dates are the wealth of the desert people.

Once having reached their full-bearing period, date palms usually yield for a century or more.

Each tree produces about a hundred pounds of fruit a year. Although these trees thrive in the dry desert air, they must have plenty of water around their roots. Numerous different kinds of dates, which furnish food for both people and animals, are grown on the Sahara oases.

In the land of Egypt in northeastern Africa is the greatest oasis in the world. Where the

Nile overflows and where irrigation has been used the watered land becomes a garden of growing things. The Nile delta is one of the earth's most fertile places. 

You may remember that the dry Sonora- 

Colorado region of North America is in the same latitude and has the same kind of climate as the Sahara desert. Part of this region, like the valley of the Nile, has been made useful through irrigation. Because it produces so many crops which are similar to those raised in Egypt, the lower Colorado region is known as the American Egypt. The valuable longfibered Egyptian cotton and the date palm flourish in the irrigated soil of the North American desert just as they do in the oases of the Sahara.

Salt is found in the western and central parts of the Sahara, and forms an item of caravan trade. 

Kalahari Desert. 

On page 190 find the desert south and west of the high grasslands of southern Africa. This is the Kalahari desert, which is not so dry as the Sahara because the continent is much narrower in the south and the desert is therefore nearer the ocean and is influenced by it.

The southeast trade winds would normally bring rain to this part of the African continent, but the Southeastern highlands steal their moisture. As the winds blow westward over the central part of the plateau the rainfall becomes lighter and lighter, until there is finally no moisture and the land is arid. You will remember that the Atacama desert in South

America was caused in the same way by the Andes mountains, which robbed the moisturebearing winds before they reached the west coast.

The great drawback to the development of the arid Kalahari region is the lack of drinking water. Sea water is distilled near the coast.

In the interior reservoirs have been built, and in places deep holes, called bore-holes, have been drilled into the soil to get at the water which is deep down under the earth. These wells, however, have not been very successful, for the water is usually brackish, or salty. 

Because the rainfall is greatest in the northern and eastern parts of the arid Kalahari region the scrub growth is densest in these

sections. At the end of the rainy season a species of wild melon springs up on the edges of the desert. These melons contain water that can be used by men and beasts. On the scattered brush of this desert grazing can be carried on, especially the raising of goats, which can thrive where cattle and sheep would be unable to find sufficient food. 

The lack of good drinking water and the sparse scrub growth make nomads of the black people of the region. They move their herds and flocks from place to place to find pasturage. 

The Bushmen, one of the desert peoples, do not keep domestic animals but hunt game with their poisoned arrows.

There are diamonds in the beds of small rivers in the western part of this region. Copper and lead are also known to be present. 

HAVING A MEDITERRANEAN CLIMATE 

Once you get safely across the deserts of

Africa you may proceed into much more pleasant regions. If you are

AFRICAN REGIONS traveling north this will be into the French countries of Morocco, Algeria, and 

Tunisia. Traveling into the southern and southeastern parts of Africa, you reach what is known as White Man's Land. 

The two regions, the southernmost and northernmost parts of Africa, have been longest known to the white man.

Atlas District. The French colonies of 

Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia have a Mediterranean climate like that of southern California, with mild, rainy winters and hot, dry summers. The Atlas district is in about the same latitude as southern California, and the moisture-laden westerly winds visit both of these sections during the winter. We have also discovered this type of climate at the Riviera and in the Central valley of Chile. 

The Atlas district is one of the most clearly defined of the African climatic belts, for it is bounded on the east and north by the Mediterranean, on the west by the Atlantic ocean, and on the south by the Sahara desert. This district includes and is greatly influenced by the Atlas mountains.

The best farm lands are on the Tell, the narrow coastal plain between the Atlas mountains and the sea, and on the plateaus between the ranges of mountains. The summer droughts limit the natural crops to hardy plants. 

The forests and mines of the Atlas mountains enrich the region. On the mountain · slopes grow forests of cork oaks. These trees live to be very old, and once a tree has reached the age of twenty-five years, the natives may strip the bark every eight or ten years. Cork products are made from this bark. Mulberry trees are grown for their leaves, which are fed to silkworms. The mines of the district yield iron ore and some lead and zinc. Another valuable mineral of the region is phosphate rock, which is necessary in the manufacture of fertilizers.

The South African Belt. The South African 

Mediterranean-climate belt is small and lies entirely in the southern part of Africa about the Cape of Good Hope. The southwest part lies in the path of the westerly winds which blow from the Atlantic and bring rain in winter. In summer the region is dry and hot. The southeastern part of this climatic belt is fairly moist because of the moisture-laden southeast trade winds. On the lowlands the crops are subtropical. 

Like northern Africa, this region is in about the same latitude as southern California, although in the Southern hemisphere. It has the same type of climate and crops. The elevation of southern Africa, the narrowness of the continent at this point, and the influence of the great bodies of surrounding water, all combine to make the climate cooler and more healthful and pleasant than that of other sections of Africa.

Like all other regions which have a Mediterranean climate, the section about the Cape of Good Hope grows quantities of fruit. 

You cannot go very far inland in southern

Africa without starting to climb, for most of this region is plateau. The land of South Africa rises in a series of terraces and as you climb you notice that, just as in North Africa, hardier crops and fruits are grown on the upper slopes and plains. You begin also to see more grazing lands on which are pastured cattle, sheep, and goats.

The mountains of both continents rob the southeast trade winds of their moisture. Moreover, a cold current, the Benguela, flows along the west shore of Africa and has much the same effect as the cold Peruvian current has on the coasts of Chile and Peru. Because of the

A CONTINENT FOR COLONIZATION 

Now that we know something about the surface and climate of Africa, let us see why so 

CONTINENT 

much of its land was left unknown THE DARK and feared when a section of the continent was highly civilized and other parts of the world were rapidly being settled. The answer is that it was very dangerous to explore this continent which had no easy way of entrance. When explorers and their men attempted to cross Africa overland from north to south, they soon reached the dreaded Sahara with its glaring heat, lack of water, and danger of attack by robbers. For many years the Sahara was the camping ground of Arab slave traders, who were not at all particular about whom they seized to sell as slaves. Whether they sold an explorer or a native chief-it was all the same to them. 

Those explorers who attempted to enter the continent from the sea met with many other difficulties. In the first place, they had great difficulty in finding a suitable harbor at which to land. In spite of its great size, Africa has a very regular coast line with few capes, peninsulas, and islands to form protected harbors where landings and settlements can be easily made. Of course the coast has some harbors; but an exploring party lucky enough to find one and to start up a river was soon stopped by the cataracts at the edge of the interior plateaus.

The explorers who pushed on and reached the interior found still other dangers awaiting them. Africa lies almost entirely in the Torrid zone, and the hot, damp shores and interior are very unhealthful for white men. In the grasslands were lions and other dangerous beasts. In the jungles the explorers might be bitten by snakes, or by the wicked little tsetse flies that carry sleeping sickness. Or they might run into a band of black cannibals, more dangerous than any beasts. There were numberless unpleasant things that might happen to strangers in Africa. 

So you can very easily see that Africa was not an easy continent to explore. But even such a continent could not remain forever unknown. Gradually Europeans established a few trading posts along the coasts. Part of the trade that they carried on was disgraceful. 

They bought black people from native slave hunters and carried them off to be sold in other lands. The ancestors of most of the negroes in our country were carried off in that manner. 

PIONEERS 

But slowly the world changed. People came to realize how wrong it was to force a man, whether he be black or white, to become a slave. Men of science learned how to fight the diseases of the low, hot, damp lands of Africa. Missionaries and explorers went to Africa and made friends with the natives. Today the worst stage in the development of Africa is over. The pioneers' task is the hardest. They are the ones to test the dangers and it is they who secure the information that makes development possible. 

Livingstone. The two best known African explorers were David Livingstone and Henry 

M. Stanley. Livingstone was a Scottish missionary who spent the best years of his life in 

Africa. He made friends with the natives, doctored them, and taught them the Christian religion. He fought unceasingly against the slave trade which in his day was still being carried on. Livingstone was so beloved by the black people that when he died they carried his body many long miles down to the coast so that it might be sent home and laid to rest with his countrymen.

During his explorations along the Zambezi river, Livingstone discovered Victoria falls.

He crossed the continent to the west coast of Angola. He discovered several of the great 

African lakes and stood upon the banks of the Congo river, which he thought to be the upper part of the Nile. 

Stanley. On his last journey into Africa, Livingstone was gone so long without sending 133

AFRICA 

any word back to civilization that Henry M. 

Stanley, a Welshman, was sent by a New York newspaper to look for him. The story of Stanley's search and final discovery of Livingstone is an interesting tale of adventure. Together 

Livingstone and Stanley penetrated farther into the unknown continent, and after Livingstone's death Stanley continued the work. One of his great feats was tracing the course of the Congo river. The two men filled in many of the blank spaces on the map of Africa. Their own names are now printed on that map. Near 

Victoria falls, on the Zambezi river, is the town of Livingstone, and on the Congo river are 

Stanley falls and Stanley pool. Find these places on the map, page 132. 

INTEREST 

When Stanley and Livingstone had shown the way, European nations followed in their footsteps and took control of sec- 

EUROPEAN tion after section of Africa. The 

IN AFRICA opening of Africa came at a very good time for the nations of

Europe. Their home lands were becoming overcrowded. Their factories needed more raw materials and more buyers for their goods. 

Colonies give nations raw materials and markets. America, filled with independent countries, no longer offered a chance to colonize, and Asia and the valuable islands of the world were already occupied. The European nations therefore turned to the development of Africa, and in spite of the difficulties set about making settlements and opening commerce with them.

The African dependencies of European na tions are of three kinds. Colonies, properly speaking, are lands owned by the European nations. They may be settled by colonists from the home country or simply managed by a few white people sent out by the mother country. 

Others of the dependencies are protectorates.

These are governed by their own rulers under the direction and protection of a powerful nation, which receives trade advantages in return for its help. The third class of dependencies are called mandates. The mandates were colonies of Germany and Turkey which were set free at the end of the World War. It was felt that they were not ready to govern themselves, so each was placed by the League of Nations in the care of some strong nation which agreed to protect it against all enemies and help it to prosper and develop. All three classes are generally called colonies. In all of them, the protecting nation gets the very valuable privileges of receiving the dependency's raw materials and of using it as a market for finished goods. In return, the nations invest huge sums of money in the dependencies to improve health conditions, to open roads and provide transportation, to help agriculture, and to keep order. They have given work to large numbers of natives and have started schools. Africa promises to develop greatly under their care, and we can no longer look upon it as the Dark Continent.

1. The greater part of Africa was unexplored for a long time because of the many dangers to be met in the interior. It was called the Dark Continent. 

2. Some of the obstacles to the early exploration of the continent of Africa were the Sahara desert, which acted as a barrier to the interior; the lack of good harbors; the falls and rapids near the mouths of the rivers; and the tropical jungles with their unhealthful conditions, wild beasts, disease-producing insects, and savage native tribes. 

3. Trading posts which carried on the slave trade were the first settlements to be established in Africa by people of modern European countries. 

4. By the time pioneers had explored parts of Africa, the European countries were becoming overcrowded. 

Their factories needed more raw material and their merchants were looking for new markets. So the nations of Europe turned to Africa to secure new colonies. 

5. A colony is owned and governed by a powerful nation. A protectorate has its own government under the direction of a powerful nation. A mandate is a former colony which is helped and protected by a powerful nation until it can govern itself. 

6. Powerful nations get many benefits in trade from their dependencies, but make many returns in protection, education, and development.

PROJECTS EXPLORERS 

1. In a life of Theodore Roosevelt, find the story of his exploration of the Amazon river. In what ways was this trip like the work of Stanley and Livingstone? What advantages had Roosevelt over these 

African explorers? 

2. Read of the explorations of Byrd and Amundsen in the polar regions, and of those of Roy Chapman

Stanley.

Following European colonization of Africa, the only lands left independent were Egypt, Liberia, and Ethiopia. Liberia is still free, but Ethiopia has been conquered by Italy. 

Egypt's independence is protected by Great Britain. Most of the African continent is now controlled by Great Britain and France, with smaller parts belonging to Belgium, Italy, Portugal, and Spain. In much of the continent, however, the actual governing is done by the chiefs of local tribes. But no matter whether a dependency is a colony, a protectorate, or a mandate, the controlling nation handles the trade and receives the supplies of raw products.

Great Britain's dependencies are the most important in the continent. By treaties or by settlement the British have obtained control of a third of Africa. Their empire includes rich tropical possessions in western Africa and an almost unbroken chain of lands in the east and south. They have special privileges in Egypt, and the proposed route of the Cape-to-Cairo railroad runs for 7,000 miles from Egypt to

South Africa through territory most of which is owned or controlled by Great Britain.

BRITISH DEPENDENCIES 

The most valuable of these British dependencies lie in the temperate southern tip of the continent and on the plateaus and highlands just north of

IN SOUTH AFRICA it. They include the Union of South Africa, Southern 

Rhodesia, Bechuanaland, and Southwest

Africa. The Zambezi river marks the northern boundary of the region. 

The Union of South Africa is a federation or combination of the Cape of Good Hope (generally called Cape Colony), Natal, Transvaal, and the Orange Free State. The British received Cape Colony and Natal by treaty with the Netherlands. Transvaal and the 

Orange Free State were conquered by Great Britain about 1900, but were promptly given self-governing powers. The Union of South 

Africa is now a dominion, like Canada and the Irish Free State, with all the powers of an independent nation. Southern Rhodesia is a selfgoverning colony with very nearly the same powers as South Africa. It is half of a great district claimed for Great Britain by Cecil 

Rhodes, an Englishman living in South Africa, who developed the South African gold and diamond mines and planned the Cape-to-Cairo railroad. Southwest Africa was once a German colony and is now a mandate of the Union of 

South Africa. 

The seacoast of southern Africa has a Mediterranean climate. Not far from the coast the land rises rapidly to the coastal mountains. 

Behind these is the great veldt, with its average altitude of 4,000 feet. Natal, between the sea and the Drakensberg mountains, has a warm, damp climate. The Orange Free State and Transvaal are on the veldt behind the mountains. Southwest Africa on the Atlantic coast and Bechuanaland northwest of Transvaal are largely in the Kalahari desert region. 

Between Transvaal and the Zambezi are the high subtropical grasslands of Southern Rhodesia.

A great deal of South Africa lies in the temperate zone, and the high altitude gives the rest a climate cool enough for white people. 

South Africa is therefore known as a "white man's country." About one-third of the population is white, and more than a half of these are Boers, the descendants of the Dutch who first colonized the country. The languages of the English and Boers are both official, and public notices are always written in both. One of the difficult problems is the settlement of the rights of the black inhabitants. These people, the Kafirs, are skilful farmers, and occupy a great deal of the best agricultural land. 

The Boers wish to take away their privileges, but the British protect them.

In recent years this district has produced a large part of the world's gold supply.

Diamond mining is open-cut mining, that is, the mining begins at the surface. When the diamonds are free from the clay they look like glassy pebbles and are called "rough" diamonds. They are sent to Holland or Belgium to be cut and polished.

tinent. At Cape Town, on the southwest coast, begins the proposed Cape-to-Cairo railroad. Its line now extends through dry 

Bechuanaland into Southern Rhodesia, running almost parallel to the southeastern coast. 

A network of branches covers the eastern region, and a line runs northwest through 

Southwest Africa to Walvis Bay.

The commerce of the countries of South Africa moves through a very few ports, for the regular coast line has few protected bays. 

Cape Town is the law-making capital of the Union and the second city in size. It is modern and beautiful, with all the conveniences of civilization. Behind it is a famous flat-topped hill called Table mountain. The harbor is enclosed by great breakwaters and will admit deep-water ships. Its only disadvantage is its distance from the busiest parts of the Union, which lie far northeast. 

Port Elizabeth serves eastern Cape Colony. 

Durban, in Natal, has the best port of the whole region, and it is much nearer the natural wealth of South Africa than is Cape Town. 

Durban is a great port of call and an important coaling station. Walvis Bay handles most of the trade of Southwest Africa.

The map on page 132 shows us that a good deal of Transvaal and all of Southern Rhodesia are separated from the nearest the nearest seacoast by the Portuguese colony of Mozambique; and we see railroad lines from Transvaal to the 

Mozambique port of Lourenco Marques and from Southern Rhodesia to Beira. These ports and railroads handle most of the imports for 

Transvaal and Southern Rhodesia and there are British customs officials at both ports. Both have artificial harbors.

Commerce and Products. The countries of 

South Africa, like Canada and many other young countries, are a land of raw materials. 

They import most of their manufactured goods. 

Since the climate is too dry for extensive agriculture and there are many people engaged in mining, a great deal of food is brought in. 

This includes wheat from Canada and Australia. Clothing, automobiles, machinery, and foodstuffs enter the country through all the ports.

South Africa is noted for its production of precious minerals. Gold is its most important export. This comes from many mines in a great district called the Rand, around the city of Johannesburg, the largest city of the Union.

In recent years this district has produced twothirds as much gold as the rest of the world put together. There are also valuable gold mines in Southern Rhodesia.

40 50 Gold is mined in many parts of the world. Only a few countries, however, produce large quantities of this metal. This graph shows the world production of gold. Each unit of the graph scale represents ten million dollars worth of gold. What part of the gold produced comes from Africa?

Less valuable but not less interesting is the diamond trade. Diamonds are the third export in importance of the country. South Africa produces most of the fine diamonds for the world's rings, necklaces, and other jewelry.

The best are those of the famous diamond center at Kimberley, in northern Cape Colony.

Some less valuable stones, called alluvial diamonds, come from old river beds in Southwest Africa and other parts of the country. "Rough" diamonds look like small glassy pebbles. They are found in the hard clay of ancient volcanoes, which is known as blue ground. The blue ground is mined and brought to the surface, where it crumbles in the sun and air for some months. Machines then wash off the earthy material, leaving a mixture of rough diamonds, pebbles, and rock fragments.

This mixture is poured onto tables smeared with grease. Diamonds stick to grease, and

AFRICA 

rock does not. When the tables are shaken back and forth the worthless material rolls off and the diamonds remain. They are then sorted and sent to Antwerp and Amsterdam to be cut into finished jewels.

The workmen in the diamond mines agree to stay for certain periods. They are given living quarters in strongly fenced and guarded enclosures, and are not allowed to leave until their time has expired. When they do leave they are carefully searched, for men have often tried to carry away the precious stones.

Most of the gold and practically all the diamonds are exported through Cape Town. 

Some of the gold goes by way of Durban. The great value of these minerals and the number of workers at the mines provided enough trade to pay for building the costly railroads of the region over the eastern highlands and the sparsely settled veldt. But do not exaggerate the value of the minerals. Such common farm products as the corn crop of Iowa and the dairy production of New York are worth as much as the gold of South Africa. 

Other mineral products of South Africa include silver and tin. A good deal of coal is mined in Natal and Transvaal. This is exported to India and is used to supply ships at 

Durban and Lourenco Marques. Southwest

Africa mines and exports copper. Southern 

Rhodesia sends out through Beira large quantities of asbestos and of chromite, a valuable mineral used in making hard steel.

Though there is not much crop raising in the dry uplands of South Africa, Natal's warm, moist climate permits a large sugar crop, which is exported from Durban. Bananas, citrus fruits, and pineapples are also raised here.

Cape Colony raises and exports apples, pears, peaches, and other temperate fruits, which sell at high prices in northern markets when northern fruits are out of season. Great vineyards yield grapes which are used to make wines and jellies or are dried as raisins and currants. 

Tobacco is an important export of Southern Rhodesia.

The products of the grazing lands are even more valuable than those of the crop lands. 

The high grasslands have great flocks of merino sheep, and wool is the second export in value of the whole region. The hair of Angora goats from the drier highlands is shipped out to be made into mohair cloth for upholstering furniture and automobiles. There are cattle in the better northern grasslands, particularly in Southern Rhodesia and northern 

Southwest Africa. Chilled meats are exported from Walvis Bay. Hides and skins of all these animals are exported. There are ostrich farms in South Africa and when ostrich feathers are in fashion the plumes are a valuable article of trade.

Pretoria, in Transvaal, is the executive capital of the Union. In this city is directed all the business of carrying out the laws made in 

Cape Town. 

Like all of Africa, the British dependencies can be much further developed. The water power of Victoria falls in Rhodesia can be made to supply light and power to thousands of square miles. The climate of the region makes it one of the few places where Europeans can settle, and there is a possibility that South Africa may become a great center of population. 

BRITISH DEPENDENCIES IN WEST AFRICA 

From the Tropic of Cancer the Atlantic coast of Africa sweeps south and east in a great curve of three thousand miles to the mouth of the Niger river. The map on page 198 shows us that this coast has been cut up into many sections. 

When the coast was colonized the powerful nations came to an agreement on their shares. 

Germany once had her portion, but now the coast is divided among Great Britain, France, and Portugal, with one independent sectionthe little country of Liberia. 

We see that Great Britain holds four sections of this coast. These colonies are second in importance among her African possessions, but they are valuable for very different reasons than South Africa. This is not a white man's country and has little mineral wealth, but it supplies tropical vegetable products which temperate countries need and cannot grow. 

Gambia is farthest west of these colonies.

Sierra Leone, about five hundred miles southeast of Gambia, was purchased by Great Britain as a home for freed negro slaves. It has proved a valuable investment. The Gold Coast lies farther east, along the Gulf of Guinea, with the colony of Ashanti lying inland from it. 

The Gold Coast includes part of the former German colony of Togo, the remainder of which is a French mandate and is still called by the name of Togo. Farthest east and most important is Nigeria, including in its southeast corner a mandate of part of the former German colony of Cameroon, the rest of which is held by the French as a mandate. On the map these colonies do not look very large and impressive, but Nigeria alone has seven times the area of England, and it is farther by water from 

Nigeria to Gambia than from New York to 

New Orleans.

Our map shows us that these colonies lie within fifteen degrees of the Equator and the map on page 124 shows us that all but the Gold Coast reach from the coast through the equatorial rain forests into the low grasslands of the Sudan. Most of the coast lands on the 

Guinea coast consist of mangrove swamps though in some places there are narrow sandy beaches. Back of these strips of coast the land rises to the jungles, which gradually give way to more open forests containing valuable hardwood timber, such as mahogany, cedar, rosewood, ebony, and satinwood. This coastal region has the typical hot, damp climate of the tropics. The rainy season often lasts for ten months with from 70 to 140 inches of rain.

The heat, dampness, and danger of fever make these tropics particularly unhealthful for white people, and only a few traders, officials, missionaries, and mine operators live in them. 

North of the coastal lands, however, the swamps and rain forests gradually give place to the low plateau grasslands of the Sudan.

Here the climate is subtropical; the air is hot but comparatively dry. The rainfall is reduced to 25 to 30 inches a year, and in some parts of the region white people can live quite comfortably. This belt extends west to the Atlantic and includes practically the whole of Gambia.

North of the Sudan, beyond the limits of the British colonies, the Sahara begins.

The population of the West Africa region is almost wholly negro, and contains a great variety of tribes. Sierra Leone has many descendants of the freed slaves, some with considerable education. The Hausas, a people of the Sudan, are a mixture of the Arab and Negro races. They are an agricultural and trading people, intelligent and active. For centuries they have traded horses, mules, cattle, camels, and their woven and leather goods to the tribes of southern and western Africa. The forests of Ashanti are the home of a west coast people who were long supreme among their neighbors. They also are intelligent, good farmers, and keen traders. They are skilful in making pottery, cotton cloth, and gold wares. 

Many of the jungle tribes, however, are very low in intelligence and habits. Some of them were originally cannibals. These peoples learn slowly, and their backwardness makes it very hard to develop their districts. 

Transportation. Trade with North Africa began in the interior long before the arrival of Europeans. For a thousand years, Arab caravans have met the negroes from the interior at such cities as Kano and Kuka, in Nigeria, and have exchanged European goods for ivory, gums, cattle, sheep, camels, and, in the old days, slaves. Kano is the largest purely native city north of the Equator. 

The natives still use these markets and the European traders still come to them; but traffic no longer follows the caravan routes across the desert. It now flows from the interior to the coast, and by ocean steamers on to Europe. 

Transportation is not an easy problem. There are few good harbors. Wherever a good port could be found or established it has been made the sea terminal of a railroad line and a point of exchange for products of the interior and imported goods from Europe. The only exception is Bathurst, in Gambia. This city lies. at the mouth of the Gambia river, which allows ocean-going ships to steam 150 miles straight into the colony and receive its products near their sources.

The ports of Nigeria are Lagos and Port OWC-12

AFRICA 

Harcourt. Lagos, the principal port, lies near the ocean on a harbor sheltered by a sand bar. 

Port Harcourt is about forty miles from the sea on a river which admits vessels of medium draft. The port was established in 1914 to export coal from nearby fields and is a useful coaling station. From both these ports railroads reach inland to Kano, and connect with each other and with the Niger river. This great river is usually navigable for the smaller sea-going vessels through most of the year, and carries considerable traffic. It is, however, uncertain, and the railroads are now the principal means of serving the colony. 

Takoradi and Accra are the ports of the 

Gold Coast. Accra has little protection, and ships lie a mile offshore and load and unload by lighters. Takoradi has a deep harbor protected by breakwaters. Railroads from these ports cover the Gold Coast and Ashanti, reaching as far inland as Kumasi. 

Freetown, in Sierra Leone, is the best harbor on the west coast and is the terminus of the Sierra Leone railroad. This harbor alone has repaid Great Britain for the establishment of the colony. Its deep and sheltered waters make it a port of call for all ships to West Africa and give the British an advantage in the trade of the whole region. 

Along the coast, calling at all these harbors and at those of the other colonies of the region, trading ships move up and down. These are not great liners like those of the north Atlantic trade, but they carry valuable freights. 

Commerce and Products. The little cargo steamers which call along the coast bring manufactured goods, mostly from Great Britain, including cotton cloth, machinery, tobacco, and hardware. They also bring supplies of coal, and automobiles from the United States. 

In return, the steamers take away tropical vegetable products and other raw materials for manufacture in Europe. These exports are much the same for all the ports. In the forest regions the oil palm yields nuts and oil, and cacao plantations established all along the coast produce large crops. In the Gold Coast the natives established a cacao industry with no help from the whites. Mahogany and other cabinet woods are exported in valuable quantities.

The Sudan grasslands send out hides and skins by way of the Gambia river and the Nigerian railroads. The Sudanese also raise tons of peanuts, which are exported to Europe to be crushed for their oil.

Nigeria has other valuable resources in the coal about Port Harcourt and in tin ore, which is shipped to Great Britain. The plantations of the Cameroon district began the cultivation of coffee under the Germans and have now a valuable export trade.

The Gold Coast received its name from the quantities of gold grains which were mixed with the sands of its rivers. For many years its natives have used the precious metal in gold work. Now the gold mines are worked by Europeans. Other exported minerals are alluvial diamonds and manganese. There is a high grade of bauxite which will prove useful in making aluminum at some future time. 

The Gold Coast, Ashanti, and Sierra Leone ship kola nuts to Nigeria and other colonies of this region. These nuts are chewed by the natives much as some people chew tobacco. 

They have a stimulating effect and are much in demand in the markets of Kano and Kuka. 

Sierra Leone has also an increasing trade in cultivated ginger, and Ashanti has established rubber plantations.

The great problem of the British in West Africa is to educate the natives, whose methods of agriculture are simple and poor, and who are, by nature, very lazy. The British are attempting to teach them better ways. The colonies are already very valuable, but they will become even more so if the natives can be taught skill and industry. 

Great Britain's equatorial colonies on the Indian ocean are in many ways much like those on the Atlantic, but they are 

BRITISH DEPENDENCIES IN EAST AFRICA 

not so important. They have a hot, damp belt of rain forest on the coast which provides tropical products needed by temperate countries, and they rise gradually to drier grasslands in the interior. Being farther from 

Europe, these colonies were developed later

than the west coast colonies and are not so far advanced.

The British East African states include Uganda, Kenya, Tanganyika, Zanzibar, Nyasa land, and Northern Rhodesia. They lie wholly in the tropics, for they extend from 5° north of the Equator to 18° south. The Equator runs through the center of Kenya. Zanzibar is a tropical island lying close to the coast. 

Two colonies touch the ocean, Kenya to the north and Tanganyika to the south. The coastal belt has the usual mangrove swamps and dense tangled tropical forest from which the land rises to the high southern grasslands and slopes down again on the west to the level of Lake Victoria and Lake Tanganyika. 

Mount Kilimanjaro is in Tanganyika and

Mount Kenya is in Kenya. These peaks lie between the ocean and the lake district. The highlands about them are fairly cool in spite of the tropical latitude, and there is plenty of rain. They offer a good opportunity for agriculture and are increasingly used by white settlers. The Kenya highlands are the higher and have the greater white population. The lake district to the west is very much lower and therefore very much hotter, and beyond Lake Victoria it gradually merges into the rain forest of the Congo basin. The part of Kenya between the Equator and Ethiopia is hot, dry, and of little value.

Northwest of Kenya is Uganda. Most of 

Uganda lies in the high grasslands, but the southwestern part is tropical and well forested.

The White Nile rises in Lake Victoria and flows through the western part of Uganda. 

Nyasaland and Northern Rhodesia lie in the high grasslands west of Lake Nyasa. Northern

Rhodesia extends to the Zambezi river and is the upper part of the great area secured for the British by Cecil Rhodes. 

Government. Though the dependencies in

East Africa have forms of government which are different in name, there is not much real difference among them. There is almost no self-government. Kenya and Northern Rhodesia are colonies. Uganda and Nyasaland are both governed by the British as protectorates. Zanzibar is ruled by a sultan, but is actually governed as a protectorate by the 

British. Tanganyika was formerly a German colony, and is now a British mandate. These states work together in money matters, and 

Kenya, Uganda, and Tanganyika have the same customs arrangements. Kenya handles all of Uganda's taxes on imports and exports. 

Transportation. Transportation in East Af rica is poor as yet. There are two ports for the mainland, Mombasa and Dar es Salaam. Mombasa is the port of Kenya and Uganda. It is built on a coral island, and because its harbor will accommodate ships of any size it has become one of the most important ports of the east coast of the continent. The city is picturesque in appearance, but has the narrow, winding streets and other disadvantages of most oriental cities. Dar es Salaam, in Tanganyika, is a beautiful little city with a small but perfectly sheltered harbor.

The rivers of the region are not of much use for transportation, and the plans for railroads are not yet fully carried out. Nyasaland and 

Northern Rhodesia have no easy connection with the other East African colonies. Nyasaland has no railroad, and its trade moves down the drainage basin of Lake Nyasa into Portuguese territory. Northern Rhodesia has rail connections with South Africa, and a line runs northwest through Belgian Congo to connect with Congo river boats. There is a break here, however, in the Cape-to-Cairo railroad route, for there is not yet connection with Tanganyika. The latter colony has the best railroads of the group. A line connects Dar es Salaam with Lake Tanganyika, and a branch runs north to Lake Victoria. A shorter line connects the coast with the northern interior and joins a branch of the Kenya railway. Kenya has an important line from Mombasa to the highland city of Nairobi and from there to 

Lake Victoria and the upper Nile in Uganda.

This railroad carries nearly all Uganda's trade. 

A branch connects with Tanganyika.

For the proper development of the country there must be railroads to connect the uplands with each other and to connect Nyasaland and 

Northern Rhodesia with the eastern coast.

The Cape-to-Cairo railroad, when finished, will

AFRICA 

connect Northern Rhodesia through Tangan yika with Uganda. The lakes will continue to serve as valuable connections with the railroads.

Natives. The East Africans are of the best 

African types. The Buganda tribe of Uganda, the Masai tribe of Kenya, and the Bantu people farther south are intelligent, and make good farmers or herdsmen. In this land of dangerous wild animals the native villages are carefully protected. The huts are generally built in a circle inside a thick hedge of thorn trees. Another thorn hedge inside the village protects the flocks at night from lions and other prowling beasts of prey. The natives have ideas of decoration that to us seem queer. 

Many have great holes in the lobes of their ears, which are so stretched out that the holes will hold wooden and ivory boxes or other articles as big as baking-powder cans. The women of some tribes wind copper wire in long coils about their arms, legs, and necks.

Game Lands. British East Africa is a fa mous big-game country. It has the African elephant, the largest land animal of the world. 

East African elephants are not caught and tamed like their Indian cousins but are hunted for their ivory. The rhinoceros of the grasslands is next in size to the elephant. The giraffe, nearly twenty feet tall, feeds from the branches of the highest trees of the region. 

The thickets along the water-courses shelter the huge African buffalo. Over Uganda, Kenya, and Tanganyika graze great herds of zebras and of the clumsy kongoni, or hartebeeste. Besides this ungainly and ugly antelope, there are a hundred other varieties, from the great eland and sable antelope to the gazelles and the tiny bush-buck. Lions prey at night on the grass-eating animals and sleep by day in the high grass.

Nairobi is the center of the game district, and its citizens make a business of equipping hunters with necessary goods, and providing guides and native porters for the long caravan trips which the sport requires. 

Commerce. Like other African lands, East

Africa is a source of raw materials and a market for manufactured goods. Its imports are about the same as those of West Africa; to 

Zanzibar, Mombasa, and Dar es Salaam come cotton cloth, hardware, machinery, and other manufactured goods from Great Britain. The well-watered grasslands of East Africa supply more exports than the grasslands of West Africa. The great herds of the northern colonies provide many hides and skins. Around Lake 

Victoria is a splendid cotton country. Much cotton is raised on native farms, and the Kenya and Tanganyika railroads bring out hundreds of bales for export. Coffee, too, is grown and exported. There is a widespread cultivation of corn and other grains in the East African lands, but most of the grain is used in the colonies. The coastal plain exports sisal fiber, sugar, and some copra. 

Both Nyasaland and Rhodesia suffer from the presence of the tsetse fly, an insect whose bite gives cattle and horses a fatal disease.

Large herds cannot be developed, and the shortage of draft animals makes it necessary for native porters to carry goods to market. 

These colonies are well suited to the production of cotton, but lack of proper means of transportation makes the raising of cotton impractical. Tobacco has been adopted as a valuable crop which does not cost so much to transport, and Nyasaland and Northern Rhodesia are raising good quantities for export. Northern Rhodesia has valuable mines of copper, lead, and zinc.

Zanzibar includes the nearby island of Pemba in its government. The two grow 90 per cent of the world's cloves. Cloves are the unopened flower buds of a small tropical tree. 

They turn red and are picked just before the tree is ready to blossom. After picking they are allowed to dry until they become brown and hard, which is the state in which we buy them.

Zanzibar was once the center of the East 

African slave and ivory trade. In the old days, traders forced the natives to carry ivory and other products to the coast, and then they sold the carriers with their loads at Zanzibar. 

Slavery has long been forbidden in all the civilized countries and their dependencies. Some ivory is still exported.

The British have in East Africa the same problems of educating the natives that they have in West Africa. There are the further problems of opening up the country by railroads and getting rid of the tsetse fly. There is room for a considerable white population in the cooler agricultural areas, and the rest of the region can be developed under the management of white men to support far larger native populations and to produce more raw materials. 

One of the most promising British dependencies extends north of Uganda for about 

ANGLO-EGYPTIAN SUDAN 

1,300 miles to the southern border of Egypt. This is Anglo-Egyptian Sudan. The north-and-south length of this country includes three climatic belts. Its southern end is hot, damp, and heavily wooded, lying close to the Congo rain forests. The northern part is in the burning desert of the Sahara. The district between is the eastern end of the Sudan grasslands.

The desert region reaches northeast to the Red sea coast. On the coast is a narrow, semiarid belt of low scrub which rises to the coast ridges of the Abyssinian highlands. From the ridges the land slopes down to the Nile valley, and then stretches westward in flat plains. 

The Nile flows north through the whole length of Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, and all its important branches join it in this country. The fertile southern part is well watered. In the northern desert section there is a narrow strip of cultivated land on either side of the river.

Transportation. For a long time the Nile was the only means of entering the country, and this fact naturally joined the Sudan with 

Egypt rather than with the grasslands to the southeast.

Now the usual means of entry is through 

Port Sudan on the Red sea. Railroads extend to Khartum and even beyond and connect this port with the fertile agricultural country of the Nile. The Nile is shallow in many places and steamers cannot travel all the way up it. It is, however, navigable through most of the Sudan, and carries the products of the south to be shipped by rail through Khartum and Port 

Sudan. Khartum is an attractive modern city set in the bleak surroundings of a desert.

Products. The Anglo-Egyptian Sudan raises a corn-like grain called durra, and crops of wheat and barley. The people raise large herds of cattle, and flocks of sheep and goats. The important crop of the country, however, is cotton grown on irrigated land. The British have built one of the world's largest irrigation dams on the Blue Nile, just above the point where it joins the White Nile, and the irrigated fields produce large crops of the long-fibered Egyptian cotton. The cotton area is being rapidly extended and the exports from Port Sudan to 

Liverpool are increasingly important.

This increase of cotton production, however, is hindered by two difficulties. First, the Arab and negro natives are not willing workers, so it is not easy to get the necessary labor. 

Second, there are difficulties with Egypt. The

Anglo-Egyptian Sudan is governed by Egypt and England, acting together, though England has the real control. The Egyptians object to the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan using Nile water for irrigation for fear that they will be left without enough water for their own crops along the lower river. The British, however, are going ahead with the Sudan development.

Besides cotton, the exports include gum arabic, ivory, and hides and skins. Gum arabic is a resin scraped off small acacia trees. It is used as a glue to gum postage stamps and envelopes and also to stiffen candy. Ivory is secured by natives who hunt wild elephants. Both of these products are sent in large quantities to the United States. The imports, as we should expect, are cotton cloth and other textiles, hardware, metal goods, coal, and tobacco. 

The Anglo-Egyptian Sudan is sparsely set tled. Increased population would lead to increased production and greater capacity for buying foreign goods.

British Somaliland is on the north coast of the dry section of East Africa which projects like a horn between the Gulf of Aden and the Indian ocean.

It has a little grazing on the high plateau back of the sea OTHER 

BRITISH DEPENDENCIES

AFRICA 

coast and exports hides and skins to the United 

States. Berbera, the capital and seaport, lies directly across the Gulf of Aden from Aden, a British possession in Arabia, and the colony is useful to Great Britain principally because it helps guard the eastern gateway to the Suez canal.

Many colonies are far distant from their home countries. Such colonies must be reached by ships, and ships need supplies and protection. Ships cannot carry enough fuel for very long voyages without giving up valuable cargo space, so coaling stations are necessary. 

There must also be naval vessels near the shores of colonies to prevent pirates and smugglers from doing damage, and to protect the sea routes in time of war. These naval vessels, too, need supply bases. 

England has a number of such coaling stations and supply bases near Africa. In the 

Atlantic are the islands of Ascension and St.

Helena, on the natural route of ships from 

England to Cape Town. Mauritius lies in the 

Indian ocean, 500 miles east of Madagascar, on the route from Cape Town to India. It is valuable for exports of sugar and copra. There is a fine coaling station in the Seychelles islands, a thousand miles north. These islands export copra, cinnamon, and a valuable fertilizer called guano.

1. Except for the independent countries of Egypt and Liberia, Africa is divided among several European nations. England and France control most of it. Belgium, Italy, Portugal, and Spain control smaller parts. 

2. The most valuable British dependencies lie in 

South Africa. They include the Union of South 

Africa, Southern Rhodesia, Southwest Africa, and

Bechuanaland. The Union of South Africa is a dominion, composed of Cape Colony, Natal, Orange 

Free State, and Transvaal. 

3. South Africa is more suitable for white settlement than other parts of the continent, and one-third of its people are white. More than half of these are Boers, the descendants of the Dutch who first colonized the country. 

4. South Africa has the most and best railroads of the continent, but only a few good ports. The best are 

Cape Town and Durban. The imports of Transvaal and most of the trade of Southern Rhodesia move through the Portuguese ports of Lourenco Marques and Beira. 

5. South Africa's chief products are gold from the

Rand, wool from the sheep of the veldt, and diamonds from Kimberley. Other exports include sugar from Natal, Angora hair, hides, and coal. 

Southern Rhodesia exports asbestos and chromite. 

6. Great Britain's four dependencies in West Africa lie partly in the tropical rain forests and partly in the western Sudan grasslands. Nigeria is the largest and most important. These produce tropical

vegetable products which temperate lands cannot grow. The climate is not healthful for white people, and only a few live there. Transportation is not easy, for there are few good harbors and navigable rivers. These colonies buy cotton cloth, hardware, and other manufactured goods, and export palm oil and palm kernels, cacao, coffee, and mahogany from the rain forests, peanuts and hides from the grasslands, and tin and other minerals. 

7. The British dependencies in East Africa are less developed than those of West Africa. Kenya and

Other exports include hides and skins, tobacco, coffee, sisal, and copra. Zanzibar supplies most of the world's cloves. The region needs railroads to connect the colonies with each other and to connect the southern inland colonies with the coast. British 

East Africa is a famous big-game district. 

8. The Anglo-Egyptian Sudan extends along the upper 

Nile river from the rain-forest region to the Sahara desert. Its chief export is cotton, and trade is carried on through Port Sudan on the Red sea. 

9. Great Britain has minor African possessions which help supply her ships and guard her sea routes. 

British Somaliland helps guard the eastern entrance to the Suez canal. St. Helena and Ascension are island coaling stations on the route from England to South Africa, and Mauritius lies on the route from Cape Town to India.
