INTERESTING PEOPLE OF THE FRENCH LANDS IN AFRICA 

3 5. (1) French Line. (2) (3) Keystone View Co., N. Y. (4) (5) Keystone-Underwood, N. Y. 

1. A snake charmer in a Morocco town. This man is entertaining townspeople and visitors from the desert by his skill in handling poisonous snakes. There are few theatres in Morocco, and many traveling showmen make their livings by street entertainments. 

2. Dancing girls of a desert tribe. These young women have been trained from childhood as dancers. They give performances in the cities of northern Africa. They save their earnings and exchange them for gold coins, which they wear as ornaments on their costumes. If they marry all the gold goes to the husbands. 

3. Women of a savage tribe from French Equatorial 

Africa. This tribe lives in the rain forest, near the Equator. The women pierce their lips and wear wooden disks in the holes. As their lips stretch, they put in larger and larger disks. 

4. A desert horseman in an oasis of date palms. A little stream makes this spot productive, and the dates from the palms are exported from the seacoast cities. The horseman wears a wide cape with a hood that can be drawn over his face. This protection is needed in a land where any strong wind may bring a sand storm. 

5. A peanut seller in Marakesh, Morocco. All that one needs to go into business in Marakesh is something to sell and a mat to sit on. This man is a Jew. Jews do much of the business in North Africa.

HERE AND THERE IN FRENCH AFRICAN LANDS 

(1) Publishers' Photo Service, N. Y. (2) (4) French Line. (3) Keystone-Underwood, N. Y. 

1. The docks at Casablanca, Morocco. The French have built this great pier to protect the harbor from storms, and ships are loaded and unloaded at its inner edge. The French are making North Africa a valuable possession. 

2. A market in Tunis, the chief city of Tunisia. Loaves of bread are piled on the counters of a bake shop. In the square are townspeople and desert dwellers, and a sailor from a French warship. The domes of a beautiful white mosque can be seen in the background. 

3. Threshing in Morocco. In Morocco the farmer spreads the grain stalks on a floor of baked mud and drives the farm animals to and fro over them until the 

We can grain has been trodden loose from the straw. well believe that the grain is not very clean. The French are introducing better methods as fast as they can. Compare this way of threshing with the method used in the 

Central plains of the United States. 

4. The courtyard of a tannery in Fez, Morocco. The 

Moors, as the people of Morocco are called, have long been famous for the manufacture of a fine quality of leather made from the skins of sheep and goats. The skins are cleaned and the hair or wool is removed. 

Then they are soaked in chemicals in clay tubs like those in this yard. The chemicals turn the skins into leather. 

Notice the leather hung on the walls to dry.

FRENCH LANDS IN AFRICA 

After Great Britain, France has the greatest colonial empire, the richest parts of which are in Africa. Including the island of Madagascar, the French dependencies in Africa are even larger in area than the British African dependencies. These French possessions supply 

France with raw materials, markets for manufactured goods, and lands for settlers from her crowded districts, just as the British dependencies supply Great Britain.

The important French dependencies are three states in the Atlas district of North 

MEDITERRANEAN DEPENDENCIES OF FRANCE Africa. The colony of Alge ria lies directly south of France. It has seven hundred miles of seacoast on the warm Mediterranean and is only about as far by sea from Marseille as Baltimore is from 

New York. East of Algeria is the protectorate of Tunisia, at the narrowest part of the central 

Mediterranean. All ships on voyages between western Europe and the Suez canal must pass 

Tunisia's shores. West of Algeria the protectorate of Morocco extends past the Strait of Gibraltar and hundreds of miles down the 

Atlantic coast.

Algerians have practically all the rights of Frenchmen. They have a governor, but they send representatives to the French parliament and have nearly full control of their own taxes. 

Morocco is ruled by a sultan and Tunisia by a bey, but both monarchs must follow the directions of France.

The three countries are very much alike. 

The rich, fertile soil of the Tell runs along their 

Mediterranean seacoast. Behind the Tellare the grass-covered plateaus of the Atlas mountains, with their herds and crops of hardy grains. 

South of the mountains stretches the sandy, sparsely settled Sahara desert. Tunisia, at the eastern end of the group, has less highland and desert than Algeria and Morocco.

These states have, of course, a Mediterranean climate, with winter rains and hot, dry summers. Most of the streams flow only in winter, and on the Sahara side of the mountains the hot sands drink them up as soon as they leave the hills. Morocco lies next to the 

Atlantic waters and has a cooler summer climate than Algeria and Tunisia.

The native people of this region are mostly Arabs and Berbers. Many of the Arabs live in the cities and towns. Some are farmers. Most of the Berbers are herdsmen in the Atlas range or live on the western plains of Morocco. Both races are of the Mohammedan religion. As this religion teaches that it is right to make war on those of other beliefs, the Berbers, being a very warlike people, have continually stirred up a great deal of trouble. Besides the natives there are great numbers of European colonists. The population of Algeria, more than one-eighth as great as that of France, includes thousands of Frenchmen. The busy farmers of the Tell are mostly French. Tunisia is only a short trip from Italy, so naturally it has many Italian and Sicilian settlers, a large part of whom live in the cities. Morocco has a smaller European population, partly because it is farther from France than the others. Its 

Europeans live principally in the towns. 

Cities. These states have a number of fine ports through which their travel and trade move easily. Algiers, the capital of Algeria, is one of the very busiest of all French seaports. It is reached by steamer from Marseille in a day and a night. When we consider that Cape Town is two and a half weeks from England by sea, we can appreciate how much this nearness helps France. Algiers stretches for ten miles between high hills and the shore of the Bay of Algiers. Along the shore is a fine modern European town; the natives have homes on the hills behind. Algiers is a busy coaling station. Oran is another Algerian port. Its population is mostly European, and its fine harbor is protected by a long pier, or jetty. 147

AFRICA 

Tunis is the capital of Tunisia, and has a fine harbor kept deep by dredging. As it is halfway between Gibraltar and Suez, it has become an important port of call on the sea route between those two points.

Tangier, in Morocco, is an international port. That is to say, it does not belong to any one nation but is governed in the interests of all nations. It has been slow in developing. 

Casablanca, a fine French port on the Atlantic, is more important and one of the busiest cities of North Africa. The largest vessels can dock at its piers. Inland from Casablanca is Fez, the capital, an ancient center of Mohammedan learning. It is now a very important trade center for the mountain regions and is noted for the manufacture of fine leather and other hand-made goods. Marakesh, in southern 

Morocco, is the largest city of the protectorate.

It lies on the edge of the desert, and is a great trade center.

Transportation. These cities are all connected by railroads built by the French. These run from Marakesh through Casablanca, Fez,

Oran and Algiers to Tunis. Branch lines cover all the Tell and extend south into the important mountain sections. This chain of railroads delivers the products of all the region, except parts of Morocco, at convenient points for transportation to France, and permits rapid travel from any part of the colonies to any other. With warlike tribes in the mountains, rapid transportation of armies has been a great help to the French in keeping order. Many excellent motor roads also aid in developing the country and getting goods to market. 

Products and Commerce. The disadvantage of a Mediterranean climate is that all the rains come in the winter, when they do not help the growth of the crops. This has been partly overcome in all these countries by French enterprise. The French have greatly improved the irrigation methods of the natives. They have sunk wells in dry parts of the region, and many American-made windmills have been put to work pumping water onto Algerian and 

Tunisian fields. Where there are rivers large enough, the French are using them to supply water for irrigation projects. They are also teaching better methods of cultivation and of caring for the vineyards and olive orchards which are so important in the commerce of the region. The improvements in transportation bring produce from a greater distance than formerly, and therefore allow more land to be used for farming. Finally, the warlike Berbers of the mountains have been forced to give up their old habits of robbing and killing the farmers, and agriculture has become safe in many square miles of new country. 

North Africa is among the best customers of

French industries. It imports manufactured goods of every kind, particularly cotton cloth, metal wares, agricultural implements, wagons, and automobiles. Algiers and Tunis are users of great quantities of coal for supplying ships. 

The thousands of white immigrants are great buyers of European goods.

In return for their manufactures, France and other European countries secure from North Africa a great variety of raw materials. The olives and olive oil of the Tell help make Marseille the oil center of the world. The coast lands also export oranges, figs, other fruits and almonds and vegetables. Their tons of grapes are pressed out and exported as wine. They have also begun to grow tobacco. The drier highlands send the mother country the sheep and wool of their grazing regions, and huge quantities of such hardy grains as wheat and barley. Tunisia was once called "the granary of the world," and is still a source of supply for much of Europe. Cork from the mountain oak forests is exported all along the coast. 

Dates are brought to the seaports from the far oases of the Sahara. Camels once brought them, but now they come swiftly in light and fast automobiles as well as by camel.

Although not a mining region like South Africa, the Atlas district has valuable minerals. Phosphate rock, a useful part of fertilizers, is shipped to France from all ports. 

Lead and zinc are exported from Algeria and

Tunisia. There are also rich iron districts. 

Their ore goes to England for smelting, for France has plenty of iron in her industrial regions and England has seacoast coal districts with little iron.

FRENCH LANDS IN AFRICA 

149 Tunisia has special exports of esparto grass and sponges. Esparto is a grassy plant with a tough fiber useful in the manufacture of ropes and strong paper. The sponges are gathered from the Mediterranean. 

The French colonies in North Africa are to 

France what South Africa is to Great Britain, a possible home for many of her people, and they have the additional advantage of being right at her door, as we might say. The French have done great things in improving the region and educating its inhabitants, and under their direction northern Africa is becoming practically a part of the home country. 

FRENCH DEPENDENCIES 

We have already seen from the map on page 132 that the part of Africa just north of the Gulf of Guinea has been cut up and divided among Euro 

IN WEST AFRICA pean powers, and that Great 

Britain has several large sections. France has still more. Under her control are most of the center of the region and five colonies along the coast. The coast lands are the colonies of Mauritania, Senegal, French

Guinea, the Ivory Coast, and Dahomey, which includes the mandate of Togo to the west. The center contains the inland colonies of French 

Sudan, Niger, and Upper Volta. 

Like the British dependencies in the same part of Africa, these French colonies have a variety of climates. Mauritania is almost all desert. The north of Senegal is also arid, but the south lies in the Sudan grasslands and has about the same climate as its neighbor, Gambia. French Guinea, the Ivory Coast, and

Dahomey have their coasts in the rain-forest belt, with hot mangrove swamps along the ocean and tropical hardwood forests in the hills. Upper Volta lies in the moister Sudan region and has a fine climate for agriculture. 

French Sudan and Niger are partly in the 

Sahara desert, and the grassland along their southern edges has only a light fall of rain. 

Wars in the north and the old slave trade in the south have, in the past, greatly reduced the numbers of the natives. The grasslands of 

Mauritania, Senegal, French Sudan, and upper

French Guinea are inhabited by small numbers of Arabs and Berbers and by tall, strong negroes who make good farmers and herdsmen and supply the French army with fine soldiers. 

The rain-forest negroes of French Guinea and the Ivory Coast are shorter and less advanced. 

The climate is not good for white people, and there are only enough Frenchmen to manage the affairs of the colonies and direct the natives.

Transportation. Like the rest of the coast, French West Africa suffers from a lack of good natural harbors. Dakar, in Senegal, is the best.

Two great jetties allow ships of any size to anchor in safety, and vessels of considerable size can lie alongside its docks. Less important ports, which will not admit large vessels, are Konakry in French Guinea, Bingerville in the 

Ivory Coast, and Porto Novo in Dahomey. 

Transportation is by rivers and railroads.

The interior plateau is highest near the coast, and streams rising among its hills flow in great circles before reaching the Atlantic. The Gambia and Senegal rivers flow north and west. 

The Niger is the most important river and is the principal highway for most of the French territory. From its source it flows 800 miles northeast to Timbuktu, in the interior of French Sudan, then swings east and southeast around Upper Volta and Dahomey before it turns south to the Atlantic through British 

Nigeria. The most important railroad of the region runs east from Dakar to Bamako on the upper Niger, where it connects with boats for 

Timbuktu and the interior. The Senegal river is used to some extent. At its mouth is the little port of St. Louis. From Konakry, Bingerville, and Porto Novo run other railroads which serve the back countries of these ports. Upper 

Volta and Niger have almost no transportation.

Timbuktu, on the most northerly part of the Niger, is one of the great historic trading centers of Africa. In old times it was the point where camel caravans from the Sahara met the river traffic from the south and west to exchange European goods for ivory and gold.

Now the camel is little used in reaching the city, and the products go out by river, by railroad through Dakar, or by motor-truck in other directions.

AFRICA Commerce and Products. French colonies trade with many countries, but principally with 

France. From Bordeaux and Marseille ocean steamers reach Dakar and the other Atlantic ports. British vessels also stop at the same harbors. The colonies use cotton cloth from

England, hardware, tobacco, firearms, and a variety of manufactured goods. Rice is grown in Senegal, but more is imported. There is coastwise trade in kola nuts as in the British colonies.

The exports are much the same as those of 

British West Africa. The dry grasslands of 

Senegal, French Sudan, and upper French

Guinea ship through Dakar great quantities of peanuts. These go to Marseille, where their oil is extracted. The cattle of the native herders supply hides for export. Cattle from the grasslands of French Guinea are sent to other colonies. The French have begun cotton growing in French Sudan just as the British have in Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, and their irrigated plantations are now exporting a good deal of cotton. Upper Volta is moist enough to raise cotton without irrigation and should become an important cotton region when transportation makes it possible to get the cotton out. 

Mauritania is mostly desert, but has some trade in gum exported through Dakar. The great present obstacle to trade in Upper Volta and Niger is the absence of railroads and other means of reaching their interiors. 

From the French rain-forest districts palm oil and kernels go to Marseille. The Ivory

Coast ships fine mahogany and other cabinet woods and has profitable cacao plantations. 

Coffee-planting has been started and promises well. French Guinea exports some rubber from the interior. It has a healthy business in gum copal and a prospect of developing the cultivation of pineapples and bananas to an important industry.

We see very easily that West Africa means to France just about what it means to Great Britain. The products of any colony are likely to be the same as those of its next-door neighbors, and the whole coast buys the same goods from Europe. The problems of the French are like those of the British. They must teach the natives habits of industry and better ways of doing things, and must try to build up an active population able to do the necessary work of the colonies.

FRENCH EQUATORIAL AFRICA 

Some six hundred miles from its mouth the 

Congo river is joined by a great northern tributary, the Ubangi. This river rises just south of Anglo- 

Egyptian Sudan and flows west and south to join the Congo.

Between the Congo-Ubangi river and the British colony of Nigeria lies a vast tract of land, French Equatorial Africa. This includes three quarters of the former German colony of 

Cameroon, mandated to France. The rest of 

Cameroon is now a part of Nigeria.

French Equatorial Africa extends north and south for two thousand miles. The coast district is very wet and rainy. It has dense forests, mangrove swamps, and great stretches of open lagoon. During the rainy season the rivers flood the country. Farther north the land rises, and the Congo and its branches cut deep, narrow valleys as they flow down from the plateau in cataracts and rapids. North of the Ubangi the forest gives place to the Sudan grasslands. Farther north, beyond Lake Chad, are the sands of the great Sahara.

The population is small, even for Africa, and is of a different sort in each different part. In the Sudan are the intelligent Hausas and other part-Arab tribes with some farms and extensive herds. The natives of the forest region are backward and savage. Among them are cannibal tribes and the shy Pygmies of the deep jungle. There are very few white people.

Transportation is very difficult, and the region is little developed. Brazzaville on Stanley pool is the only important town. The rivers are navigable for short distances, but cataracts cut off the interior from access from the sea. 

The trade of this region is not yet very important to France. Timber and palm oil and kernels are exported from the southern districts and here cacao plantations are rapidly developing and tobacco is grown. Around 

Lake Chad is an increasing trade in livestock. 

But the growth of great commerce must wait for the development of transportation which

FRENCH LANDS IN AFRICA 

151 the French have already begun. 

Off the southeastern coast of Africa lies Madagascar a French colony and the third largest island in the world.

MADAGASCAR Its southern end crosses the 

Tropic of Capricorn. Its interior is a wide plateau, with mountains near the narrow plain of the east coast. The west coast has a wider lowland. The east coast catches the rain of the hot southeast trade winds and is covered with tropical forests. The rest of the island is drier and is covered with grasslands.

The natives are closely related to the people of the East Indies. They are industrious and skilful farmers, and grow rice as well as any people in the world. There are few French, but France has been making harbor improvements and building good roads and railways to open the country to trade. The principal railway runs from the port of Tamatave to Antananarivo, the capital. 

The important cultivated crops include rice and manioc, which the natives use to make flour and the French use to make tapioca. 

The vanilla bean has been introduced and is now a thriving product, and there are cacao, sugar, and coffee plantations. Raffia fiber, which is taken from the leaves of a kind of palm, is exported to be used in making baskets and furniture.

Cattle are raised on the grasslands and their hides and meat are sold in France. Important minerals of the island are graphite and mica. 

Graphite is used for the leads of pencils and in lubricating grease and stove blacking. Mica is a mineral which can be split into transparent sheets. It is used for windows in stoves and for making electrical wares.

OTHER FRENCH DEPENDENCIES 

French Somaliland, like British Somaliland, is important only for its one seaport. Jibuti is the only French harbor on the route through the Suez canal and serves as a coaling station for French ships. It is the terminal of the railway from Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia. 

The dry French colony has little trade, and Jibuti's commerce is mostly in goods shipped to and from Ethiopia.

Reunion is a tropical island in the Indian ocean, east of Madagascar. Its population is largely French, and its principal export is sugar.

1. The most important colonies of France are Algeria,

Tunisia, and Morocco in the Atlas district of Africa. 

These colonies are just across the Mediterranean sea from Marseille. They all extend from the fertile Tell through the Atlas highlands into the 

Sahara desert. They have a Mediterranean climate.

The native inhabitants are Arabs and Berbers, and there is a large population of immigrants from Europe. Algiers and Tunis are the principal ports, and there are fine railroads. 

2. The three North African countries give France a home for surplus population, a source of raw materials, and a market for manufactured goods. The 

French have greatly improved all three countries. 

The principal exports to France are olives and olive oil, fruits and vegetables, wines, sheep and wool, grain, cork, dates, and phosphate rock. Iron ore is exported to England. 

3. France has a large share of the coast lands of West 

Africa and controls practically all the interior.

These colonies have about the same climates and peoples as British West Africa. A sparse population of natives is controlled by a very few white people. The colonies supply palm oil and palm kernels, cacao, and mahogany from the rain forests and peanuts and hides from the grasslands. In the 

French Sudan, France is attempting to develop cotton growing. 

4. French Equatorial Africa, including most of the former German colony of Cameroon, extends through rain forest, grasslands, and desert country. 

The territory is little developed, because transportation is difficult. 

5. Madagascar, the third largest island of the world, is a French colony off the southeast coast of Africa. 

It has a tropical rain forest on the east side and grasslands on the west. The people are principally 

East Indian in their origin. Products include rice, cacao, hides, mica, and graphite. 

6. Less important French African possessions are 

French Somaliland and Reunion. Jibuti in French 

Somaliland is a coaling station for French ships on the Suez route and handles the trade of Ethiopia. 

Reunion is a tropical island near Madagascar.

1. A native potter at work in the Congo basin. young potter has hardly more tools than he has clothes, but he turns out all the jars needed by the people of his village. The weather in the Congo basin is always warm, and most of the natives wear few clothes. 

2. Canoes and fish nets on the bank of the Congo. 

Native canoes in Africa are made by hollowing out logs by burning and with the use of crude tools. These dugout canoes are heavier and more clumsy than the birch-bark canoes of the American Indians, but they are the principal means of travel in many parts of Africa. 

3. The chief of a Congo tribe, armed with spear and shield. Like the early American Indians, the savages of 

Africa decorate themselves when preparing for battle. 

This chief is wearing his best clothes, and a helmet made of feathers. He is a skilful fighter with his heavy spear. 

4. The native section of a plantation in Belgian Congo. 

One long thatched roof covers many huts, in which the plantation workers live. The Belgians have established many plantations in the Congo basin, and export from them rubber, sugar, and coffee. 

5. A native queen of Belgian Congo. Her headdress of pearl horns shows that she is a person of nobility. Ladies of her tribe do not pierce their lips, but they decorate their legs with hundreds of rings of grass, adorned with little copper bells. Walking must be awkward for them.

SCENES IN LIBIA AND EGYPT

1. A desert well in Libia. This Italian colony lies east of Algeria, and is for the most part in the Sahara desert. 

The ancient well is used to irrigate the oasis in which it was dug. The water needed in the palm grove is pulled to the surface in buckets by an ox or a donkey, and is dumped into a little reservoir from which it flows out to water the land of the oasis. The date palms of the desert oases provide Libia with a large part of her exports. 

2. Desert nomads camping in a grove of date palms in

Egypt. This family roams from oasis to oasis with its camels, donkeys, and dogs. 

3. The Assuan dam in the Nile river, Egypt. This dam was built by the British to help control the flood waters of the Nile. The dam stores water when the Nile is full and lets it out as it is needed when the natural flow of the river is slight. Besides providing water for the irrigation of much of Egypt, the Assuan dam is used to keep the river sufficiently full for navigation. 

4. River boats on the Nile. These flat-bottomed boats have brought cargoes of cotton from the irrigated fields of lower Egypt to be loaded on steamers at Alexandria. 

The cotton raised in Egypt is of very fine quality. 

5. The pyramids of Egypt. These tremendous tombs of ancient kings were built by the early Egyptians from blocks of stone. They are among the wonders of the world.

BELGIAN CONGO OTHER COLONIES AND INDEPENDENT NATIONS 

The tiny country of Belgium owns the vast Belgian Congo, a colony seventy-seven times its own size. This colony includes most of the rich Congo basin which is a low plateau extending west from the boundaries of British East Africa to the lower reaches of the Congo river. The Equator crosses the plateau, and the climate is hot and wet. The colony is covered with dense rain forests and wooded savannas. The densest jungle is in the east and northeast, where the country has changed only a little since Livingstone cut his way through it. The thick growth keeps out sunlight, and the forests are dark and gloomy. Wild animals and dangerous insects are plentiful.

Such a climate is not fit for white people, and even the natives are affected by it. The colony is not thickly populated. The tribes are generally very backward, and some of them are even cannibals. The few Belgians must leave most of the rule to native chiefs, and have not been able to get entirely rid of savage practices.

The colony has the same transportation difficulties that we saw in its neighbor, French 

Equatorial Africa. The Congo and its branches are the principal means of carrying goods. 

Trading companies have warehouses along the river banks, to which natives carry their produce on their heads or in canoes. Small steamers collect the produce from these stations. 

But the Congo has great falls and rapids where it has cut its way through the edge of the plateau to the coast plain and in other places. 

Some of these falls are less than a hundred miles from the ocean. So railroads have been built around the difficult spots, and it is now possible to travel by rail and steamer from the mouth of the Congo to Cape Town, Beira, or 

Dar es Salaam. Parts of the interior are very hard to reach and there goods move slowly. 

The towns of Belgian Congo are mostly trading or mining centers. Banana, just at the mouth of the Congo river, has a fine harbor. 

European traders have been established here since the sixteenth century. Matadi is the farthest point on the Congo which ocean steamers can reach. A railroad connects it with 

Leopoldville, above the cataracts.

Elisabethville is in the rich copper district of the colony. Copper is a leading export of the colony, and the district around Elisabethville is one of the world's great copper regions. 

This district also produces tin, gold, silver, and diamonds. 

Palm oil and nuts are the great vegetable exports of the basin. The oil is refined in Antwerp. Rubber is brought from the interior, and rubber plantations are being set out to produce more and better rubber. The wild rubber is obtained from vines, and is less valuable than the tree rubber of other regions.

Sugar cane, cotton, and coffee have been introduced and have proved successful. Gum copal is another important product. Rice and manioc are raised by the natives for their own use. 

Ivory is still brought down river from the eastern end of the plateau.

Much of the trade of Belgian Congo is with Great Britain, for Belgium does not supply the great quantities of cotton cloth its colony needs. But Belgium supplies iron and hardware, and Belgian companies control the trade. 

The colony is a source of great wealth to the mother country. As transportation improves and as education increases the skill and industry of the natives, Congo products in the world's trade should greatly increase.

Italy's African possessions are less rich than those of England, France, or Belgium. They are mostly dry and hot. The colony which offers the greatest POSSESSIONS opportunities for development is IN AFRICA Ethiopia.

ITALIAN 

Ethiopia. Before its capture by Italy in 

1936, Ethiopia was an empire. Once before, in 1893, Italian armies had invaded the coun- 153

AFRICA 

try, and had suffered a severe defeat. But

Italy needed a rich colony to which her surplus population could move, and, having grown strong since her defeat, and with modern airplanes and war machines to help her, she at length succeeded in capturing Ethiopia.

Ethiopia occupies the Abyssinian plateau and part of the high grasslands southeast of it. 

The trade winds, rising to the highlands, bring heavy rains that produce swollen rivers which cut deep ravines through the plateau. Here is the source of the Blue Nile, the largest tributary of the Nile river. Although the country is near the Equator, its variations in height give it variations of climate. 

The soil of Ethiopia is fertile and well watered. The lower lands and the valleys are hot the year round, and sugar cane, cotton, and tropical and subtropical fruits such as bananas, figs, and oranges are grown. On the higher slopes are coffee trees. Coffee grows wild in Ethiopia. In fact, it was from the 

Ethiopian province of Kaffa that coffee got its name. On the plateau above the coffee regions live most of the Ethiopian people, in a climate which is mild during the whole year. At this level grow the more temperate crops-barley, corn, wheat, and vegetables of many kinds. 

Grazing is the most important occupation. 

The grasslands pasture cattle and the higher levels support sheep and goats. There are also wild animals of many kinds, lions, leopards, zebras, elephants, and many species of antelopes. These live in the wilder districts. 

The people are black of skin, but are members of the white race with no negro blood. 

They belong to a Christian church. Because of their religion, they have been constantly attacked by the African Mohammedans, but they have successfully resisted the attacks. 

The Ethiopians have been so long hemmed in by their mountains that they are not a progressive people. The only community of any size is Addis Ababa, their capital. Outside the city the roads are little more than trails and goods are carried mostly by pack animals. 

The only railroad in the country connects 

Addis Ababa with Jibuti in French Somali land. 

Jibuti handles almost all the trade of the country. The imports are cotton cloth and other manufactures. In return, Ethiopia exports hides, skins, and coffee. There are minerals in profusion, and the mountain streams offer splendid water power. The development of Ethiopia to a colony of importance is entirely possible. 

Libia. Libia is almost all desert. There is only a narrow strip cultivated along the coast. 

Behind this a few hills mark the rise of the Sahara table-land. The climate is arid, and agriculture is uncertain. Barley is grown, and it is thought that olive and fruit trees may be profitable. But, as the map on page 124 shows us, Libia does not have a Mediterranean climate like that of the Tell and has very little rain at any time of the year.

Libia is, however, the nearest of Italy's colonies to the home land, and many Italians have left their crowded native country to make their homes here. They are working energetically to succeed. Since their trade in olives, grapes, and citrus fruits will not support a large population, they have developed three other really important trades. Esparto grass is shipped to England for manufacture into paper. Sponges are gathered off the coast. 

Dates are brought in from the oases of the desert and exchanged at the coast for the manufactures of Italy and other European countries. The caravan trade, although now lessened by the French and British railway lines, is still important. 

Tripoli, the capital, is a picturesque modern city on a cape stretching into the Mediterranean. The desert almost touches the town, and caravan routes center here. The Italians have dredged a deep harbor and built fine warehouses and docks with loading machinery. 

Other Italian Possessions in Africa. Eritrea is a narrow, sandy ribbon of shore along the Red sea northeast of Ethiopia, with a small amount of fertile land on the inland plateau. 

The climate is hot most of the year. Italy has done little to develop the country, and the chief wealth of the land is in the herds of cattle and camels of the natives. Cotton-growing has been started by the Italians. From the coast

Italian Somaliland is hardly more valuable than French and British Somaliland, except that the southern part is watered by the courses of two rivers. Along the banks of these streams the Italians have begun to raise cotton, sugar cane, rice, and corn. The coast is rocky and dangerous, with only one harbor of any value. The principal exports are the hides of cattle, and tree gums, like gum arabic, frankincense, and myrrh, which are obtained from the saps of trees of the plateau. Gum arabic is used in making varnishes and glues.

And frankincense and myrrh are valuable in making incense and perfume. 

Portugal was once a rich and powerful nation with a wide-spread empire in all parts of the earth. Her venturesome sail 

POSSESSIONS 

PORTUGUESE ors were among the first to ex- IN AFRICA plore the coast of Africa and to claim land there. Today her

African colonies are almost all that remain to her. These are not so profitable as the colonies of France and England, partly because Portugal has not the money to develop them by building railroads and highways. They have, however, future possibilities.

The most important of Portugal's African colonies are Angola and Mozambique, on the west and east coasts of southern Africa. 

Angola. From the Atlantic coast, Angola rises to the high grasslands by a series of irregular terraces covered with vegetation. Like the pampas section of Brazil, Angola lies in the path of the southeast trade winds, which lose most of their moisture on eastern highlands. 

Its grasslands lie between Belgian Congo on the north and the British dependencies of East and South Africa, on a high plateau that slopes on the east to the Congo and Zambezi basins. 

The coast is so unhealthful that the capital was moved in 1928 from Loanda to Nova Lisboa in the high interior. The plateau is well suited to growing forage crops and especially to pasturing stock. Cattle, sheep, and goats are raised.

Crops include sugar cane, cotton, coffee, corn, peanuts, and the castor beans from which castor oil is made. Bananas and other fruits grow well, and fruit preserving is an industry. 

Palm oil and coconuts are exported. Their value could be increased with more scientific care of the trees.

The mines and the ocean add to the wealth of the colony. Preserving and salting fish is an industry, and dried fish are an important export. Angola colony has beds of copper, gold, diamonds, and sulphur. British concerns work the deposits of petroleum and asphalt. 

Natives work the iron and salt deposits. 

The Angola government includes Kabinda, a small Portuguese colony north of the mouth of the Congo with a sheltered Atlantic harbor.

Kabinda has a transit trade in palm oil and jungle products from the Congo basin.

Transportation is not as good as the country needs. The harbors of Loanda and Benguela need improvements to protect ships from storms and allow them to tie up to docks. 

Railroads run inland from Loanda and Benguela. The Benguela railroad runs through 

Angola to the copper district of Belgian Congo.

It brings copper to the port, and forms part of a transcontinental railway to the east coast. 

Mozambique. The colony of Mozambique lies on the Mozambique channel in southeastern Africa opposite Madagascar. This is one of the oldest European colonies on the continent. British colonies lie on three sides and are responsible for much of its trade. 

The eastern highlands are broken in Mozambique by the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers, and the coastal plain is wide. This region is low, hot, and swampy. The interior is in the high grasslands, and is more temperate and healthful than the coast.

The country has great natural wealth, but, like Angola, needs development. Lourenco 

Marques and Beira have good harbors, and railroads from them cross the country into 

Transvaal and Southern Rhodesia. Beira is the port for Nyasaland. The railroads do not serve the Portuguese territory as well as they do the British, and most of their trade is in transit goods for the Transvaal gold mines and the Rhodesian interior. Progress has been greatest where Portugal has given large companies

AFRICA 

grants of land to develop or where British money is invested.

Plantations established on the hot, moist coast grow sugar cane and cotton, and there is a coconut industry about the town of 

Mozambique. Peanuts and oil seeds are raised in the moister grasslands, and sisal hemp is grown in the northern part of the colony. The bark of the mangrove trees, useful in making tanning extract, is stripped off by the natives and either shipped abroad or treated in plants in Mozambique. Sugar and coconut products are the other principal exports. There are valuable but undeveloped coal fields, gold mines, and tin deposits. 

Portuguese Guinea. Portugal's portion of 

West Africa is Portuguese Guinea, a little country between Gambia and French Guinea. 

The coastal rain forests just reach this state. 

Its rain-forest coast has a hot, damp climate, and its interior lies in the low grasslands. It has many small rivers, along which grow dense forests.

The inhabitants are mostly natives or halfbreed descendants of the Portuguese. They produce all the material exported from the colony. The exports are peanuts, palm oil and kernels, hides, and rubber. Rice and millet are the chief food crops.

Island Possessions of Portugal. Portugal owns two small islands in the Gulf of Guinea and the 

Cape Verde and Madeira island groups in the 

Atlantic ocean. 

Portugal's islands in the Gulf of Guinea are 

St. Thomas and Prince's Island. Their principal product is cacao.

The Cape Verde group west of Senegal contains fourteen islands of volcanic origin. They are very hot, with tropical vegetation. The people are largely of negro blood. The most important product is coffee.

Madeira is the most important of the Madeira islands, off the coast of Morocco. Mountains and deep ravines give the Madeiras beautiful scenery. The islands raise early vegetables and fruits for the European market.

Both these groups lie on the steamship routes from Europe to Brazil and Argentina and are important coaling stations.

Spain, like Portugal, has lost all but a little of a once great colonial empire. Today there is nothing left to her but a few 

DEPENDENCIES small African colonies and some SPANISH 

nearby islands, all of less value IN AFRICA than the African lands of any of the other nations. These colonies lie in or near northwestern Africa and along the coast of the Gulf of Guinea. 

Spanish Dependencies in Northwest Africa.

Spanish Morocco, a small territory in northern Morocco, around the city of Tetuan; a still smaller area, Ifni, in southern Morocco; and the larger territory of Rio de Oro, southwest of Morocco, are Spain's possessions in northwest Africa. These lands are surrounded by French territory except where they border the sea. 

Spanish Morocco is not much different from French Morocco except that it is less well developed. The warlike Berber inhabitants of the hills have given Spain trouble which it required the help of France to put down. Wine and cork are exported. Tetuan, the most important city of the colony, is famous for the manufacture of Morocco leather and glazed building tiles.

Ifni is semi-arid, with crops of dates, hardy grains, and vegetables. Rio de Oro, the largest of the Spanish colonies, is almost altogether desert. The sparse Arab and Berber population are herdsmen. The coast waters of both 

Ifni and Rio de Oro abound in fish, and fishermen from the Canary islands use them.

The Canary Islands. Off the coast of Rio de 

Oro are the Canary islands, perhaps the most valuable Spanish colony. They are on the steamship route from Europe to South Africa, and vessels calling at their harbors bring many tourists. Fishing and agriculture are valuable sources of trade. The volcanic soil is very fertile, but rainfall is light and the land must be irrigated. The most important crop is bananas. 

Spanish Guinea. The small colony of Rio 

Muni, on the east coast of the Gulf of Guinea, and the volcanic islands of Fernando Po and Annobon are governed together under the title of Spanish Guinea. The governor lives on 

Fernando Po. These tiny colonies lie in the rain-forest belt and have the usual products of

OTHER COLONIES AND INDEPENDENT NATIONS 

157 this hot, damp region. Palm nuts and rubber are gathered in the forests, and cacao, coffee, and sugar cane are raised on plantations. 

The little independent nation of Liberia lies on the Atlantic ocean between Sierra Leone

LIBERIA 

and the Ivory Coast. It was founded in 1847 as a home for freed American slaves, as Sierra Leone was founded for freed British negroes. It is the only African country ruled by negroes. The population consists partly of the descendants of freed slaves and partly of African natives. The country is independent, but is protected and helped by the 

United States.

Liberia is in the rain-forest belt. It has low, steaming marshes along the coast and densely forested hills over most of the country. The more civilized negroes live in coast settle- . ments. They have imitated the communities of the United States, and Monrovia, the capital and chief port, looks like one of our southern towns. Palm oil and kernels, rubber, and coffee are exported. Another valuable export is piassava, a fiber used in making brushes. Rubber plantations have been established by American tire manufacturers. The raising of rubber should make Liberia increasingly wealthy, for it is much nearer to the great United States market than the East Indian plantations which now supply so much of the world's rubber. 

EGYPT 

Egypt, the only important independent

African country, is one of the oldest countries of the world. Before Bible days it had a great civilization and a strong government. The early Egyptians are thought to have discovered the use of metals and the art of making glass, and to have been the first to use written language and a calendar. Since early days, however, Egypt has been conquered many times and has advanced but little. 

Egypt is really part of the Sahara, and without the Nile river the country would be like the rest of the desert. Once each year the heavy equatorial rains pour down the highland slopes, adding great quantities of water to the Nile and carrying into it much rich soil. When these rain waters reach the valley of Egypt, the river overflows its banks and floods a narrow strip of land on either side. These narrow strips of land and the broad delta of the Nile are the cultivated lands of Egypt.

Until comparatively recent times the natives depended on the overflow of the Nile to water their dry desert lands, and in some parts of the valley they still do. They enclose their fields in embankments which hold the flood waters for weeks so that the ground becomes thoroughly soaked. As the waters soak into the ground they leave a rich soil on the surface. 

Seeds grow quickly in this muddy soil. 

Besides this natural means of irrigation, the natives early learned to build great pools or reservoirs to hold back the flood water. When the dry season came they let this water into their fields through ditches. They also used large wooden water wheels to pump river water into irrigation ditches.

In recent times the British have helped Egypt by developing an irrigation system which includes a tremendous dam at Assuan. 

Now water is furnished whenever needed, and two and often three crops are grown each year. 

A farmer can make a living on a smaller piece of land, and the Nile delta and flood plain support a larger farming population than any other region of similar size. As the climate is warm, farming can be carried on the year round. Grain, rice, vegetables, and clover feed the people and animals of the country and are exported in small quantities. The great crop is the long-fibered Egyptian cotton, the best in the world, which has been for centuries the great export of the country. Half of each year's output is exported to England, some is manufactured in Egypt, and much is sold to the United States to be used in making automobile tires and fine cotton cloth.

The British have a particular interest in Egypt because the country contains the Suez canal, which is the sea gate to Great Britain's faraway possessions, India and Australia. 

Partly to protect the canal, the British held control of Egypt for many years, and although the country is now fully self-governing the British still help it tremendously. 

The Suez canal adds a great deal to the commerce of Egypt. Port Said is a coaling station for ships going through the canal. These ships

AFRICA 

also make Alexandria one of their main ports of call. The city sends cotton to Europe and the United States and fresh vegetables from the Nile delta to Europe. Most of Egypt's exports and imports pass through Alexandria. 

Cairo is the largest city in Africa. It is located where the Nile valley ends and the delta begins, and it is the junction for the railroads of Egypt. Trains meet here from Alexandria on the coast, Assuan on the river, and Port 

Said on the canal. Cairo is also the northern terminal of the unfinished Cape-to-Cairo line. 

The city is a tourist center. It contains a museum of treasures taken from the tombs of the ancient Egyptian kings. In the foreign quarter are fine hotels, beautiful parks, and wide streets. The native section is noted for narrow, winding streets and queer bazaars where, in their little stalls, the merchants usually make the articles they sell. The city is largely 

Mohammedan, and the domes and slender minarets of the mosques are to Cairo what the skyscrapers are to New York and Chicago.

More than a million people live here. 

1. Belgian Congo includes most of the rich plateau of the Congo basin, a region of heavy rain forest. 

The Congo is the principal means of transportation, with railroads around its obstacles to navigation. The colony is peopled with backward negro tribes and a few whites. In the southeast corner is a rich copper district. Vegetable products include palm oil and palm kernels, rubber, and gum copal. 

Ivory is brought down the Congo from the eastern part of the plateau.

The Blue Nile rises in the country, which is well watered and suitable for agriculture. Hides, skins, and coffee are exported. Ethiopia is rich in minerals and water power. Libia is largely desert, but the Italians have done much to make it a valuable colony. Tripoli is the capital and has a fine modern harbor. The colony has an important trade in esparto grass, sponges, and dates. Eritrea and 

Italian Somaliland are dry and unimportant.

Your study of the regions and of the political divisions of Africa has given you an idea of the continent's many natural resources. There are rich mines. There are great forests of valuable timber. Many of the continent's most valuable resources, such as the oil palm, grow wild without need for cultivation. There are fertile regions suited to the growing of large crops.

The backward population, the tropical climate, and poor transportation, however, hinder the development these resources. of When the governments of Europe began to consider

Black Natives. 

The millions of black people in Africa have been cut off by the Sahara from contact with the more enlightened white people to the north. They have therefore made little progress during the centuries when the people of the other continents have been advancing. When 

Europeans came to 

Africa, the slave trade was still being carried on and the tribes were constantly at war with one another.

The Dutch found that white men could live in the southern tip of Africa and they built their colonies there. The facts that this part of Africa is in the Temperate zone, is high, and is cooled by the ocean make it suitable for colonization. 

White Natives. Northern Africa has white natives as well as black. Their skins are much darker than the skins of American or European whites, but they are members of the same race. 

The negro peoples of Africa differ widely from one another. The fact that they belong to the black race has not united them into a single nation. There are hundreds of negro tribes with different customs and languages. 

The tribes do not even resemble one another in appearance. The men and women of one tribe may be a coffee-colored people with big, strong, well-formed bodies. Another tribe may have woolly hair, flat features, and short, 160

stocky bodies which are black and shiny. 

These people have many ways of beautifying themselves which seem odd to us. They pierce their ears, their noses, or their lips, and thrust ornaments of ivory or gold through them. It is the custom of one tribe to shave the heads. Other tribes wear very elaborate headdresses built up with the aid of mud. 

In the jungle regions the natives wear few, if any, clothes. In parts of Africa it is the custom to make clothes of grass. Some of the 

African women know how to skin the bark from certain trees and soften it so that it may be made into garments. Since the white men have been trading in Africa, American cotton cloth has been one of the chief items of import. 

The natives do not need any patterns or sewing machines to make the goods into clothes. 

They simply drape it about their bodies. 

The African family usually lives in a hut shaped somewhat like an immense beehive, built of branches and thatched with grass. In a tribal village in a forest clearing the huts will be set about a chief's dwelling. Often a village will be built in a circle, inside of which the cattle and sheep can be penned, safe from the attacks of wild beasts.

The African natives have a curious method of telegraphing information from one village to another. It is done by means of drums. Every village has an official drum-beater. He uses a code which has been handed down for generations from father to son. If something happens in one village, and the natives wish to let the people in the next village know about it, the beater beats the message on his drum.

When travelers are passing through the country, news of their arrival and departure is flashed from village to village by this signal system.

The tribes are not all equally ignorant. In many of the coastal settlements the natives have considerable culture and education, and some tribes of the interior, such as the Masai of British East Africa, have developed into really strong nations. In the interior jungles there are still tribes that are fierce and warlike. 

These less civilized tribes, like the Pygmies, are great hunters, depending on game for their food. The herdsmen near the deserts are nomads, wandering from place to place to find pasture for their flocks. The tribes of the grasslands and plains are usually settled herdsmen who also cultivate gardens. Near the

European settlements in South Africa many Kafirs and Zulus work in the mines and on the ostrich farms and plantations. 

These civilized and semi-civilized tribes are the workers on whom Africa must depend for its future development because the warm climate of the greater part of the continent saps the strength of white men so that they can do no more than direct the work of the government, the mines, and the plantations. When white men have offered to buy the natural products of the continent-ivory, rubber, and palm oil-the natives have collected them; but they have seldom started new industries themselves. Through their contacts with white men, however, the natives are gradually gaining in wisdom. Great Britain has adopted the policy of training the natives in British territory so that they can assist in the development of the British possessions and share in the colonial governments.

TRANSPORTATION 

Difficulties of transportation, too, have prevented the more rapid growth of the African continent. Because the regular coast line has few good natural harbors, it has been necessary for the colonizing countries to build ports and make expensive harbor improvements. The waterfalls and rapids near the mouths of streams have made it necessary to build railroads before the interiors of the colonies could be developed or even thoroughly explored. With railroads built around the rapids and waterfalls, the rivers and lakes of the continent have proved a valuable means of communication and transportation. Regular steamship lines on Lake Victoria and Lake Tanganyika carry freight and passengers to and from the railroads. The Congo river, too, is an important means of east-west communication. 

At present most of the railroad lines of Africa extend but short distances from the coasts. The route of the proposed Cape-to- 

Cairo railroad will be the longest system con-

AFRICA 

necting a series of colonies. About two-thirds of the railroad line has been completed. Although the northern and southern sections of the line have not been joined, parts of Central Africa can be reached by railroad from the east coast and steamers and railways carry goods and passengers from Central Africa to the west coast. The heart of the continent, therefore, is open from the north, south, east, and west.

The airplane is beginning to play an important part in the development of Africa. Great barriers to communication, such as the Sahara desert and the dense Congo jungles, are quickly overcome by this new means of transportation. 

OUTLOOK FOR AFRICAN TRADE 

Trade and production will increase in Africa when the natives have been trained and educated and the means of transportation have been

AND PRODUCTION improved. The tropical prod ucts of Africa-cacao, oil nuts, rubber, and timber-are needed by the world. Africa has many products which the continent can produce in great quantities, but at present these products are unused because they cannot be brought to markets cheaply enough to compete with those of other regions.

When African products of good quality can be marketed as cheaply as those raised in other parts of the world, the industries of many countries may be affected. In tropical Africa rubber plantations can be developed which will compete with southeastern Asia and Brazil for the rubber trade. Coffee plantations are rapidly increasing in Africa, which is the native home of the coffee plant. These plantations will compete with Brazil for the coffee industry. Africa's great possibilities as a grazing country may take from the United States, Argentina, and Australia some of their trade in hides, skins, and meats. The cotton exports of the Sudan may affect our southern states and India. The east coast lowlands may compete with Yucatan in the production of sisal hemp. Already the cacao region of West 

Africa is rivaling the cacao trade of South America.

The more accessible coast lands and the cooler regions of Africa are developing most rapidly. In these regions the natural wealth, such as minerals and the tree crops, has been developed first. Gold, diamonds, and copper have been the most valuable of the minerals. 

Rubber, coconuts, palm oil, and cacao have been the most important of the tree products. 

Now that the continent is being developed more intensively, the cultivated crops, such as peanuts, cotton, and sugar, are being introduced by Europeans into regions which seem best suited to them. You have seen that cotton is being developed in the Sudan and sugar and sisal along the moist coast plains. Larger and better herds are being raised on the grassy plains. 

Manufacturing. So far there has been little industrial development in Africa. There are possibilities in the water power of Victoria falls and other places on the great rivers and in many undeveloped coal deposits; but these are more than offset by the disadvantages. 

First, the climate is too hot to encourage the development of manufacturing centers. Second, the natives lack the enterprise and education needed to start important manufactures for themselves. Most important of all, the continent is principally composed of colonies of European nations, and these nations want the colonies as a source of raw materials and as a market for finished goods. They will encourage an increasing population with greater power to produce raw materials and to buy manufactures, but they are not likely to encourage industries which compete with those of the home countries. Only in temperate 

South Africa, where coal is mined and the population is largely white, industrious, and inventive, are we likely to see any development of manufacturing.

Imports. Africa is and for many years will continue to be a buyer of manufactured goods. 

The products imported now are surprisingly uniform in all parts of the continent. Cotton cloth, clothing, and hardware are in great demand. Farm and mining machinery and railroad supplies are needed to cultivate the land, work the mines, and build railroads. The 

United States has quite a trade with the Afri-

can continent, which buys our manufactured goods. But in trade with Africa the large manufacturing nations of Europe have an advantage over the United States, for they own possessions in Africa and the colonies naturally trade largely with the mother countries. 

CITIES OF AFRICA 

As Africa is just beginning to develop and is largely unsuited to manufacturing there are few cities or even large towns on 

TOWNS AND the continent. Cities usually grow up where people can make a living through manufacturing or trade. The few cities of size in Africa are located principally in the northern and southern parts of the continent and have grown up as seaports, mining centers, or trading centers. 

The best-known of the African seaports are 

Alexandria, Algiers, Tangier, Mombasa, Durban, Cape Town, and Port Elizabeth. Some of the mining centers are Kimberley, Johannesburg, and Elisabethville. Among the trading centers are Cairo and Timbuktu. Some of these communities have grown very large, but none of them compares in importance with the great cities of the United States and Europe.

Although Africa has a much larger population than South America it is far behind that continent in development, transportation, and govern

semi-civilized people than 

Africa. Much more of South America than of

Africa lies in the Temperate zone, so that the climate in many parts of the South American continent is more healthful and better adapted to manufacturing. The deserts of South 

America are smaller and are more productive than are those of Africa. Transportation is better on the South American continent. In 

South America as in Africa there are few naturally good harbors; though in both continents many are being built and the poorer ones are being improved, South America has made the greater progress. 

The future development of Africa will be less haphazard than was that of our own continent which has been over 400 years reaching its present condition. Today men know how to overcome tropical diseases and have a knowledge of irrigation, scientific farming, and mining engineering. Railroads, the telegraph, the telephone, airplanes, and automobiles will all help in developing the continent. Though 

Africa may never develop into a densely populated industrial continent, other lands as they become more crowded will look to it to supply a great part of the food and raw materials they require. 

Some of the governments controlling African colonies are investing huge sums in these possessions. France and Great Britain are fast developing their colonies, and Italy and Belgium are following their example. Portugal and Spain, however, lack the wealth at home to spend money abroad, and their colonies are not far advanced.

But other things are just as important as money and government in developing colonies. 

A colony with many resources usually develops faster than a colony with few. A colony with a healthful temperate climate is more likely to be settled than a colony of unhealthful climate. 

If easily reached from the mother country, a colony has a better chance for early development than a colony that is hard to reach. 

Algeria is near Europe and has a healthful climate and some resources and a strong home government. British South Africa has advantages of wealthy home government, climate, resources, and transportation. Such colonies have advanced the farthest. 

Such colonies as Mozambique, Spanish

Guinea, and Eritrea are far behind either because they have poor climates, or desert land, or few resources, or are hard to reach, or most commonly because their home governments cannot afford to develop them. 

As new resources are discovered, new transportation provided, and new industries begun, Africa's development will not be slow. Even the most neglected of African colonies must some day join the march of progress.

1. Towering peaks in the high mountain region of Asia. 

Across Asia from the Aegean sea almost to the Pacific, and northeast from northern India nearly to the Arctic ocean stretch great ranges of mountains. Asia is cut into several distinct sections by its mountain walls. The 

Himalayas, some of which we see in this picture, are the highest of them all. Mount Everest, at the right, is the loftiest mountain in the world. It is 29,141 feet high. 

2. A horseman of the high desert plateau of Mongolia.

Mongols, like Arabs, move from place to place in search of pasture for their horses and sheep. On the whole wide plateau there are fewer people than in one of our large cities. 

3. Life on the Arabian desert. These Bedouins are wandering Arabs, who move from place to place with their flocks of sheep and goats, searching for pasture. The long-legged camel is strong and fast. Instead of hats, these Arabs wear head cloths which can be drawn over their faces to protect them from sand storms. 

4. Jerusalem, Palestine, a holy city to Christians, Jews, and Mohammedans. The various types of buildings show us that people of many different races have helped to build this city. Palestine is now being made a home for

1. An ancient street in Damascus, Syria. It is known as "the street called straight." Way back in Bible times it looked much as it looks today. The street is narrow and lined with shops. Notice the arches overhead. When the sun is very hot, a cover can be drawn across them to shade the street below. In the picture we see Arabs with head cloths and Syrians with tall felt caps. 

2. Bagdad, in Iraq. Bagdad is the largest city in southwestern Asia. The British, who have a temporary mandate over Iraq, have taught many modern ways to the people of this country. Notice the well-paved street and the automobiles among the quaint old houses of ancient times. 

3. Weaving rugs in Persia. Persian rugs have long been famous for their beauty and wearing quality. These children are doing the slow, careful hand work that makes these rugs so costly and beautiful. There is little machine manufacturing in Persia. 

4. The harbor of Vladivostok, the only important Pacific port of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. Vladivostok does not have great piers and modern dock machinery, but it is the terminal of the Trans-Siberian railway, and many Siberian products are exported here. The steamer at the dock is perhaps loading with soy beans for China.

THE CONTINENT OF ASIA 

Asia is the largest continent. It is so large that it is sometimes regarded as the mainland, of which Europe is only a peninsula extending toward the setting sun!

Look at the map of Asia on page 168. Its most southern point, in the Malay peninsula, is 

SIZE 

only about two degrees north of the Equator. The most northern point of land lies within 13° of the North Pole.

Asia's most western part, in Asiatic Turkey, is about 26° east longitude, and its most eastern point, only a few miles from Alaska, touches the 170° west meridian. In all, Asia has an area of over 17,000,000 square miles. What a giant continent it is beside Australia, with less than 3,000,000 square miles, or Europe, with less than 4,000,000. In fact, Asia alone is larger than North and South America together or 

Europe and Africa.

Asia is a continent of extremes of climate. 

It contains the coldest permanently settled region in the world, and one of the world's hottest deserts. It has sections of extremely heavy rainfall, and other sections where there is almost no rain at all. 

CLIMATE 

The northern and central parts of Asia lie in the belt of the prevailing westerly winds. 

Blowing over the land surfaces of Europe and northern Africa, these bring little moisture to Asia. Consequently its interior and the northern coastal lands have little rainfall. Southwestern Asia, too, is a region of little rain. 

This section is in the path of the northeast trade winds, which blow first across the Asian mainland and so have little moisture left for the southwest region.

The eastern part of Asia's southern coast and the southern part of Asia's eastern coast have what is known as a monsoon climate. In summer, the direct rays of the sun heat the great interior of the continent, and the air above the heated lands grows warm and rises. Cooler air blows inland from the sea to take the place of the rising air. These winds from the sea are known as summer monsoons, and they bring heavy rainfall to the coastal lands of southeastern Asia. In winter the air over the interior is colder than that over the sea. So the air over the sea rises and the cold air from the interior flows out towards the sea. These winds from the interior are known as winter monsoons. They are dry, and bring a dry season to the coastal lands.

SURFACE 

In surface features also Asia presents some striking contrasts. Here we find the highest mountains and plateaus in the world, forming a highland region so lofty that it is spoken of as the "Roof of the 

World." And only a few hundred miles to the west of these highlands, we find lands below sea level! In the northwest part of the continent are broad, barren lowlands with but few people, and along the eastern and southern shores are other lowlands, smaller but more fertile, crowded with millions of inhabitants. 

Probably the most striking of all the land features of this great continent is the Himalaya range of mountains-those highest mountains in the world. Three of their peaks tower more than a mile higher than the tallest peaks of the 

Western hemisphere! The highest of these 

Asian peaks is Mount Everest, 29,141 feet in height. Although many have tried, no one has as yet been able to reach its summit. Mount 

McKinley, the highest peak in North America, is 8841 feet lower than Mount Everest, and Mount Elbrus, the highest European peak, is 

10,676 feet lower. So you can see what a giant this Asian mountain is!

Besides the Himalayas, there are other, lesser mountain ranges in Asia. These, with the Himalayas, form an east-west mountain chain from the shores of the Aegean sea nearly to the Pacific, and they cut southern Asia off almost completely from the northern part of the continent. Another series of mountain ranges extends northeast from the western end of the Himalayas almost to the shores of the 167
