THE CONTINENT OF ASIA 

169 Arctic ocean. These mountains form a great barrier between eastern and western Asia. 

Thus the great central highland region divides the continent into several sections, each of which is cut off from the others by mountain ranges. Look for this on the map, page 166. 

Now let us study the map on page 168. 

Within the central highland region are some of the largest and highest plateaus of the world. The highest of these is Tibet, a cold, little-known plateau, more than 12,000 feet above sea level. The plateaus of Iran, Pamir, Turkestan, and Mongolia have altitudes of from 3,000 to 10,000 feet.

What an irregular coast this great continent has to the east and south! Indenting its shores we find eight seas-The Bering, COAST LINE 

Japan, Yellow, East China, South

China, Arabian, and Red seas, and the Sea of Okhotsk. We also find the gulfs of Tongking, Siam, Oman, and Aden, the Persian gulf, and the Bay of Bengal. Just as there are many seas, bays, and gulfs extending into the land, so are there many peninsulas extending out into the water.

RIVERS 

One would expect the rivers of Asia to flow in all directions from the central highlands, and a glance at the map shows that they do so. We have already learned how unfortunate it is for Russia in Asia that all her great rivers-the Ob, Yenisei, and Lenaflow north into the ice-blocked Arctic. The 

Amur, the Hwang, and the Yangtze are three of the great rivers that flow into the Pacific, or into small seas along the eastern coast of Asia. 

The Mekong, the Brahmaputra, the Ganges, the Indus, the Tigris, and the Euphrates flow generally south. Two less important rivers flow westward into the Aral sea. Most of the great rivers flowing east or south carry much silt. They have rich deltas at their mouths, and leave a coating of fertile soil in their valleys when they overflow their banks. But even with their gifts of fine soil, the floods are terribly dreaded for they destroy crops, homes, and thousands of people.

Most of this great continent is waste land, and will probably always be barren. The mountains are so high and forbidding that few 

WASTE LANDS 

people live among them. The plateaus are either deserts in the path of the dry westerlies, or are so cold and high that only a few of the most hardy grains can be raised there. The tundras of the north can be made to produce only moss and some grass, so that the few people there must depend for their living on the reindeer herds they raise. Although not really waste land, the 

Taiga or great forest belt south of the tundras is of little value until some way can be found to get the wood to market. The lands of the 

Kirghiz steppe and the Lowland of Turan to the south of the forests are dry plains, with just enough rain for the growth of scanty grass. 

Some of these waste lands may some day add greatly to the mineral wealth of the world. No one can be sure of that yet, because so much of Asia's area is still so little known that the mineral value can only be guessed at. The mines that are known are very rich, and indicate the presence of other deposits of hidden wealth. 

FRUITFUL LANDS 

Besides her waste spaces Asia has fertile and productive lands, some of which are very rich indeed. There is the great Siberian wheat belt with its good soil, a continuation of the European belt, stretching across northern Asia as far as the headwaters of the Yenisei river. The whole extent of this belt is only roughly known. 

The northern latitude at which the hardier kinds of wheat can be grown has not, as yet, been discovered. Not till the railroads open up this country, and it becomes more thickly settled, will the northern and southern limits of this vast belt be accurately known.

The other productive sections of Asia lie in the eastern and southern parts of the continent. Here the lowlands and the great river basins, with their rich alluvial soil, produce abundant crops. Rice, wheat, and millet are raised in huge quantities to feed the millions of inhabitants. Silk and tea are important exports of the eastern river valleys, and rubber, cotton, teakwood, tea, and jute come from the southern lowlands. Many of these sections are producing all the crops that can be raised in them, but the far southeastern lowlands on the

ASIA 

Indo-China and Malay peninsulas could be made even more productive if they were more densely settled.

DOMESTIC ANIMALS 

The domestic animals of Asia vary greatly in different regions. Reindeer and shaggycoated ponies, able to withstand severe cold, draw the sleighs and wagons of the northern plains.

Camels are used in many of the desert areas. 

The finest horses are raised in the Arabian plateau region. In some of the southern countries, huge elephants do heavy work in the forests. Where there is enough food for them, great-horned water buffaloes help in the work of farming. In many parts of Asia there is too little food for the people, and none at all for domestic animals. Here human labor is very cheap, and men do unaided the heaviest farm work and carry to market great loads of goods on their backs, or in baskets hung from wooden yokes across their shoulders.

TRANSPORTATION 

Transportation is very poor in most of Asia.

In some sections, men called coolies draw twowheeled carriages or carry on their shoulders sedan chairs slung between poles. These carriages and chairs take the place of horse-drawn carriages and automobiles.

The rivers of India and China are crowded with queer-looking boats bringing goods from far inland. Good roads are almost unknown, except in seacoast trading districts and parts of India and Japan. Railroads are scarce except for the Trans-Siberian railroad and lines in India, China, and Japan. What few railroads there are have done much toward opening up the countries through which they run and stimulating the manufacture of goods too bulky to be carried with profit to the outside world in any other way. Today airlines connect some of the more advanced countries with each other and with countries of the west. 

MANUFACTURING 

Throughout most of Asia, manufacturing is limited to slow, patient hand work. Beautiful rugs are woven by the women and girls of several countries. In the hurry of our own civilization, workmen cannot find time to make rugs by hand. But our machine-made rugs are much less beautiful than the soft, lovely, handwoven rugs of Asia, and a good Persian or Chinese rug sells for a great deal of money in America.

Can you imagine our busy people having the time or patience to raise silkworms and to unwind, slowly and carefully by hand, half a mile of silk fiber from each cocoon? Thousands of people in Asia engage in this work which gives us soft, lustrous silks.

But, little by little, Asia's people are being trained in the use of machinery, and in time it is hoped that they may be able to depend on manufacturing and trade for much of their food, rather than almost entirely on the uncertainties of agriculture.

POPULATION 

Asia has a great population most of which centers in the productive parts of the continent. The waste lands are almost empty, and the productive lands are very crowded. The steppe, the tundras, and most of the plateaus are inhabited only by small bands of nomads. Lack of good transportation prevents dense settlement of the vast extent of the Taiga or of the Siberian wheat belt. So Asia's people are crowded into the productive river valleys, along the eastern and southern coasts, and in parts of the islands of Japan. These sections are so crowded that there are only tiny farms for the workers, and these farms have to produce all the crops possible. When the great rivers flood the land or when the rain-bringing summer monsoons fail it means death by starvation to thousands of people. Just to keep alive is a struggle in most of these thickly populated sections. Even Japan, with her scientific handling of crops, finds it hard to feed all her people. 

Asia is a land of many races. In the north, the people of the yellow, or Mongolian, race are the most common. In the south we find members of the white, or Caucasian, race, but they have dark skins. The Malays belong to the brown, or Malaysian, race; and there are members of the black race to be found in the island interiors off the coast of Asia. 

The dark-skinned whites of Asia differ from the European and American whites in several

THE CONTINENT OF ASIA 

171 ways-in religion, in education, and in many of their social customs. The two leading religions of the Asian white race are Mohammedanism, in which the Arabs believe, and Brahmanism, the belief of the Hindu people who live in India. A third great religion of 

Asia, Buddhism, includes most of the members. of the yellow race. Because of the coming of

European whites, Christianity is beginning to gain in Asia, though it has fewer followers than any of the other three. 

Education in Asia is very different from that in Europe or North America. Most of the people are so taken up with the struggle to get enough food that they have no time for education. In many of the countries of Asia, children must work long hours in the fields, just as their parents do. The boys and girls have much less opportunity for play than children have in America. In fact, many of them never learn to play. Their whole life is work, work, work. There are, however, a few schools for children of the wealthier families. Many of these young people later come to our own country to carry on their education. In general, however, the people of Asia are uneducated and superstitious.

Writers of our race have often called Asia the land of mystery. The ways of the Asiatics are so different from our ways that it is often hard for us to understand why the people do things as they do. Asia is mysterious, too, because much of it is still unknown to us. Asia is like the women of some of her countries, who hide their faces behind veils. Future development of Asia's unguessed natural resources and better transportation will in time lift the veil of this strange continent, and lead to a more complete understanding between 

East and West.

1. Asia is the largest continent in the world. 

2. Asia has extremes of climate. The northern and central parts, which lie in the path of the prevailing westerlies, and the southwestern part, which lies in the belt of the northeast trade winds, have little rainfall. The southeastern part of the continent has a monsoon climate, with a rainy season in summer and a dry season in winter. 

3. The Himalaya mountains are the highest mountains in the world. They are part of an east-west mountain chain which separates northern and southern 

Asia. Another mountain chain, running northeast and southwest, separates eastern and western Asia.

Among the Asian mountain ranges are the lofty plateaus of Tibet, Pamir, Turkestan, and Mongolia. 

4. The coast line of Asia is irregular; it has many peninsulas and is indented by many seas, bays, and gulfs. 

5. The rivers of Asia flow in all directions from the central highlands. Those flowing east and south carry much silt and have broad, rich deltas. Those flowing north are ice-blocked for much of the year. 

6. Much of central and northern Asia is unproductive land-desert, untamed forest, or tundra. 

7. The most productive lands of Asia are the Siberian wheat belt, in the west-central part of the continent, and the broad fertile river valleys in the east and south. Rice, wheat, millet, silk, tea, rubber, cotton, teakwood, and jute are raised in the river valleys. 

8. The important domestic animals of Asia are the reindeer and pony in the northern section, the camel in the desert regions, the horse on the Arabian plateau, the elephant and water buffalo in some of the southern countries. 

9. Transportation is very poor in most of Asia. Railroads and good roads are scarce. Most transportation is carried on by means of river boats and human porters. 

10. Most of Asia's manufacturing is done by hand.

Oriental rugs and beautiful silks are among the leading products. Machine manufacturing is slowly gaining. 

11. Asia has a great population, most of which is concentrated in the productive river valleys, along the eastern and southern coasts, and on the Japanese islands. The steppe, the tundras, and most of the plateaus are inhabited only by small bands of nomads. 

12. In Asia one finds members of the white, yellow, and brown races; there are negroes on some of the nearby islands. Mohammedanism, Brahmanism, and Buddhism are the three leading Asiatic religions. The great part of the population of the continent is poorly educated and superstitious.

Some of the oldest civilizations of the world had their beginnings in southwestern Asia thousands of years ago, even long 

ANCIENT EMPIRES 

A LAND OF before ancient Rome spread the mighty arms of her empire west across Europe and east into Asia.

In those lands which lie between Turkey and India many nations have flourished and perished, and great empires have been built up and destroyed.

Should you visit these lands today you would find that the people live much as they did way back in Bible times. There has been little progress. In fact, you might think that the change has been in the opposite direction, for many of the great ancient cities are now but heaps of ruins, and few new cities have been built to replace them. As we visit the lands of southwestern Asia let us see why the ancient empires have faded away and whether the future holds any possibilities of new and prosperous nations rising in their place. 

Although southwestern Asia looks small when compared to the entire continent, yet it 

SIZE AND 

is really a great area-five times 

POPULATION as large as the countries of 

Great Britain, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Germany combined. The total population, however, is only about forty million, less than two-thirds that of Germany alone. So you can see that the region, as a whole, is not thickly settled. 

Southwestern Asia is a dry country, as you will see from the map on page 181. Most of 

RAINFALL 

it has less rainfall than any other part of the continent. This great section lies in the belt of northeast trade winds, which have come so far over the land areas of Asia that they have little moisture left. What rain does fall comes in the winter.

The surface of the region is mostly high and rugged. In its western part lies the broad desert plateau of Arabia. This is

SURFACE 

fringed along the Red sea and the

Persian gulf with a coastal plain seldom more than fifty miles wide. To the northeast of the plateau of Arabia is the high desert plateau of Iran, hemmed in by mountains which make it almost inaccessible from the surrounding countries and give it the greatest extremes of continental climate. North of the two plateaus lies a mountain system, extending westward from the Himalayas to the Aegean and cutting off southwestern Asia from the plains regions to the north.

Between the two plateaus is the one fertile spot of the whole region, a valley in which lies the rich, alluvial plain of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. In summer this is one of the hottest places on earth. There is little rain and the burning, blistering sandstorms which sometimes rise in the nearby desert regions and swoop down on the settlements do not help to make them pleasant places in which to live. But people stay because the river waters moisten the fertile soil, and vegetation flourishes. The valley once supplied millions of people with food, and it may be made to do so again. 

There are few streams in southwestern Asia, the Tigris and the Euphrates being the only large, navigable ones. A few small sunken streams and springs provide oases in the deserts, and about these there are usually settlements. The greater part of the Arabian plateau, however, is so dry and has so few oases that most of it is still unexplored. In such a land of deserts, mountains, and few streams, transportation is limited largely to camels, horses, and donkeys. The people are naturally kept apart by a lack of swift and easy means of transportation and communication.

of Iran is known to have many and varied mineral resources. The Tigris and Euphrates valley has valuable oil deposits. Elsewhere in the southwestern section the mineral deposits are either limited or unknown. 

Strange as it may seem, barren southwestern Asia contains seven entire countries and part of an eighth. Most of the

COUNTRIES Arabian plateau lies within the borders of Arabia. Along the eastern end of the Mediterranean sea stretch Palestine and

Syria. East of Palestine, largely in the desert, is Trans-Jordan, and still farther to the east is Iraq, formerly known as Mesopotamia, most of which lies in the fertile valley of the Tigris and the Euphrates. The high plateau of 

Iran, with its surrounding mountains, is divided between Persia and Afghanistan. In the north, mountainous Asia Minor forms a part of the country of Turkey. Find these countries on the map, page 174. 

Southwestern Asia, as has been said, was the home of some of the greatest nations of 

HISTORY 

early history, and scientists today find many relics of ancient times in the ruins of its cities. We read of these nations in the Old Testament. Among the first to settle in the region were the Babylonians and the Chaldeans, who made their homes in the Tigris and Euphrates valley. The rich and beautiful city of Babylon was the home of great kings. North of Babylon lived the fierce and savage Assyrians. These people conquered the Babylonians. But later the Babylonians conquered the Assyrians, overthrew their capital city of Nineveh and founded the Babylonian empire.

East of all these peoples lived the rich and powerful Persians. After the fall of Nineveh the Persians conquered the new Babylonian empire. Then they extended their conquests and became for a time the most powerful nation in the world. They overran nearly all the land between India and the Red sea, and were stopped only with great difficulty by the 

Greeks from conquering all civilized Europe. 

From a city called Ur, south of Babylon, came the Hebrews. They were a wandering shepherd people who spent many years seeking a new homeland. They lived a long time in the deserts of Arabia and finally settled in Palestine. Their small numbers led to their being conquered time and again by many strong nations. They were intelligent, proud, and capable people, and their writers left us the Old Testament books of the Bible. 

As Europe developed, southwestern Asia became a crossroads for travel between

Europe, India, and Egypt. This might have been an advantage to the region, but rivalry among foreign countries led to wars which laid waste the land. The Macedonians took the region from the Persians, and the Romans took it from the Macedonians. Each army destroyed or stole what it could. The old civilizations grew weaker. Arts, sciences, and irrigation projects and other public works were neglected. 

Then about 1,300 years ago Mohammed, an

Arab of Mecca, founded a new religion which held that there is one god, and that Mohammed is God's prophet. His followers set out to force their religion upon the world by means of the sword. Believing that those who were killed in battle by unbelievers were sure to reach Paradise, these early Mohammedans were fearless. Men who did not adopt the religion were enslaved or killed. Mohammedanism rapidly spread over all southwestern Asia and northern Africa, and even penetrated 

Spain and Balkan Europe. 

The people of southwestern Asia are today mostly Mohammedans. Although the Arabs were once the most learned race of the western world, they have not attempted to go beyond the teachings of Mohammed for wisdom. The common people dislike believers in other religions. They object to the introduction of new ideas of any kind. This makes them backward and slow to learn. Consequently they have not developed the resources of their region, and they have let the old civilizations die out. 

The last great conquest in southwestern

Asia occurred in the fifteenth century, when the Ottoman Turks from central Asia, also 

Mohammedans, conquered the whole region.

The Turks were oppressive masters, and during the period of their rule nothing was done

ASIA for the benefit of the people. It was not until the World War that the Turks lost their hold and the peoples of most of the region were freed from their oppression. 

The ancient trade routes of southwestern

Asia are still the main arteries of travel and 

TRADE 

trade, and methods of transportation

ROUTES over many of them have progressed little since earliest times. Camel caravans still carry goods from the Mediterranean ports east to the Tigris-Euphrates valley and the high plateau lands, just as they did hundreds of years ago. The old caravan route from the Mediterranean across the Isthmus of Suez to the Red sea lost its former importance with the opening of the Suez canal. 

In this region there are, even today, very few railroads, and these follow mainly old routes of trade. The longest railroad extends from Russia, through Turkey, across Syria, Trans-Jordan, and Arabia to the city of 

Medina. A few short railroads lead from the seacoasts to inland cities. There is one from

Beirut to Damascus in Syria. There is another from Jaffa, the seaport for Jerusalem, to 

Jerusalem. Still another runs from Jaffa along the Isthmus of Suez to Cairo, in Egypt. In the Tigris-Euphrates valley, running generally parallel with the rivers, there are several hundred miles of railroad between Bagdad and the Persian gulf. Travel on any of the railroads of this whole section is hot, slow, and difficult.

CITIES 

Many of the cities of southwestern Asia are among the oldest and most interesting in the world. Although they have little commercial importance, they attract thousands of travelers each year. So little have these cities changed from ancient times that tourists visit them to see their historic ancient buildings and how people lived in the days of long ago. 

The most famous of these cities is Jerusalem, a holy city of the Jews, Mohammedans, and Christians. To the Jews it is sacred as the capital of Palestine, their Promised Land. 

Here they sought peace and happiness after long persecution by Egyptian kings. To the

Mohammedans it is holy because it contains the Mosque of Omar, one of the most famous of their temples. And to Christians the city and all its surroundings are holy, because they are the scene of the life and work of Jesus Christ.

Mecca and Medina, too, are holy cities to 

Mohammedans. Mecca is the birthplace of 

Mohammed, the founder of their faith, and it is the desire of every Mohammedan to visit Mecca before he dies. The chief occupation of the people there is the care of the pilgrims. 

Medina is the burial place of Mohammed, and it, too, is visited by great numbers of pilgrims each year.

Damascus, in Syria, is another city of interest to Mohammedans. It is the burial place of Fatima, the only child of their leader. This city has long been a trading center. The city has several times been destroyed and rebuilt. 

Bagdad, on the Tigris river, in Iraq, is the largest city of the southwestern countries. 

Trade from east and west meets there. You may have read of Bagdad in some of the stories from the Arabian Nights. Perhaps you have seen pictures of it. It is a charming 

Mohammedan city with its tall, slender minarets and the rounded domes of its mosques standing out against the sky. Date palms and other subtropical plants flourish in the gardens of Bagdad. But like most oriental cities it has narrow and dirty streets, and it is often unbearably hot. Bagdad was once on the principal trade route from Europe to India, but it has lost much of its importance to the 

Suez canal.

Aden is a newer city, belonging to Great Britain. It stands at the extreme south of 

Arabia and is strongly fortified, for it guards the eastern entrance to the Red sea and so to the Suez canal. It is set in a desert, and there is not a blade of grass nor a single tree near it. 

Fresh water is obtained by boiling sea-water and cooling the steam until it condenses. This process makes it expensive. Aden is an important coaling station. 

Great Britain, Germany, and Russia have always been interested in the countries of southwestern Asia. Great Britain needs to control the Suez canal and other approaches to

India and Australia.

Germany, before the 

INTEREST OF EUROPEAN NATIONS IN SOUTHWESTERN ASIA 

World War, wanted to extend the Berlin-to-Constantinople railroad as far as Bagdad. By this she hoped to establish a means of direct trade with the east. Germany was defeated in the war, and the plan could not be carried out. Such a railroad would have diminished the traffic through the Suez and might have weakened Great Britain's hold on India. Russia once hoped to get control of the Suez canal, and having lost that hope has long desired a route to the Indian ocean through Persia.

Syria. At the close of the World War, a number of small countries in southwestern

Asia, long held by the Turks, were given to 

Great Britain and France as mandates.

France was given a mandate over Syria, which has about 60,000 square miles of territory and about 3,000,000 people. Irrigation is essential to agriculture there, and as yet only about one-fifth of the suitable land is planted. Cotton, tobacco, and silk are the chief crops. Imports far exceed exports, but the exports are rapidly increasing. 

Throughout Syria modern methods of transportation and better roads are becoming more general. This is shown by the increasing number of automobiles which yearly cross the Syrian desert to Bagdad, and to Teheran, the capital of Persia. The years since the 

World War have been marked by revolts and unrest, and the French have been too busy keeping peace to play a great part in the improvement of the country. In the future, however, they should be able to help Syria greatly in becoming an important nation. 

Palestine and Trans-Jordan. Great Britain has mandates over the countries of Palestine and Trans-Jordan. An early provision which the government in Palestine made was for the return of Jews from all over the world to their own country, now largely inhabited by Arabs. 

The return must be gradual, until industry and the food supply in the country make it possible to support more people. The number who may come back yearly is regulated by immigration laws. An old Arab legend said that the Jews would never return to their country until the Nile should flow into Palestine. Strangely enough, water from this river is now being turned through a great pipe to supply water for the city of Jerusalem. 

The whole world is glad to see the restoration of the Holy Land. Old streets and buildings are being repaired and rebuilt, and new ones are under construction. The draining of swamps, one of the greatest needs, is being carried on. Much of the money for these improvements is donated by Jews in all parts of the world.

The river Jordan, so famed in the Old Testament, flows between Palestine and Trans-Jordan, through a valley which is below sea level. It connects the lovely lake called the Sea of Galilee with the Dead sea. The 

Jordan has waterfalls with great possibilities for electric power. Some power is already being used to run railroads and to supply light for the cities. The Dead sea lies over 1200 feet below the Mediterranean, and it is rich in valuable salts.

The land about the Sea of Galilee is being reforested. Means are also being taken to protect and restore the fisheries in the sea, for these are not now so rich as they once were. 

Palestine has enormous agricultural possibilities. Only water is needed for the fields to produce an abundance of crops.

Trans-Jordan is a desert country, inhabited only by wandering Bedouin tribes. It has a king of its own, but his government is weak and British soldiers are needed to keep order.

The country has few products and does not seem destined to progress very rapidly. 

Iraq. A temporary British mandate is making the country of Iraq important. Iraq lies in the old, fertile valley of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. Old irrigation works are being repaired, and new ones built; and once more as in long ago days the valley is yielding varieties of fruits and grains. Most of the people are Mohammedans, and the lower classes of this faith always look with displeasure on new ideas of any kind. They still plow with primitive wooden plows drawn by

ASIA oxen or water buffaloes. But agricultural machinery, in time, will find its way there. In the northern part of the valley coal, iron, and salt are found. Oil wells around Mosul are being extensively worked by British companies. Turkish, French, Dutch, and American groups also have interests in the petroleum which is very plentiful there. The petroleum resources, however, are only partially developed. 

Advantages of Mandates. Not all the advantages of the mandate system go to the protected countries. France and Great Britain spend much money and sometimes sacrifice the lives of soldiers to help the mandated countries, yet they profit through the development of trade. Great Britain's position in Palestine, Trans-Jordan, and Iraq gives her the further advantage of having troops and a few harbors near the Suez canal, which might be very useful in case of war, and the still further advantage of keeping other strong nations from the borders of India. 

Arabia, Persia, and Afghanistan. Arabia, Afghanistan, and Persia are independent countries. They are under no mandate; but their foreign affairs are largely under the direction of the League of Nations. Many of the Arabs are such wanderers that they are quite free from any real government at all. They follow the directions of their leaders. These wanderers are called Bedouins. They roam about the deserts with camels, sheep, goats, and horses. The Arabs are skilful riders, and the horses that they raise are among the fastest and most graceful in the world. The tribes stay in one place only so long as the pasture there is sufficient for the needs of their animals. Then they move on. This way of living makes them thoughtless and carefree, and most of them consider robbery a good way to supply their needs.

The Arabs are tall, slim, fine-looking people, somewhat dark in complexion. Their eyes are deep and dark, used to looking long distances over desert sands. Arab women are fond of jewelry-hammered bits of metal or polished pieces of glass or stone, which they wear about their necks and arms, and in the form of earrings. One may buy this jewelry in the bazaars, or open-air shops, of the Arabian cities. Here a merchant spreads his goods under an awning and sits tailor-fashion, his legs crossed under him, waiting for you to buy.

Persia, the country once famous for the strength of its armies, owes most of its fame at present to the beautiful rugs made by its people. Rug making is carried on in all the countries where the Turks have ruled, but especially in Turkey itself and in Persia. The city of Tabriz, in Persia, is the greatest rugmaking center. The rugs are woven of sheep's wool dyed many and beautiful colors. Even in the factories most of the work on them is done by hand, and often it takes several people many months to complete one rug. The rugs bring enormous prices in other countries, and lately the demand for them has so increased that machinery has been installed to turn them out in greater quantities. The machine-made rugs, however, are not so fine as those which are made by hand. They are not so soft nor so rich looking, and they will not wear nearly so long. 

Persia, though over 600,000 square miles in area, has very few railroads. A plan is now under way to build a railroad to connect the Persian gulf with the city of Teheran near which valuable iron and coal deposits have been discovered. The new railroad will be of great benefit. It will take years to build it, but here, as in the Andes, the mineral wealth to be obtained will make up for the expense. 

Persia also has copper and zinc mines; and turquoise, a beautiful blue-green stone, is found in small quantities. In Persia, as in Iraq, British firms have petroleum interests.

Afghanistan is so located between Russia and India that it is a buffer between the two. 

Kabul is the capital city. There are no railroads into this country. The chief entrance is by the Khyber pass from India. This narrow pass leads for over thirty miles through a wild, mountainous, undeveloped region. Until recent years travel through the pass was difficult, and one had to go on foot or horseback.

Now, however, there is a fine military road

which the British have built for the use of their troops defending India. But in Afghanistan, even in the most civilized sections, good roads are very, very few. Plans are being made by the Ameer, as the ruler is called, for extending motor roads between several of the larger cities. Agriculture and grazing are the most important industries. Varieties of fruits are grown. There are a few factories where shoes and other leather articles are made. 

Turkey in Asia. The greater part of the country of Turkey lies in southwestern Asia, occupying the peninsula of Asia Minor and extending east beyond the eastern end of the Black sea. The land is mostly arid plateau. 

Only along the coasts is there enough rainfall for agriculture. Irrigation, though widely practiced, is crude and primitive. Tobacco, cotton, cereals, figs, almonds, grapes, and olives are grown. On the drier lands sheep and cattle are raised. Tobacco is the principal export. The chief cities are Smyrna (Izmir), a seaport with some textile mills, and Angora (Ankara), the capital of both European and 

Asiatic Turkey. 

LIVING 

In all parts of southwestern Asia living conditions are much the same. Nearly everywhere the great poverty is 

CONDITIONS plainly seen. Though there are a few fine dwellings, most of the houses are uncomfortable, their rooms close and small. Windows are rare, for the people want to keep out the hot sun from their homes. In their attempts to do this they shut out the air as well, and several people often crowd together in a space that has scarcely breathing room for two. 

Looking down on any of the cities—Jerusalem, Bagdad, Teheran, or Damascus-you would be amazed to note the flatness of the roofs. You might wonder why the people did not build sloping roofs to shed the rain, until you remembered that here there is little rain to shed. The people use their roofs for porches. In the very warm weather they sleep on them.

Even the wealthier homes have few tables or chairs. A wealthy home is usually recognized by the number of beautiful rugs and mats thrown about here and there, over balconies, over the edges of the roofs, or hung over the doorways. The rugs also serve as table cloths and bed coverings. One can get along very nicely without them, however, and the poor people usually sell those they make. 

Lack of sanitary measures has caused fever and other diseases in all these countries. 

Here, as in the Philippine islands, Central 

America, and the Panama Canal zone, modern methods of science are helping to better health conditions.

What does the future hold for the countries of southwestern Asia? Their location at the crossroads of three con 

THE SOUTHWESTERN tinents gives them untold THE FUTURE OF commercial possibilities. COUNTRIES 

With more and better railroads and roads, they should become important trade centers. Such railroads and roads would also make possible the working of mines, which would lead to great industrial growth. Along the coastal plains and in the oases, dates, oranges, figs, melons, and grapes grow abundantly. Cotton is raised in the lower part of the Tigris-Euphrates valley and in Syria. Wheat, rye, barley, and other grains are raised in irrigated sections. More land cultivated by better methods can increase the variety and output of the crops. Such progress, however, depends upon good governments, willing to spend money to improve the country; to assure the common people that their rights and property will be protected; and to encourage the education which is needed and which has begun. Freed from the misrule which has held them back in the past, the countries of southwestern Asia should have a brighter future.

ASIATIC RUSSIA NORTHERN AND CENTRAL ASIA 

Several thousand miles across northern

Asia, from the Ural mountains to the Bering sea, stretches the vast expanse of

Asiatic Russia. This great territory is part of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. Its northern part, called Siberia, is made up mainly of three great regions-the tundras, the Taiga, or Forest belt, and the Siberian Wheat belt. There are rugged mountains in the southern and eastern parts of the country. The southwestern part of Asiatic Russia, east of the Caspian sea, is a region of plains and deserts. This region includes the 

Kirghiz steppe and the Lowland of Turan. The map on page 168 will show you these regions.

Russia is extremely cold in winter. In fact, the region

The length and warmth of the summers increase as one goes south from the Arctic Circle. From 10 to 20 inches of rain falls yearly in the forest belt, chiefly in the summer time. Elsewhere the rainfall is scanty the year around. 

The Tundras. In the extreme northern part of Asia are the tundras. Their frozen wastes stretch along the Arctic ocean, whose icejammed waters shut out communication on the north. On the south they are walled in by 181 guses. They are similar to the Eskimos in the northern part of our own 

North America, and to the Lapps in 

Scandinavia. They depend largely on their herds of reindeer for meat, clothes, milk, and transportation. 

Their homes are rude huts of mud, wood, or reindeer skins. They dress in reindeer skins and in the furs of the wild animals they kill in the forests. Those who have visited the region tell us the 

Tunguses are brave, kind, and generous folk.

They make up in good nature and hospitality what they lack in household goods and other possessions. 

The Taiga. The evergreen forest belt cov ers an area fully as large as the United States of America, and its trees are one of the richest natural resources of Asia. They are not yet extensively used, because there is no means of getting their lumber to market. The 

Taiga resembles the great northern forests of our own continent and, like them, has sparse population. The forests are the home of many fur-bearing animals-the wolf, the fox, the OWC-14

ASIA bear, and the squirrel. All are sources of wealth, and trappers and hunters seek them for their valuable pelts.

The people of the Taiga build their houses of rough timber. They eat wild berries and herbs and the streams supply them with fish. 

They seem never to mind the loneliness or hardships of the strange, half-civilized life they lead.

Not far south of the forest belt there are a number of scattered settlements. The 

Trans-Siberian railroad runs near this region, and since its coming a few settlements have grown to be cities and trading centers. Chief among these are Omsk, in western Siberia, and Irkutsk, on a river which flows into Lake Baikal. When the hunters and trappers have a sufficient supply of furs they ship their products to market from one of these stations.

Russia has no great hold on the people of the tundras or the Taiga. Their manner of living makes them, like the Arabs, hard to control. Their lives are wild and free. Time spent out of doors hardens them to extremes of weather and makes them strong and healthy. 

The Wheat Belt. Wheat growing in Siberia centers around Omsk. The soil here is rich and deep, for the Siberian wheat belt is a continuation of the fertile black earth belt, European Russia's great grain-growing section.

Here streams from the Altai mountains and other ranges on the southeast are used for irrigating the land. Besides wheat, the people raise rye, barley, oats, potatoes, beets, and hay. 

Grazing Lands. South of the wheat belt there are grazing lands. These extend south through the region of the Kirghiz steppe and on into western Turkestan which lies in the 

Lowland of Turan. Here, also, there are desert lands. On the west the grazing lands border the Caspian sea, that great body of salt water without an outlet. About the Caspian seal hunting is an important industry, and in its waters the natives catch many sturgeon, great fish valuable for food. The sea of Aral, another salt sea, lies in the center of this region. Like the Caspian, this sea may be a source of wealth in the future, for quantities of salt can be taken from it.

The grazing lands consist of grassy plains. 

Besides stock raising, the growing of wheat and other grains is carried on here. Near the 

Persian border is an irrigated cotton belt that produces nearly as much fiber as Egypt. Mulberry trees are raised, and silk worms are fed on their leaves. Some of the people weave rugs and mats of silk or wool. These are marketed in Omsk and in the principal cities of southern Turkestan, Bokara and Tashkent. 

The peoples of the plains are the Kirghiz, the Turkomans, and the Cossacks. The 

Kirghiz and Turkomans are mostly shepherds.

They are nomads who roam about from place to place, stopping wherever there is suitable pasture for their flocks. They have large herds of sheep, goats, and horses, and the meat and milk of these animals provide them. with food. The Cossacks live in small villages and raise scanty crops and tend herds. They are daring horsemen, and have long furnished 

Russia with famous cavalrymen. 

Mountains and Plateaus. Eastern Siberia is formed largely of old, worn-down mountain ranges which run generally northeast and southwest. Gold, iron, coal, and silver are known to exist in these mountains. The gold and coal have been mined to some extent, but otherwise the mineral resources are largely undeveloped. 

Rivers. From the northern slopes of the mountains rise and flow three great riversthe Ob, the Yenisei and the Lena. Winding through forest and tundras they at length reach the Arctic ocean. But, as they are often frozen, and as their mouths are frequently jammed with ice, they are of little use except for watering the land. They cannot carry lumber to market because the ocean into which they empty is almost useless for navigation and because logs floating in them would be held by the ice jam near the Arctic. ice also unfits the rivers for navigation by large ships, and only crude and primitive vessels are used on them during the open season. 

Like the many small streams in northern

North America, the rivers supply fish for food and are useful for local travel to the settlers The

NORTHERN AND CENTRAL ASIA 

183 along their banks. 

Future. Asiatic Russia owes her slow development partly to her natural disadvantages and partly to a long period under an indifferent government. The present Russian government has shown some interest in the development of the country, and the future may tell a different story. Modern engineers have both the knowledge and the skill to open up this great region by railways and highways. 

These would bring machinery to the forests and mines and would carry away their lumber and ore. At present it is as though the mineral and lumber wealth were shut up in a great storehouse, waiting for the future to draw upon it.

CENTRAL ASIA 

Mountains and Plateaus. The high mountains which lie south of Asiatic Russia and extend through central Asia are a continuation of the high mountain regions of southern Europe. The greatest range is the Himalayas. The smaller ranges include the Kuenlun, the Altai, the 

Hindu Kush, and the Tien Shan. Look for them on page 174. These mountain ranges enclose several of the highest and driest plateaus in the world. 

You would think the people who live in this mountain region very strange and interesting. 

They are divided into tribes. In certain respects, all the tribes are much alike. All are fond of bright colors and both men and women dress in queer, gaily colored costumes, and wear a great deal of jewelry. Each tribe, however, has its own leader and its own customs. 

There are bands of robbers who seize the tradesmen's caravans and who live by helping themselves from their neighbors' fields and shops. Other people of the region are nomads who wander far and wide seeking pasture for their herds. But there are many, as well, who live peaceful, quiet lives in settled villages, farming and caring for their sheep, goats, and yaks. A yak is a kind of ox. 

Chief among the plateaus is Tibet. This plateau lies between the Himalaya mountains on the south and the Kuenlun range on the north. It is known as the "Roof of the 

World," for one must climb passes well over 

15,000 feet in height to reach it.

Future. The mountain lands of central 

Asia lie partly in Siberia and partly in China. 

Like Siberia, they are backward because the governments which rule them have been unprogressive. The people have so long been shut off from civilization that they dislike and distrust foreigners. So they have been very slow to adopt any modern methods or machinery which Europeans and Americans have tried to introduce to them. But in our study of the countries of southwestern Asia we have seen that the civilization of Europe and the New World is spreading in Asia and is increasing the progress of Asiatic countries. 

It may take a long time for modern means of transportation-railroads, highways, and airways to open up the mountain regions, but that they will do so seems very sure. Then these various peoples will progress along agricultural, industrial, and educational lines. 

1. Siberia occupies the entire northern part of Asiatic

Russia. It consists mainly of three great regions, the tundras, the Taiga, and the Siberian Wheat belt. 

There is also a region of plains and deserts, and a rugged mountain region rich in minerals in Asiatic Russia. Three great rivers of the country are the 

Ob, Yenesei, and Lena. 

2. Asiatic Russia has very cold winters. The length and warmth of the summers increase as one moves south from the Arctic circle. The country is sparsely populated. Because of natural disadvantages and the lack of railroads and good roads to connect settlements the country is slow in developing.

The Hindus will not eat beef because they believe that cattle are sacred. They do not object, however, to using their bullocks for work.

Elephants live to be very old and sometimes a mahout's son and grandson will take his place in caring for the same elephant.

How the name of India once stirred the countries of Europe!

INDIA- 

A LAND OF WEALTH AND STORY 

It meant gold and precious stones, silks and spices. It meant a great market from which the West could buy these products. Attempts to find the shortest possible water route to India led to the discovery of the New World. 

India is a stirring name still to those who know the country. Perhaps you have read some stories by Rudyard Kipling, an English writer who spent many years in India, and who pictures it as a strange land with people very different from us. In reality it is even stranger and more unlike our country than any stories can make it.

POSITION, SIZE, AND POPULATION 

India is a British colony. The greater part of it occupies the central peninsula of southern 

Asia. Its location in respect to the other countries of Asia is similar to that of Italy in respect to the countries of Europe. The country lies between 8° and 37° north latitude, which means that it is in both the hot Torrid zone and the North Temperate zone. East and west, India extends from about 62° to about 

101° east longitude. 

India's northern frontier lies in the high ranges of the Himalaya mountains. These mountains separate India from the country of 

Afghanistan and the Chinese dependencies of 

Sinkiang and Tibet. The Himalayas send off shoots and spurs of lower ranges to the southeast and the southwest, and cut off the Indian peninsula from the two states of Burma and Baluchistan, which are, however, included in the Indian empire. The southern part of the country is a triangular peninsula, which narrows to a point in the extreme southern portion. The peninsula is washed on the east by the waters of the Bay of Bengal and on the west by the Arabian sea. The coastline is regular, so the country has few good bays or 

INDIA 

harbors.

India's greatest north-south and east-west lengths are about 1900 miles each. The country is well over half the size of the United States in area, and it is twenty times the size of the mother country, Great Britain. Its population is enormous. Over 300,000,000 people swarm its valleys and plateaus, working its farms and crowding its cities. In the far recesses of the hills some live as primitive a life as the wild animals.

SURFACE 

Mountain Slopes. India is divided into three distinct regions—the mountain slopes, the lowland plains, and the central plateau or upland. The Himalaya mountains are the highest in the world. The lowest passes by which they may be crossed are from 15,000 to 19,000 feet above sea levelfar higher than those of the Andes or the Alps. 

Mount Everest, the highest peak in the world, is 29,141 feet in altitude.

The name Himalaya means "abode of snow," and the mountains are rightly called. 

Their heads are snowcapped and often, from a distance, one cannot tell where the mountains end and the sky begins. Miles and miles of glaciers lie between their ridges. As you would expect, the upper slopes are very cold, though the winds which blow against them from the south are warm. The warm air, as it strikes the cold rocks, forms many clouds.

These break and scatter and come together again, drifting constantly across the faces of the peaks. Men go to high mountains in dry regions to study the stars. The formation of clouds could well be studied in the high, moist air of the Himalayas.

The temperature rises as one travels down the mountain slopes, and population, which is sparse in the upper mountain regions, increases. The European or the American in this section finds it most desirable to live at an altitude of about seven thousand feet. At such a height the air is cool, pleasant, and healthful 185

INDIA 

187 and one is well above the dangerous feverbreeding swamps and marshes. Many government officials and business men have their homes in towns along the mountain slopes. 

Rivers and Lowland Plains. Three great rivers flow through northern and north central India. Two of these, the Indus and the 

Brahmaputra, rise on the plateau of Tibet, north of the Himalayas. The third river, the 

Ganges, is formed by the drainage from the southern slopes of the Himalayas. Down the mountains for thousands of feet these three great rivers twist and wind to the second region of India-the lowland plains. These plains extend across the country at its widest point, and in the northwestern part they are about a thousand miles from north to south. 

The great rivers have all helped to build up the plains by bringing to them rich, stoneless soil. Turning to the map on page 168, let us follow their courses. 

From its source the Indus flows northwest, turns sharply near the northern point of

India, and flows southwest through lower ranges and valleys to the Arabian sea. The upper Indus flows through a region of moderate rainfall and has many tributaries. The lower Indus resembles the lower Nile river in Egypt, for it has no tributaries and flows in an almost straight line through the dry, sandy Thar desert. The Indus has built up a deep, rich delta about its several mouths. 

The Ganges and the Brahmaputra rivers rise not far from each other, but their sources are separated by a ridge of mountains. The 

Ganges tumbles down the slopes nearly due south and then flows east, nearly halfway across the entire plain. Rich, alluvial soils fill its basin. The Brahmaputra flows eastward through the mountains, following a valley of its own making, then descends irregularly southward to the plain and joins the Ganges not far from the Bay of Bengal. These two rivers have one delta in common, which is larger than the delta of the Indus.

The Dekkan. The third region of India is an upland plateau called the Dekkan. This plateau includes the great southern part of the country which lies south of the river plains. A range of mountains, the Western 

Ghats, rises from the Arabian sea coast and forms the western edge of the plateau. The range has no natural passes. Opposite it, along the Bay of Bengal, are the Eastern

Ghats. These are lower, slope to a junglecovered coastal plain, and are broken by several streams which flow into the bay. Through the river valleys railroads have been built to the interior of the Dekkan.

The Dekkan plateau ranges in height from 

1,000 to 3,000 feet above sea level. The Ghats have a few peaks above 7,000 feet in altitude where the eastern and western ranges come together at the point of the peninsula. The surface of the plateau is generally flat, but is broken here and there by low ridges of rock. 

CLIMATE 

The protecting mountains on the north, the warm waters on the east, south, and west, and the country's tropical location all help to make India a warm land. 

But because of its varied altitude it has a wide range of climate. It is also in the belt of monsoons, those strange winds which blow inland from the sea in summer, and seaward from the land in winter. These monsoons provide India with a rainy season and with a dry season. 

Summer Monsoon. The rainy season is in the summer. It is brought by the southwest monsoon, which arrives about the first of June and continues through October. It blows inland from the Indian ocean and brings heavy rains. The distribution of this rainfall differs with the land surface. The Western Ghats are drenched on the windward side. Some of the hills in northeastern India receive at this period an amount of rainfall equalled in few other regions. The average annual rainfall is in places more than forty feet. The rainfall is lighter across the Dekkan, and parts of this plateau are quite dry. It is heavier again along the plains, except in the northwestern corner, which is so protected by mountains that it receives scarcely any rain at any time. 

Winter Monsoon. The dry, or winter, monsoon begins early in November and continues through December. During this period the

ASIA 

prevailing winds are from the northeast. Before reaching India they blow over interior 

VERY HEAVY RAINFALL HEAVY RAIN FALL MODERATE RAINFALL LIGHT RAINFALL VERY LIGHT RAINFALL SUMMER MONSOON 

India's summer monsoon, or period of heavy rainfall, is caused by the moisture-laden southwest winds which sweep in off the Arabian sea and the Indian ocean.

When these winds reach the mountains they are forced to rise and, becoming cool, they drop their moisture. 

VERY HEAVY RAINFALL HEAVY RAINFALL MODERATE RAINFALL LIGHT RAINFALL VERY LIGHT RAINFALL WINTER MONSOON 

In winter the monsoon winds from the northeast sweep down over India. They have traveled over great areas of land and have little moisture left. Consequently during this time India has very little rain except along the coasts. 

Asia, so they bring little rain and have a drying and cooling effect. Following the winter monsoon there is calm, clear, cool weather which lasts during January and February. The skies are blue and unclouded. The sun is warm, and the air is fresh and clean. This is the time when the foreigner would most enjoy a visit to the country. Then follows the hottest period of the year, the months of 

March, April, and May. Because 

Relation of Monsoons to Farming. 

India has varied altitude, her farmers, like those of the plateau regions of the central 

Andes, can raise a variety of crops. The monsoons are also an aid to the farmer. They allow him to grow crops that require a great deal of moisture in the summer, and crops that are drought-resisting in winter. Among the farm products which may be thought of as summer monsoon crops are rice, jute, sugar, and cotton. Winter monsoon crops include wheat, millet, and other grains.

When the summer monsoon is late or fails entirely the farmers suffer. The crops fail, and thousands of people in India die of starvation. 

The farmers are now being taught to rely less and less on the monsoon, and to store up water in reservoirs which can be drawn upon in the event of severe drought. But famines, caused by lack of rain, still cause great disaster. 

Even the occasional failure of the monsoons has not prevented India from being an agricultural country. The soil, for 

AGRICULTURE 

the most part, is well suited to this purpose, and the vast numbers of people living there can best assure themselves of enough to eat by raising their own food. 

Besides this, manufacturing is still largely undeveloped, being mostly carried on by hand in native homes and bazaars. The few factories in the various cities employ only a small part of the people. So agriculture is really the only great occupation open to the bulk of the Indian population.

Farms and Farm Methods. The farms in 

India are small. In parts of the Dekkan and in the Ganges basin they are so close together that they appear like one great garden. During the various planting and harvesting times armies of people are busy there. Most of them work with primitive tools, but some machinery has been introduced and is in use on the farms of the wealthier landowners.

INDIA 

189 Cotton. India, you may remember, is the home of cotton. Long before the United 

States took the lead in cotton production, western markets were supplied with it from parts of the Dekkan, and from the Indus region. Both of these sections are outside the area of India's heaviest rainfall, and do not have too much moisture to prevent the cotton bolls from ripening. The Indus region is so dry that irrigation is necessary and has been carried on there for a long time. 

Indian cotton has shorter fibers than American cotton and does not make so fine a cloth. 

But it mixes well with wool for varieties of textiles and is in demand in Great Britain for this purpose. 

Most of the natives dress in cotton clothing, and some cotton is manufactured in India. Much of the raw product, however, is sent to Great Britain, made into cloth and clothing there, and then sent back to India.

Sugar. In the irrigated lands around the upper Indus in the foothills of the Himalayas, sugar cane is an important product. Crops are raised in the summer months when the wet season brings rain to help the irrigation system, for sugar cane requires much moisture. 

Because it can be raised during only a part of the year, this crop is not so important to India as it otherwise might be. 

Jute. Jute, a plant fiber valuable for making burlap bags, string, and rope, is exported by India to all parts of the world, including the United States. To raise jute, harvest it, and prepare it for use is a long, laborious task. 

So it is easy to understand that thousands of people in India may be kept busy supplying the great demand for this product. Jute is plentifully raised along the rivers and in the broad Ganges valley where the soil is deep and there is plenty of moisture. 

Wheat and Other Grains. India raises great quantities of wheat, partly for home needs, and partly for export. Much of it is shipped from 

Karachi, a growing port at the mouth of the 

Indus. You may remember that wheat needs moisture for the first few weeks after planting. 

After that it does not require much moisture. 

For this reason it can be grown in the Thar desert, where irrigation allows it to get a start. 

The wheat farms in India are not on so great a scale as those of our own wheat belt. In general, the land is plowed with poor tools and must be gone over again and again before it is in the right condition for seeding. Many natives are employed to do the work which one great machine is made to do in our country. But the results are very good-so good that India is a competitor of the United States in the sale of wheat. 

Other grain crops, including barley, sorghum, and millet, are grown. Millet is used as food for both cattle and men, and is commoner than wheat among the poorer people. It is grown mostly on the western part of the Dekkan, though crops of it are raised in nearly every part of the country. 

Rice. The greatest food crop of India is rice. In much of the country it is the main dish at nearly every meal. The yearly yield is well over 20,000,000 tons. Rice growing is heavy labor. The grain requires a muddy soil, and the young stalks must be transplanted by hand. One farmer cultivates only a small plot of ground, but his hard work results in a very

This kind of farming produces more food from an acre than our kind; but in the United States each farm worker produces a great deal more than a farmer in India.

ASIA 

Tea. The British have developed tea plan tations along the slopes of the Himalayas and the Ghats. This crop, like cotton, jute, and rice, requires a great deal of labor. But in 

India labor is cheap because there are so many people living there, and the tea-plantation owners can afford to employ hundreds of workers. The natives drink some tea, but most of it is exported.

Other Crops. The natives of India raise for export a number of crops from whose seeds oil is extracted for food or for use in making paints, varnishes, and inks. These crops include peanuts, and flax from which we get linseed oil. Poppy seeds are also exported for their oil, but the poppy is most valued for the juice of its unripe fruit, which hardens into opium. 

This is a very valuable drug, but a very dangerous one, which should never be taken except at the advice of a physician. Other products of India's farms are spices and tobacco. 

Irrigation. We have mentioned irrigation in the Indus basin and in the Thar desert.

These and many other sections of the country have been irrigated for a long time by various methods. In early times water was stored in wells from which it was brought to the surface by means of crude hand pumps. Ditches were dug near the wells, and through these the water flowed to the fields. Gradually methods improved. Steam and electric pumps were brought into use and wide networks of canals and ditches now cover the areas where they are most needed. River waters, too, are being used to irrigate dry areas for farming. 

Great Britain has accomplished a great deal along this line. Old, abandoned irrigation works have been rebuilt and extended and new ones are under way. Two of these, in the 

Indus basin, are among the largest ever undertaken anywhere in the world. Within ten years it is believed these projects will have added several millions of acres to the farm lands of India.

Like the farmers in other parts of the world, the farmers of India have certain domestic animals to help them with their work. Of these the most important is the water buffalo, very useful

USEFUL ANIMALS 

in the rice fields, and the bullock, a valuable draft animal. Donkeys and horses are hitched to rude wooden carts and haul heavy loads.

Goats are raised for dairy purposes and for their hides. Goat and cattle hides are an important export, shipped largely to the United States. On the grassy western part of the 

Dekkan, great herds of goats and sheep are pastured. Elephants, because of their great strength, are used for travel in the jungles, where usually the trees and scrub growth are so thick that only an elephant can break through. These animals are also used in lumbering, for they can haul and lift heavy logs very easily. Camels are used in the dry sections because they can go so long without water. 

TRANSPORTATION 

All through the farming regions there are thousands of small villages. Most of the people of India live in them, so as to be near the country's food supply. The villages are connected by roads. There are even some well-paved modern highways, which the British have built. 

On these roads one sees every kind of transportation. Government officials and well-to-do citizens drive by in automobiles. Native farmers lumber along in their crude carts, drawn by bullocks or donkeys. There are horses and elephants, carrying riders on their backs. But perhaps commonest of all are the large numbers of people on foot, who often travel long distances. 

Over forty thousand miles of railways have been built in India, connecting all sections of the country. British engineers are largely responsible for the planning and laying of the roads, and British-built engines and cars run on them. While Bombay, the nearest large seaport to the Suez canal, is the chief railroad center, Calcutta, Madras, Delhi, and Benares are also important.

The newest and fastest means of transportation, the airplane, is also coming into use in India. Many of the large cities are now connected by air lines, and there is regular service between Delhi and London, England. By steamer, it takes fifteen days to reach India from England, but airplanes make the trip in

INDIA less than five. In the future, as more air ports are established along the route and night flying becomes practicable, we may expect to see this time cut even lower. 

In this agricultural country there are few cities, but some of the few are large and im- 

CITIES 

portant. The great ports are Bombay on the west coast, Madras on the east coast, and Calcutta on the Ganges river. 

Bombay has a splendid natural harbor, and is the principal seaport for the export of cotton and oil seeds. It has a number of cotton mills. 

Madras is on the open seacoast, but has built a fine harbor by extending great walls into the sea. It ships cotton to Japan and hides and skins to the United States, and has a trade in tobacco and spice. Calcutta is the largest city of India. It was once the capital, but as its location is not central, the seat of government has been moved to Delhi. Calcutta is a great port, eighty miles from the sea on one of the mouths of the Ganges river. Its export trade is in jute, tea, and hides and skins. One of the interior cities is Lucknow which makes fine tapestries and brass wares. Hyderabad, a picturesque walled city in the rocky part of the Dekkan, is a trading center ruled by a native prince.

The cities of India are famous for their beautiful buildings, particularly their temples, which are gorgeously designed and richly ornamented. The splendid temples of Delhi, Agra, and other cities of northern India illustrate the artistic skill of the workmen who built them. Besides the temples there are the government buildings and the homes of wealthy natives and people who have come from Europe. As is customary in the cities of warm regions, the houses in India are often built with balconies on the second story. 

These balconies are cleaner and cooler than porches built near the street. They usually jut out over the sidewalks and shade the passersby from the fierce rays of the sun.

The streets in the poorer sections are narrow and of rough material, so they are not very comfortable to travel over. The new and improved streets of Bombay, Calcutta,

Delhi, and some of the other leading cities are as broad and smooth as those of the large cities of Europe or North America. They are made beautiful by palm trees and parkways.

PEOPLE 

Traveling through India, one is attracted by varieties of plants and trees, curious insects, beautifully colored birds, and strange animals. But nowhere does one discover anything more strange and interesting than the people themselves. They are of many races, varying in color from those as blackskinned as Africans to those as white-faced as 

Europeans. One hears many strange languages, for hundreds of native dialects are spoken. In a crowded bazaar, the natives all chattering in their queer tongues sound like so many birds. 

Native Princes. India has many native princes, who store their wealth and keep it in one family from generation to generation. 

These princes make their own surroundings as magnificent as possible. They ornament their homes with gold and silver, with precious stones and rich sculptures. They travel about in splendid coaches or in costly automobiles.

They might well employ such wealth to aid the development of industry in their country, or to help the poor. But even such contact as they have already had with western peoples and European civilization has not yet taught them to do this, and the vast majority of their countrymen are wretchedly poor. 

The Poor. The poor live, almost without clothing, in miserable huts made of mud, straw, or thin wood. Many crowd into the cities where they work in tiny shops in great bazaars. They make articles as fast as they can, for there are thousands of such shops, and the best and quickest workmen get most of the business. Hard as they work, the poor people of India are usually able to earn only their shelter and enough food to keep them alive. 

This is true as there are so many of them that labor is cheap and wages are very low. There is little machinery. Jewelers, stone-cutters, carpenters, weavers, and almost all Indian workmen do their work with their hands. 

There are numerous religions in India. 

There are about seventy million Mohammedans, following the teachings of the prophet

ASIA 

RELIGIONS AND 

Mohammed. There are

THE CASTE SYSTEM nearly twelve million 

Buddhists, whose god is known as Buddha. There are nearly five million Christians. But the great mass of the people, well over two hundred million of them, are Hindus, worshipping many gods, the greatest of which is Brahma. 

Brahmanism greatly affects the lives of its followers, for it divides the people into many castes, or social groups, according to their trades. The members of one caste cannot mingle with those of another caste, and a person must always remain in the caste in which he is born. This means that the son of a silversmith must be a silversmith, the son of a shoemaker must be a shoemaker, though he may not choose to be so at all. This offers a man no encouragement to better himself if he belongs to a low caste. Brahmanism thus retards the general progress of the people as a whole. 

The Hindus believe many things which seem most strange to us. For instance, the cow is considered a sacred animal. Therefore the native Hindus will not drink its milk or eat its flesh. A cow is allowed to go where it pleases.

It may even roam the city streets unattended, no matter what trouble it causes to traffic or pedestrians. Sometimes it is decorated with a wreath of flowers.

Benares is the sacred city of the Hindus, as Mecca is the holy city of the Mohammedans. 

It is on the bank of the Ganges, which is believed to be a sacred river. Every year thousands of Hindu pilgrims visit the city to worship in its famous temples and to wash away their sins in the sacred waters of the river.

INDIA UNDER GREAT BRITAIN 

Great Britain assumed a tremendous task and a great responsibility when she attempted to make this vast crowded country of strange people a part of her empire. For a long time a few British officials and a small army ruled successfully this country of more than 300,000,000 people. They were able to do this because, in the first place, they ruled fairly and stopped the bloody wars between different groups, which in the past had caused much suffering. In the second place, the many different religions, races, and castes prevented any united rising against them. Both Mohammedans and Hindus are likely to be fanatical, that is, to hate and despise people of other religions than their own. So they were not fitted to work together. The members of the different Hindu castes were even unwilling to mix with each other. As a result, the British met no united opposition. Today, however, India is beginning to object strongly to foreign government, and Great Britain is attempting to set up a sort of government that will satisfy the wish for independence, will prevent conflicts among the different groups, and will protect British property and trade advantages. 

Of course, Great Britain profits from her control of India. She has developed the country's natural resources, and much of India's wealth has helped to enrich her government and her merchants. She has developed India into a great source of raw materials for 

British factories, and a great market for

British goods. But she has also done much to help India. Besides increasing and improving transportation and extending irrigation projects, she has improved sanitation and lessened disease. She has also established schools where, regardless of caste, a person may become skilled in his own type of work, and so may increase his use to the country as a whole. The great problem of securing enough food will probably always be present in India, but British agricultural schools are doing much toward enabling the natives to get the most possible use out of their land and to prevent famines.

India was formerly a mass of native states under despotic rulers who were constantly at war with each other. Today there are still several hundreds of such self-governing states, but they are under the supervision of the British government. The rest of the country is divided into provinces. Each province has a governor who conducts the affairs of his own. section and is sometimes assisted by native officers, for, like all people, the people of India wish some share in their own affairs. The 

British have largely done away with war be-

INDIA tween the native states, and have corrected many of the evils of the old system of government.

It is also in the belt of monsoons. These give the country a wet season in summer and a dry season in winter.

The wet and dry monsoons make possible the raising of crops which need a lot of moisture as well as those which need little. The soil throughout is well suited for farming. Manufacturing is little developed.

CEYLON 

Off the southeastern tip of India, in the warm waters of the Indian ocean, lies the island of Ceylon. In the beauty of its scenery it compares well with any spot in the world. 

It is not a part of British India, but a separate colony, controlled for over a century by Great Britain. It is very densely settled. 

SURFACE 

In size, Ceylon is a little larger than West Virginia. From north to south it measures 

272 miles and from east to west 137 miles. Four-fifths of Ceylon is lowlands and one-fifth is a mountainous plateau which rises some 7,000 feet above sea level in the south central part of the island. 

CLIMATE 

Ceylon lies near the Equator and is tropical in climate. April is the hottest month. In 

May the monsoon winds from the southwest begin, bringing deluges of rain to the southwestern slopes of the plateau. In November come the northeastern monsoons. These bring dry weather to India, but they bring rain to practically the whole island of Ceylon for they gather moisture from the Bay of Bengal. After these winter monsoons, Ceylon has nearly two months of mild, clear weather followed by a hot period in 

March and April. See the monsoon maps on page 188. 

Only about one-quarter of the island of Ceylon is cultivated. The soil is fertile and 

PRODUCTS 

most of the people are farmers. 

Coffee was once the chief product of the island, but a pest destroyed the plants and the raising of tea took its place. 

Tea. Tea raising has become the most important industry of the island. There are great tea plantations all over the southwestern slopes of the plateau, where the rainfall is heaviest. Tea requires at least sixty inches of rainfall a year for its best growth. On the eastern and northern slopes there is not enough rain for this crop. The soil is enriched with fertilizers which increase the yield of tea leaf. The plants mature so fast that there are 195 several pickings from the shrubs each year. 

White men, chiefly English, own most of the tea plantations and hire the natives to work

Rubber. Rubber production is becoming an important industry in Ceylon. In our study of Brazil, we found that the rubber there is laboriously gathered from wild jungle trees by the natives. In Ceylon, rubber trees are cultivated on plantations. This makes the work of rubber gathering easier and the yield larger.

In a recent year Ceylon exported more than three times as much rubber as Brazil, and over half of it went to the United States. Possibly there is Ceylon rubber in the tires on your family automobile or your bicycle. 

Other Products. Rice is a leading crop of the hot, damp coastal lowlands, but the natives do not raise enough to feed the population and a great deal is imported. Coconut palms, raised on large plantations, yield copra and coconut oil for export. Cacao and cinnamon and other spices are also exported. Ceylon has been known from early times for her precious stones -sapphires, rubies, amethysts, and garnets.
