SOUTHEASTERN ASIA INDO-CHINA AND BRITISH MALAYA 

In the southeastern corner of Asia, east of India, lie Indo-China and British Malaya. 

Indo-China includes

Burma, which we studied as part of British India, French Indo- China, and the independent kingdom of Siam. 

British Malaya contains the Federated Malay States and the Straits Settlements. 

Surrounded by water-the South China sea, the Bay of Bengal, and the Indian Oceanthese countries are on the water highway for all the ships passing around southern Asia. 

They are easily reached by sea from the Dutch 

East Indies and from Australia. 

Surface. Southeastern Asia is a region of jagged highlands and fertile lowlands, of abundant grasslands, dismal swamps, and almost impenetrable jungles. In the north are young, rugged mountains. A range of these follows along the eastern coast of French Indo- China and another reaches through the west part of Siam and on south to the tip of the Malay peninsula. Rising in the mountains and flowing south through valleys to the sea, are three great rivers: the Mekong, which forms part of the border between French Indo-China and Siam; the Menam, flowing through Siam, and the Irrawaddy, flowing through Burma. 

These rivers bring down rich soil from the mountains to their valleys and to their deltas. 

In the wet seasons, the rivers overflow their banks, and as they recede they leave the land richer, just as the Nile does after flood time in Egypt.

Climate. The climate of the region is tropical. April and May are the hottest months and are very unhealthful for white men. The thermometer sometimes climbs to 100° in the shade at noon, and the air is moist and sticky. 

Even the natives, who are used to the hot weather, have little energy. 

The monsoons have a strange effect on the Malay peninsula and Indo-China. As in India and Ceylon, the summer monsoon from the southwest brings heavy rainfall to most of this region. The eastern coast of French Indo- 

China, however, is sheltered by the mountains and so receives little rain at this time. On the other hand, the winter monsoon from the northeast, which brings a dry season to most lands in its path, picks up moisture from the South China sea and brings rain to eastern Indo-China. So this section has its rainy season while other lands are dry. In the dry season, during the winter months, there is so little rain on the west coast of Indo-China that vegetation withers and dries up. Besides being in the monsoon belt, the Malay peninsula is also in the belt of equatorial rains, so there is a good deal of rainfall there all the yearmuch more than in Indo-China.

French Indo-China belongs to France. It is about the size of the state of Texas, but has three times as many people. The capital is Hanoi, FRENCH INDO-CHINA 

a modern city about the size of Albany, New 

York. Saigon is the chief port, with an excellent harbor for ocean vessels. Situated in a region of rice fields, Saigon has large rice mills, and rice forms the principal export from its docks.

The Mekong river is the main transportation route of the country. There is only one railroad, running inland from Hanoi across the Chinese border, but the French have built many miles of good roads. Airplanes, too, are used for transportation, and an airway connects Hanoi with Saigon, while other lines connect the two cities with Bangkok, Siam, and Rangoon, Burma. 

The wealth of French Indo-China lies mainly in agriculture. The soil is very rich, especially in the southwestern part. The country is a leader in the production of rice, exporting more than any country except Burma. Other products raised on the lowlands are sugar, cotton, and spices. On the higher lands, coffee and tea are raised. Rubber is grown on great 197

ASIA 

plantations covering many thousand acres, and almost all of it is exported. The teak tree is found in the forests. From it comes a very hard, durable timber, called teakwood, used in building ships and in making furniture. An oil is extracted from the wood for medicine and from its leaves a red dye is made. Fishing is an important industry along the rivers and on the coast of French Indo-China. In the mountains are coal, tin, and lead.

The country of Siam lies between French 

Indo-China and Burma. Siam is an independent kingdom, her freedom being guaranteed by both Great Britain and France, between whose provinces she lies. In area, Siam is over four times the size of Pennsylvania, though its population is only a little larger.

The northern and western parts of Siam are mountainous, and contain many parallel northsouth mountain ranges. The central part of the country is a flat, fertile plain, largely occupied by tropical jungle.

The climate of Siam is very hot and moist. 

There is so much rain when the summer monsoons blow in from the sea that the lowlands are flooded and people go about in boats. The soil is very rich and during the dry season much of Siam is irrigated. Rice and teakwood are the two most important products. Elephants are used to drag the great heavy teak logs to the streams where they are floated to mills or shipping points. Cotton, tea, tobacco, coconuts, and sugar-the usual tropical products are also raised. Siam has great natural resources. Besides its agricultural products, there are tin, zinc, coal, iron, and precious gems. The Siamese people are not very energetic as a nation, and Chinese do much of their work.

Bangkok, on the delta of the Menam river, is the capital of Siam and an important seaport. It is a modern city, a little smaller than 

Boston in population. There are rice mills and some manufacturing establishments in Bangkok. The most important exports are rice and teakwood. One of the interesting sights of the city is the floating houses on the canals. 

There are over 100,000 people who have no other homes than these primitive huts built on rafts. BRITISH

1. Natives planting rice on the Dutch island of Java in the East Indies. One laborer is carrying young rice plants on a stick across his shoulders. Rice is the chief food crop of Java, although many other crops are raised. 

2. Rubber trees on a great plantation in Sumatra. The company which owns this plantation has more than ten million trees under cultivation. The white line on the nearest tree is a groove in the bark through which the rubber sap is flowing to the cup on the ground. 

3. A scene in the mountains of the Philippine islands. 

See how the road curves back and forth over the hillsides between the valley and the mountain top. This avoids steep grades but makes travel much longer. The mountains, in places, are so steep that direct roads are not practical, and agriculture in such country is very difficult.

Philippines. Manila bay is in the background. This bay is one of the largest land-locked harbors in the world, and Manila is the principal trade center as well as the capital of the Philippines. The city is only slightly above sea level and at one time was one of the most unsanitary cities in the East. Today it is a modern city in every way with excellent sewage and water systems.

INDUSTRIES OF THE PHILIPPINES 

1. Coconuts on a raft, ready to be taken to market. 

Coconuts grow in clusters on a palm tree known as the coconut palm. This tree is a native of the Philippines and the East Indies and of tropical America. 

2. Husking coconuts. The nuts are broken with an axe or by striking them on a sharp iron spike, as shown in the picture. The pieces are allowed to dry, and, as they dry, the meat shrinks away from the shell, which is then removed. The dried meat, called copra, when crushed or boiled, yields an oil which is used in the making of soaps and candles. Certain fats which are used in place of butter for cooking or eating also come from this oil. 

3. Threshing rice with an American-built thresher on a plantation in the Philippines. While an enormous amount of rice is raised on the islands none is exported. It is entirely consumed by the inhabitants, and large quantities are imported besides. 

4. On an abaca plantation on the island of Mindanao in the Philippines. The plants grow to a height of from fifteen to twenty-five feet. Manila hemp, a fiber of the abaca tree, is stronger and lighter than most other hemps, and is widely used in making ropes and twines of all sorts. 

Hundreds of Filipinos earn their livings by preparing the fiber of the abaca tree for shipment to other lands.

THE EAST INDIES AND THE PHILIPPINES 

South and west of the busy port of Singapore, and separated from it by only the narrow Strait of Malacca, is the great island of Sumatra, which extends northwest and southeast for more than a thousand miles. East of the southern end of Sumatra lies the rest of the 

East Indian archipelago, a chain of islands four thousand miles long. Next to Sumatra on the southeast is Java, smaller but the most important of the entire group. North of Java is 

Borneo. East of Borneo are the island of

Celebes and the Molucca islands, and farthest east is New Guinea. New Guinea is the largest of the East Indies, and Borneo is the second in size. Hundreds of other smaller islands are included in the archipelago. Northeast of Borneo and directly south of Shanghai in China is a very interesting group of islands, the Philippines. They are so much like the East Indies in their geography that we can study both island groups together.

The Equator runs through the middle of

AND 

CLIMATE 

the Philippines lie in the Torrid zone. The East Indies are surrounded by the warm waters of the 

Pacific and Indian oceans. Con sequently they have a hot and moist climate, with plenty of rain in all parts. 

Most of the islands have volcanoes, and since the soil of volcanic lands is rich and fertile they have heavy and plentiful vegetation. 

They are wonderfully suited to cultivation of tropical crops, and agriculture is very successful wherever it has been intelligently undertaken.

The only places, in fact, where crop growing is difficult are on the slopes of the mountains. Mountains are found in all the islands, and some of them are so steep that they cannot be plowed, and some are even so steep that the rains have washed them bare of soil. 

The East Indies belong principally to the 

Netherlands and Great Britain. Great Britain

MOTHER COUNTRIES 

holds Singapore and part of the 

Malay peninsula. Singapore is a very valuable trade port for the island group. The British also control Sarawak and North Borneo on the northern coast of Borneo, and the eastern half of New 

Guinea. The Dutch control Java, Sumatra, southern Borneo, Borneo, western New Guinea, Celebes, the Moluccas, and most of the smaller islands-altogether sixty times as much territory as the mother country. These East 

Indies are a great source of wealth to the 

Netherlands. Until recently, the Philippines were a dependency of the United States. 

Manila, the capital, is the chief port. 

PEOPLE 

The natives of all the islands are principally of the brown race. They are intelligent and can easily learn western methods of agriculture. They can produce huge crops from the fertile fields and hillsides of the islands. The Filipinos are somewhat different from the rest. Though most of the islanders are Mohammedans, the great mass of the Filipinos are Christians. The East Indians are not very ambitious, and are usually willing to follow directions of European managers. 

They do not have much to say about their own governments. The Filipinos, on the other hand, are self-governing. During the time when their country was a United States possession, they were given a share in their government and were educated to the idea that they would some day be independent. In 1935, they began a ten-year trial period of freedom under a Filipino president and legislature. During this period, the Philippines are to be protected by the United States. Our government and many 

American firms have invested large sums in developing the islands, and we are therefore much interested in the future of the Philippines.

In the East Indies, Dutch and British managers direct the work of the natives and carry on the foreign trade. Great plantations have been developed, on which Europeans see 201

ASIA 

to it that the best methods are followed and that the natives work faithfully. The result has been a great increase in the tropical products which these plantations send to our temperate world.

Java is the most fully developed of all the plantation islands. Here the Dutch have 

DEVELOPMENT 

made a network of good automobile roads, have built up a fine port at Batavia, and have taught the natives the best ways of cultivating the many products of the island. Java has a population of almost 700 people to the square mile, the densest population of any entire country in the world. Batavia is the capital and largest city of the Dutch East Indies. Its harbor is not naturally good, but the Dutch have greatly improved it and made it an important place in the trade of the islands.

The other islands are less fully developed. 

The Dutch have made an excellent start, however, in Sumatra and other colonies and the British have done the same in their section of Borneo. The products of the islands are constantly increasing and there is no reason why they should not increase as long as the temperate industrial countries are ready to buy them.

These products are of the greatest importance. The people live on rice and sago, and, like many tropical people, they raise other materials to meet western demands. 

Their exports include sugar, rubber, coffee, tea, cacao, coconut products, spices, cinchona, tobacco, and many other tropical products which we find in our markets. The hardworking natives, under their European managers, turn out much of the rubber for our automobile tires. The rubber is the thickened sap of rubber trees, which are planted in groves. The sap is collected in little cups placed to catch it as it flows from cuts in the bark. It is heated in wide, shallow pans over a fire until the sap hardens into sheets of "crepe" rubber, which are shipped by way of 

Batavia or Singapore to the great markets.

The United States buys most of this rubber. 

The "crepe" soles on some sport shoes give us an idea of what crepe rubber looks like when it leaves the plantations. 

Between Borneo and New Guinea are the 

Celebes and the Moluccas, or Spice islands, famous today for the same products as in the days of Columbus. In Columbus' time spices were more valuable than they now are, for they were necessary to the preservation of food. 

Nowadays we preserve food by refrigeration. 

Columbus was looking for a short route to these same Indies when he made his famous first voyage to the New World. The Moluccas still provide nutmeg, mace, and many other spices. 

TRADE 

The trade of the islands is largely carried on by little steamboats which move from one small port to another, picking up the spices, rubber, copra, cacao, or sugar of the planters and leaving in return cotton cloth, hardware, and other manufactures.

These cargo boats carry their wares 

Manila, Batavia, or Singapore and deposit them in warehouses until the great oceangoing steamers can transport them to Europe and the United States. Singapore is the principal port for this trade. to In addition to the more usual products of the East Indies, the British have valuable oil fields in Sarawak in northern Borneo, and export all kinds of petroleum products to the surrounding markets. The eastern end of New 

Guinea, which is governed by Australia, has valuable exports of copper in addition to its copra and rubber. From the Philippines we get a fine fiber plant, Manila hemp, from which are made the ropes used on most of the world's ships. The Filipinos send the United States many cigars and fine embroideries which find a ready sale in our markets.

FUTURE 

Because of the heat and dampness of the climate, not a great many white settlers are apt to make their homes in the East 

Indies. But the islands are a rich source of necessary raw materials, and they buy from Europe and the United States a great many manufactured articles. It is most likely that they will develop under European guidance into busy agricultural countries, with increasing populations which will supply more and more products and will buy more and more

CHINA AND MANCHUKUO 

CHINA The Chinese nation is very much older than When the Romans were fighting to build their empire, China was already an old country. The Chinese people 

OLD 

CHINA were a cultured and thoughtful race when our ancestors were European barbarians. 

Long years before Columbus stepped foot on North America, the Chinese were using the mariner's compass. While Europeans were still fighting and hunting with bows and arrows, the Chinese invented and used gunpowder. They were making beautiful silks and satins and velvets with which to clothe their emperors and empresses long before the people of Europe learned to make fine cloths. 

They were using carved blocks to print their books when monks in Europe were slowly and painstakingly copying manuscripts by hand. 

While the nations of Europe were as a whole unable to read or write, the Chinese were reading and rereading and memorizing the words of their favorite poets and philosophers. 

Confucius, who lived about 2400 years ago, was one of the wisest men that China ever had, and one of the wisest men CONFUCIUS the world has ever known. The

Chinese today still treasure his words. Confucius gave to the Chinese the Silver Rule. 

This says that you must not do to others the things you would not want others to do to you, which is simply another way of wording our 

Golden Rule. His many wise sayings have guided the Chinese people for centuries. 

But all the time, in spite of their advanced state, the Chinese were developing little habits 

CHINA'S ATTITUDE 

and ways of thought that were going to hinder them later when the rest of the world began to progress rapidly. For one thing the Chinese were building up a dislike and distrust of all foreigners. They felt that the people to the west were barbarians, wholly inferior to themselves, and wanted nothing to do with them. 

Then, too, the teachings of Confucius led the Chinese to worship their ancestors. Even today many a Chinaman pays more heed to the beliefs of his dead father, grandfather, and great-grandfather than he does to those of the people of his own day. Partly as a result of this looking backwards, the Chinese have practically stood still, while the nations of the western world have raced ahead. Ancient

China gave us gunpowder, the compass, printing, and silks; but there she stopped. From the western nations, in the meantime, have come discoveries and inventions in almost a steady stream-the railroad and steamship, telegraph and telephone, automobile and airplane, radio and electric light, and many hundreds of other useful things. Swiftly, China was left behind. And she really wanted to stay behind, to be left alone with the tombs of her ancestors and her old familiar customs.

She wanted no foreigners in her land with their hustling ways, their eagerness to try new things, and their endless rounds of business. 

The surroundings of China have helped to keep the Chinese backward. Her boundaries are very hard to cross, and for many long years only the boldest

BOUNDARIES 

of explorers succeeded in entering this shutaway country. On the east is the Pacific ocean, which remained unexplored and almost unsailed for many years after the Atlantic became a common highway. On the south and southwest are forests, high mountains, valleys, and rivers. To the west tower highlands, mountain peaks, and lofty plateau deserts.

Many of these regions were, and still are, inhabited by fierce wandering people and robbers, who added one more danger to the path of any travelers wishing to enter the country. 

The Great Wall. Behind her barriers China remained practically undisturbed during many years. East, south, and west were well protected, and it was only from the north that 204

1. The Great Wall of China. More than two thousand years ago the Chinese built this wall as a defense against savage tribes from the north. Their task was greater than the building of the pyramids by the Egyptians, for the Great Wall winds over 1200 miles across the hills and valleys of northern China. Notice how well it has lasted through the centuries. 

2. A Chinese junk. Junks are flat-bottomed, squarelooking sailing boats. Often their sails are made of matting woven from long grasses, and their sterns and prows are hand-carved with Chinese designs. The Chinese were among the earliest navigators and invented the compass. 

But most of them still make boats like those which their ancestors made. 

3. A street in Shanghai, a Chinese seaport of great importance in foreign trade. Crowded China has no room for wide sidewalks or automobile boulevards. Shops in the market district crowd in until there is barely room for two hand carts to pass. Most of China's business is done along streets like this. 

4. River life in Shanghai. China's fertile lowlands are so crowded that there is not enough land to raise crops for the great population. Many thousands of people live on the water in queer little houseboats, so as to use as much land as possible for farming. The people of the houseboats are poor, and these floating homes are far from comfortable.

1. Sorting cocoons in a Chinese silk factory. Within each cocoon in every one of these trays is a silkworm which has fed on mulberry leaves and then spun the cocoon about him. The fine silk fibers which the silkworms spin are made into the silk thread and silk cloth with which we are familiar. The workers in this factory are selecting the perfect cocoons for silk making. 

2. Farmers husking wheat in China. Wheat is one of

China's important crops, but in China wheat is not harvested and threshed with machines as it is in our country. These people are grinding the wheat in hand mills to remove the husks, so that the wheat can be made into flour. Notice the bamboo fence in the background. 

3. Chinese rice fields. Notice how the separate fields are bordered by earth banks which keep the water in. 

The brook furnishes the water for irrigation. Probably all of these Chinese and many others depend for their living on these fields. In our country this amount of land would most likely support only one farmer and his family. 

4. A bamboo thicket in China. The Chinese have hundreds of uses for bamboo. They eat the green bamboo shoots and make bottles and building materials from bamboo stems. Baskets and chairs, fences, masts of small boats, walking sticks, and even fine paper are made from bamboo. We know this plant best in the form of fishing rods, but that is one of its least important uses.

From its many watch towers sentries used to scan the horizon for a glimpse of the wild intruders from the north.

The Chinese wall served very well to keep out small bands of raiders, but it was of little use against the great Mongol army which attacked the country in the thirteenth century, under the leadership of a crafty general, Genghis Khan. Not only did Genghis 

Khan conquer

China, but most of Asia, and he created a mighty empire stretching from the China sea to the Dnieper river in Europe. Then about three hundred years later the Manchus, from

Manchuria in the north, overran the country. 

Each of these conquests placed a new line of emperors on the Chinese throne.

Despite the great size and importance to which China grew, her people still wanted only to be left alone, shut off from the outside world. But this was not possible. Men from the western world persisted in going adventuring, exploring, and trading. Today the nations of the world are seeking new markets for the products of their sive future. The

Chinese are waking up. The old empire has passed and the 

Chinese of today have established a republic. This Chinese republic is of vast size, equaling in area about half of the whole continent of North America.

The population is greater than that of 

North America by more than two hundred million people.

The republic is made up of several different parts, some of which are but loosely bound 

CHINESE REPUBLIC 

together. The part of the republic known as China proper is in southeastern Asia-the land of bamboo groves, of soaking fields of rice, of ancient walled cities, and of queer Chinese sailing craft, called junks, which slowly ply up and down the rivers and canals. China proper includes the great fertile flood plains of the

Hwang and Yangtze rivers. It is made up of 

18 provinces, or states. Besides China proper, the republic of China includes three dependencies: Mongolia, Sinkiang, and Tibet. Find these on the map, page 174. Manchukuo was the Chinese dependency of Manchuria until 1932, when it declared its independence, set

ASIA up a home government, and adopted its new name-Manchukuo. 

DEPENDENCIES 

Mongolia. This Chinese dependency, about one-third the size of the United States, has a population less than that of the city of Philadelphia. Mongolia is a high, bleak desert country. Here is the Desert of Gobi, one of the highest deserts in the world. The Mongolians have bronzed faces, high cheek bones, and hard expressions. They wear heavy coats and high boots and look very rough and dirty. They are nomads, living in tents, and roaming the desert with their camels, horses, goats, and sheep. In days past the galloping hoofs of the Mongol horsemen have struck terror to both Chinese and Russian settlements. 

Sinkiang. Sinkiang, or Chinese Turkestan, has proved of little importance to the Chinese republic. It is a sandy desert, covering a low plateau surrounded by lofty mountains. Perhaps 2,500,000 people, mostly wandering herdsmen, live there. Close to the highlands there are a few small irrigated areas, where cereals, fruits, and vegetables are raised.

Wool, cotton, and raw silk are other products of this region. 

Tibet. Tibet, the third dependency, is the highest country in the world. It is a plateau country, cold and dry. Perched up near the clouds, Tibet is a bare land with treeless mountain slopes and wind-swept passes. The only highways lie through these mountain passes, sometimes as high as 18,000 feet above sea level, where the snow is whirled by the winds about the traveler's head. Bands of robbers infest many of the highways. 

Most of the 2,000,000 people in Tibet are farmers and stockbreeders. They raise several varieties of grains and some vegetables, including peas. Many roam about the hillsides with flocks of sheep, or with herds of goats and other grazing animals. They raise the yak, an odd-looking, long-haired animal resembling a shaggy ox. The yaks are valuable as beasts of burden, and they also supply milk. Some of the farmers who own them engage in dairying. 

Many Tibetans are hunters, and furs are one of the exports of the plateau. The chief export of this country is wool. Musk from the musk deer is also exported for use in making perfumes.

The Tibetans are not a hospitable folk, and do not pretend to be. They wish for no visitors, and for many years tried to keep all foreigners out of the country. Even today they are apt to show the traveler quite plainly that they see no reason for his presence and do not care to have him. For the most part they are unfriendly and inquisitive and often dangerous. 

In the plateau of Tibet, high above the rest of the world, the Hwang and the Yangtze rivers rise, and from there they go winding down to water the Great plain of China proper.

The Indus and Brahmaputra rivers of India rise in Tibet.

Climate of Dependencies. The climates in all these dependencies of the Chinese republic are extreme, often either too hot or too cold. The westerly winds sweep across the plains and the highlands, but they have already covered great stretches of land on their long journey from the Atlantic ocean, and have lost most of their moisture. This accounts for the general dryness and bleakness of the provinces.

CHINA 

PROPER 

China proper is very different from any of the dependencies. Here much of the land is low and fertile, the climate mild, and the population dense. Here you may see a Chinese farmer in a spreading straw hat and a garment that looks like a kimono, cultivating a well-soaked field with a crude hoe such as his ancestors used before him. Here you may see city after city down whose streets go silk-clad men and women, taking tiny, shuffling steps, and looking as if they were thinking thoughts that we westerners could not possibly understand. This is 

China proper, the land of graceful pagodas, or temples.

If it were not for the Great plain of China proper, well-watered, level, and fertile, the millions of inhabitants would fare very badly.

This plain is an excellent agricultural region. 

The wants of a Chinaman are very simple. Give him a little to eat, a little to wear, and some sort of a shelter, and he is content. But there are so many people in China that even with

CHINA their modest desires it is often hard to feed them all, and in lean years starvation is a frequent and dreaded visitor. 

Size and Population. China proper is about half the size of the United States, but it has over two and a half times as many people. Of the nearly 400,000,000 people in the Chinese republic, less than one-twelfth live in the dependencies. The others swarm over China proper, crowding especially what is known as Middle China. When you consider that this is an agricultural country and that a very limited area of productive land must support an immense population, you will begin to have some idea of the Chinese food problem. You can form your own opinion as to why the Chinese have become such excellent and thorough farmers. 

Climate. China proper is affected by the monsoons, which bring heavy rains in the summer, or growing season. These rains are heaviest in the south. The temperature of the country also varies from north to south, ranging from a cool temperate climate like that of our New England states to a tropical one like the climate of the West Indies. 

North China. The northern part of China proper lies in China's Great plain. Here the summers are warm and there is moderate rainfall. The winters, however, are very cold, as the westerly winds have to cross great stretches of cold land before reaching this eastern country. China proper has been almost stripped of her forests, so wood as fuel is almost unknown. As her coal mines have not been developed, coal is scarce. In consequence, there is much suffering among the poor people during the cold winters. Wool clothing is rare, and to keep warm the people usually wear heavily quilted cotton garments in cold weather. 

The people of North China are large and alert and healthy, somewhat like the vigorous 

Manchus living to the north of them. They are intelligent, and are keenly interested in the affairs of the government of their country. But they are even less eager for new ideas than the southern Chinese, and have opposed with arms some of the proposals of the new republic. 

North China is drained and watered by the famous Hwang, or Yellow, river which has one of the most fertile deltas in the world. 

This river has caused so many floods and so much despair and suffering among the people that it is known as China's Sorrow. Rising in the high plateau of Tibet, it rushes down through lands so stripped of their forests that they cannot hold back the water, and on across the vast, fertile flood plains. The Hwang is a changeable river, overflowing its banks, changing its mouth, shifting its course, and sometimes sweeping crops and houses and helpless people along with it. During some of its floods the Yellow river has drowned thousands of people. It is, in its worst moods, a great, yellow, dangerous monster.

The Hwang is of little use for navigation, for there are many rapids and sandbars in its course, which interrupt the passage of boats. 

But it helps to provide the soil in which to grow good crops. In its upper course it flows through an area of loose, yellow soil, or loess, which has been carried in dust storms from dry central Asia by the wind. The river gathers up this rich soil, carries it down to the plain, and spreads it over the fields. So highly is this soil regarded that its yellow color has become the imperial color of China. It is among the richest soils of the world, and without it there would probably have been much more starvation than there has been in China. 

In this northern part of China the farmers grow millet, peas, beans, and other grains and vegetables, but little rice. Many people in our country make the mistake of supposing that the Chinese grow only rice and live entirely upon this product. On the contrary, they grow a large variety of vegetables and grains. The peninsula of Shantung is noted for its crops of peanuts, many of which find their way to our country. 

North China's great city of Peiping, formerly known as Peking, is one of the oldest and most famous cities in the world. For many centuries it was the capital of China. Inside its great outer walls are four separate walled cities—

ASIA 

the Chinese city on the south; the Tatar, or 

Mongol, city on the north; the Imperial city within the Tatar city; and the Forbidden city within the Imperial city. In the Chinese and 

Tatar cities are the shops and homes of the people and the modern public and government buildings. The Imperial city contains many temples, as well as the palaces, courtyards, and gardens of former emperors, kings, and princes. Within the Forbidden city lie other palaces and temples, most of them very ancient. 

Until recent years no foreigners were permitted to enter this inner city. Peiping, with its great wall, its gates, and its cities within a city is very mysterious and fascinating.

On the coast, only a few miles from Peiping, is its seaport of Tientsin. Tientsin is fast becoming a modern factory city. It is also one of the few railway centers of China. Railway lines from Tientsin connect with Manchukuo and the Trans-Siberian railway and also with many important Chinese cities farther to the south.

Leaving Tientsin, we might board a Chinese boat and go down the Grand canal, which is over 1200 years old, nearly 800 miles long, and one of the most famous transportation routes of China. The Grand canal connects the harbor of Tientsin with the Hwang and the Yangtze rivers, thus joining North China to Middle China. Many Chinese craft sail this popular waterway. The canal leads through rich, well-watered fields, past farms, villages, and walled cities.

Middle China. Middle China lies directly south of North China. Here, the climate is warmer, the rainfall heavier, and the population even denser. We would be amazed at the number of very large cities, cities the size of 

Buffalo, Philadelphia, Cleveland, and other great centers of population of our own country. But only a small fraction of China's population lives in cities, compared to the citydwelling population of the United States. 

These many cities show that this is the industrial and commercial section of China.

The city of Shanghai is located near the mouth of the Yangtze river. At this famous seaport, great quantities of manufactured goods from America are landed to be sent inland. From here leave the silks, tea, bamboo, and firecrackers which the Chinese send to our country. Shanghai has large and modern factories which specialize in making silks and cottons. In fact, Shanghai is the center of cotton manufacturing in China. This is very natural since the basin of the Yangtze river has the finest cotton fields of all China. There are oil refineries in Shanghai and other industries as varied as those of any ordinary American city. 

Nanking is the capital of the republic. The government was removed to Nanking to give it a more central location than that of Peiping and to remove it from northern influence.

Nanking is located on the Yangtze, and is a little smaller than San Francisco. It is an old textile center. Here, in years gone by, the silks and the satins and the velvets of imperial yellow were woven for the emperors. Nanking is still a center for the silk industry for which 

China has long been famous. You will find many textile factories throughout Middle China.

Eight hundred miles up the Yangtze, which may be navigated by ocean steamers for that distance, is the inland port of Hankow, a large distributing center and an iron manufacturing city. There are many tea factories in Hankow.

The tea is shipped from Hankow by caravan into Tibet and Mongolia, or down the river to the port of Shanghai.

The great Yangtze river, which waters and drains Middle China, is not quite so unruly as the Yellow river in the north, but nevertheless it has extensive, well-watered, and rich flood plains, and it also brings down much rich soil from the highlands. Unlike the Hwang, it is navigable far inland, and so provides Middle China with a fine water route.

In spite of its many growing industries Middle China is an agricultural section, and every bit of land is made to produce its share of food. 

The abundant rains of this region make possible the growing of rice, which must have its roots in water during the growing season. 

Here rice is a staple article of food for every day in the week and every week in the year. 

Tea and cotton are both highly important

CHINA crops. Much tea is used by the Chinese, but nevertheless there is enough left over to supply many foreign countries, including our own. 

The cotton of this region is sent to the Chinese cotton factories. 

Journeying south in Middle China, we pass watery fields of rice, bamboo forests, and little river and canal villages of mud houses. These all look rather dreary and tumbledown. We notice, as we travel, that the climate is becoming both warmer and more moist, and the appearance of the landscape is mountainous rather than level. The Great plain of China is being left behind. 

South China. Southern China is a warm, moist section, with more highlands than plains. 

The Tropic of Cancer crosses it just north of Canton, so that it lies in both the Torrid and the North Temperate zones. This section is drained by the Si, or West, river, sometimes called the Si Kiang. The basin of the Si is low and fertile, well fitted for agriculture. Here are raised large crops of rice and tea. Much silk is also produced.

The summers of South China are long and hot, and the monsoons bring this section heavier rains than any other part of China. 

Another great difference is in the people. The inhabitants of South China are smaller and less energetic than those of North China. 

South China is an important agricultural section, though it lacks the rich, extensive flood plains of Middle and North China. Here one finds the mulberry and bamboo trees, as · well as the fields of tea, of rice, and of cotton. 

Sugar cane is a common product, and there are also certain tropical products, including bananas and spices. There are, too, rain forests of mahogany and ebony.

Canton is the most important city of this region and a great tea-exporting center. It also has many silk mills. Most of the Chinese in our country come from its vicinity. Canton has been very prominent in the affairs of the republic.

Hong Kong is a British city and a famous seaport. It is located on an island, southeast of Canton. Once it was a poor fishing village. 

When the Chinese ceded it to the British they probably thought they were not giving them much. Today Hong Kong is one of the greatest ports of the world. It handles the oceangoing trade of Canton, which cannot be reached by deep-sea vessels, and has a very large commerce in goods going from one part of China to another. It is the greatest center of the rice trade in the world, and the great variety of other imports and exports include cotton yarn, tin, and coal. There are a number of factories.

AGRICULTURE 

If you were to know the Chinese and talk with them as friends you would learn many interesting things about them. 

You will remember that in IN CHINA

Spain the people think that agriculture is work unfit for a gentleman. In China, on the other hand, they think there is no more honorable occupation than that of agriculture. 

The reason for this is most natural. There are many millions of people, all needing food in order to live. What could be more honorable for a man, they will ask you, than to till the soil to produce food for himself, his family, and his fellowmen? 

Nature favors agriculture in China. To 

China she has furnished the rich yellow soil, and the winds and the rivers to bring it down to the plains and spread it out. During the growing season she sends heavy rains, so that the crops will have enough moisture. 

During the long years in which they have been engaged in agriculture, the Chinese have, through hard work and application, acquired almost unbelievable skill. They plant every available foot of ground. They terrace the hillsides and plant crops there. Many of them with their families, their chickens, and their pigs, live in boats on the waterways, so that they will not need to waste the ground which a house would cover.

A Chinese farmer is careful to give back to the soil what he takes from it, so that it will not become barren. After he has planted a field with a crop which uses up the nitrogen and other plant foods in the soil, he plants that field with crops which give these foods back to the soil. He uses everything that could possibly serve as a fertilizer, including the hair

ASIA 

cut from the heads of his family. He even scrapes from the banks of the rivers and the canals the rich soil they have brought down from the mountain slopes, and by many hours of back-breaking work spreads that soil over his fields so that they may produce food for him. The tools used by the Chinese farmer are usually very crude, but labor is cheap and skilful, and the land so carefully tended produces two or three crops a year.

Cheap, skilful labor is especially important in the cultivation of tea, as a great deal of TEA patience and careful picking is needed to separate the best grades of tea leaves from the poorer. The cultivation of tea is very common in China. A family usually produces a certain amount of tea, uses what it needs, and sells the rest. India and Ceylon have passed China in their production of tea, but China produces some of the finest grades. In parts of interior China the tea is pressed into bricks, which are even used for money. 

There is very little livestock in China because the ground is too valuable to be used for EGGS pasture or forage crops. So the Chinese use little meat, butter, cheese, and similar products. They have, however, many chickens and ducks which produce great numbers of eggs, but these are chiefly for export. 

China exports many millions of eggs each year, either frozen or prepared in other ways to keep them from spoiling.

The mulberry tree is very much in evidence in China, for raw silk must be provided for the silk mills, both of China and of

From your study of the silk industry in other countries you will doubtless recall that it was first started in China, and the secret was jealously guarded there for centuries. During that time China was the only country that could supply this beautiful, shining textile, and its fame on that account alone spread over the known world. Merchants from the west sent many caravans traveling across deserts and high mountain passes to reach this ancient country and buy its beautiful silks. 

At last some silkworms were smuggled out of China, although the person who did the smuggling must have known that to be caught would mean certain death. It is generally believed that the worms were hidden in the hollow tube of a bamboo cane and thus carried across the mountains and into the western countries. However it was done, China is now yielding a little to other countries in the production of silk, although she still exports large shipments of it, both in the raw and finished state. The manufacture of artificial silk, or rayon, has also hurt the silk industry of China.

China is an ideal country for the exacting tasks of the silk industry, for the population is large and labor very cheap. In addition, the 

Chinese are a calm, patient people, and it takes patience to unwind the soft cocoon in which the silkworm winds itself.

BAMBOO 

Our western eyes would be especially interested in the groves of bamboo trees so common in China. The bamboo is used in many different ways. The shoots are cooked and served like asparagus, and very good the Chinese consider them, too.

They are also salted, or pickled, or candied and then eaten. The hollow stems are used as bottles, as cooking vessels, for fuel, for the masts of boats, and in building the lattice work of houses. They are made into writing pens, into bamboo baskets, and into chairs. To us the most familiar use of bamboo is in fishing poles. 

In traveling through China you would notice particularly the river life. The waterways, especially the Si and Yangtze, are sometimes as choked with boats as a city street is with automobiles. There 

RIVER LIFE

CHINA 

211 are boats of farmers, boats of beggars, fishing boats, and you might even see a pirate's boat.

Some of the boats are junks, which have sails, and others are sampans, which are poled along. Thousands of China's poor live on the water, and people are born, grow up, marry, and die in their river homes. Little children play with homemade life preservers tied about them in case they should fall into the water.

One reason for all this water life, as we know, is that land is so scarce and so precious that people feel they must not waste a bit even by living on it. Often a man will build his houseboat, carry soil to it and make a garden on the deck. It is a common sight to see a pig or a flock of chickens or ducks living on a boat.

Some of the boats appear to be most ramshackle affairs, and so thickly do they cluster on the water that they seem to be in constant danger of ramming one another. Besides the junks and sampans of the Chinese themselves, you will see on the larger waterways steamboats belonging to the Japanese, British, Americans, or other peoples.

Fishing is an important occupation along all the rivers, and in a country where animals are so scarce fish is a highly-prized article of food.

The difficulty of exchanging products between the different sections of China has led 

TRANSPORTATION 

the Chinese to be self-supporting. They carefully cultivate every possible bit of ground, and they waste nothing that can be used. Having few luxuries, they have learned to get along with the barest of necessities. Each community must struggle to provide for its own needs. 

Often one section will be flood-swept and starving, while another section is enjoying plenty. If transportation were good, this would not happen. The problem of transportation will probably bother China for many years to come.

The waterways are still the chief travel routes, and the extensive flood plains are crossed by a multitude of canals. But even at best river and canal travel is slow.

The roads of China are about as bad as one could imagine in a settled country. Some are nothing but paths. Others are sunk deep in the land and are rough from centuries of travel, making the going highly unpleasant for the traveler. During the heavy rains the roads become sloshy lanes of mud. Because of these exceptionally poor highways China has clung for long years to her human carriers. Pounds and pounds of tea and cotton and silk are carried on the backs of coolies to the seaports, the railroad centers, and the manufacturing cities. 

Wheelbarrows with very high wheels are common in China, not only to cart building materials and farm products, but to carry people as well. The one wheel of the wheelbarrow is much better adapted to the rough roads than are the two or four wheels of carts. 

Small carts are used, however, and baskets as well, and almost every other means by which men can take products to market. The means of transportation that interests tourists most is the sedan chair, fastened to two long poles, and borne on the shoulders of coolies. Almost every American tourist takes at least one ride in a sedan chair when he is in China.

These various slow methods of transportation seem very interesting, quaint, and even funny to us, but by making travel and the exchange of products very difficult they have decidedly hindered the progress of the country.

When foreigners first began building railroads in China the natives were much opposed. 

It was thought that the railroads angered powerful spirits, and all sorts of misfortunes were laid to them. The Chinese even bought one foreign-built railroad and destroyed it. 

Today, however, with the gradual spread of western ways and ideas, the Chinese are accepting railroads and are using them. The

Chinese coolies still resent them, for they feel that if the railroads start carrying freight there will be no need for coolies. The problem of starvation is always uppermost in the Chinese mind. But the railroads are spreading over the country. Air travel, too, is showing progress and China now has an air line between 

Shanghai and Hankow.

ASIA 

Lack of transportation is chiefly responsible for the undeveloped state of the mineral deposits of China. This country has 

MINERALS 

more coal than all Europe. It has large deposits of iron of fine quality, and petroleum as well. But very little has been done with them. Among the few mineral exports of China are copper and antimony. Antimony is used in different medicines and in hardening certain metals. 

MANUFACTURING 

Her coal and iron will be highly important if China turns to manufacturing, as she may have to do in order to take care of her increasing population. Even the rich yellow soil can produce just so much and no more, and many Chinese are beginning to realize that they cannot depend solely upon agriculture forever. The building of great factories would supply work for large numbers of Chinese, and the sale of the goods would bring sufficient wealth into the country to enable the people to buy from less crowded lands a greater quantity and variety of foods than can be raised in China. 

The Chinese manufactures today include silk and cotton textiles. Cotton is of great importance, since the poorer Chinese depend upon this material for their clothing. Ornamental pottery is made in lovely colorings and patterns by the Chinese, and has been made for many centuries. Our chinaware gets its name from this country. China makes many of the firecrackers that we use in our celebrations. In the larger cities are flour mills, iron and steel works, glass factories, and oil refineries. Two advantages for manufacturing which China has are the cheap and plentiful labor and the abundance of raw materials. 

Many of the Chinese factories are run by 

Japanese or British or British or American money, although the Chinese are beginning to resent the use of their natural resources by foreigners.

China cannot be wholly blamed for her resentment toward foreigners, for other nations have not always treated her fairly. 

RELATIONS For many centuries China refused 

FOREIGN 

to allow foreign ships to stop in her harbors. But the various nations induced her to open port after port to them and once a foothold was gained they turned the resources of the country to their own advantage. Japan, Russia, Great Britain, France, and Germany all secured special privileges and pieces of territory. Then they established ports and opened up new sources of raw material. The peninsula of Shantung, rich in coal, has been held by one nation after another. Germany took possession in 1897, Japan seized it during the World War, and China has only recently regained it. 

Japan still controls Kiaochow, Shantung's chief port.

CHINA'S PROBLEM 

The foreign powers established rich cities in the lands they held in China, to which many of the richer Chinese moved. Today the republic wants to recover these cities. But Europe and the United

States have invested great sums in them, and do not feel sure that the Chinese government can protect their interests. They see that there has been almost continual civil war since the country became a republic, because the people in one part do not understand the people in another part and so the various sections do not work together for the common good. They see that the many generals of the Chinese armies have usually been more eager to win personal power than to help build a good government; that bandits have killed foreigners and robbed almost at will in many parts of the country; and that the government has not yet been able to control these troubles. The heads of the present Chinese government have been educated in the United States and Europe to understand the principles of a republican government. So there is hope that they will finally be able to control the country. But when they now ask the great powers to give up their holdings in China, the powers tell them that China must first establish a government which they can trust.

The future of the Chinese is uncertain. It depends on their ability to set up for themselves a strong government and to educate their people to live under it and to accept its new ideas. When they have done this, they can take their place among the commercial nations of the world.

MANCHUKUO 

213 

MANCHUKUO 

Manchukuo shows promise of becoming one of the most progressive sections of Asia. In the years when, as Manchuria, it was still a part of the Chinese republic, both Russia and Japan fought to gain this rich section. At last, with the help of Japanese armies, Manchuria declared its independence and became a separate country. At the head of the government is a native-born emperor, but the country is actually controlled by Japan. 

Manchukuo has about 30,000,000 people. In the east and the north are dense forests and mountains, but the central part is a vast treeless plain. The country has rich deposits of coal, iron, and gold. Its forests produce much valuable lumber, and they are inhabited by many fur-bearing animals. These are hunted and trapped, and their furs are tanned and shipped to the great fur centers. On the plains, cattle graze. On the rich lowlands, great crops of grain are grown-wheat, corn, millet, and barley. Among these, wheat has long held the chief place. The soy bean is increasing in importance, and it is estimated that 20,000,000 acres are devoted to that crop alone. The oil of this bean is used for lubrication and lighting, and the oil cake that is left after the oil is removed is used for cattle food and for fertilizer. The soy bean, like clover, puts back into the soil a valuable plant food, called nitrogen, that other plants take out.

Many Chinese farmers, fleeing from flood, famine, and fighting, have emigrated to the agricultural lands of Manchukuo, which are growing in population and industries. Manchukuo has flour mills and many tanneries, and among its various manufactured products are oil, carpets, cotton, silk, leather, and steel.

Mukden, one of the chief cities, is a great fur center.

The natives of Manchukuo are taller and stronger than are the Chinese people farther south. The wealthy people dress in rich silks of brilliant colors, and the women wear ornaments of gold and silver in their hair.

For many years Japan has controlled parts of Manchukuo. These she still holds. The seaports of Dairen and Port Arthur and the 

Southern Manchurian railroad are owned by the Japanese.

The foreign-built railroads of Manchukuo have greatly helped the development of the country. From southern and central China, great loads of tea are shipped over the Trans-Siberian railway to Moscow and on to western countries. Along the railway in southern Manchukuo, factory towns have sprung up, and their growth will be helped by the numbers of immigrants and the plentiful supply of coal and iron.

1. China has had a famous past. She developed the mariner's compass, a means of printing by carved blocks, gunpowder, and the silk industry. The 

Chinese preferred to remain cut off from the nations to the west of them, and this attitude was strengthened by the mountain barriers which formed their boundaries. The northern boundary of China was the Great Wall, which she built to protect herself from invaders. 

2. The Chinese republic is made up of China proper and three dependencies-Mongolia, Sinkiang, and Tibet. 

3. Mongolia is a high, bleak desert country. Its few people are nomads. Sinkiang is a sandy desert plateau, peopled by wandering herdsmen. Tibet is the highest country of the world. Its people are unfriendly to foreigners. They are mostly farmers and stockraisers. 

4. China proper is about half the size of the United 

States, but has over two and one half times as many people. It has a monsoon climate, which brings heavy rains in the summer, especially in southern and central China. The climate varies in temperature from temperate to tropical and the crops vary with it. China proper includes the 

Great plain, a rich agricultural region. 

5. North China has warm summers and cold winters.

The people of this section are alert, healthy, and intelligent. The famous Hwang, or Yellow, river drains North China, and gives it fertile flood plains.

This river has caused much suffering and death by its heavy floods. The products of North China are grains and vegetables. The peninsula of Shantung is noted for peanuts. 

6. Middle China includes the basin of the Yangtze river. Here the climate is warmer and more moist,

ASIA 

and the population even more dense than in North China. This is the leading industrial and commercial center, and the cities of Shanghai, Nanking, and Hankow are large manufacturing cities. Shanghai is the port for American products. Nanking is the capital of the Chinese republic. Middle China is intensively cultivated, and the leading crops are rice, tea, and cotton. 

7. South China is hilly and warm. The West, or Si, river drains this section. Here the people are smaller and less energetic. South China produces most of the products of Middle China, and also fruits and spices and other products of a tropical region. The mulberry and bamboo trees are grown here. Canton is the chief city. Hong Kong is one of the famous ports of the world, and is under 

British control. 

8. Agriculture is necessary in China as the dense population needs vast amounts of food and it is hard to exchange produce between the different sections. 

The soil is fertilized, and even the hillsides are terraced and made into agricultural lands. Little livestock is kept because the ground is too valuable to be used for pasture or forage crops. The chief domestic animals are pigs and chickens. China exports many millions of eggs each year, besides her tea, silk, and rice. 

9. The means of transportation in China are mostly very slow and crude. China proper is covered by a network of canals across the flood plains. 

The Grand canal is about 800 miles long and for centuries has been an important route for transportation. Railroads are very recent and are few. 

The roads are bad. Goods are carried on the backs of men, or in wheelbarrows and small carts. People are carried in wheelbarrows and in sedan chairs. 

The Yangtze is navigable far inland and is a busy water route. 

10. China has much coal, iron, petroleum, and other minerals, but they have been but little developed on account of poor transportation and the generally backward state of the country. Manufacturing has been little developed but is growing. 

11. The Chinese have been unfriendly to foreigners, partly because they do not think people from other nations should come in and develop their resources. 

Foreign powers have secured possession of territory which they have developed into rich cities. 

The Chinese wish to recover these. 

12. China's problem is to develop a government strong and permanent enough to insure the safety of the country and to educate its people to live under such a government and accept its ideas. 

13. Manchukuo, formerly a Chinese dependency, is now an empire, under Japanese control. The country is rich in lumber, coal, iron, and gold. Agriculture is carried on extensively, grains and soy beans being the chief crops. There are many fur-bearing animals. Japan owns the Southern Manchurian railway and the ports of Dairen and Port Arthur.

JAPAN 

Among the most ancient empires of the world is the island Empire of Japan, off the east coast of Asia. For centuries it was the "Hermit Empire." Its people lived in natural seclusion, cut off by surrounding waters from other peoples and keeping their ports closed to all foreigners. They loved their country passionately and were so busy building up their own strange and beautiful civilization that they wished no interference from outside sources. Their rulers were garded as sacred. 

None thought of disobeying them, and their lives and property were staunchly defended. re-
