QUAINTNESS AND BEAUTY IN OLD JAPAN 

(1) (2) Copyright E. M. Newman, from Publishers' Photo Service, N. Y. (3) American Mail Line. (4) Publishers' Photo Service, N. Y. 

1. A canal scene in Tokyo, the capital of Japan. The flat lower section of Tokyo is interwoven with canals. 

At any time of day you may see hundreds of barges like these carrying merchandise to or from steamers at the port of Yokohama. The canal boats are generally pushed by men with long poles, for labor is so cheap in Japan that it does not pay to use engines or tug boats. 

2. A street in Tokyo. Little wooden shops with tiled roofs are built close to the street. Many of them have their wares displayed outside. The interiors of the shops are attractive, and the goods are tastefully displayed, for the Japanese are an artistic people. Both freight and passengers are carried in two-wheeled carts. 

3. Fujiyama, the sacred mountain of Japan. This wonderful cone-shaped mountain, always capped with snow, reaches nearly three miles towards the sky. It is a volcano which has been asleep more than 225 years. People come from all parts of Japan to see it, and Japanese artists have painted it in many pictures. 

4. Cherry blossom time. The Japanese have festivals to celebrate the beauty of the blossom season. The fragrant blossoms vary in color from faint pink to the deepest shades. When the petals fall, they fall all at once like an April shower. Many Japanese cherry trees have been set out in our city of Washington, where they add to the beauty of the city in the spring..

LIFE AND WORK IN JAPAN 

5 

(1) (3) (4) Copyright E. M. Newman, from Publishers' Photo Service, N. Y. (2) Corticelli Silk Co. (5) Publishers' Photo Service, N. Y. 

1. Tea gathering. On this Japanese hillside women are busily picking tea leaves, using both hands as they work. 

Their baskets are fastened to their sides. Tea leaves are picked many times a year. The Japanese use two-thirds of their own tea crop. The English people use even more tea than the Japanese. 

2. Moths which have developed from silkworms. Many million bushels of silk cocoons are produced annually in 

Japan. Silkworms spin them of very fine fiber. Most of the cocoons are heated to destroy the worms inside, and are used for making silk. Others are left until the worms develop into moths, which lay eggs from which more worms are hatched. In leaving the cocoon the moth ruins the silk fiber by breaking it. 

3. Visitors to the rice fields. These tourists are drawn by coolies in jinrickshas over a road which is built higher than the fields. The rice is growing in soft mud between the rows of grass. 

4. Spinning silk thread from silk fibers. The fibers from the cocoons are so delicate that many must be combined to make a single thread strong enough to weave into cloth. These Japanese are spinning on simple home machines. The threads they spin are called raw silk.

We buy much raw silk from Japan. 

5. Lantern makers. The Japanese excel in artistic work.

These men are making gay paper lanterns which are used for decoration in Japan and many other countries.

JAPAN 

SIZE AND POSITION OF THE JAPANESE EMPIRE 

west in the Pacific for a distance of over 

2000 miles, from about the 50° parallel north latitude to a little south of the Tropic of Cancer.

The Japanese islands have been likened to the figure of a great fire-breathing dragon, a creature quite famous in the ancient legends of 

China and Japan. Hokkaido forms the head of the dragon. The body is made up of Honshu, the largest island, and of Shikoku and Kyushu, to the south of it. These islands are all known as Japan proper because they belonged to the ancient empire. Taiwan, or Formosa, and the string of tiny islands which trail off from 

Kyushu make the dragon's tail. The Kuril islands, north of Hokkaido, are the smoke from the beast's nostrils.

The Japanese islands have a position off the eastern coast of Asia somewhat similar to that of the British Isles off the western coast of Europe. The area of Japan proper, however, is greater than that of Great Britain and Ireland. Chosen, formerly called Korea, a peninsula off the northeastern coast of China, and a part of the island of Sakhalin near the Sea of Okhotsk, also belong to Japan. The total area of the empire is over 260,000 square miles. 

Japan is more than half again as big as our state of California, and more than five times as big as New York state.

Japan is largely mountainous. The mountains are richly forested. Waterfalls rush down their slopes and lovely lakes lie in 

SURFACE 

the valleys below them. Two main mountain ranges, one in the north, another in the south of Honshu, meet in the middle of the island. None of the mountains is very high.

The average peaks are only about 7000 feet above sea level.

Fujiyama, on the island of Honshu, is the highest peak in Japan, and is a long-inactive volcano. It has an altitude of over 12,000 feet and is visible from far out at sea. It is an almost perfect cone and from a distance is one of the loveliest sights in the world. This mountain is celebrated in Japanese art. The people think of it as a sacred mountain, the home of the Goddess-who-makes-the-blossoms-of-the- trees-to-flower. They speak of it as "O Yama," which means Honourable Mountain.

Earthquakes in Japan are frequent. In some places near the sea they occur almost daily. 

Though many of them are so slight that they can only be detected with instruments made for the purpose, others have caused enormous destruction, and even killed thousands of people. Changes in the surface of the country have been brought about by these earthquakes, and by volcanic eruptions. 

Like the British Isles, the Japanese islands rise from a broad continental shelf. The land has been slowly sinking for thousands of years, so there are many drowned valleys, through which the sea reaches far inland. As a result, there are numerous fine bays and harbors.

CLIMATE 

There is quite a wide range of climate in Japan, due to the wide range of latitude and to the varied altitude. Taiwan, Kyushu, Shikoku, and southern Honshu are subtropical in climate. Farther north, the climate is temperate. But, as in many island countries, the climate throughout Japan is mild and even because of surrounding waters. 

Moisture from these waters makes the air damp and the foliage of Japan very green. So far as color is concerned, we might call Honshu the Emerald Isle of the East. The moisture in the air forms mists over the islands which add to their beauty a certain fairy-like, unreal quality, especially noticeable in distant views. 

Like India and Indo-China, Japan has a monsoon climate. In summer, the winds blow from the south and southeast. In passing over the Pacific ocean, they pick up much moisture, so the islands have heavy rainfall in summer, especially on their southern and eastern coasts. 

In winter, the winds come from the north and northwest, from the heart of Asia. These winds are dry and cold. Sometimes they bring light falls of snow to northern Japan. In the fall, terrific wind storms, or typhoons, sometimes strike the islands, damaging crops, destroying buildings, and often taking a toll of human life. It is Japan's misfortune that the typhoons strike most frequently in Sep-

ASIA 

tember, when the all-important rice crop is beginning to ripen.

The southern and eastern coasts of the Japanese islands are generally warmer than the northern and western coasts. The North

Equatorial current, also called the Japan current, which warms the northwestern coast of our own country, flows along the southeastern coast of Japan. It affects climate there in much the same way that the Gulf stream through the Atlantic ocean affects the climate of the 

British Isles and western Europe. Down along the western coast of Japan flows a cold current from the Arctic region. This has a cooling effect on the temperature of that section. 

PEOPLE 

A great many people live in Japan and her nearby possessions. Although the total area of the entire Japanese empire is less than one-eleventh that of the United States, the population is more than two-thirds as great. The population is centered in Japan proper, which is even more densely settled than the British Isles. It is here that most of the cities are located. The interior is less densely populated than the sections nearer the coasts. 

The Japanese belong to the yellow race.

They look somewhat like the Chinese, but are generally smaller. They are a pleasant-faced, soft-voiced people, and they are very intelligent. They are noted for their politeness, their thrift, their industry, their patriotism, and their bravery. They work from eight to twelve hours a day, but they are such quiet, efficient workers that they do not appear to be working so hard and steadily as they really are. Even the women and children work, but laws have been passed recently which prevent their being employed such long hours as the men.

Customs. In parts of Japan people still cling closely to many of the older customs, especially to those which do not interfere with progress. 

Many of these customs are very picturesque and greatly interest the traveler to Japan. On entering a religious temple, for instance, the Japanese customarily remove their shoes and leave them at the door. One wonders how the hundreds of people in one of the great temples will ever be able to find their own shoes again.

Meal time in Japan is always a period of relaxation. Around a bowl of stew squat the members of the household, each with his own smaller dish which he fills from time to time from the bowl. In place of knives and forks, the Japanese have chopsticks-wooden sticks which are used much like a pair of tweezers to carry food to the mouth. Often a meal lasts for hours, and enjoyable hours they are, too, for the Japanese know the secret of relaxing after a hard day's work. Some of the storekeepers will even serve you tea as you examine their picturesque goods. Dress.

Where native costumes are worn, there is not much difference in the dress of the old and the young. A little girl wears her hair piled neatly on top of her head as her mother does. She wears a long kimono which folds across her body in front and is held in place by a very wide sash. When she is dressed up, her costume is in the same style as when she is working or going to school, but it is usually made of much finer material and is handsomely embroidered in soft colors.

The men and boys wear loose, tunic-like coats with high necks and wide sleeves. Their trousers are tight-fitting, and are fastened in at the ankles. Servants often wear their master's initials in Japanese letters on the backs of their tunics. A group of them from the same house would remind you of an American football team with their school letters or numbers on their sweaters.

Religion. As in most oriental countries, there are several religions in Japan. Buddhism has the most followers. Next in numbers is 

Shinto, the original Japanese religion, which has many gods. Christianity has been slowly but steadily gaining in Japan, and now stands third.

Love of Beauty. The Japanese have an in stinctive love of beauty which is perhaps the result of the natural beauty of their island country. This love of beauty is expressed in much of their handiwork, especially in embroideries and in painting. Visit an art store in one of our cities. Ask to see some imported 

Japanese prints or water colors. You will see

JAPAN 

219 how delicately they are designed and colored. 

Favorite subjects are birds, flowers, trees, and the scenes from home life. 

Homes. Japanese houses are as artistic as the Japanese prints show them to be. They are usually made of heavy paper material and of light woods, such as bamboo. The walls are sliding partitions which in fine weather are thrown open, so that one going by can see into the home. There is little furniture. Rugs and mats are used to sit on and to sleep on. Tables are little more than tiny trays on very short legs.

The home is the real center of family life, for the Japanese are a great home-loving people. It is a fortunate visitor who is invited as a guest into a Japanese home, for outsiders are rarely admitted to a family circle. Once a guest is invited, however, he is treated with a fine hospitality and is made to feel very much at home.

JAPANESE GARDENS 

The visitor to Japan never fails to be delighted with its gardens and its foliage. There is scarcely a time when the air is not sweet with the fragrance of some particularly abundant flower, or the eye is not given a feast of colors. Many and beautiful varieties of flowers are planted around the little houses. They border the paths and walks and trim the window ledges.

Shrubs whose leaves change color with the seasons are planted for their foliage alone, and these are brilliant even in the winter time. The 

Japanese gardeners have learned to trim these shrubs so that some of them have the shapes of birds and animals. Imagine yourself in a garden like this in the moonlight. You would find it a fairyland indeed.

Among the best loved of the Japanese flowers are the cherry blossoms. Every year a cherry-blossom festival is held. Japanese boys and girls in their best clothes gather in the flowering orchards to play games and to dance and sing. The older people, too, take part. We send messages to each other on St.

Valentine's day. In much the same way during the festival time the Japanese write verses for each other and tie them to the branches of the cherry trees.

MODERN WAYS 

These sights and customs are typically Japanese and are not generally found in any other country. In the larger Japanese cities, however, such as

Tokyo, the visitor may see many things that will remind him of cities and countries of the West. Tokyo is the capital city of Japan, and has more than 2,000,000 people. The newer buildings there are being built of steel and concrete. Roads are broad and are paved with asphalt. Automobiles and electric trolley cars are numerous. In the restaurants and in many of the homes, chopsticks have been replaced by western tableware-knives, forks, and spoons. Little by little, the picturesque

Japanese clothes are being discarded. Many 

Japanese business men now wear suits like those of Americans or Europeans, and the soldiers and sailors of the empire are dressed in uniforms not much different from those of any modern army or navy.

But much more important than new buildings and changes in table manners and dress are certain changes which have been brought about in Japanese school systems and in the government. When the country first opened its doors to western civilization, teachers were brought in to instruct the children. Many young people were also sent to other countries to learn about new and better ways of doing things. Today most of the teachers in Japan are trained native Japanese and the school systems are very much like our own.

In much the same way changes have come about in the government. The Emperor, who was once an absolute ruler in Japan, now rules according to a constitution and is assisted by cabinet ministers and a council with whom he consults on all important matters. There is a 

Parliament much like our Congress. The power and influence of military men, once very great in the country, is decreasing.

Because of her enormous population, Japan, like Great Britain and India, is confronted with the serious problem of how to get enough food for her people. Of late years this has been much easier to do,

NEED OF FOOD- COLONIZATION MIGRATION AND 

because grain, fruits, meats, and other articles

ASIA are imported. Besides this, many Japanese have migrated to other parts of the world, especially to the Hawaiian islands and Brazil.

In these countries they work on plantations or build homes for themselves. Japan is so thickly populated that the Japanese are accustomed to work for very low wages. They do this even when they migrate to other countries. 

On this account, our own country has restricted the immigration of Japanese workmen, for they will work for such low wages that our own workmen cannot compete with them.

The addition of new lands to her empire in recent years has helped Japan take care of her over-crowded population. Thousands of Japanese have been transported to Sakhalin to develop the natural resources there. Over 300,000 

Japanese colonists live in Chosen. The conditions in the colonies are not yet very favorable, but they are steadily improving and the people there can live almost as they do at home, carrying on fishing, agriculture, and the arts. They are helping to increase Japan's wealth by working the mines, forests, and farm lands in these possessions. In Chosen, stock raising is extensively carried on. Millions of dollars of Japanese capital are invested in Kwangtung, a part of Manchukuo, leased by Japan for a period of ninety-nine years. About 

200,000 Japanese live here. Many other Japanese settlements are scattered throughout

Manchukuo and in parts of China. The Japanese government encourages settlement on the mainland of Asia and has sometimes even used the powerful Japanese army and navy to gain new lands there.

In the Japanese empire less than one-sixth of the land can be farmed, since so much of it is mountainous. But the suit 

AGRICULTURE 

able land is all intensively cultivated. The slopes are terraced as they are in 

Italy and in parts of South America, and these terraces make more room for planting. The land is divided into very small farms, usually not more than one acre in size.

Rice is the chief food and the chief crop. It is grown in all of the islands and in Chosen, largely along the coasts. Wheat, millet, barley, and other grains are also raised. The growing of mulberry trees ranks next to rice cultivation in importance. They are grown extensively in 

Japan proper. These trees also flourish in 

Chosen. As elsewhere, the leaves of the mulberry tree are used for feeding silkworms, and the Japanese export quantities of raw silk and also manufacture much of it at home. Taiwan raises acres and acres of tea. It is of excellent grade and flavor and is sold to many countries. 

Coal and copper are abundant minerals in Japan. There are coal deposits containing many millions of tons. Petroleum is another valuable resource. Not enough iron is found in Japan to supply the country's needs; so iron ore is imported. Foundries have been established, and steel and iron products are turned out in large quantities. In Chosen there are gold, silver, and copper mines. In the past, American companies have held mining rights in Chosen, but a recent law prevents foreigners from holding such rights in the future.

NATURAL RESOURCES 

The forests of Japan furnish lac, a sticky, reddish substance deposited on the branches and twigs of trees by little insects which carry it in their bodies. From it is made a varnish called lacquer. Lacquer gives a glossy finish which is very pleasing, and it is extensively used on paper, steel, and wooden articles. 

Bamboo trees are plentiful in Japan, and this wood is a most important one in that country. It is light and hollow and is used in making pipes, fish poles, and frames for houses. 

Its supply is easily kept up because bamboo trees grow rapidly.

Taiwan supplies most of the world's camphor, another valuable tree product. Camphor is the gum of the camphor tree.

The com- mercial camphor consists of white crystals, and is used in medicines and in making celluloid.

FISHING 

Since there is no land in Japan proper which can be given over to the raising of animals, the people eat little meat except such as is imported. They eat fish instead, which are caught in great quantities in the shallow waters offshore. These fishing grounds are like the splendid ones about the British 

Isles, Newfoundland, and the fiord coast of

Norway. The continental shelf provides ex-

JAPAN cellent spawning grounds.

Like the people of other countries where fishing is an important occupation, the Japanese are also a seafaring

SEAFARING-THE AND NAVY MERCHANT MARINE people. Although their country's policy of having nothing to do with foreigners prevented the development of commerce before 1854, the Japanese have, since that time, become a leading trading nation. 

During the World War a great shipbuilding boom started in Japan. Besides increasing the number of her fishing boats, it built up her merchant marine so that today this includes over 2000 vessels. Japanese steamship lines reach all parts of the world. Japan has also developed a powerful navy, surpassed only by those of Great Britain and the United States. 

Seafaring offers another outlet for Japan's crowded population, much as it does for that of Norway, whose rugged coasts discourage agriculture.

While shipbuilding was developing in Japan, her manufactures, too, were increasing and 

MANUFACTURES 

improving. The Japanese have long been skilled in the making of fine porcelain and chinaware, and in the weaving of silks and tapestries. Paper articles, such as fans and lanterns which we use for decorations, and matches, toys, and fancy buttons are exported. Originally these articles were all made by hand. Now many of them are made in factories by machinery.

Japan imports quantities of raw cotton, and her textile mills are becoming more and more numerous. Each year she exports millions of yards of cotton textiles and thousands of bales of cotton yarn. The number of industrial establishments in Japan, including cotton mills, silk mills, machine, toy, and paper factories, has more than tripled in the last thirty years.

There are now about fifty thousand factories, employing nearly two million people. Although 

Japan cannot yet compare with the United

States or Great Britain in the number or value of manufactured goods, she is the leading manufacturing country of Asia.

The building of ships and the increase in the output of manufactured articles naturally increased the commerce of

Japan. In 1854 only two COMMERCE, TRANSPORTATION, 

Japanese ports were open AND CITIES to American vessels. Fortyone ports are now open to foreign trade with all nations. Kobe is the most important port.

Its neighbor, Osaka, the largest city of the country, has a fine harbor. Yokohama is the port of Tokyo, the capital, and handles most of the trade with the United States. Nagasaki is the main port of Kyushu island. Niigata, on the west coast of Honshu island, carries on trade with the Russian port of Vladivostok.

Tamsui is the chief port of Taiwan, and Fusan is the most important seaport of Chosen.

Osaka and Tokyo have each more than two million people. Other important cities are 

Nagoya, Kyoto, Hiroshima, and Kanazawa on the island of Honshu, and Keijo in Chosen. 

Japan is excellently located for trade with densely populated India and China and with the United States. By way of the Suez canal her ships reach the ports of the crowded European countries. Even Australia may be easily reached. Of all these countries the 

United States is Japan's best customer. We take from forty to forty-five per cent of her exports. We supply her with from twenty-five to thirty per cent of her imports.

Transportation in Japan is made possible by a network of railroad lines, covering the islands of Hokkaido, Honshu, and Kyushu, and the peninsula of Chosen. There is also a railroad running the length of Taiwan. In addition, Japan has a modern airline, running from 

Tokyo across southern Honshu, Shikoku,

Kyushu, and up along the Chosen peninsula to 

Port Arthur, in southern Manchukuo. Thus, by railroad and air line, the chief cities of

Japan, those on the coasts and those inland, are connected with each other and travel within the country is made rapid and easy. OWC-17

ASIA 

1. Japan was for many years shut off from other peoples and kept her ports closed to foreigners. 

In 1854 a treaty was signed which provided for trade between our country and Japan. Contact with western peoples has since combined with her location, climate, natural resources, and the qualities of her people to make Japan the foremost nation of the Far East. 

2. The Japanese islands lie off the eastern coast of 

Asia, mostly between the Tropic of Cancer and the 50° parallel north latitude. The empire also owns the peninsula of Chosen. The total size of Japan is greater than that of Great Britain and Ireland. 

Its population is over two-thirds that of the 

United States. 

3. Japan is largely mountainous, though none of the ranges are very high. Fujiyama, the sacred mountain of Japan, is over 12,000 feet above sea level. 

Frequent earthquakes and volcanic eruptions occur in Japan. These disturbances have had their effect on the land surface. Because of the gradual sinking of the continental shelf, there are many indentations and fine harbors. 

4. Japan has a wide variety of climate because of her varied altitude and latitude, but surrounding waters help keep it mild and even. Rainfall is generally plentiful. Along the southeastern coast the climate is tempered by the warm Japan current. 

A cold current from the Arctic cools the western coast. 

5. The Japanese people belong to the yellow race. 

They are polite, intelligent, thrifty, industrious, brave, and patriotic. They have a great love for beauty and are very progressive. 

6. One of Japan's problems is to secure food for her large population. Food products are imported. 

Sakhalin, Taiwan, Chosen, and Kwangtung afford room for colonization. The chief agricultural products are rice, wheat and other grains, and tea. 

Other products are silk, coal, copper, bamboo, lacquer, and camphor. Japan is rich in fisheries. 

7. The Japanese are a seafaring people. Japan has a merchant marine numbering over 2000 vessels, and an excellent navy. 

8. Industrial establishments have tripled in Japan within the last thirty years. The principal manufactures are cotton and silk, iron and steel goods, china, and small wares. 

9. The building of ships and the increase in manufactures in Japan have greatly increased her commerce. Many ports are now open to foreign trade of all kinds. The country is well located for trade with India, China, and the United States. 

10. Transportation is made easy by railways and air lines. Among the chief ports are Yokohama, Kobe, Osaka, and Niigata. Osaka, with over two million inhabitants, is the largest city in Japan. Tokyo is the capital and second largest city of Japan. It contains over two million people.

SCENES IN AUSTRALIA 

5 

(1) (3) (5) Publishers' Photo Service, N. Y. (2) Australian National Travel Ass'n. (4) Official Secretary of Australia in U. S. A. 

1. Giant eucalyptus trees in a Queensland forest. The most valuable tree of Australia is the eucalyptus. There are many varieties of this tree, some rivaling the sequoias of California in height. Eucalyptus timber is very strong and durable. From the leaves of the tree a valuable medicine oil is obtained. 

2. A kangaroo mother and her baby. This is perhaps the best known of Australia's strange creatures. There are many varieties of kangaroo, some as small as rabbits and others as tall as men. They travel rapidly, leaping along on their powerful hind legs. The young kangaroo is carried in a pouch on the mother's body. 

3. Fern trees in an Australian jungle. In the warm rain forests near the east coast there are great areas of dense forest growth. Ferns like those you see in the picture grow to the height of moderate-sized trees. 

4. Growing cotton in a river valley in Queensland. This looks like a view in our own Southland. Australia is slowly developing her cotton-growing industry in warm northern river valleys where the soil is fertile and the growing season is long. 

5. An open-cut tin mine on the island of Tasmania, Australia. Many metals are mined in Australia. One of the main centers for tin mining is on the island of Tasmania. Here hand labor is used in loading the ore cars and in moving them about.

IN THE AGRICULTURAL REGIONS OF AUSTRALIA 

15 (1) (2) (3) (4) Publishers' Photo Service, N. Y. 

1. Two pure bred Merino rams. Most of the sheep raised in the dry grasslands of Australia are of this breed, which is grown for its wool rather than for its meat. The 

Merino sheep are not large, but their skin hangs in loose folds. This increases the amount of space on which wool can grow. Merino wool is of a very fine quality and brings a high price in the market. 

2. The "show" floor of an Australian wool warehouse.

The bales of wool from the sheep ranches are brought to the warehouse. On this floor they are opened for the inspection of buyers from many countries, who come to Australia to buy wool for cloth factories. Australia produces far more wool than any other nation. 

3. Loading wheat at a country station in the wheat region. The wheat is not stored in elevators and shipped in bulk as it is in our land. It is packed in sacks, and because the harvest season is so dry in Australia these sacks of grain can be piled outdoors without danger of getting wet. Horses, instead of motor trucks, are used to haul the wheat to the railroad. 

4. An Australian dairy farm. On its grasslands, Australia raises beef cattle. In the temperate southern and eastern parts of the continent, however, there are many herds of dairy cattle like this one. They supply the cities with fresh dairy products and provide a great deal of butter and cheese for export.

CONTINENT  

Australia is, to most people, an almost unknown continent. Because it lies between the 

Pacific and Indian oceans, far

THE LONELY from other continents, one can not reach it quickly and easily. 

Africa is 4500 miles away, North America is 6000, and Europe is half way around the world. 

Even Asia, the nearest continent, is 1800 miles distant. It is small wonder, then, that Australia is seldom visited by the average traveler. 

IMPORTANCE 

Australia holds, however, an important place in the world's affairs. It is a land of raw materials. Australia's millions of sheep and cattle supply all parts of the world with meat and wool. Textile mills of our country and Europe depend on Australia for the special grade of wool from which they make their finest cloth. The grain lands of Australia supply crowded Great Britain, the mother country, with wheat and other grains. Australia competes with Denmark, the Netherlands, France, and Switzerland in the manufacture of fine cheeses. Great ships leave Australian ports every day laden with wool, hides, grains, fruits, dairy products, and frozen mutton, lamb, and beef. Some of the world's supply of gold and other metals also comes from Australia. In this industrial age, such a land of raw materials is bound to be important.

SIZE 

Because Australia is an island, far from any other large body of land, it appears on a map of the world to be much smaller in relation to the other continents than it really is. Europe, so close to Asia and Africa, looks much larger than Australia, but as a matter of fact Australia is nearly three-quarters the size of Europe, and has an area about as great as that of the United States. From east to west the continent extends 2400 miles; the distance from north to south is 1970 miles. The railroad from Sydney on the east coast to Perth on the west coast is 3000 miles long, nearly as long as a road from New York to San Francisco. The north-south extent of Australia is so great that bananas, sugar cane, and other tropical products are grown on the hot northern coast, while in the cooler southern section grapes, apples, and pears are the principal fruit crops.

SHAPE 

In shape, Australia has been compared to a clamshell. Take one of the half-shells of a clam. Put it down, hollow side up, with its hinge edge for the south. 

Chip a few pieces out of the upper edge so that it will look like the northern coast of Australia, and you have a fairly good model of the continent. 

You will notice that the southern coast curves gently inward. The broad bay formed by this curve in the coast line is called the 

Great Australian bight. Just east of the bight, narrow Spencer gulf cuts into the land. Like the sides of the clamshell, the eastern and western coasts are fairly regular. The eastern coast is paralleled, for the entire northern half of its length, by the longest coral reef in the world—the Great Barrier reef. The northern coast is very irregular, being indented by many small bays and gulfs and by the great Gulf of Carpentaria. On either side of this gulf, long capes extend out into the ocean-Cape Arnhem on the west and Cape York on the east.

SURFACE 

In surface, too, Australia resembles our clamshell, for it is high near the edges and somewhat lower in the interior. The highest mountains extend in a long north-south range not far from the eastern coast. Near the western and northern coasts are lower mountain ranges. In the very center of the continent is another small group of worn-down mountains. Although in places the mountains extend down to the sea, the highlands of the eastern, western, and northern coasts are generally paralleled by long stretches of narrow coastal plain. The interior of the continent has low, level grassland plains in the east while the western part consists of a 225

flat, desert-covered plateau. 

Unlike other continents, Australia does not have an important system of rivers and lakes. 

There is only one important river system in 

Australia, the Murray-Darling, which is formed by the Murray and the Darling rivers.

They rise in the southern part of the great eastern mountain range, unite, and flow as a single stream west and then south to the ocean.

Both branches are navigable for several hundred miles. There are several other rivers flowing from the inland region to the coasts, but they are all short. Australia has few lakes. 

There are some in the southern part of the continent but most of them are shallow and salty, almost disappearing during periods of drought.

CLIMATE 

Australia extends from about 11° to about 39° south latitude, and therefore lies partly in the Torrid zone and partly in the 

South Temperate zone. Since the continent is south of the Equator, conditions of climate are just opposite to those we know. 

In Australia one goes north, towards the Equator, to find warmer weather, and south to find cooler weather. The coolest weather comes in June, July, and August, though no part of Australia is ever very cold. The hottest months are January and February. The continent as a whole is very warm, with the temperature in the interior sometimes going as high as 130°.

Australia lies mainly in the path of the southeast trade winds. These bring much moisture from the Pacific ocean, but as they rise to cross the eastern mountain range, they lose their moisture. Consequently, the eastern coastal plain and the eastern slopes of the mountains receive much rain, while the lands farther to the west have a drier climate. During the hot season, the extreme northern part of the continent is in the belt of equatorial calms. Northern Australia is also swept by monsoons from the northwest. The monsoons are caused by winds sweeping from the sea to replace the heated air rising over the land.

The rainy belt and the monsoons combine to give the northern coast very heavy rains during the hot months from November to April. During the cooler season, which lasts from 

May until October, the prevailing westerlies bring rain to the southwestern corner of the continent, and also to the strip of coast about the mouth of the Murray-Darling river. The central part of Australia receives little rain at any season.

ANIMALS 

Australia has the strangest animals in the world. Europe, Africa, and Asia are all connected, and North and South America are joined by the Isthmus of 

Panama. In past ages, Asia and North America were connected by a neck of land. So it was possible for animals to go from one continent to another and many species, or kinds, found in widely separated regions are closely related to one another. Australia, however, lies far from other continents. Animals could not go to and from Australia, and totally different species are found here than in other lands. 

The kangaroo is perhaps the best known of the Australian animals. There are many different kinds, some as small as rabbits and some as large as men. All of them have long, thick tails, long hind legs, and short, weak forelegs. 

They travel very fast on their hind legs, with giant hops, and when sitting still they balance themselves on their hind legs and their tails. 

The mother kangaroo has a pouch on her stomach in which she carries her babies until they are old enough to take care of themselves. 

One of the world's queerest creatures is the platypus, a furry animal the size of a large woodchuck or house cat. The platypus has webbed feet, a bill like a duck, and a poison spur on its heel. Unlike most animals, the platypus brings forth its young from eggs. 

The echidna, or spiny ant-eater, is another

Australian animal that lays eggs. 

Australia has fish that can live out of water for long periods because they have both gills and lungs. There are flying squirrels that can glide through the air long distances from tree to tree. Along the coast are penguins, and pelicans and sea cows. These sea cows, or dugongs, have fat tails, thick flippers, round bodies, and rounded snouts. They live in the water and grow to be fifteen feet in length.

The mother carries her young hugged to her breast. It is said that in ancient times sailors, seeing dugongs in the distance, have reported sighting mermaids.

The parrots of Australia are beautiful with their many flashing colors. The lyre bird has a tail shaped like the musical instrument called a lyre. The cassowary is a bird five feet tall, with long, heavy legs and a scrawny neck. It has almost no wings and carries a tall horny crest on its head. The emu is another large bird, much like an ostrich, with tiny wings and powerful legs and feet. The kookooburra, or laughing jackass, is a bird of the kingfisher family with a loud, high-pitched scream.

Some of the animals found in Australia were taken there by men. The dingo, or wild dog, was carried to the island continent ages ago by natives. Though it is sometimes tamed and used for hunting, it is more commonly found as a wild animal. Dingoes kill many sheep, so the ranchers do all they can to rid the country of them.

The rabbit, another imported animal, has proved a more serious pest to the ranchers and farmers than the dingo. Many years ago an 

Englishman brought a few rabbits to Australia as pets. Here they found plenty to eat and few natural enemies. The rabbits multiplied, and it was not long before there were millions. They ate the grass intended for cattle and sheep, and also harmed gardens. The 

Australians were forced to build long wire fences to keep the rabbits out of the fields. 

Frequent rabbit drives are now held during which the rabbits are driven into great fenced enclosures where they can be killed easily and quickly. In recent years rabbit meat has become a valuable export. The fur is made into felt.

In an attempt to raise rice in the low, hot, marshy lands around the Gulf of Carpentaria, another Englishman imported a number of water buffaloes from Asia. When the rice fields were abandoned, the water buffaloes were turned loose, and they soon greatly increased in number. Hunters, however, have killed many of them.

Camels have been introduced into the hot desert of the interior, and have proved very useful as beasts of burden. Though they are well adapted to their new home, their numbers have not greatly increased.

PLANTS 

The plant life of Australia is no less queer than the animal life. Here you may see ferns that are as tall as trees, and trees that would seem very strange to you.

The bottle tree has a very tall light-colored trunk with foliage growing in a clump at its top. The eucalyptus tree, which grows to immense heights, sheds its bark instead of its leaves. The grass tree has a trunk about ten feet high at the top of which grow long, thin grasslike leaves.

When you walk through an Australian forest, you will notice that many trees have grey or blue leaves instead of green. You will also be surprised to see that in spite of the many trees there is sunlight in the forest. Look closely at the leaves and you will see that they turn their edges toward the sun so that the sun does not strike their flat surface but shines past them onto the ground. Leaves that grow in this way keep their moisture better than those whose surfaces are exposed to the sun. 

In recent years Australia has suffered from a plant pest that has been almost as serious as the worst of its animal pests. This plant is the prickly pear, a kind of cactus. It was brought to the grasslands to serve as a food for grazing animals, but it did not prove to be a success as fodder. In the absence of its natural enemies the prickly pear soon spread throughout the eastern part of the continent, using up the plant foods of the soil and choking out all other vegetation, even trees. The scientists came to the rescue. They imported large numbers of a moth called the cactoblastis, from whose eggs come caterpillars which eat the prickly pear plant. This plant is now well under control. When the last of the plants is dead and their natural food is gone, it is believed that the cactoblastis, too, will die. 

The first explorers to reach Australia found it inhabited by a race of black savages, whom they called "blackfellows."

These natives are very dull and backward. Scientists who have studied the 

THE NATIVES

races of man tell us that they belong to the most primitive race known. They build no houses, and many of them wear no clothes.

Their weapons consist of the spear and the boomerang. The spear is thrown great distances by means of a throwing stick with 'a notch in one end. The blunt end of the spear is placed in the notch, and the stick held by the other end gives the effect of a longer arm in throwing. The boomerang is a heavy curved stick which, when properly thrown, will kill even large animals instantly. A boomerang which misses its mark will usually follow a curved course and return to a point behind the thrower.

The Australian natives resisted the first white people who came to settle on their shores, but could not stop them. Little by little, the natives were forced to give up their best lands. 

The natives seldom cultivated the soil but lived almost

WHITE 

SETTLEMENT 

The first white settlement in Australia was made by the English in 1788. In that year an 

English prison colony was established near the site of the present city of Sydney. Soon other prison colonies appeared, for England was finding Australia a convenient place to ship her undesirable citizens. For many years the great majority of Australian settlers were prisoners.

As the system of deporting criminals died out, a new class of English people packed up and started for Australia. They were attracted by the tales of the great lands that could be theirs for the asking. Then gold was found and many others came attracted by the gold that could be theirs for the digging. These immigrants were sturdy people who felt that their mother country was much too crowded to enable them to make their fortunes at home. 

Some found gold and became fabulously rich. 

Most of the gold hunters, however, failed in their search.

More people made fortunes on ranches than in gold mines. As the fame of Australian wool spread, the importance of sheep raising increased. New settlers came. The continent and the island of Tasmania were divided into states and territories, and became known as the Commonwealth of Australia. commonwealth This is part of the British empire, but the 

Australians actually govern themselves. 

To encourage newcomers the 

Australian government helps them in all possible ways and the British government offers to send British families to Australia without charge. They are even provided with land on which to settle. Great Britain realizes how valuable Australia is to her as a source of raw materials and foodstuffs, and she is anxious to have more of the continent put to OVER 125 use.

WHITE MAN'S CONTINENT 

The total population of Australia is less than that of the city of London and is only about one-eighth of that of the tiny mother country. On the eastern and southeastern coasts the population is most dense, but it becomes sparse towards the interior, for frontier life is hard and dangerous. One reason that the population has not increased so rapidly in Australia as it has in other new countries is that Australia welcomes only members of the white race. The people feel that if they admit other races, large numbers of laborers will flock to their land, which will bring wages

down and put white men out of work. They feel that they are protecting the white laboring man in preventing the entrance of other peoples, and it is their intention to keep Australia a white man's continent, even if it does take much longer to build it up. 

Politically, Australia is divided into six states and three territories. Five of the states

Capricorn it becomes milder. The southern section of the coastal plain has a temperate climate. 

The hot, moist lands of the east coast of Queensland are a plantation country, growing tropical fruits, sugar cane, tobacco, and some cotton. Pineapples, olives, oranges, and bananas are grown here to supply the cities to the south. Queensland produces enough sugar for the needs of Australia and some to spare, and

still has miles and miles of land that has never been cleared and put to use. A shortage of labor is one reason for these uncleared lands. 

In the temperate southern part of the eastern coastal plain are many towns and cities. 

This is a region of mixed agriculture. The farms are small and crowded closely together, but they are very well cultivated. Wheat, corn, and other grains are produced in large quantities. Vegetables are grown for the nearby cities. Fruits from the orchards help to swell the exports of Australia. Dairy farms, with their fat, sleek cows, supply the population with fresh dairy products, and have enough left over to make fine cheeses and butter for export.

Among the east coast cities is Sydney, the largest and most important city on the continent. Sydney is the seaport that handles most of the products from the grazing and agricultural lands. It is one of the most modern and progressive cities south of the Equator, with a population that is almost wholly white. More than a million people live in Sydney, and the city is almost as large as Detroit. Travelers tell us that in beauty the harbor of Sydney is rivaled only by that of Rio de Janeiro. It is a busy port, with ships from all nations constantly coming and going. An enormous commerce is carried on here each year, as Sydney has much of the import trade of Australia, which, as you might guess, is largely in textiles, petroleum, farm machinery, and automobiles.

With its busy harbor, its skyscrapers, its pleasant homes, its parks, and its well-paved streets, Sydney reminds the American traveler of bustling cities at home. There are some factories here and in other Australian cities. The work of most of these factories consists of getting wool, meat, fruits, and dairy products ready for export. Most of Australia's factories are in New South Wales and Victoria. 

Western and Northern Coastal Plains. The western coastal plain lies between the western mountains and the Indian ocean. In the north, near the Tropic of Capricorn, it is hot and dry. 

Some sheep are raised here. Farther south the climate is mild and rainfall is abundant. Here wheat and temperate fruits are raised, and mixed farming is carried on. In the extreme south, lumbering is an important industry. 

Perth, with a population about equal to that of Omaha, is the principal city. 

The heavy rainfall of the northern coastal plain gives it damp tropical forests. There are few inhabitants and no important industries. 

Australia has several mountain ranges. Of these, the eastern range is by far the most important. It is known as the Great

HIGHLANDS 

Dividing Range, for it divides the river systems which flow east into the Pacific from those which flow in a westerly direction.

The Great Dividing Range cannot be compared in height and extent with the greatest ranges of the world, but it is nevertheless a recognized mountain system. Mt. Kosciusko is over 7300 feet high. In the north the mountains are covered with trees, but towards the south they are bare and extend upward in rocky peaks. 

The chief city of the eastern mountain region is Canberra, the capital of the commonwealth, laid out in imitation of our capital city, Washington. The government buildings are very beautiful, and the streets of the city radiate out from them like the spokes of a wheel.

Canberra is a new city, and it is being made larger and more attractive every year. 

A westward extension of the Great Dividing 

Range is known as the Victoria highlands. Between this wooded mountain section and the coastal hills to the south lies a fertile valley. 

Here wheat, temperate fruits, and sheep are raised. 

The chief city of Victoria, and the second in size in Australia, is Melbourne, a seaport lying in the Victoria valley on a deep bay. In 1837 Melbourne was a little forsakenlooking town with a few houses, a few turf huts, and a very few people. Now, only about a hundred years later, it is a beautiful and a busy metropolis, with parks, fine buildings, public baths, picture galleries, and museums. 

Melbourne is larger than Cleveland. For many years it served as the capital of Australia. 

The other mountain ranges of Australia are low and not very important. A short highland extends inland from Spencer gulf. The Darling

range runs north and south parallel to the southern end of the western coast. There are still other mountains in the west and north. 

The Macdonnell range rises from the center of the continent. These mountain systems are all old and worn down.

Products. The highlands of Australia yield many valuable products. The Great Dividing 

Range has heavy forests of valuable wood. 

This wood is of such strength and texture that it is used for paving blocks and will last for years under the heaviest traffic. As in our country, the mountains are stores of minerals. 

The Victoria highlands, the western ranges, and the Great Dividing Range produce copper, gold, silver, tin, coal, and lead. The coal deposits of New South Wales and Queensland run into billions of tons. The silver mines of 

New South Wales are among the richest in the world. Queensland, Victoria, and Western

Australia are the leading gold sections. Gold is still a valuable mineral product, but production has fallen to a small fraction of its former amount. Coal has been found in every state in 

Australia, and silver also. Tin and iron are mined in several places. Not only the mountains, but the grasslands and the desert have large deposits of minerals. Many of the deposits have never been thoroughly worked, because of a lack of people and of means of transportation.

West of the Great Dividing Range lie the great plains of Australia. This is a region of 

THE GRASS- LANDS 

little rainfall, for the mountains to the east rob the trade winds of much of their moisture. The natural vegetation consists of tall grass, scrubby trees, and bushes. For this reason, the Australians speak of their grassland plains as "the bush." 

Agriculture. The grasslands are chiefly used for agriculture and for stock raising. The soil is very rich, and there is sufficient rainfall in the southeastern section for the growing of wheat and other grains. Here we see mile after mile of waving wheat. We also see modern agricultural machines-reapers, binders, and harvesters-most of them made in the United States. We miss, however, the great barns and grain clevators of the North American wheat belt. They are not needed in Australia, for the harvesting season is so dry that the wheat may be put in sacks and piled up out of doors to await shipment without danger of being spoiled by the rain. 

Despite the limited rainfall the southeastern part of the grasslands is being used for agriculture. This is possible through the use of dry farming and irrigation. Dry farming is a method of cultivating the soil so that a covering of loose dirt is left on the surface. This lessens evaporation, and helps the soil to hold moisture for a long time. Thanks to dry farming, many sections of the southern grasslands that were once considered useful only as grazing lands are now producing fine crops of wheat.

Irrigation in Australia is carried on by two methods. Rivers are dammed, and the storedup water is let into the fields through irrigation ditches. There is a great irrigation dam in the Murray river which supplies enough water to the surrounding lands for the growing of immense crops of wheat. A few other 

Australian rivers, too, have been dammed, but most of the streams are so small, and dry up to such an extent in dry weather, that they are practically useless for irrigation.

Australia's other method of irrigating is practiced in few other places in the world. It has been found that much of the water which falls on the eastern slopes of the Great Dividing Range flows westward under the mountains, between layers of rock. When a well is drilled through the top layer of rock, this water rises to the surface. Such wells are called artesian wells. There are many of them in the 

Australian grasslands north of the Murray Darling basin, and they are used for irrigating large areas of the plains. The irrigated lands make fine pastures for sheep and cattle, but are not used extensively for agriculture because they are so far from markets. In the future, when Australia's railroads are extended throughout this region, it may become an important wheat-producing center.

Getting the wool to market has been a serious problem to the rancher, although it is becoming less difficult as the population grows and transportation systems are extended. The railroads, however, do not reach most of the sheep ranches of the interior, and often it is a matter of weeks to haul the wool "clip" to the railroads. The wool is carried in great wagons drawn by many yokes of oxen or many teams of horses. Near the settled coasts sheep are widely raised for their mutton.

In addition to the sheep, many herds of beef cattle are also raised on the great plains. Although the sheep industry overshadows the raising of beef cattle in Australia, the herds of cattle are very large indeed and the total beef trade is enormous. When it is time for the cattle to be sold they are driven to market, often a journey of many miles and many days on the road. Large herds may be seen in the bush, patiently making their way over the winding roads, cropping food along the way, or stopping at a water hole to drink. Most of the wool and the meat from the grasslands is sent to Sydney for shipment. The beef and the lamb and mutton are frozen solid in preparation for the 14,000 mile trip to England, a part of which is through the Torrid zone. The ships that carry these products have refrigerating systems and rooms whose temperature may be regulated so that the food will not spoil. The meat may be kept in a freezing atmosphere, but the temperature of the dairy product rooms must be very carefully regulated, for these products will spoil if they are frozen. They must be kept just soneither too hot nor too cold.

In the southern part of the grasslands, which includes the basin of the Murray-Darling river, there are prosperous farming communities.

Here the climate and agriculture are much like those of the United States between Kansas and the Gulf of Mexico. Rainfall and irrigation supply sufficient moisture to raise rich pasturage for dairy cattle, which must have better food and more water than beef cattle, so this is a region of large dairy farms. 

Fruit Products. The southern grasslands are also a region of fine orchards which produce cherries, peaches, apples, and other fruits.

There are many vineyards of luscious grapes as well. These fruits, of course, all ripen in our winter months and they find their way to northern markets in the cold months of January and February. Some are shipped fresh, others canned, and fruits like grapes and apricots are dried. There is much wine made in this section.

Life in the Grasslands. Life in the bush is lonely, for often the ranches are many miles apart. Yet the people are neighborly, and think little of riding ten or fifteen miles on horseback to pay a call and chat a little while. 

From time to time a traveling school-teacher arrives, sets up his tent, and teaches the children from the nearest ranches for a week or two. Many of the children receive part of their education in this way and part through correspondence schools. Where there are railroads, the government furnishes the children with free passes to the nearest school. As you can see, it is difficult for the children who live on the great Australian grasslands to become educated. Yet Australia has a smaller per cent of people who cannot read and write, in proportion to population, than our own country has. 

The people of the grasslands have one great fear-drought. Although the yearly rainfall is slight, it ordinarily brings enough moisture to keep alive the forage upon which the sheep

and cattle depend. Some years the rain fails. 

For days and weeks and months not a drop falls. The grass withers and dies. The rivers shrink, and some disappear entirely. The lakes dry up. Sheep and cattle drop in their tracks and the ranchers can do nothing. The output of wool and meat is cut down. Profits grow leaner and leaner, and many stock raisers are ruined. In one period of drought, extending over five years, more than sixty million sheep perished. One can scarcely wonder that the people of the bush fear droughts. 

In the west-central part of Australia stretches a plateau varying from 1000 to 2000 feet in altitude. In the extreme north, where the monsoons and the PLATEAU belt of equatorial calms bring rain, THE WESTERN this plateau is covered by grasslands where cattle and sheep are pastured. In the southwest, where the prevailing westerlies bring a little rain over the low range of the coast mountains, are more grasslands with more cattle and sheep. All the rest of the plateau is a dry, hot desert.

The Australian desert is one of the least inviting places in the world. There are no streams. Its few "lakes" are shallow sheets of salt water, unfit to use. The rocks and the sand are hot to the touch. One's very finger nails get dry and brittle. The safest way to travel here is by caravan. Europeans have brought camels to this country, and they have proved very useful in the desert region. 

About the middle of the last century, gold was discovered in the Australian desert. When the news spread to the settlements of the east, men set out for the gold fields, many ill-prepared to face the hardships of the journey and of life on the desert. Some of them had never even seen a desert. They piled their belongings onto any kind of a conveyance and started out in search of gold, expecting to return home rich in a few months. Imagine entering a desert pushing a wheelbarrow, as some of these men did! They did not know the location of water holes, and many arrived at the gold fields with tongues and lips swollen from lack of water. In their search for gold men lost their health, their reason, and even their lives. 

But still others came. Desert towns sprang up overnight, ugly little towns set down in a burning waste. The city of Kalgoorlie was the most important of these settlements, and millions of dollars worth of the precious yellow metal has flowed through this town. Perth is the exporting center for the gold. 

How is it possible for people to live in the desert city of Kalgoorlie, so far from any source of water? From a huge reservoir near 

Perth, about three hundred miles away, water comes by pipe. The water is sold, and is so valued that some people think it is a scandalous waste to use it for bathing. Camels carry water to some of the mining camps. 

When the transcontinental railroad was being built across the Nullarbor plains, the problem of supplying water to the workmen was a very great one. These plains cover a low, flat limestone plateau between the western plateau and the Great Australian bight. They stretch for many hot and stifling miles without a water hole, and the railroad was built with great suffering and at huge expense. It connects the cities on the east coast with the cities on the west coast of Australia. 

South of Australia lies the island of Tasmania, one of the states of the Australian commonwealth. Tasmania is known 

TASMANIA 

as the Switzerland of the southern

Pacific. It is about as large as Massachusetts, New Hampshire, and Vermont together, and lies in about the same latitude south of the Equator as these states do north. Tasmania is a healthful, beautiful, rugged little island, with the fresh, wild loveliness of a mountainous country. It is a land of plentiful rainfall and a mild climate. Its mountains, waterfalls, forests of fern trees, and beautiful harbors call forth exclamations of wonder. The weather is delightful and many visitors from the dry lands of Australia come here in search of both health and recreation. 

Tasmania is also known as the Apple Island because of its famous apples. It does a large business in canning fruits and making jams. It is a sheep-raising state, and grows fine purebred sheep. It has valuable deposits of tin. Its exports include the products of its orchards,

its grazing lands, and its mines. The busy little city of Hobart is the capital of Tasmania. 

In its museum are many interesting relics of the early races of the world, and well-known scientists take the long journey to Hobart to see them.

On the map, the two islands of New Zealand seem to be quite near Australia, but they are 

NEW ZEALAND 

really 1200 miles to the southeast. New Zealand is an outpost of the white man in southern waters, but a very progressive and independent outpost. 

It is part of the British empire, with its own dominion government. The scenery of the islands is crowned with the grandeur of snowcapped mountains and glittering glaciers. It also has many of the natural wonders that we find in our Yellowstone National park, including geysers and bubbling underground springs. 

Unfortunately, New Zealand sometimes suffers from earthquakes which do enormous damage to life and property.

Like Australia, New Zealand has its odd forms of life. It has a wingless bird with a long bill, called the kiwi, which feeds at night and lays huge eggs. Then there is the kea parrot which has been known to kill sheep by tearing open their backs to eat the fat around their kidneys. A tiny New Zealand mouse carries its young in a pouch. There are black swans as stately and beautiful as our white ones. The swamp hens of the islands have bright blue bodies and red legs. There is a lizard which has a blind third eye between the regular seeing pair. In this country, as well as 

Australia, rabbits which were brought in as pets are now a costly nuisance. In the vegetable kingdom we find the caterpillar plant, which looks like a caterpillar with a horn growing out of its head.

New Zealand is a land of pastures and one of the leading sheep countries of the world. Mutton from the islands is very popular in England. Wool, butter and cheese, meat, and hides and skins are the principal exports. 

The brown-skinned natives of New Zealand are called Maoris. They are brave and intelligent, unlike the Australian bushmen. By a courageous fight against the white men they forced the latter to grant them a share in the government. There are Maori members in the dominion parliament. They have quickly learned the ways of the Europeans, and many of them are now shopkeepers, teachers, and professional men.

New Zealand has a progressive government. 

Women were voting in the islands before the beginning of the twentieth century, more than twenty years before they were given the vote in the United States. The government of New 

Zealand has seen to it that the land is well divided up among small landowners. The laws favor the laboring people. Aged folks are pensioned, so that no poorhouses are needed in 

New Zealand. Auckland, the largest city, and 

Wellington, the capital, are prosperous modern cities. To tourists, New Zealand presents a smiling face, with green scenery all the year round, and a climate something like that of our 

Puget sound section-cool in winter, but not too cool, and warm in summer, but not too warm.

1. Australia is an island continent, far from any of the other continents. It is important to the world as a producer of raw materials. 

2. In size Australia is about as large as the United 

States. The Great Australian bight indents the southern coast. Along the east runs the longest coral reef in the world. Australia is high near the edges and somewhat lower in the interior. 

The highest mountains, the Great Dividing Range, extend in a long north-south chain not far from the eastern coast. There are other lower mountain ranges near the western and northern coasts.

The western part of the interior consists of a low, flat desert plateau and the eastern part of low, level grassy plains. There is only one large river system in Australia, the Murray-Darling. 

3. Australia lies partly in the Torrid zone and partly in the South Temperate. The coolest weather comes in June, July, and August and the hottest months are January and February. The continent as a whole is very warm. The southeast trade winds bring heavy rains to the eastern coast. The monsoons and the equatorial rain belt bring heavy rains to the northern coast in the hot season. Dur-

ing the cool season the prevailing westerlies bring some rain to parts of southern Australia. The interior of the continent has little rain at any time. 

4. Australia has many strange animals and plants which are unlike those found anywhere else in the world. 

5. The native Australians are of very low intelligence. 

The first white settlements were English prison colonies. Australia is still thinly populated and the British and Australian governments help immigrants all they can. Only white men are welcomed to the continent. 

6. Politically Australia is divided into six states and three territories. The most important mainland states are Queensland, New South Wales, and Victoria. The island of Tasmania is one of the states and Papua on the island of New Guinea is one of the territories.. Australia is a dominion of the British empire. The capital city is Canberra. 

7. The eastern coastal plain of Australia is fertile and has heavy rainfall. The climate in the north is tropical and in the south is temperate. The chief industry is agriculture. Here lives the greater part of the Australian population and here are located many cities, including the largest and most important on the continent, Sydney. The western coastal plain is hot and dry in the north and there sheep are raised. In the south there is mixed farming and lumbering. Perth is the most important city. The northern coastal plain consists mainly of damp forested tropical lands with heavy rainfall. There are few inhabitants and no important industries. 

8. The Great Dividing Range consists of fairly high mountains extending north and south not far from the eastern coast. Canberra, the capital of Australia, is located in this mountain region. The 

Victoria highlands are an extension of the Great

Dividing Range. In Victoria lies the important city of Melbourne. The remaining mountain systems of Australia are lower and less important. 

The mountains of Australia yield valuable lumber and minerals. Copper, gold, silver, tin, lead, iron, and coal are all mined there. 

9. The grasslands of Australia lie west of the Great

Dividing Range. Here there is little rainfall. The natural vegetation consists of tall grass, scrubby trees, and bushes. Parts of the grassland are used for the raising of wheat and other grains. Parts are used for stock raising. The land is irrigated by streams and by artesian wells. Sheep are raised in the drier lands and cattle where there is more moisture and the pasturage is richer. Dairy cattle are raised in the rich grasslands of the Murray- 

Darling basin. Here, too, there are many orchards and vineyards. Wool, meat, hides, wheat, and dairy products are among the important exports of the country. Droughts, which occur occasionally, do great damage. 

10. In the west-central part of Australia is a flat plateau from 1000 to 2000 feet in altitude. In the north and southwest, grasslands support cattle and sheep. Much of the plateau is a dry, hot desert. 

Gold is found in the desert. Perth is the port of the region. 

11. South of Australia lies the island of Tasmania, a beautiful rugged island where the weather is mild and delightful. Tasmania is noted for its apples and other fruits, its sheep, and its tin. Hobart is the capital city. 

12. New Zealand consists of two islands 1200 miles southeast of Australia. It is a part of the British empire but it has its own government. 

It is a mountainous country with rugged, snow-capped peaks. New Zealand has geysers and bubbling underground springs. It also has many odd forms of animal and vegetable life. The natives of New 

Zealand, the Maoris, are very intelligent people and have adapted themselves to the white man's ways. 

The government is very progressive. Auckland and Wellington are the principal cities.

CLASS PROJECT SOME TRIPS TO AUSTRALIA 

Divide the class into six groups, each group to take one of the following trips. Let a spokesman from each group describe the route taken, and what is to be seen in the Australian seaport and the interior behind it. 

1. From San Francisco to Adelaide, Australia. 

2. From Montreal to Brisbane, Australia. 

3. From Vera Cruz to Perth, Australia. 

4. From New York to Sydney, Australia. 

5. From Valparaiso to Auckland, New Zealand. 

6. From Rio de Janeiro to Hobart, Tasmania.

REFERENCE TABLES AND MAPS 

On the following pages will be found a series of reference tables and reference maps. 

The reference tables have been especially planned to meet the specific needs of THE OLD WORLD CONTINENTS, and will be found very valuable in the pupils' work. They include carefully built and thoroughly up-to-date tables of areas and populations, and tables of the lengths of principal rivers.

The reference maps cover the continents of the Western hemisphere. These, with the maps on the Old World Continents included in the text, give the pupil a complete set of maps on all the continents for general reference use.

The live teacher will see to it that full and effective use is made of reference tables and maps. 

One of the best means of fulfilling the aims of the geography course is to teach the pupil to use the reference method systematically, without specific direction on the part of the teacher. At frequent intervals, early in the course, the responsibility of looking up in the tables such facts as areas and populations of countries studied, populations of important cities, and lengths of principal rivers, should be placed on the pupil. Where references are made to North America or South America, the maps covering the areas or localities mentioned should be used, in order to clarify text comparisons and to keep fresh in mind regions and locations already studied. Such training will strengthen the pupils' work in geography and will help lay a foundation of sound research habits for the future.

THE IROQUOIS SERIES OF GEOGRAPHIES AND WORK BOOKS 

By 

ABRAMS BODLEY-THURSTON 

A new and complete series of Geographies and Work Books presenting the subject of Geography from the modern point of view. Emphasis is placed on the natural regions and their effects on the lives and activities of the people who live in them. Political units, too, are fully recognized and judiciously treated. 

The text stories are full and rich in content and simple in style. At the end of each unit are: a summary of the facts which the pupil should remember, topics for discussion, question and map exercises, and projects. Many graphs and tables supply important statistics. Complete pronouncing indexes, cross-referenced for ease of use, make the finding of any topic an easy matter. 

A wealth of illustrations and varied maps enliven and supplement the texts. The pictures were chosen for their geographic values and their artistic qualities. They are grouped at the beginnings of the units and at strategic points in the text to provide interest-arousing preliminary views of the chapter contents. The maps show the locations of all places mentioned in the text, and are especially clear and easy to interpret. 

HOME GEOGRAPHY. A book for beginners in Geography which introduces the child to the study of 

Geography through the region he knows best-his own surroundings. A text and work book combined.

PEOPLES OF OTHER LANDS. A basal text, providing studies of type regions of the earth and of the reactions of their peoples to their environments. 

A WORK BOOK TO ACCOMPANY PEOPLES OF OTHER LANDS. A work book, built to key with 

PEOPLES OF OTHER LANDS, and providing in full for map work and other pupil activities. 

NORTH AMERICA AND SOUTH AMERICA. An exceptionally readable basal text which gives the pupil distinct, clear cut impressions of the natural regions and countries of the continents of the 

Western hemisphere.

A WORK BOOK ON NORTH AMERICA AND SOUTH AMERICA. A companion book to NORTH 

AMERICA AND SOUTH AMERICA, providing varied, well-balanced material for pupil activities.

THE OLD WORLD CONTINENTS. A basal text on Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australia, fixing essen tial points by sharp, clear contrasts between regions and between countries.

A WORK BOOK ON THE OLD WORLD CONTINENTS. A companion book to THE OLD WORLD 

CONTINENTS, providing modern drills and tests and map exercises for all pupil activities. 

NORTH AMERICA. A basal text, presenting a well-rounded treatment of the regions and countries of our own continent of North America.

SOUTH AMERICA AND THE OLD WORLD CONTINENTS. A basal text covering all continents ex cept North America. Rich in teaching aids.

A WORK BOOK ON SOUTH AMERICA AND THE OLD WORLD CONTINENTS. A companion book to SOUTH AMERICA AND THE OLD WORLD CONTINENTS, providing drills, tests, map exer cises, and other features for pupil activities. 

WORLD GEOGRAPHY. An advanced basal text grouping geographic facts in new and significant ways to show relationships. Treats the basic activities of mankind, the great facts of commerce and industry, and the factors which make for the strength of nations. A fitting capstone for any Geography course.

A WORK BOOK ON WORLD GEOGRAPHY. A companion book to WORLD GEOGRAPHY. Particu larly rich in varied material-modern tests, drills, map and graph exercises for pupil activities.

A COMPLETE HISTORY SERIES FOR THE GRADES 

Southworth and Southworth

An exceptional new series of basal texts in history for the grades. Noted for simple, complete presentation of the subject, many splendid illustrations and maps, and varied and effective teaching helps. 

THE STORY OF LONG AGO. Greek and Norse myths, the story of Early Man, and Old World his tory to the fall of Rome.

THE STORY OF THE MIDDLE AGES. Old World history from the fall of Rome through the Period of Exploration.

AMERICA'S OLD WORLD BACKGROUND. Greek and Norse myths, the story of Early Man, and the history of the Old World from the Dawn of Civilization through the Period of Exploration.

THE THIRTEEN AMERICAN COLONIES. The American Indians before the coming of the white man, the Period of Exploration, the Colonial Period, and the Intercolonial Wars.

EARLY DAYS IN AMERICA. The Period of Exploration, the Colonial Period, the Intercolonial Wars, the Struggle for Independence, and the adoption of the Constitution.

AMERICAN HISTORY, COMPLETE EDITION-Illustrated. The complete history of our country from the beginning of the Period of Exploration to the present day.

A WORK BOOK IN AMERICAN HISTORY. Built to key with AMERICAN HISTORY, COMPLETE 

EDITION, but usable with any complete standard text. Contains a wide variety of modern tests and other pupil activities.
